papers.abstract: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation -- doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within $\sim 1.3$M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at $2\times$ higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: https://chenshuo20.github.io/PixVid/
authors: Yanke Song, Shuo Chen, Chris Rockwell, Guande He, Nan Liu, Desai Xie, Tianpei Gu, Yong-Hyun Park, Aryan V S, Dennis Yuren Menn, Ming-Hsuan Yang, Xun Huang
bullets: Addresses latent compression limits on resolution, frame-level conditioning, and response latency.
Keeps the diffusion transformer while replacing the VAE decoder with a convolutional pixel-rendering head.
Finds clean-video prediction and a larger noise shift important for generation quality.
Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, it is competitive with the latent baseline using approximately 1.3M training clips.
Achieves 2× higher resolution at the same per-frame token count, preserves depth-conditioned editing under fast motion, and responds to actions on the next frame.

figures.caption: Figure 11. Detailer head architecture (patch size p=16). Top: the DiT’s pre-head tokens s, combined with the timestep embedding as SiLU(et + s), form a feature map on the token grid. A bottleneck convolution and L= log2 p=4 up blocks upsample it 2× per level to full resolution, and an output convolution predicts x̂0. Feature sizes are per frame, where D is the DiT width and Cℓ the width of up block ℓ. Bottom left: each up block is a 2× transposed convolution followed by a causal 3×3×3 convolution and SiLU. Bottom right: all convolutions are causal in time (kt=3): output frame t only reads frames t−2 to t, so in frame-by-frame generation the head keeps the previous two frames as a streaming cache.

Figure 2. Lifting a pretrained latent video DiT to pixel space. Top: the pretrained latent model. A linear pixel-latent alignment, fitted offline, is fused with the pretrained patch embedding to obtain a pixel patch embedding. Bottom: PixVid. A timestep calibration rescales noisy pixel input to the signal-to-noise ratio the pretrained DiT was trained on. The DiT is initialized from the latent model, and a convolutional detailer head replaces the linear head and VAE decoder to predict the clean video directly.

Figure 15. High-Resolution Video Generation. Left: text-to-video samples generated by our pixel model at a resolution of 1664× 960. Right: native-resolution crops of the boxed regions. Our method preserves fine pixel-level details such as fur, whiskers and architectural details because the model directly generates pixels without a VAE that compresses and reconstructs them.

Figure 6. Control-to-screen latency. Control inputs, e.g. turn right (→), turn left (←), and look down (↓), arrive over time (top row). Colors indicate which control each generated frame reflects. Latent model: controls are reflected in the next block. With block size N this means a wait of up to N − 1 frames. We use N = 4 for this visualization. Pixel model (ours): generates one frame per control, so controls are reflected with zero wait, making it better suited for real-time interactive generation.
Figure 5. Depth-conditioned Editing. Our pixel model enables precise video editing under high motion, while the temporally compressed latent model morphs and blurs fast-moving objects.

Figure 9. Impact of prediction target. With the same convolutional head, v-prediction produces grainy frames at 80× the estimated noise of x-prediction, while x-prediction produces clean ones. Metric details are in App. B.6.

Figure 8. Impact of output head. Under x-prediction, a linear head maps each DiT token to its pixel patch independently, causing visible grid-like artifacts, while our convolutional head removes most seams. Metric details are in App. B.6.

Figure 7. Responsiveness. SolarWM receives one pose per fourframe latent, resulting in inaccurate motion when the direction changes; here continuing to look up when it should look down. PixVid handles direction changes natively.

Figure 3. Patch-size adaptation. To obtain 1×2p×2p patches, the new patch embedding weight is obtained by fusing 2×2 average downsampling with the pretrained 1×p×p patch embedding. A new up block L+1 is prepended to the detailer head and initialized as nearest neighbor upsampling. With token count unchanged, we train at 2× resolution at the same DiT cost.

Figure 10. Sampler-state precision. We use the same prompt and initial noise in every column. With a bf16 sampler state, UniPC drains pixel-space sample color (red), while Euler keeps it. Color kept is mean OKLab chroma relative to an fp32 sampler state.

Figure 13. Inference cost vs. resolution for a 21-frame clip with the 14B DiT (100 passes; Tab. 12). Doubling the resolution gives a latent model 4× the tokens and raises its FLOPs 6.9×, while PixVid keeps 30× 52 tokens per frame, so only its detailer grows and its FLOPs rise by 17%.
Figure 14. Text-to-video comparison on prompts from Movie Gen Video Bench [69]. We show frames 0, 10, and 20 of each 21-frame video from Wan2.1-T2V-14B, PixelUMM, and PixVid at 480× 832.
Figure 16. Depth-to-video comparison on fast motion. PixVid can generate high-quality outputs under sharp and fast motion.

Figure 12. Comparison with One-latent SolarWM. SolarWM and PixVid show relatively small motion errors and produce moderately realistic videos. In contrast, One-latent SolarWM follows the controls less closely, here severely overestimating the motion, and looks less realistic.
Figure 17. Camera-controlled autoregressive generation. We show 8 consecutive generated frames at 16 fps for simplicity.

papers.selection_reason: Lifts latent video diffusion to pixel space for higher resolution and controllability; fits video generation research.
papers.title: Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space
papers.tldr: PixVid lifts a pretrained latent video diffusion model into pixel space to enable higher-resolution, framewise, and more interactive video generation.

papers.abstract: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.
authors: Ellis Brown, Chris Hoang, Shengyi Qian, Shang-Wen Li, Mike Lewis, Marjan Ghazvininejad, Luke Zettlemoyer, Lucas Beyer, Mengye Ren, Jakob Verbeek, Saining Xie, Hu Xu
bullets: The study disentangles visual pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement under controlled compute and data.
A vision encoder trained jointly from scratch performs on par with a pretrained encoder, making a separate visual-pretraining stage unnecessary.
Removing dedicated vision capacity harms visual understanding, even when the backbone is enlarged by an equivalent parameter count.
Vision-only modules integrated into early backbone layers perform comparably to pre-fusion encoders and may reduce time to first token.
Findings persist across backbone sizes, free encoder-pretraining assumptions, and pretrained language-model initialization.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled study of vision encoding choices in multimodal LLMs; directly relevant to multimodal foundation model design.
papers.title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
papers.tldr: Dedicated vision capacity matters more than a pretrained visual encoder, and it can be integrated early within the multimodal backbone rather than placed before fusion.

papers.abstract: Model architecture shapes the scaling behavior, training efficiency, and inference cost of LLMs, making it a central focus of both industry and academia. In industry, teams such as those behind DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi routinely introduce architectural innovations, yet public reports rarely document which ideas succeeded, which were abandoned, and why. In academia, limited compute and inconsistent baselines often restrict evaluations to small-scale, single-point comparisons, making it difficult to establish whether improvements hold at larger scales or translate into broader impact. ArchSpace addresses both gaps as a public platform for Recording, Reviewing, and Referencing Architecture Researc}: each proposal is recorded with its experiments and reasoning, reviewed by the community, and referenced by later work. To evaluate ideas before costly large-scale training, ArchSpace leverages scaling laws to predict model loss at larger scales from smaller experiments, a practice widely adopted in industry. We provide initial references that make the platform usable: Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines, fitted scaling laws, and a reusable training recipe. Ideas validated through this review can in turn become new baselines, and ArchSpace thereby aims to broaden the range of ideas that shape the next generation of models.
authors: Jie Wang, Tong Zhu, JiaHao Kuang, Zhe Xu, Yunkai Chai, Dehong Zheng, Yu Cheng, Tao Ji, ZhouHan Lin, Qi Zhang, Bowen Zhou
bullets: Addresses poor documentation of successful, abandoned, and unexplained architecture choices in industry.
Helps academia overcome limited compute and inconsistent baselines that hinder large-scale evaluation.
Records proposals with experiments and reasoning, enables community review, and links validated ideas to later work.
Uses small-scale experiments and fitted scaling laws to predict loss at larger model scales.
Provides initial Qwen3.5 and OLMo3 baselines plus a reusable training recipe; its scope is an initial platform and reference set.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The ArchSpace contribution workflow. Phase I compares the proposed architecture with its baseline across the scaling ladder; the three settings differ in their reuse of model size, token count, learning rate (LR), and batch size (BS). Phase II tests whether gains persist through longer training and evaluates downstream capabilities. Reviewed records support future reference. Here, ̂︀𝐿 denotes predicted loss; 𝐶 is training FLOPs, 𝑀 training FLOPs per token, 𝐷 the training token count, 𝜂 LR, and 𝐵 BS.

papers.abstract: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: https://test-time-baking.github.io
authors: Chin-Yang Lin, Ryo Hachiuma, Jaesung Choe, Min-Hung Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Yen-Yu Lin, Wei-Chen Chiu, Yu-Lun Liu, Cheng Sun
bullets: Targets efficient decoding for decoder-only large view synthesis models without reconstructing 3D geometry.
Trains a TTT fast-weight MLP to imitate cross-view attention rather than replacing it outright.
Separates camera-only context tokens from image-content ground-truth tokens to resolve modality misalignment.
Reports up to 23× rendering speedup with quality comparable to state-of-the-art across several benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Pipeline. Our model stacks L identical blocks of Intra-view Attention, FFN, Test-Time Baking, and FFN. In the reconstruction stage, each context view is duplicated into a context pair, where the context ground-truth token X(ctx-gt) carries RGB and pose while the context rendering token X(ctx-rend) is pose-only and matches the modality of the novel rendering token X(nv). At each TTB layer, the inner-loop update bakes the fast-weight MLP via MSE loss to map X(ctx-rend) toward the cross-view attention output of X(ctx-gt). The baked MLP is applied to serve three token streams: it propagates both X(ctx-rend) and X(nv) to the next layer, and provides feedback to X(ctx-gt) as an auxiliary signal. In the novel-view rendering stage, each token retrieves global scene information in O(1) from the baked MLP, instead of O(N) via cross-attention. The rendering loss is backpropagated through the inner-loop baking process to train the model end-to-end.
Figure 5: Qualitative comparison on DL3DV. TTB preserves fine details on par with DVSM [58], while LaCT [77] and LVSM [25] produce visible blur.
Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on in-the-wild datasets. TTB generalizes to out-of-domain scenes and preserves fine details consistent with the in-domain results.

Figure 2: Motivation. We show three variants of the inner-loop optimization in TTT-style fast-weight MLPs. (a) TTT with KV binding [77] learns from raw value tokens projected from X(ctx). (b) TTB without context pairing targets the cross-view attention output instead, collaborating with attention rather than replacing it. (c) Our full TTB additionally pairs each context view: X(ctx-gt) carries image content and supplies the cross-view attended target, while X(ctx-rend) is camera-only and matches the modality of X(nv). The t-SNE plots show that only (c) aligns the modalities from the first block.

Figure 7: Scene representation size as V grows at 544×960 resolution, measured on a single A100. The DVSM [58] KV-cache grows linearly in V (hollow points: linear extrapolation where DVSM ran out of 80 GB memory), TTB’s baked fast weights stay constant, and TTB-duplicate grows with the number of copies K=V/16 while remaining 21× smaller than the KV-cache.

papers.tldr: TTB bakes cross-view attention into lightweight MLPs at test time, enabling up to 23× faster novel-view rendering while maintaining state-of-the-art quality.

papers.abstract: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines.
authors: Guangyuan Sui, Yunzhong Hou, Chi Harold Liu
bullets: UAV VLN is difficult because small 3D motion errors can cause navigation failures or collisions.
The framework predicts feature prototypes associated with possible outcomes and linearly combines them to estimate the target region’s visual features.
These imagined local visual representations provide context for generating waypoints and actions.
Experiments show substantial improvements over existing baselines.
The abstract does not specify datasets, numerical gains, or detailed limitations.

papers.abstract: Video diffusion models are able to generate samples with high-quality appearance and textural qualities. However, content produced by these methods is known to exhibit significant physical errors. This is because, in a classical video generation setting, all physical reasoning must take place simultaneously and exclusively within the diffusion process.We propose to resolve these issues by redistributing the task of physical reasoning onto a language model-backed keyframe generation module, which allows for explicit reasoning in language, and fine-grained control over the appearance of the video at important moments in the video. We then condition a video generation model with these keyframes, reducing the role of the diffusion model to the simpler task of interpolating between physically-correct intermediate states, rather than inferring an entire sequence with diffusion. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Physics-IQ Verified benchmark and PhyGenBench.
authors: Felix O'Mahony, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Roberto Cipolla, Ayush Tewari
bullets: Video diffusion models often generate visually strong videos with substantial physical inconsistencies.
A language model-backed module explicitly reasons about and generates physically meaningful keyframes.
A video generator is conditioned on these keyframes, simplifying diffusion to interpolation between intermediate states.
The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on Physics-IQ Verified and PhyGenBench.
The approach focuses on improving physical reasoning through explicit keyframe planning.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Conditioning model detail. Keyframes are inserted into the typical conditioning stack of blank frames at locations designated in Equation 3. This is then passed to the VAE, and is subsequently treated as normal conditioning in the Wan pipeline. The conditioning is concatenated with a mask indicating which keyframes are filled, and with the latent noise before being passed to the transformer. The mask and latent conditioning is appended before each denoising step.

Fig. 9. Left: Conditioning Wan2.2-5B on 𝑁 equally spaced ground truth keyframes, for 𝑁 between 1 and 6, raises the Physics-IQ Verified score from 27.7 to 67.4. Right: Editing the final keyframe with the same image edit model used in our pipeline yields a new video, here with the inner petals recoloured.

Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed method. We design a keyframe module which reasons about the physical evolution of a given scene and produces keyframes with timestamps and an expanded caption. These are then used as the conditioning signal for Wan2.2, resulting in videos with more accurate physical plausibility.

Fig. 6. Physics-IQ Verified score against cost per video for the image-to-video models of Table 1, with costs as listed on the Physics-IQ Verified leaderboard [Anates Labs 2026] on 8 October 2026. Costs follow the leaderboard’s normalization, which scales generation cost to 24 fps and 1280-pixel-wide output and then adds any language-model cost; for K2V this is the leaderboard’s Wan2.2 generation cost plus our planning cost from Table 4. The dashed line traces the cost score frontier, and vertical bars show the standard deviations of Table 1.

Fig. 7. Left: Compared to vanilla Wan2.2, the quality of our generations (measured by mean squared error above physical variance) does not rise over the 5 seconds of a video. Beneath, keyframe density shows that our approach distributes keyframes relatively evenly throughout videos on Physics-IQ Verified, with spikes at 0s and 5s, as these keyframes are required for each video. Right: The time taken to produce keyframes shows that the language model spends compute efficiently, spending more time on scenes which require more careful planning and less time on simpler scenes.

Fig. 3. Keyframe module detail. A VLM planning agent orchestrates a recursive loop producing keyframes. The first frame is passed to an image editor with an instruction from the VLM to produce the appearance of the frame later in time. The VLM reviews this frame and, if deemed correct, the frame is added to a stack of keyframes. The VLM repeats this process, now passing the top image to the image editor to add to the keyframe stack. Once all keyframes are produced, the model finishes, returning an expanded caption describing the motion of objects in the video with the keyframe stack.

papers.abstract: Remasking allows diffusion language models to revisit generated text, but effective correction requires knowing when and what to revise. Our diagnosis on Sudoku reveals two gaps. Hidden states contain error information that token confidence does not reliably expose, and remasking an isolated error usually reproduces it when the surrounding context remains fixed. These findings motivate DiVR , a verifier that predicts whether a partially generated sequence will reach a correct answer. Trained on the final correctness of the model's own trajectories, DiVR decides when to regenerate a block and which alternative to retain, while the generator itself stays unchanged. On five reasoning benchmarks with LLaDA-8B-Base, DiVR raises the average accuracy of the fine-tuned generator from 35.3\% to 43.4\% at $1.9$-$3.5\times$ the cost of greedy decoding, above search baselines that use $3.8$-$7.4\times$. It also complements post-training such as supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and generalizes to other generators, including Dream.
authors: Minhae Oh, Jeonghye Kim, Jinwoo Koo, Yeongoon Kim, Jimin Seo, Minsik Seol, Jungwoo Lee
bullets: Token confidence can miss errors, and remasking isolated errors often reproduces them because context remains unchanged.
DiVR verifies whether a partially generated sequence is likely to become correct using the model’s own completed trajectories.
It decides when to regenerate a block and which candidate to retain without changing the generator.
On five reasoning benchmarks, accuracy increased from 35.3% to 43.4% with 1.9–3.5× greedy-decoding cost, versus 3.8–7.4× for search baselines.
The verifier complements supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning and transfers to other generators, including Dream.

Fixed counts the greedy errors that guided decoding corrects, out of 413 on GSM8K, 377 on MATH-500 and 322 on Countdown, and the repair block is the first block at which an alternative replaced the original. TPR and FPR treat a wrong greedy answer as positive and a first-block score below θ as a flag. Most repairs begin in the first block.

A rule regenerates when the raw score is below θ, and predictions apply the development-fitted Platt map to the state each action leads to. The gap is predicted minus realized success of the chosen action, with a 95% bootstrap interval.

papers.abstract: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce Spatial Foundry, a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview.
authors: Ethan Lin, Yang Song
bullets: Combines floor plans, RGB images and panoramas, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, 3D instance boxes, and camera-trajectory video.
Uses shared scene coordinates to align visual, geometric, and temporal observations.
Editable source scenes enable new camera paths and controlled object changes.
Supports applications including 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance perception, video generation, world modeling, and scene editing.
Scope is focused on furnished residential 3D scene configurations and controlled spatial variations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Aligned observations and 3D representations. The two-floor scene provides floor plans, a colored surface-point preview, editable mesh geometry, perspective RGB, a panorama, metric-depth visualization, instance-box overlays, and a camera trajectory. This static overview uses UV textures and material Base Color for point coloring, display-space floor separation for interior visibility, and a color map for depth visualization.

Figure 5: Application areas supported by aligned scene data. Diverse furnished environments provide paired layout and 3D content. Instance annotations connect observations to objects and metric geometry. Shared scene states support multiple observer viewpoints, while editable assets provide controlled object changes. The examples illustrate the data correspondences used for spatial perception, generation, and world modeling.

Figure 3: Scene construction and data generation. Residential rules and functional motifs condition GPT-6 layout generation. Human review checks doorways, room circulation, and stair connectivity. Blender assembly combines the accepted layout with Infinigen assets, materials, and furniture. Reference geometry supports virtual scanning and calibrated rendering, while camera trajectories and object-state changes produce aligned temporal observations.

Figure 4: Functional layout motifs. Kitchen arrangements vary from one-wall and galley layouts to L-shaped, U-shaped, island, and peninsula configurations. Bathroom motifs vary the combination and placement of fixtures. These schematic patterns illustrate the functional priors used to diversify layouts and guide circulation review.
Table 1: Aligned data modalities. Coordinates, camera calibration, instance identifiers, and timestamps connect the representations within each scene.

papers.tldr: Spatial Foundry is a multimodal, editable dataset of 5,280 furnished 3D residential scenes designed to support research on spatial intelligence across views, geometry, and time.

papers.abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.
authors: Peiwen Li (Yale University), Harshit Verma (Yale University), Sophia Zhou (Yale University), Haiwen Wang (Yale University), Ngoc Bui (Yale University), Heng Chang (Tsinghua University), Fei Fei (Goodvision AI), David van Dijk (Yale University), Rex Ying (Yale University)
bullets: Targets memory selection when future tasks are unknown and repositories evolve.
Builds compact memory from repository-location and executable-check anchors using segment-level prospective valuation.
Adapts the actor with rollout-based memory valuation, provenance-gated credit, and rewards favoring resolution with fewer steps.
On ChainSWE, raises resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, while reducing steps by 17% and cache-aware tokens by 11% versus an untrained actor without memory.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of CoReMem. (a) Prospective segment valuation of memory. A memory m written from the trajectory τk is valued by the change ∆y(m | bk) it causes on task k+1, run from the inherited tree Sk with and without m. Removing each of the seven segments of τk gives its value νc, and the segments that pay are kept as anchors A(m). (b) Cost-internalizing on-policy valuation. A group of G sessions mixes sessions with their own memory (m), no memory (∅) and a misplaced memory (m̃) under the reward Ri, and V̂b = R̄m − R̄∅ is the memory’s value on-policy. (c) Step-level provenance-gated value credit. Only the steps that the gate ωt marks as acting on an anchor from the memory receive the value credit.

Figure 7: Evidence for M2 and M3. Top, steps per task and resolve rate of the with-memory arms in training order, where up and to the left is better and the larger marker is the full method. Bottom, paired differences in the memory benefit to resolve rate and in the step cost of a misplaced memory, blue for 27B and green for 9B as above, with 95% intervals.

Figure 2: What crosses coding-task boundaries and where memory is valued and optimized. Existing settings keep memory within one task, transfer general experience across independent tasks, or carry memory while resetting the repository. Our setting carries both repository state and memory to unseen future tasks. The ⟲ and ↓ symbols indicate whether memory is valued and optimized on its source task or on future tasks.

Figure 6: Steps, resolve per token and resolve per dollar against no memory for the API-served models. Top, each point is one memory layer on one model, and the shaded quadrant is where a memory lowers steps and raises resolve per thousand total tokens, which CoReMem w/o training reaches on all three models. Bottom, the change in resolve per dollar at list prices, with full numbers in Table 3 of App. D.

Figure 1: Memory on the next task. A memory written at the end of one flake8-simplify task hands two anchors, a location (WHERE) and a check (VERIFY), to the next task on the same repository; the post-trained actor model acts on them at steps 1 and 6 and skips the exploration it would otherwise start with (step counts illustrative).

Figure 5: From segment values to the memory design. The median change in steps (νc) and in thousand actor tokens (κc) when one segment is removed from the current task’s trajectory (Eq. (3); 27B actor model). Blue bars mark segments whose removal adds steps. The right columns give the field each segment becomes in the memory design, kept as a main field (blue), in reduced form (light blue) or dropped (gray), and what the next task gets from each of them.
Figure 10: A real memory and its anchors. The memory has 889 characters and 18 anchors.

Figure 8: Training dynamics of the 27B actor on the test sessions with the memory. Lines are means over three replays and bands their standard deviation. Update 0 is the untrained actor, also drawn as the dashed line. The number beside each panel is the paired difference at update 20.

Figure 9: A real trajectory split into segments (flake8-simplify, training split, frozen 27B actor). Verbatim except [...] cuts and the omitted command fences; segment labels and step numbers are ours.

Figure 11: The instruction under which the actor writes its memory, verbatim from the deployed file. It states what the next session can see, fixes the memory’s two blocks and five line types, sets the rules and shows the finished shape. Bold, shading and gray placeholders are ours.
Table 3: Cost and outcome of each memory layer for the API-served models on the test set. Overall columns as in Table 1, with the list-price cost per session and resolve per dollar.

Table 2: Anchors the next task can act on, per memory layer. 27B frozen actor model, test set; an anchor is used when it occurs only in the memory and appears in a message of the next task’s session; brackets give 95% intervals over the test chains.
Table 7: The seven segments of a trajectory. The first five partition the transcript, and the last two come from the boundary.
Table 8: From segments to lines. Results of the segment study (App. I). Counts are boundaries where the segment helped and hurt the next task. BH marks the multiplicity correction across segments.

Table 4: The post-trained actor on SWE-bench Verified. All 500 instances, one task each, no memory, 3 replays per row. The untrained row serves the zero-update adapter on the same path, and tags give the change against it (∗∗ for a paired 99% interval that excludes zero). Raw counts tokens with no credit for caching, and Limit hit is the share of instances that end at the step limit.

Table 5: The memory layer off the training distribution: successive tasks of one repository on an external dataset. SWEContextBench (SCB) pairs are two-task chains of one repository in one image, the next task opening at an independent checkout from the first, so only memory crosses the border. CoReMem w/o training writes its memory under the instruction of Figure 11; we updated the writer instructions by adding that the next session starts from a new checkout without the earlier changes, that the memory should not include a summary of or reason for the changes, and that the memory should only include one clause per DID line. The adapted instructions were written after observing the first runs on the set, whose memories were getting cut off because of note length.
