papers.selection_reason: Improves frozen VLM performance for morphing attack detection via validation-guided prompt selection, a form of test-time adaptation without parameter updates.
papers.title: Validation-Guided Prompt Selection for Differential Morphing Attack Detection
papers.tldr: Validation-guided prompt selection substantially improves frozen vision-language models for differential morphing attack detection without fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Remote sensing change detection usually relies on large collections of temporally aligned, pixel-level annotations, which limits its scalability across regions, imaging platforms and application domains. Recent zero-shot approaches reduce the need for supervision, but they often localize fine-grained changes poorly because their features are coarse or inconsistent across time. We present SpotDiff, a training-free, plug-and-play framework for zero-shot change detection built by composing complementary vision foundation models. SpotDiff uses DINOv3 for semantically robust features, AnyUp to reconstruct them at pixel resolution, and SAM 3 for text-guided region-of-interest proposals, which an inference-time multi-scale strategy (SWIMS) makes reliable on small objects. Change is then measured by comparing the reconstructed features of the two dates inside the proposed regions, with no learnable components, fine-tuning or change labels. To our knowledge, SpotDiff is the first change detection method to use a universal feature upsampler, which alone adds 13.8 F1 over bilinear upsampling of the same features. On LEVIR-CD, SpotDiff reaches 82.46 F1, 2.06 points above the strongest prior training-free method, and on the multi-class SECOND benchmark it improves building change detection by 10.3 IoU and the six-class average by 2.2 IoU. Qualitative results on PlanetScope (3 m) and Sentinel-2 (10 m) imagery show that the same pipeline transfers across resolutions without modification. Our results indicate that composing modern foundation models is an effective route to scalable, label-free change detection.
authors: Anit Upadhyaya, Ata Akbari Asanjan, Chaitanya Jalluri, Subash Yeggina, Jeremy Kravitz
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable change detection without temporally aligned pixel-level labels.
Combines DINOv3 features, AnyUp pixel-resolution reconstruction, SAM 3 region proposals, and the SWIMS multi-scale inference strategy.
Measures feature differences within proposed regions with no learnable components, fine-tuning, or change labels.
Improves over bilinear upsampling by 13.8 F1; achieves 82.46 F1 on LEVIR-CD and gains on SECOND building and multi-class detection.
Transfers across PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 resolutions without pipeline changes.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of SpotDiff. The Similarity Module encodes both images with a frozen vision foundation model, reconstructs pixelresolution features with a universal upsampler and computes their per-pixel cosine similarity. The Region of Interest Proposal Module segments instances of the prompted category in each image with multi-scale inference (SWIMS) and fuses them across time. The Change Detection Module marks a candidate instance as changed when its mean similarity falls below a threshold. No component is trained.

Figure 4. Cross-resolution results of the class-agnostic variant (τ = 0.7) on medium-resolution imagery, using the same models and settings as on sub-meter data. Magenta: pixels with cosine similarity below τ (changed). (a) PlanetScope at 3 m: deforestation, urban and port changes. (b) Sentinel-2 RGB at 10 m: building, road and land-clearing changes.

papers.abstract: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.
authors: Donglin Yang, Xiangyu Wang, Yantong Zhong, Wenhao Zheng, Zihan Ding, Yue Liao, Hongsheng Li, Ke Xu, Si Liu
bullets: Targets the underexplored problem of converting concise language, egocentric vision, and UAV dynamics into continuous object-relative flight actions.
UAV-Flow includes 30,692 real-world expert trajectories across eight motion categories and 10,109 simulation trajectories with task-specific completion criteria.
FlowVLA uses mixed real-simulation imitation pretraining followed by Tail-Aware GRPO online post-training.
On 273 held-out simulation episodes, FlowVLA reaches 75.58% mean success after pretraining and 93.16% after TGRPO post-training.
Real-world indoor and outdoor experiments show robust execution of object-relative commands.

papers.abstract: State space models (SSMs) are an emerging alternative to Transformers. SSMs offer linear-time inference and parallel training, but most implementations make the parallel scan efficient by making the recurrence diagonal: each channel of the hidden state is multiplied by an input-dependent real or complex number. These numbers commute, so the state records which inputs occurred but not their order. We formalize this with representation theory, which explains and fixes the state-tracking failures previously reported for SSMs. The state update defines a linear representation of the monoid of input sequences, and we show that an SSM tracks a group at every sequence length exactly when that group is a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices. Two consequences follow. Diagonal real- and complex-valued SSMs can track only commutative groups, while the transition matrices of any SSM that can track a group must split into independent blocks over the real, complex, and quaternion numbers. We then introduce HyperSSM, which adds quaternion channels while keeping linear-time inference and parallel training. Trained only on final answers, HyperSSM solves the group tasks of recent state-tracking benchmarks exactly with at most five state numbers. This includes $S_5$ with 32 generators, where previous SSMs are at chance, and HyperSSM generalizes to sequences 25 times longer than those seen in training. Because the theory says what the transitions must encode, the learned weights of the linear recurrence can be interpreted directly. We demonstrate this by recovering the calibration of a real gyroscope, the rotations of imperfect qubit gates and the geometry of protein backbones.
authors: Anif N. Shikder, Ramit Dey, Jan Minac, Lyle E. Muller
bullets: Diagonal real- or complex-valued SSM transitions commute, so they cannot represent noncommutative group structure or reliably track input order.
The paper characterizes exactly when an SSM tracks a group: the group must be a quotient of the group generated by its transition matrices.
Any SSM capable of tracking a group must decompose into real, complex, and quaternionic blocks; this motivates HyperSSM.

HyperSSM solves group-tracking benchmark tasks exactly using at most five state numbers, including an $S_5$ task where prior SSMs perform at chance, and extrapolates to sequences 25× longer than training.
The learned recurrence weights are directly interpretable and recover structure from gyroscope calibration, imperfect qubit-gate rotations, and protein-backbone geometry.

figures.caption: FIG. 4. Applications: Physical systems in which the state is represented as an ordered product of rotations. Median error as a function of sequence length; training lengths are shaded; mean ± standard deviation over three random seeds. (a) Orientation of a moving body measured by a real gyroscope (BROAD; held-out recordings); physical model: integration of the sensor readings. (b) Bloch vector of a qubit following a gate sequence, with imperfect gates (2% under-rotation and 2◦ axis tilt); physical model: simulation using ideal gates; HyperSSM achieves errors below the lower axis limit (10−3 degrees) at all sequence lengths; complex diagonal SSM uses three layers. Details on Clifford gates and ideal Clifford+T gates are provided in SM S11. (c) Orientation of residue j relative to the frame of residue i, computed from the torsion angles, on held-out PDB proteins; physical model: reconstruction using standard bond geometry. In all three cases, HyperSSM uses a single quaternion channel (four state variables); the complex diagonal SSM uses 128 state variables.

FIG. 1. Order in a linear memory. (a) One step of a selective SSM; shaded, the tracking regime (no decay, x0 = 1, one transition per symbol). (b) After a word w, a channel holds the ordered product Q(w); it tracks the group if a continuous readout recovers π(w) from Q(w) at every length. (c) A complex channel stores a phase; turns add, and order is lost. (d) A quaternion channel stores a 3D orientation; 90◦ turns about x and z in either order give different states. (e) q and −q are the same rotation; a sign-invariant readout tracks A5, a sign-aware one tracks Q8. (f) H tracks A5 but not S5; M2(H) tracks S5.

Channels evolve independently, mix only in the readout C, and are computed by the same parallel scan.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a quaternion state-space model with representation-theoretic analysis of recurrent memory, directly relevant to LLM architectures and recurrent memory mechanisms.
papers.title: Symmetry in Time: A Representation Theory of Linear Recurrent Memory
papers.tldr: A representation-theoretic analysis shows why diagonal SSMs lose sequence order, and HyperSSM fixes this with quaternion-valued state channels while preserving efficient inference and training.

papers.abstract: Embodied interaction requires an agent to integrate multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors to effectively communicate its intentions, including speech, body motion, and facial expressions. We present XBot-Omni, a Thinker--Talker--Actor architecture that extends the Omni paradigm to robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expressions, with ``X'' representing the extensibility to robotic-specific modalities. The Thinker processes text, images, audio, and video to formulate contextually appropriate responses, which are then realized by the Talker and Actor through speech and coordinated bodily expressions, respectively. In this report, we innovatively introduce the concept of ``Actor'' as a dedicated component for embodied agents: a coordinated, streaming module that leverages the native representations of the Thinker and Talker within an end-to-end pipeline, introducing only modest latency overhead. This unified architecture enables multimodal generation conditioned on omni-modal inputs directly to prevent information loss in staged designs. We comprehensively evaluate XBot-Omni across seven benchmarks, demonstrating strong multimodal understanding capabilities on both general-domain and robot-centric videos, as well as high-quality, natural, and well-coordinated motion generation. Furthermore, our results validate its capability to generate embodied multimodal responses directly from omni inputs, meeting the diverse requirements of embodied interaction. XBot-Omni enables robots not only to perceive the omni world but also to express themselves through speech and bodily behaviors, extending Omni models from conversational interaction to embodied communication in physical environments.
authors: Kerui Gu, Xing Fu, Shuoyang Sun, Cheng Peng, Jingru Duan, Huayu Gu, Zhenyu Chen, Jiaxin Huang, Cheng Wen, Rui Zhen, Kairui Chen, Zhihui Peng, Shaoli Huang
bullets: Addresses embodied interaction by jointly integrating multimodal perception with verbal and nonverbal behaviors.
Uses a Thinker–Talker–Actor pipeline: the Thinker understands omni-modal inputs, while the Talker and Actor produce speech and coordinated bodily expressions.
Introduces the Actor as a dedicated, streaming embodied-output module that reuses native Thinker and Talker representations with modest latency overhead.
Directly conditions multimodal generation on omni-modal inputs to reduce information loss from staged designs.
Evaluation across seven benchmarks reports strong multimodal understanding and high-quality, natural, coordinated motion generation for embodied responses.

papers.title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction

papers.abstract: Robots that learn from demonstrations should extrapolate their policy despite state perturbations such as sensor noise, scene variation, and compounding errors. One approach to this robustness is regularization. Prior regularizers consider each state on its own and limit how sensitive the policy is to any perturbation at that state. By contrast, we explore how the policy's output shifts when given the same perturbation at different states. Our insight is that, locally, the robot should respond to state perturbations in a consistent manner: e.g., if changing an irrelevant object position does not impact the policy at one state, that same change should not shift the policy output at a nearby state. Applying this insight, we develop inner product regularization (InneR). We show that the inner product on action space induces an inner product on state space through the policy Jacobian (the Fisher information for stochastic policies), and that the null space of this inner product governs which state perturbations have a first-order effect on the policy. By clustering states whose inner products are aligned, averaging the inner products within each cluster, and minimizing the smallest eigenvalues of that average, InneR shapes the learned policy so that nearby states share a common null space. InneR enforces consistent responses to perturbations without limiting policy expressiveness, and can be appended to existing imitation learning pipelines for deterministic or stochastic policies. In simulated experiments, InneR makes learned policies more robust to irrelevant state dimensions and shifts between training and test distributions, whereas norm penalties often perform worse than behavior cloning. On a real robot arm performing three manipulation tasks, InneR raises the average success rate of a diffusion policy from 18% to 57% without additional data.
authors: Benjamin A. Christie, Tianyu Qiu, Amy H. Choi, David Fridovich-Keil, Dylan P. Losey
bullets: Addresses poor policy extrapolation under sensor noise, scene variation, and compounding errors.
Uses the policy Jacobian to define a state-space inner product and identify perturbation directions with little first-order effect on actions.
Clusters states with aligned inner products, averages within clusters, and minimizes the smallest eigenvalues to create shared local null spaces.
Can augment existing deterministic or stochastic imitation-learning pipelines without restricting policy expressiveness.
Improved robustness in simulation; on a real robot arm, diffusion-policy success rose from 18% to 57% across three manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 6. Drone landing simulation from Section 8.1. Plots show the landing success rate as state dimension n increases (higher is better). papers.abstract: The proliferation of user-generated video content has made accurate and robust no-reference video quality assessment (NR-VQA) a highly important challenge. Existing research increasingly relies on architecturally complex multi-branch pipelines or computationally intensive fine-tuning of single-branch backbones. In this paper, we investigate whether a single frozen video foundation model can serve as an effective NR-VQA backbone, and propose HiVE-VQA, the first framework (to our knowledge) to apply a JEPA-based video encoder to this task. HiVE-VQA extracts token grids from multiple depths of a pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and stacks them into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume, which a compact 3D convolutional head fuses across its layer, spatial, and temporal axes, combining low-level distortion cues from shallow layers with the semantic and temporal context captured at greater depths. The encoder remains frozen throughout, so only the head is trained: 5.2M parameters (5.7\% of the total), with no auxiliary multi-modal models and an inference cost that is invariant to video resolution. Trained solely on LSVQ and evaluated without any fine-tuning, HiVE-VQA outperforms 17 state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in SROCC and PLCC on both intra-dataset (LSVQ-test, LSVQ-1080p) and cross-dataset (KoNViD-1k, LIVE-VQC) benchmarks. These results indicate that hierarchical, depth-wise fusion of features from a single frozen video foundation model provides a more effective and efficient basis for NR-VQA than task-specific multi-network fusion. Code and model checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RobHam99/HiVE-VQA.
authors: Robbie Hamilton, Fan Zhang, David Bull
bullets: Targets robust NR-VQA without complex multi-branch pipelines or backbone fine-tuning.
Stacks token grids from multiple encoder depths into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume.
A 3D convolutional head fuses layer, spatial, and temporal information while the encoder remains frozen.
Trains only 5.2M head parameters, with inference cost invariant to video resolution.
Trained on LSVQ and outperforms 17 SOTA methods across intra- and cross-dataset SROCC and PLCC benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated locomotion, balance regulation, and manipulation under frequent contacts, making teleoperated demonstration collection difficult: a practical controller must simultaneously provide precision, stability, and contact awareness. We propose FORGE, a force-aware multi-granularity control system with a coarse-to-fine command space spanning velocity navigation, planar foot placement, wrist-pose tracking, and optional force-conditioning inputs. Policy training requires no full-body human motion trajectories or joint-angle references; deployment consumes only sparse bilateral wrist poses relative to the pelvis, coarse motion commands, and optional desired wrist-load inputs. For sustained contact, FORGE combines a momentum observer with a learned correction trained using simulator contact-force supervision. At deployment, it estimates low-frequency, wrist-equivalent interaction forces from proprioception and reconstructed low-level arm PD torques, without wrist force/torque sensors. A quasi-static virtual-target loop uses this estimate and an optional desired applied-force input to adapt the wrist target. A frozen locomotion prior and asymmetric residual actions stabilize manipulation-induced whole-body corrections. Experiments evaluate unified-control stability, task-space tracking, quasi-static wrist-equivalent force estimation, squeezing forces during sustained contact with a rigid box, and downstream diffusion-policy execution of a squat-and-lift task across payload conditions. Website: https://bb0928.github.io/forge/.
authors: Liangjun Xing, Ke Fan, Kailin Li, Bin Wang, Xiaojie Niu, Qingwei Ben, Jiafei Cao, Wei Yao, Yebin Liu, Jingbo Wang, Weinan Zhang
bullets: Targets coordinated navigation, balance, manipulation, and sustained contact under teleoperation constraints.
Uses coarse-to-fine commands: velocity navigation, planar foot placement, wrist poses, and optional desired wrist loads.
Estimates wrist-equivalent interaction forces without wrist force/torque sensors using a momentum observer, learned correction, and reconstructed arm-control torques.
Adapts wrist targets through a quasi-static virtual-target loop while residual actions stabilize whole-body responses.
Evaluates stability, tracking, force estimation, sustained-contact squeezing, and squat-and-lift execution across payloads.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall pipeline of FORGE. The framework has three components: multi-granularity control over navigation, stance, pose, and optional forceconditioning inputs; a physics-informed hybrid force estimator and virtual-target contact-adaptation loop; and asymmetric residual actions anchored on a frozen locomotion prior. papers.abstract: Smaller language models (SLMs) make it feasible to deploy clinical natural language processing where large proprietary models are too costly, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning allows them to be specialised on commodity hardware. One obstacle persists after training: on medical tasks these models answer at far greater length than the clinical question requires. In clinical decision support and point-of-care use, where time is short, such verbosity is hard to act on even when the underlying reasoning is sound. Existing length-control methods depend on preference optimisation, reward models, or proprietary teachers that undercut the accessibility making SLMs attractive. We introduce Parameter-Efficient Conciseness Adaptation (PECA), which adds a single differentiable conciseness term to the QLoRA supervised fine-tuning objective. Because the token count is discrete and non-differentiable, PECA instead raises the end-of-sequence probability once generation exceeds a token budget, a smooth signal optimised during ordinary training, with no preference data, no auxiliary model, and a single commodity GPU. On a 1.7-billion-parameter model fine-tuned on the medical-o1-reasoning-SFT corpus, PECA reduces mean response length by 72.8% while improving multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy from 40.8% to 44.0%. A sweep over the conciseness strength traces an interpretable accuracy-to-length frontier for balancing brevity and diagnostic completeness.
authors: Tanzeel Abbas, Ahmad Kamran Malik, Nafees Qamar, Sana Liaqat
bullets: Addresses excessive verbosity in smaller models used for clinical decision support and point-of-care applications.
Adds a differentiable conciseness term that increases end-of-sequence probability after a specified token budget.
Requires no preference data, reward model, proprietary teacher, or auxiliary model, and is designed for commodity hardware.
On a 1.7B-parameter model, mean response length fell by 72.8% while multiple-choice diagnostic accuracy rose from 40.8% to 44.0%.
Varying conciseness strength produces an interpretable accuracy–length trade-off for balancing brevity and completeness.

papers.abstract: Distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) technologies such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) generate continuous, high-resolution spatio-temporal data at rates exceeding hundreds of megabytes per second, creating severe challenges for real-time storage and transmission. While neural compression methods can achieve strong rate-distortion performance on sensing data, prior approaches either require per-segment retraining incompatible with streaming, or have only been validated offline. None have been demonstrated end-to-end on a continuously streaming DAS acquisition system at scale. We present STeP-C (Spatio-Temporal Predictive Compression), a neural compression framework that decouples spatial encoding, temporal prediction, and entropy-optimized residual coding, trained end-to-end with a rate-distortion objective motivated by conditional entropy reduction. Critically, we identify entropy coding as the dominant bottleneck for streaming deployment. We address it through GPU-side symbol computation, cached probability tables, and parallel GIL-free arithmetic coding, together with FP16 inference and batched entropy coding, enabling a full real-time pipeline built around a GPU ring buffer. We validate this pipeline on a live DAS testbed, achieving a 98.85% file size reduction at 31.04 dB full-band PSNR and an average throughput of 535 MB/s, exceeding the 324 MB/s requirement for 1 kHz, 81 km DAS streams. We further show that STeP-C substantially outperforms conventional codecs at practical streaming bitrates, can be applied to unseen channel ranges within the same acquisition system without retraining, and largely maintains downstream detector consistency, with 96.62% high-confidence class agreement and 100% Jaccard similarity on detected event types.
authors: Tingfeng Li, Ming-Fang Huang, Shaobo Han, Yue Tian
bullets: Addresses the storage and transmission burden of continuous, high-resolution distributed acoustic sensing streams.
Decouples spatial encoding, temporal prediction, and entropy-optimized residual coding in an end-to-end rate-distortion framework.
Accelerates streaming deployment with GPU-side symbol computation, cached probability tables, parallel arithmetic coding, FP16 inference, batching, and a GPU ring buffer.
Validated on a live DAS testbed at 535 MB/s and 31.04 dB full-band PSNR, exceeding the stated 324 MB/s requirement.
Preserves downstream detection consistency and generalizes to unseen channel ranges within the same system without retraining.

papers.abstract: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information. It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.
authors: Zhuangzhuang Ma, Rukuan Chai, Qianqian Ma, Yanghua Wang, Branko Bijeljic, Martin J. Blunt
bullets: Addresses noisy, low-contrast CT images where conventional segmentation requires image-specific manual tuning and independent 3D models can confuse segmentation errors with physical change.
Combines spatial and temporal information in a 4D transformer framework to resolve ambiguous phase assignments across image sequences.
More accurately measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries than a comparable spatial-only 3D model in mineral-dissolution experiments.
Captures permeability increases consistent with reference segmentations and flow simulations, and transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining.
Reduces spurious rock and porosity fluctuations while identifying filling events in fluid-displacement datasets.

papers.abstract: Memory decides which LLMs an edge device runs, and how fast: capacity on a $4$ GB Jetson Nano, bandwidth on an $8$ GB Jetson Orin Nano Super. Deployed formats (GPTQ, AWQ, $\texttt{llama.cpp}$'s K- and I-quants) spend equal bits on every integer code of a matrix, although the codes are far from uniform. $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ keeps these formats but tunes GPTQ so the codes compress, Huffman-codes them losslessly in interleaved lanes, and decodes them on demand in a small unit between DRAM and L2, so GPU kernels run unchanged and DRAM moves only coded bytes. At $1\%$ and $3.5\%$ perplexity budgets, coded Phi-3-mini, Mistral-7B and SmolLM-1.7B are $5.7-31.4\%$ smaller than the best $\texttt{llama.cpp}$ format. A bit-exact $0.21$ mm$^2$ ASIC decoder unit ($1$ GHz, $7$ nm) cuts Orin latency and energy per token by up to $36\%$ and $38\%$ ($54\%$ and $44\%$ with prompt-lookup speculation). On the Nano, $\texttt{LazyWeights}$ needs $58-64\%$ less time and $53-57\%$ less energy per token than CPU $\texttt{llama.cpp}$, and runs a streamed Mistral-7B 6.6$\times$ faster at $3.89$ bits per weight. A Huffman decoder beats an rANS decoder in rate and area at equal throughput; the ASIC decoder unit runs bit-exact on a Zynq UltraScale+ FPGA (AMD ZCU102).
authors: Arnab Sanyal, Gourav Datta, Sandeep P. Chinchali
bullets: Targets memory capacity and bandwidth limits on resource-constrained edge devices.
Tunes GPTQ code distributions, then applies lossless Huffman coding in interleaved lanes.
Uses a small DRAM-to-L2 decoder, preserving existing deployed weight formats and GPU execution.
Across tested models, achieves 5.7–31.4% smaller weights within stated perplexity budgets.
Reports up to 36% lower latency and 38% lower energy per token on Orin, with larger gains under prompt-lookup speculation; also improves Nano performance and energy use.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. LazyWeights overview: entropy-aware quantization and a permatrix Huffman bundle in the cloud; on the device, a decode unit between the memory controller and L2 restores fixed-width codes. Without the unit, the GPU kernels decode in software inside GEMV (32 lanes) as the reference. Bottom: bits per weight.

Fig. 3. (a) Bundle layout: a 64×256 tile of 4-bit codes is 32 lanes of two rows; each lane is one Huffman stream of 32-bit words (code boundaries illustrative); the lanes’ words are interleaved, so one aligned read fetches the next word of every lane, and per-tile lane offsets let any tile start independently; two 4-bit codes form one 8-bit pair symbol. (b) Decode unit between the memory controller and L2 (as in Fig. 1): T engines of 32 lanes sharing an 8-word read port through a masked round-robin arbiter; a lane compares an 11-bit peek against per-length limits (no 2048-entry table), adds the length’s offset to index the symbol table, and shifts its buffer by the length.

papers.abstract: Quantifying disease-associated renal tubular remodeling is challenging because tubular appearances are heterogeneous. We introduce TuMAP (Tubular Morphotype-Aware Pathomics), a pipeline combining (1) dual-view foundation-model representations and provisional morphotype annotation, (2) compositional and within-morphotype pathomics, and (3) patient-level statistical inference. From 456,158 tubules in 358 PAS-stained kidney biopsy slides, TuMAP identified eight image-based morphotypes, seven of which showed stable subsampling assignments. Across 219 patients in six diagnostic groups, diabetic nephropathy (DN) and tubulointerstitial nephritis/acute tubular injury (TIN/ATI) each differed from minimal change disease in seven morphotype proportions, while IgA nephropathy differed in six. DN showed reduced nuclear solidity and increased eccentricity across all eight morphotypes. Area-normalized nuclear density exposed additional within-morphotype differences. TuMAP provides a framework for separating changes in tubular morphotype composition from phenotypic differences within morphotypes.
authors: Ruijie Wu, Yuechen Yang, Yanfan Zhu, Yu Wang, Shilin Zhao, Ming-Tsun Tsai, Szu-Yuan Li, Shuo-Ming Ou, Tz-Heng Chen, Haichun Yang, Yuankai Huo
bullets: Addresses heterogeneity in disease-associated renal tubular remodeling.
Uses foundation-model representations, provisional morphotype annotation, compositional and within-morphotype pathomics, and patient-level inference.
Identified eight image-based tubular morphotypes, with seven showing stable subsampling assignments.
Analyzed 456,158 tubules from 358 PAS-stained kidney biopsy slides across 219 patients and six diagnostic groups.
Distinguished disease groups through morphotype proportions and nuclear features, including reduced solidity and increased eccentricity in diabetic nephropathy.

papers.abstract: Merging independently fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model requires no data, no labels, and no gradient steps. In practice the task vectors of different tasks interfere, and the standard remedies--averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election--operate entry by entry, ignoring that each delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon. We recast merging as a subspace interference problem. For every two-dimensional weight tensor we take the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta--the input directions along which that task moves the representation most--and remove from each task vector the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces. The resulting Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set. On eight CLIP image-classification tasks JNSP merges ViT-B/16 experts to 89.45% average accuracy without using a single image, 11.88 points above the strongest parameter-wise training-free baseline (TIES-Merging, 77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic, and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). The gain holds across three backbones on the independently trained TALL release (+10.8, +12.6, +9.1 over TIES for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) and replicates there at 89.20%; controls confirm the source--a single shared subspace instead of per-task ones loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the same projection underperforms plain task arithmetic, which we report rather than hide. Code is available at https://github.com.
authors: Tian Xia
bullets: Addresses interference between task vectors during data-free, training-free checkpoint merging.
Uses top-r right-singular subspaces of each weight-delta tensor and projects each task update into the joint null space of the others.
The closed-form, order-independent method requires neither forward passes nor data, labels, or gradient steps.
Achieves 89.45% average accuracy on eight CLIP image-classification tasks, outperforming reported training-free baselines; results also replicate across multiple ViT backbones.
Performance is not universal: JNSP underperforms plain task arithmetic on RoBERTa-large.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) for data-free merging of foundation model checkpoints (CLIP, RoBERTa), addressing subspace interference in model merging.
papers.title: Joint Null-Space Projection for Data-Free Model Merging
papers.tldr: JNSP merges independently fine-tuned models without data by removing task-update components that lie in other tasks’ important input subspaces, substantially improving multi-task accuracy on CLIP benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Change detection in remote sensing conventionally relies on spatially aligned bi-temporal imagery, which may be unavailable or unreliable in practical scenarios. Recent single-temporal approaches address this limitation by learning structural evidence, such as building regions, from a labeled source dataset and transferring it to unseen target imagery using only the current image. However, adaptation to the source dataset can over-specialize pretrained features and reduce their cross-dataset generalization, a risk that this paper argues is higher when the feature adaptation is parameterized independently of the states used for prediction. To address this issue, the current study introduces SALT, a State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer framework. SALT keeps a DINOv3 backbone frozen and learns negative and positive structural states that both score each patch and, through State-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation (SALA), span the rank-2 subspace in which patch features are corrected. Directional State Alignment supervises these corrections to raise the evidence of positive patches and lower that of negative ones, while Geometry Preservation limits changes to the pairwise relations among pretrained patch features. Experiments on LEVIR-CD and the WHU aerial building dataset show that, at the pixel level and in both transfer directions, SALT outperforms four baselines reproduced under a common source-only protocol, improving over the strongest reproduced baselines by 9.45 and 5.79 points in pixel-level AP and by 27.69 and 14.25 points in IoU (LEVIR-CD to WHU and WHU to LEVIR-CD, respectively), with only 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image. In order to facilitate reproducibility and further research, the source code of SALT is available at https://github.com/gthpapadopoulos/SALT
authors: Aggelos Psiris, Georgios Angelidis, Giorgos Sfikas, Maria Vakalopoulou, Thomas Lagkas, Panagiotis Sarigiannidis, Georgios Th. Papadopoulos
bullets: Addresses single-temporal cross-dataset structural localization when aligned bi-temporal imagery is unavailable or unreliable.
Freezes a DINOv3 backbone and learns positive/negative structural states that score patches and define a rank-2 correction subspace.
Uses directional state alignment to separate positive and negative evidence, with geometry preservation limiting distortion of pretrained patch relationships.
On LEVIR-CD and WHU, outperforms four reproduced source-only baselines in both transfer directions at pixel-level AP and IoU.
Uses 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image; code is publicly available.

The four training objectives (top) supervise structural predictions, guide feature corrections, preserve feature relationships, and separate the learned states. papers.abstract: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.
authors: Hao Li, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Hui En Pang, Kairui Hu, Mingze Sun, Runmao Yao, Xinhao Ji, Xiyuan Zheng, Xuanli Chen, Yalun Dai, Yap Kim Hui, Dingwen Zhang, Yuanyuan Gao, Ziang Cao, Cheng Huang Yean, Jackson Peng, Rui Duan, Yaobo Liu, Zetong Wang, Ziwei Liu

Includes 1,589 metric-scale 3D scans and 4,230 egocentric recordings covering 74 tasks and 131 hours.
Converts captured scenes into interactive simulations and retargets human motion to whole-body robot trajectories.
Augments data through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation.
Provides a foundation for studying how physical-AI capability scales with environments and behaviors.

papers.title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
papers.tldr: Ropedia Xperience 2 provides large-scale 3D environments and human behavior recordings that can be reused to train and evaluate physical AI systems.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can supply autonomous systems with plans, predictions, and judgments, but these contributions are sometimes wrong. This review asks how a system can maximize an LLM's utility while managing its fallibility. Our answer is to adapt the system's reliance on the LLM as evidence about the LLM's performance accumulates. Systems built from imperfect components, such as noisy sensors and faulty software, have long worked in this way, and the classical methods they use can be applied to LLM-based systems as well. A system can change its reliance on an LLM in several ways, depending on the LLM's role and on the other components in the system. Each change needs an estimate of the LLM's reliability, and the LLM's role and the kind of contribution it makes determine what to estimate. Classical methods from decision theory, estimation, and online learning then turn these estimates into reliance decisions. These decisions can reduce how often LLM errors affect the system. However, some errors matter even when they are rare. An independently verified mechanism can prevent such errors from being executed. Without one, adapting reliance using reliability estimates can still keep their risk within a bound. Studies on adapting reliance on LLMs are emerging but limited, and the reviewed comparisons suggest that adapting reliance can improve system performance.
authors: Ekta U. Samani, Christopher G. Atkeson
bullets: Reviews how autonomous systems can use LLM plans, predictions, and judgments despite their fallibility.
Advocates adapting LLM reliance based on observed performance and the LLM’s role in the system.
Applies classical decision-theoretic, estimation, and online-learning methods to convert reliability estimates into reliance decisions.
Independent verification is needed to prevent rare but consequential errors; otherwise, adaptive reliance can help bound their risk.
Emerging studies suggest adaptive reliance can improve system performance, though evidence remains limited.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Blocksworld example used throughout this review, adapted from [12]. For one Blocksworld problem, the LLM generates a plan and a validator checks it. The robot executes an accepted plan as shown in (a). Feedback generated from this can be used in three different ways: (b) adding invalid-plan feedback to the prompt, (c) fine-tuning the model on outcomes from many such problems, and (d) using validator results and execution outcomes as evidence to change how the surrounding system relies on the LLM.

papers.selection_reason: Reviews methods for managing LLM fallibility in autonomous systems, focusing on adapting reliance based on reliability estimates rather than a specific technical implementation.
papers.title: Maximizing LLM Utility While Managing LLM Fallibility
papers.tldr: Systems can improve LLM-based performance by adapting how much they rely on an LLM as evidence of its reliability accumulates, while independently preventing or bounding high-impact errors.

papers.abstract: Layer-local self-supervised objectives remove the backward pass between layers, but almost all still compute their loss over a batch of samples and are therefore local in space but not in time. We introduce Temporal Regularized Learning (TeReL), a spatially and temporally local learning rule for self-supervised representation learning from sequential input streams. The key idea is to instantiate a VICReg-style objective with temporally adjacent positives and non-differentiated running population statistics, yielding a per-neuron online loss with bounded state. The objective is a soft form of Slow Feature Analysis, and its gradient is a Hebbian update of the feedforward weights and an anti-Hebbian update of one lateral matrix per layer. The aim of the experiments is to show that the rule works in a small network, not to compete with backpropagation. On a class-chunked MNIST stream, a two-layer fully connected network trained with batch size one outperforms random features (96.48% versus 95.09% linear-probe accuracy) and classical SFA, and a variant that relaxes both locality constraints is comparable to supervised backpropagation. Because training and inference use the same computation, the network can keep learning from unlabeled data during inference without loss of accuracy.
authors: Davide Wiest
bullets: Uses temporally adjacent positives and running population statistics in a VICReg-style objective.
Produces per-neuron online updates with bounded state: Hebbian feedforward and anti-Hebbian lateral updates.
In a small two-layer network on class-chunked MNIST, batch-one training achieved 96.48% linear-probe accuracy versus 95.09% for random features.
The method outperformed classical SFA, while a less-local variant was comparable to supervised backpropagation.
Training and inference share the same computation, enabling continued unlabeled learning during inference without accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Nonlinear time-optimal model predictive control (TOMPC) enables highly performant control of constrained systems, but its computational cost prohibits real-time use on fast dynamical systems. Neural network imitation of the TOMPC control law can reduce online computational costs, yet existing work mostly targets quadratic cost formulations in simulation and addresses the challenges of neural controllers in isolation. This work imitates a long-horizon nonconvex TOMPC with hard terminal constraints, whose high computational cost limits training-data generation. We present (i) \emph{self-informed sampling (SIFS)}, a data-efficient expert-sampling strategy that uses a learned time-to-go to query the expert only where the policy deviates from time-optimal behavior, (ii) a complete training and control architecture that jointly addresses dataset correlation, suboptimal expert labels, covariate shift, constraint satisfaction and model mismatch, and (iii) real-world validation on a Furuta pendulum. SIFS matches standard dataset aggregation performance in roughly one-third of the training time and with less than half the training data. The resulting controller matches the region of attraction of the expert TOMPC while raising the control frequency from 1.4~Hz to 1~kHz. On hardware, the controller swings up and stabilizes the pendulum along trajectories closely matching the expert TOMPC solution.
authors: Maarten De Baecke, Flavia Sofia Acerbo, Andrea Giusti, Wilm Decr\'e
bullets: Targets the computational cost of nonlinear TOMPC with hard terminal constraints, which limits real-time control and training-data generation.
Introduces self-informed sampling (SIFS), querying the expert mainly where the learned policy deviates from time-optimal behavior.
Combines strategies for dataset correlation, suboptimal labels, covariate shift, constraint satisfaction, and model mismatch.
SIFS achieves comparable performance to standard dataset aggregation in about one-third the training time and with less than half the data.
Hardware experiments show swing-up and stabilization along trajectories closely matching the expert TOMPC solution.

papers.abstract: This report summarizes the Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding (MUMU) track of the 8th Large-scale Video Object Segmentation (LSVOS) Challenge, held in conjunction with ECCV 2026. MUMU asks for a single unified model that jointly performs multi-concept image tagging over quality, scene, and event vocabularies, open-vocabulary object detection, and concise image captioning, within a budget of 0.5B parameters and 8 GB of peak inference memory. Submissions are ranked by a weighted task score scaled by an efficiency factor. We describe the tasks, rules, and evaluation protocol, report the final results, and review the methods of the top three teams. All three leading solutions build on the compact Florence-2-base model, but extend it in different ways: lightweight tagging heads with cross-task inference refinement, a shared low-rank adapter trained on coverage-aware multi-source data with task-dependent decoding, and a training-free pipeline that maps captions to tags and applies detection test-time augmentation. The results show that a compact prompt-based vision-language model can serve all three outputs when supervision, decoding, and cross-task cues are designed for each task, while open-vocabulary detection on novel categories remains the main bottleneck.
authors: Chang Liu, Henghui Ding, Tong Yang, Dayoung Kil, Seong-heum Kim, Qilin Xiang, Ronghao Zheng, Ziyang Zhang, Shanlin Jiang, Ruohan Shi, Qilin Fan, Chengfeng Qiu, Kaifeng Wei
bullets: Requires one model to perform multi-concept image tagging, open-vocabulary object detection, and concise captioning.
Models are constrained to 0.5B parameters and 8 GB peak inference memory, with rankings combining task performance and efficiency.

The top three solutions extend Florence-2-base using lightweight heads and refinement, shared low-rank adaptation with task-specific decoding, or a training-free caption-to-tag and detection-augmentation pipeline.
Results indicate that supervision, decoding strategies, and cross-task signals are important for compact unified multimodal models.
Open-vocabulary detection on unseen categories remains the main limitation.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art LiDAR-inertial odometry methods, including those on richer state manifolds, achieve strong global accuracy, yet their pose stream alternates between propagation and correction and can oscillate over short horizons even when globally accurate. Most existing methods follow these approaches: they either modify the filter to enable faster updates or estimate a continuous-time trajectory from raw LiDAR and inertial data. The latter involves extra optimization, delaying state updates and becoming less robust during rapid rotations or accelerations. We propose CT-SGAL-LIO, a continuous-time refinement module that smooths the posterior pose stream of a discrete SGal(3) estimator without modifying the estimator itself. The key novelty is to perform continuous-time trajectory refinement directly on the projected SGal(3) posterior: we fit a cubic trajectory over a bounded window of recent poses and evaluate it at a small fixed lag. This places the query time within the observed interval, so the refined pose is obtained by interpolation rather than extrapolation, while preserving causal operation. CT-SGAL-LIO improves relative trajectory accuracy on 17 sequences from three public benchmarks. Across 17 sequences from GRAND-TOUR, MCD, and GEODE, CT-SGAL-LIO improves short-term motion accuracy while largely preserving global accuracy. RTE improves by up to 70% on GRAND-TOUR and on all seven GEODE sequences, with 9.9-51.1% reductions. A 19.5-min R-Campus run also reduces posterior jumps by 85.4% with only a 4.7 mm change in the end-to-start gap. We plan to release our source code and results to support community validation and reproducibility.
authors: Nam Tran, Thu Tran, Toan Nguyen, William J Beksi, Tuan Dang
bullets: Addresses short-horizon pose oscillations caused by alternating propagation and correction in discrete odometry.
Fits a cubic trajectory to recent projected SGal(3) posterior poses and evaluates it at a small fixed lag.
Uses interpolation within the observed window, avoiding noncausal extrapolation and leaving the underlying estimator unchanged.
Improves relative trajectory accuracy across 17 sequences from the GRAND-TOUR, MCD, and GEODE benchmarks.
Reports up to 70% RTE improvement on GRAND-TOUR and reductions on all seven GEODE sequences; an R-Campus run reduces posterior jumps by 85.4% with a 4.7 mm end-to-start-gap change.

papers.abstract: Second-order optimizers (e.g., Shampoo, SOAP) have emerged as compelling alternatives to Adam/AdamW and promise faster per-step convergence than AdamW in transformer training. However, they still remain costly in practice, and even SOAP still pays substantial optimizer-state memory and eigendecomposition overhead. We ask whether the benefits of SOAP can be retained at nearly the efficiency of AdamW. In this paper, we answer yes with a lightweight SOAP variant, Factored One-sided Adam-Moment (FOAM). The path to practical impact is twofold: first, FOAM employs input-only preconditioning, dropping the output-side Kronecker factor to reduce memory and remove one eigendecomposition. The Kronecker structure of the Hessian shows that this is exact for a diagonal output-side curvature and nearly lossless for a near-diagonal one, as we observe empirically. Second, FOAM replaces SOAP's dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator based on row-by-column statistics. Under the K-FAC Fisher assumption with a diagonal output curvature, this estimator exactly recovers SOAP's dense second moment, and we measure only a 15-20% K-FAC violation, with negligible effect on the update. Our empirical results support the claim that FOAM matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss across scales of large language model (LLM) pre-training, uses half of SOAP's optimizer state, runs at Muon-class wall-clock time, and retains robustness across a three-fold learning-rate range. The results hold from 124M to 760M parameters, demonstrating that SOAP's gains need not require SOAP's cost. Code: https://github.com/naver-ai/foam
authors: Jaemyung Yu, Byeongho Heo, Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han
bullets: Targets the high memory and eigendecomposition costs that limit practical use of SOAP.
Uses input-only preconditioning, removing the output-side Kronecker factor and one eigendecomposition.
Replaces SOAP’s dense rotated second moment with a factored Adam-moment estimator using row-by-column statistics.
Matches strong SOAP and Muon baselines in validation loss, uses half of SOAP’s optimizer state, and runs at Muon-class wall-clock time.
Demonstrated across 124M–760M-parameter LLM pretraining and a three-fold learning-rate range.

Curves are 3-seed means smoothed over 1K steps, and grey boxes mark the regions magnified in the insets. (a) Per-step. Validation loss against training step. In the last 4K steps (inset) SOAP ends slightly below FOAM (2.791 vs. 2.796, within about one seed std), both below Muon, while AdamW stays above the inset range. (b) Wall-clock. Same runs vs. wall time, normalized so AdamW finishes at 1.0× (Muon, FOAM, and SOAP finish at 1.15×, 1.17×, and 2.31×). Within AdamW’s own budget, FOAM is already 0.04 nats below AdamW’s final loss (inset), and it reaches SOAP’s quality band at 51% of SOAP’s wall-clock time. (c) Time to AdamW’s final loss (2.847; Table 2). FOAM gets there as fast as AdamW itself (10.53 vs. 10.55 h) and slightly ahead of Muon, while bilateral SOAP needs 2.15× as long.

For AdamW, SOAP, and FOAM we sweep 5 LR points (factor 101/8), 5 WD points (factor 101/4) at the best LR, and 3 values each of β1 and β2 at the best LR/WD. All other HPs are held fixed. papers.abstract: We introduce TokenStream, an optimization-based framework that composes independently learned subject identities in text-to-video generation without a reference-video training dataset or joint optimization of each new subject combination. Learning from a single reference image makes subject appearance difficult to separate from static-image bias, while merging independently trained adapters can mix identities. Token-wise LoRA (ToRA) restricts low-rank updates to the cross-attention value projections of subject-associated text tokens, providing a separate adaptation path for each subject. A T2V-guided stream copies queries and keys from the frozen base model during early denoising to reuse its layout and motion priors while retaining personalized values. We also introduce Multi-DB, a 30-subject, 122-prompt benchmark with appearance-free prompts and varied interactions. On Multi-DB at 1.3B, TokenStream improves identity preservation from 0.422 for DreamBooth to 0.467 and textual alignment from 0.652 to 0.688.
authors: Hung Nguyen, Quang Qui-Vinh Nguyen, Khoi Nguyen
bullets: Addresses identity mixing and static-image bias when combining independently learned subjects without joint optimization or reference-video data.
Uses Token-wise LoRA to adapt cross-attention value projections for subject-associated text tokens.
Copies queries and keys from the frozen base model during early denoising to preserve layout and motion priors.
Introduces Multi-DB, a benchmark with 30 subjects and 122 prompts covering appearance-free prompts and varied interactions.
On Multi-DB with a 1.3B model, identity preservation rises from 0.422 to 0.467 and textual alignment from 0.652 to 0.688 versus DreamBooth.

Each model evaluation traverses L self-attention–cross-attention–FFN blocks. Both streams share frozen weights but incur additional guidance computation.

papers.abstract: Post-training of large language models typically combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with preference-based fine-tuning such as Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). Human-annotated and synthetically generated preference data differ substantially in per-sample cost, but prior work typically holds sample count fixed when comparing the two. In this work, we explicitly study the interplay between cost and performance by comparing the effect of post-training with human and synthetic preference data under a fixed, dollar-matched annotation budget. We train and evaluate multiple base model families across helpfulness and summarization tasks. We find that synthetic data is far more cost-efficient at low-to-moderate budgets, achieving high win rates with as little as \$200--\$400. On helpfulness, human data closes the gap only at budgets roughly two orders of magnitude larger; on summarization, it does not close the gap at any tested budget. We also find that human-annotated data varies in reliability: one widely used human preference source substantially underperforms another, and the gap persists even after standard remedies such as domain restriction and deduplication.
authors: Shourik Banerjee, Ethan Mendes, Mohit Raghavendra, Wei Xu, Alan Ritter
bullets: Compares human-annotated and synthetic preference data using dollar-matched, rather than sample-matched, budgets.

papers.abstract: How does data shape language model (LM) behavior throughout pretraining? We investigate this question through a case study on entity comparison, e.g., Between France and Brazil, which country is larger?, across nine comparison tasks spanning five entity types. We begin with controlled experiments in which we train small LMs (163M parameters) on mixtures of natural text from pretraining corpora and synthetic task data. Our analysis identifies three distinct phases of learning: (1) an early phase where the LM selects entities by frequency, (2) a middle phase where the LM selects entities by position in the prompt (first vs. last mentioned entity), and (3) a late phase where the LM selects the entity that is the correct answer. We show that the emergence of these three phases is causally determined by statistical properties of the training data. With small amounts of task-specific synthetic data, we observe only the first two phases and the model fails to learn the task; with large amounts, the model jumps directly from the frequency-based heuristic to solving the task correctly. Moreover, changing the entity frequency distribution from a naturally occurring Zipfian distribution (a small number of entities are very common and the vast majority are rare) to a uniform one weakens the frequency phase and speeds up learning of the task. Lastly, we show that the three phases of training dynamics from our controlled experiments appear in the open source model OLMo-2 32B. Together, our findings demonstrate that properties of pretraining data are causal drivers of heuristic learning and show that small-scale synthetic experiments can predict training dynamics at larger scales.
authors: Yik Siu Chan, Jing Huang, Yanai Elazar, Atticus Geiger
bullets: Across nine comparison tasks and five entity types, models exhibit three learning phases: frequency-based selection, prompt-position selection, then correct answers.
Small amounts of synthetic task data produce only the first two phases and fail to yield task learning; larger amounts skip the positional phase and enable correct solving.
Replacing naturally Zipfian entity frequencies with a uniform distribution weakens frequency-based behavior and accelerates learning.
The same three-phase dynamics appear in the open-source OLMo-2 32B model, suggesting controlled small-scale experiments can predict larger-scale behavior.

papers.abstract: Accurate environmental monitoring relies on Informative Path Planning (IPP) to deploy autonomous systems that maximize information gain. While Gaussian Processes (GPs) provide a robust mathematical foundation for modeling the environment, contemporary IPP approaches remain hindered by heuristic operational constraints and the lack of simultaneous theoretical guarantees for worst-case estimation error and approximation quality. Rather than introducing yet another heuristic, this paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of existing error bounds and algorithms to further develop the mathematical foundation for IPP. By evaluating probabilistic and deterministic bounds on reconstruction error, we establish that predictive variance is the theoretically ideal optimization objective for GP-based IPP. Furthermore, we analyze GreedyCover, a recent approach for optimizing predictive variance, and demonstrate that its near-optimal approximation guarantee matches the fundamental hardness-of-approximation limit for the problem. Comprehensive benchmarking confirms that this approach delivers superior estimation accuracy and computational efficiency compared to prominent information-theoretic objectives and optimization methods used in IPP. Finally, this theoretical analysis establishes a rigorous, near-optimal foundation for discrete offline IPP under bounded uncertainty constraints, offering clear and principled guidance for future work in continuous-space and online formulations.
authors: Kalvik Jakkala, Jennifer Wakulicz, Donald G. Dansereau, Srinivas Akella, Lantao Liu, Jason M. O'Kane
bullets: Addresses the lack of simultaneous guarantees for worst-case estimation error and approximation quality in IPP.
Analyzes probabilistic and deterministic GP reconstruction-error bounds, showing predictive variance is the theoretically ideal objective.
Proves that GreedyCover’s near-optimal approximation guarantee reaches the problem’s fundamental hardness-of-approximation limit.
Benchmarks show improved estimation accuracy and computational efficiency over prominent information-theoretic objectives and optimization methods.
Scope: establishes a rigorous foundation for discrete offline IPP under bounded uncertainty, with extensions to continuous and online settings left for future work.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in frontier models have pushed the boundaries of agentic robot control, enabling agents to perform complex robotic tasks through reasoning and interaction. However, repeated calls to these models during execution can substantially increase task completion time. Code as Policies (CaP) offers a route for coding agents to acquire physical skills through experience and retain them in executable programs, allowing the reasoning invested in development to be reused across runs. Developing reliable code policies while limiting the cost of physical experimentation remains a central challenge. We investigate human guidance as a source of priors for feasible actions and simulation as an auxiliary environment for exploring and testing candidate policies. Our findings favor robot demonstrations available on request and simulation used selectively during real-world policy refinement. These findings inform ACE-CaP-0, an agentic recipe that couples policy revision with experience acquisition through Demonstrations on Request and Simulation on Demand. Across eight real-world manipulation tasks spanning alignment, multi-object handling, and bimanual coordination, the resulting frozen programs achieve 92.1\% success (221/240 trials). Mean execution times across tasks range from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes. The programs execute with runtime perception and control, without a human or coding agent in the loop. These results highlight CaP's potential to turn experience into reliable, reusable physical skills.

papers.abstract: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.

papers.abstract: To keep long interaction contexts tractable, stepwise group-relative training for multi-turn LLM agents materializes each source trajectory into multiple response rows and valid tokens. This expansion creates an outer-accounting problem distinct from within-trajectory credit assignment: row-based outcome statistics can count one episode outcome multiple times, while token-level reduction can assign unequal aggregate objective mass across trajectories. We term these effects outcome-statistics multiplicity and objective-mass imbalance. We introduce Outcome-Mass Alignment (OMA), a two-component method that makes both accounting choices explicit. Outcome Alignment computes outcome statistics over unique source trajectories, while Mass Alignment controls aggregate objective mass after within-trajectory aggregation of optimizer-native token objectives. Neither redesigns the base optimizer's credit assignment, importance ratios, or clipping. Across matched ALFWorld GRPO comparisons at two model scales, where failed trajectories typically expand much more than successful ones, OMA improves matched-horizon endpoint success by 7.0-9.4 percentage points. Ordinary WebShop exhibits weak or reversed expansion-outcome coupling and correspondingly mixed effects, whereas in a success-oriented WebShop setting, WebShop-SOL, OMA improves success nAUC from 0.399 to 0.511. Component ablations and GiGPO and GSPO comparisons further support component separability and cross-optimizer compatibility. These results show that trajectory expansion always defines an implicit weighting rule, but its practical effect depends on how expansion couples to outcomes and optimizer-native updates.

bullets: Problem: Expanding each trajectory into response rows and tokens can multiply episode outcomes and assign disproportionate training mass across trajectories.

Scope: OMA leaves the base optimizer’s credit assignment, importance ratios, and clipping unchanged and is compatible with multiple optimizers.
Results: In matched-horizon ALFWorld GRPO experiments, OMA improves endpoint success by 7.0–9.4 percentage points; effects are mixed on ordinary WebShop but positive in WebShop-SOL.
Key limitation: Benefits depend on how trajectory expansion correlates with outcomes, so OMA is not uniformly effective across environments.

papers.abstract: Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as "corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: cornercase-dashbench.github.io
authors: Gabriel Manalu, Minh Son Hoang, Hyeontaek Hwang, Jaesung Lee, Hyojin Choi, Tran Tuan Phong, Seon Kwon Kim, Saad Wazir, Daeyoung Kim

The benchmark includes an evaluation toolkit and diagnosis of model limitations; code and data will be released.

papers.abstract: Autonomous greenhouse management increasingly requires robotic systems that integrate perception, navigation, environmental regulation, and plant-level intervention. This paper presents AgriSense, a framework combining an Isaac Sim virtual greenhouse, a quadruped mobile manipulator, RGB and LiDAR-inertial sensing, environmental control, and supervised vision-language decision support. Frozen DINOv2 and BERT encoders, together with structured environmental inputs, support joint prediction of twelve environmental references, a target zone, and an intervention flag. Checkpoint replay reproduces 41/43 zone decisions. Across five seeds on a source-grouped test set, the full, image-removed, and language-removed configurations each achieve 43/44 correct zone decisions, providing no evidence of incremental multimodal zone-accuracy improvement. The full model achieves mean absolute errors of 0.249 degrees C for temperature, 2.030 percentage points for humidity, and 0.997 percentage points for soil moisture. Sensor-only inputs match full-model zone accuracy, while language-only inputs achieve 68.64%. External real-image benchmarks reveal distribution-shift limitations. Five offline Point-LIO routes yield rigidly aligned trajectory errors of 5.22-17.32 mm. Of 40 virtual-arm targets, 32 satisfy geometric acceptance criteria and eight are rejected at boundaries. Six long-horizon climate cases and fault protocols characterize integration limits. Navigation and integrated treatment rely on simulator-state inputs; physical greenhouse performance and agronomic treatment efficacy remain unvalidated. The contribution is an evaluated decision-support and robotic-intervention framework for a virtual greenhouse.

papers.abstract: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

papers.abstract: LiDAR is a core sensor for autonomous driving, yet it is highly vulnerable to fog. Fog scattering produces strong backscatter near the sensor and attenuates reflections from objects behind it, so weak object returns are often discarded by the peak detection that converts received signals into point clouds. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL), which records the received optical signal before peak detection, retains these weak returns, but the lack of suitable data has prevented research on recovering fog-hidden objects from FWL. We present Fog-FWL, a dataset foundation for this task that consists of a real-world benchmark, Fog-FWL-Real, and a large-scale synthetic training set, Fog-FWL-Sim. Fog-FWL-Real contains 7,527 real foggy FWL frames from 8 scenes and 58 sequences, which is 579x larger than the only existing real foggy FWL data, together with histogram-level Object/Fog/Noise labels, 10,719 3D bounding boxes, and three difficulty levels defined by the attenuation of object reflections. Fog-FWL-Sim contains 12,000 frames generated by our physics-based simulator, Fog-FWL-Simulator, which integrates spatially heterogeneous fog density fields, time-resolved light transport including multiple scattering, and a photon-counting SPAD receiver model. The two subsets share the same sensor format and annotation protocol, enabling a strict sim-to-real evaluation in which no real waveforms are used for training. Our analysis shows that, under the hardest condition, object returns are included in the three strongest peaks for only 34.9% of object rays, underscoring the need for waveform-level recovery. Fog-FWL-Real, Fog-FWL-Sim, and the Fog-FWL-Simulator will be publicly released to facilitate research on fog-robust LiDAR perception.

Fog-FWL-Sim provides 12,000 simulated frames generated with heterogeneous fog, multiple-scattering light transport, and a photon-counting receiver model.
Shared formats and annotations support strict sim-to-real evaluation without using real waveforms for training.
