Handles diverse Internet videos through actor identification, optional references, and multi-shot operation tracking.
Targets improved fidelity for hand–object interactions and broader first-person data collection across tasks and scenes.

papers.abstract: Optional reasoning, retrieval, web search, and tool use can improve large language model responses but incur unnecessary computation when activated indiscriminately. This study investigates whether prompt optimization can compensate for limited router capacity and whether classification gains translate into downstream efficiency. The proposed framework uses prompt-driven small language models to make four independent capability decisions, allowing multiple capabilities to be selected per query. Qwen2.5 routers ranging from 1.5B to 14B parameters are compared across five prompting strategies, followed by an evaluation of capability-specific optimized configurations using a fixed GPT-OSS-120B downstream model on 127 questions. Under minimal prompting, increasing router capacity does not consistently improve classification performance. Prompt optimization narrows the capacity gap for reasoning and calculator routing, whereas RAG and web search retain larger benefits from higher capacity. Similar classification F1 scores do not necessarily imply equivalent downstream behavior: false-positive activations increase unnecessary computation, while missed capabilities can reduce answer quality. The 14B router achieves a mean BERTScore F1 of 0.8408, compared with 0.8418 when all capabilities are enabled, while reducing average downstream token consumption by 68.7\% (8,837 to 2,764 tokens) and median downstream latency by 80.5\% (9.79 to 1.91 seconds). These savings exclude router overhead, which is measured separately in a different inference environment and increases with router capacity. The findings demonstrate that the relationship between router capacity, prompt design, and downstream efficiency is capability-dependent. Consequently, router selection must consider error profiles and routing overhead alongside classification performance.
authors: Sailendra Kolluru, Maheshkumar Duvvarapu
bullets: The study routes queries independently to reasoning, retrieval, web search, and calculator capabilities, allowing multiple selections per query.
Larger routers do not consistently improve classification under minimal prompting; prompt optimization reduces capacity gaps mainly for reasoning and calculator routing.
RAG and web-search routing benefit more from higher model capacity, showing capability-dependent scaling effects.
A 14B router nearly matches always-on quality (BERTScore F1 0.8408 vs. 0.8418) while reducing downstream token use by 68.7% and median latency by 80.5%.
Classification scores alone are insufficient: false positives waste computation, missed capabilities can hurt quality, and router overhead increases with capacity.

papers.abstract: Advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have improved remote sensing image analysis and supported geospatial decision-making. However, fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery remains challenging for VLMs. Large variations in object scale, complex geospatial relations among instances, and limited visual detail hinder precise instance localization, visible attribute identification, and spatial relation understanding, potentially leading to descriptions that lack visual grounding. Existing datasets and benchmarks insufficiently assess end-to-end instance localization and captioning without target-specific textual cues. To support this evaluation, we introduce RICapBench, a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localization and fine-grained captioning in remote sensing. RICapBench contains 245,466 instance-level annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples spanning general remote sensing, UAV remote sensing, and dense small-object scenarios. Each annotation pairs an object's oriented bounding box with a natural language description of its visible attributes and spatial relations to surrounding instances and environmental elements. To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning, we propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric. We combine RelCap-F1 with instance localization and attribute captioning metrics into a composite metric, RICScore. Our evaluation of 15 advanced open-source and closed-source VLMs identifies instance localization as a major bottleneck for these models. LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68, but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than other task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Xldln/RICapBench.
authors: Xue Wang, Yubin Xu, Kun Tan

papers.abstract: It is common to train Large Language Models (LLMs) for agentic tasks with Reinforcement Learning (RL) from scalar rewards. However, this throws away the fine-grained information about the environment that the agent experienced during the trial (e.g., error logs). To utilize this rich information, recent works wrap the agent in a harness that refines its own inputs through reflection or compaction and hands past experience to future rollouts, but the construction of the handed-off artifacts (e.g., a playbook) is itself not learned. We want the best of both worlds: gradient updates from a scalar reward, while also utilizing environment information to hand off experience. As a concrete testbed, we fix the Agentic Context Engineering (\ace{}) harness and train one model to act, reflect, and curate task-local playbooks. Our method, \acerl{}, evaluates candidate experience-handoff artifacts by their downstream effect on future actor rollouts, and co-optimizes the role-specific behaviors (action generator, insight reflector, and playbook curator) under a fixed scaffold. Across agentic benchmarks, \acerl{} achieves higher held-out performance than baseline methods. The results suggest that agent training should optimize not only the actions in the current rollout, but also the model-written experience that future rollouts inherit.
authors: Doyoung Kim, Byeongguk Jeon, Kailin Zhang, Sherry Yang
bullets: Scalar-reward RL overlooks useful trial information such as error logs.
The work learns experience handoff within a fixed Agentic Context Engineering harness.
ACERL evaluates artifacts by their downstream impact on future actor rollouts.
One model jointly learns to act, reflect on insights, and curate task-specific playbooks.
Experiments report higher held-out performance than baseline methods across agentic benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Experience-Handoff RL. (a) Outcome-only RL compresses each trial into a scalar reward. (b) A harness runs several calls to the same model (cis; in ACE, actor, reflector, and curator) and preserves experience as a model-written context, such as a playbook, handed to the next attempt (blue), but the model never learns to write better playbooks. (c) Experience-handoff RL trains the model for the harness it runs in, from task outcomes alone. For example, ACE-RL rewards each handoff artifact for what it does to a future rollout: (i) each new context is scored by a fresh rollout, and (ii) each role is compared within its own group (stacked boxes), which lowers the variance of its credit.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are increasingly capable, yet their reasoning in complex remote sensing scenes can remain coarse-grained and insufficiently grounded in task-relevant visual evidence. We propose Gravity and Flight (G&F), a framework for scene specialization with limited supervision that separates visual and reasoning verification while coupling policy updates. It combines Evidence-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning (EoT-SFT) and Relational Transfer Policy Optimization (RTPO). EoT-SFT teaches fine-grained observation and faithful reasoning through description, analysis, and supported conclusions. RTPO independently samples responses to scene-matched image pairs with fine-grained visual differences under a shared task. Its rubric-based verification combines Gravity, which checks visual fidelity and description coverage, and Flight, which takes descriptions as premises to assess evidence use and relations between paired judgments. Their scores and task correctness yield a shared pair-level advantage that couples policy updates from both responses. Using 1,008 demonstrations and 500 training pairs for harbor specialization, G&F achieves a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone and supervised initialization by 9.76 and 4.56 points. Matched controls show gains over single-image and joint-input RL, and removing either verification view reduces performance. Applying G&F to urban specialization also improves on the base model and supervised initialization across three evaluation subsets. Project details and updates are available at https://github.com/Z0ngL1ng/Gravity-and-Flight.
authors: Yuheng Zong, Minghua Wang, Xin Zhao, Xiaobin Liu, Yongjian Dong, Chanho Eom
bullets: Targets coarse, insufficiently grounded reasoning in complex remote-sensing scenes.
Combines Evidence-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning with Relational Transfer Policy Optimization.
Uses Gravity to verify visual fidelity and coverage, and Flight to assess evidence use and paired relations.
For harbor specialization, achieves a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, outperforming the backbone and supervised initialization by 9.76 and 4.56 points.
Removing either verification view reduces performance; gains also transfer to urban specialization across three evaluation subsets.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective post-training approach to improving fine-grained perception in multimodal large language models by amortizing costly inference-time zooming operations into a single-pass recipe. However, vanilla OPD is inherently susceptible to linguistic momentum: the teacher can follow the student's erroneous prefixes, thus weakening corrective supervision. To address this, we propose Blink On-Policy Distillation (BlinkOPD), in which the teacher "blinks" at every token: it reads the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed. A first-glance gain further strengthens the correction on rollouts that conflict with the teacher. By extracting more effective supervision from each on-policy trajectory, BlinkOPD achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using only 500 training images (12x less data) than existing OPD methods. Beyond fine-grained perception, BlinkOPD also demonstrates strong zero-shot improvements across ten held-out benchmarks spanning general visual perception, visual hallucination, and multimodal reasoning abilities. Code: https://github.com/Supltz/BlinkOPD
authors: Tangzheng Lian, Hang Zhang, Guanyu Hu, Renjiu Hu, Zhensong Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Jifei Song
bullets: Vanilla OPD can exhibit linguistic momentum, where the teacher follows the student's mistakes instead of correcting them.
BlinkOPD has the teacher read each prefix twice: with visual input (“eyes open”) and without it (“eyes closed”).
A first-glance gain amplifies corrective supervision on rollouts that disagree with the teacher.
It achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using 500 training images, 12× less data than existing OPD methods.
It also improves zero-shot performance across ten held-out benchmarks covering visual perception, hallucination, and multimodal reasoning.

figures.caption: Figure 5. Overview of BlinkOPD. The student generates rollouts from the full image I and question q, together denoted by xs. Their log-ratio rt keeps the privileged visual evidence, while the prefix-induced linguistic drift shared by both cancels. A prefix-free first glance of the same teacher flags rollouts whose answer conflicts with it, and the gain is raised by a factor γ on these rollouts (Sec. 3.2). The student is trained toward the resulting distillation target (Sec. 3.3). At test time, the student runs alone in a single pass.

papers.abstract: An assistant watching a worker can prepare for an emerging need before the worker is ready to receive help.As the need evolves, the assistant must maintain preparation until a response is due, or withdraw it if the need disappears. Video anticipation and interactive response benchmarks leave this interval between early evidence and response largely unmeasured. We introduce FuGIBench (Future-Grounded Interaction), a streaming-video benchmark in which a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation, and response given a causal video prefix and a task contract. The benchmark contains 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tool tasks, in handover, ordinary-activity, and cancelled-need tracks. One primary score credits sustained preparation, incorporates response-interval alignment, and penalizes activity when the reference prescribes waiting. On a frozen set of 1,000 episodes, a reference system with a longer preparation lead has poorer response alignment, while similar handover leads accompany different levels of activity during ordinary work in matched scenarios. Together with cancellation analyses, these results show why evaluating preparation requires tracking decisions as needs develop, become actionable, or disappear.
authors: Changheng Cai, Zhichao Huang, Song Ren, Zhichen Zhao, Hongsen Liu, Chaoyang Zheng, Wenxi Wu, Yuan Fang, Wei Wang, Yang Wang, Yuchen Wang
bullets: Addresses the undermeasured interval between early evidence of a need and the moment a response is due.
Introduces a benchmark with causal video prefixes, task contracts, and three choices: wait, reversibly prepare, or respond.
Covers 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tasks and handover, ordinary-activity, and cancelled-need tracks.
Uses a score that rewards sustained, well-timed preparation and penalizes unnecessary activity when waiting is prescribed.
Analyses show that longer preparation leads do not necessarily improve response alignment, and cancellation behavior is important to evaluation.

papers.abstract: In long-horizon manipulation, a robot may need to take different actions under identical observations, depending on task progress and the outcomes of earlier attempts. We refer to this ambiguity as decision aliasing. Resolving it requires the policy to maintain memory of its execution history. To reduce the cost of processing full observation histories, recent methods build compact event memories using perceptual, semantic, or kinematic cues. However, these criteria may miss events that matter for task success. We instead propose an outcome-grounded principle: remember events that substantially change the predicted probability of eventual success. Following this principle, we introduce CGEM, a critic-gated event memory that uses a critic to select events with large estimated changes in success probability. Positive and negative changes are encoded as progress and failure records, respectively. Failure records are discarded once the corresponding subtask is completed. In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment with exactly computed success probabilities, CGEM achieves 88.0% success, compared with 0.0% for both a 36-step observation window and a kinematic event memory. Removing failure records reduces success to 1.7%.
authors: Xuanzhuo Liu, Chuankang Li, Maoqing Yao, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Addresses decision aliasing, where identical observations require different actions based on task history.
Uses a critic to gate event memory by estimated changes in success probability.
Stores positive changes as progress records and negative changes as failure records, deleting failures after the related subtask is completed.
In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment, CGEM reaches 88.0% success versus 0.0% for a 36-step observation window and kinematic event memory.
Removing failure records drops success to 1.7%, highlighting their importance.

papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) advance toward increasingly long inputs, soft context compression offers a promising approach to efficient inference by converting long inputs into compact memory slots. Under limited memory budgets, effective context compression remains challenging because task-relevant evidence varies substantially across queries, ranging from localized evidence to multiple distant spans or information dispersed throughout the full document. Instead of compressing everything indiscriminately, we propose CoMem, a query-guided selective context compression framework that learns memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query. CoMem develops Contrastive Compressor Learning to achieve query-sensitive yet context-preserving memory representations. To inject a strong prior over query-dependent evidence distributions, we devise a same-context hard negative mining strategy by pairing a single document with multiple queries, requiring the compressor to selectively retain information according to each query's distinct evidence needs. To address the restricted information flow imposed by causal masking, we further enable bidirectional attention among memory slots. Experiments demonstrate that CoMem consistently outperforms existing context compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/scar-on/CoMem.
authors: Sikui Zhang, Haowei Liu, Ziyun Gan, Chunfeng Yuan, Guangze Gao, Nian Liu, Boyu Cai, Bo Li, Xiaolei Lv, Jun Gao, Bing Li, Weiming Hu
bullets: Addresses context compression when relevant evidence may be local, scattered, or distributed across a document.
Uses query-guided memory representations conditioned on both the document and the query.
Applies contrastive compressor learning with same-document, multi-query hard negatives to distinguish differing evidence needs.
Enables bidirectional attention among memory slots to improve information flow despite causal masking.
Outperforms existing compression methods across compression ratios on question answering and RULER-NIAH benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Universal multi-modal fusion often fails not because modalities are insufficiently aligned, but because the fusion process allocates information poorly: redundant evidence is repeatedly amplified, modality-unique evidence is over-smoothed during alignment, and task-dependent synergistic evidence is insufficiently activated. We present RADIANT (Redundancy-Aware Dynamic Information Allocation Network), a task-general framework that organizes fusion around three complementary roles: suppressing redundant cross-modal overlap, preserving modality-unique evidence, and composing task-conditioned synergy through cross-modal interaction. Specifically, stable matrix-exponential projections are used to reduce interference among shared and modality-unique streams, while task memory with hard positive updates selects which synergistic interactions should be activated for the current fusion regime. Extensive experiments across six heterogeneous fusion tasks show consistent improvements over the compared methods. On FLIR, RADIANT improves downstream detection mAP@0.5 from 91.2% to 96.8%, a gain of 5.6 percentage points (6.1% relative) over GIF. RADIANT also exhibits strong direct cross-dataset transfer, with further gains from inference-time task-memory adaptation while keeping all network weights frozen. Additional ablations and sensitivity studies support the robustness of the allocation mechanism.
authors: Shenghai Wu, Yue Lin
bullets: Targets redundancy amplification, over-smoothed unique modality cues, and underused task-dependent interactions.
Uses stable matrix-exponential projections to reduce interference between shared and modality-unique streams.
Employs task memory with hard positive updates to activate relevant cross-modal synergies.
Across six heterogeneous fusion tasks, it consistently improves over compared methods.
On FLIR, detection mAP@0.5 rises from 91.2% to 96.8% over GIF; task-memory adaptation also improves cross-dataset transfer with frozen weights.

papers.abstract: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. Yet a plausible modification is not necessarily suitable for persistent adoption: candidate selection is adaptive, evaluators may be imperfect, and local gains can hide degradation against an earlier baseline. We introduce Evidence-Governed Evolution (EGE), a framework for governing adoption of self-generated agent modifications. EGE separates candidate generation from confirmatory adoption, evaluates frozen candidates on fresh paired audits, requires meaningful improvement on a prespecified primary objective, protects declared capabilities through reference-relative non-inferiority tests, and applies governance constraints before bounded canary deployment. We establish an evaluator-calibrated simultaneous lower-bound construction for a countable sequence of adaptively generated candidates. It combines candidate-wise Hoeffding bounds with independent calibration samples comparing the operational evaluator with a prespecified reference procedure. We also formalise reference replacement through bridge tests, derive a cumulative degradation bound along a versioned reference lineage, and provide an audit-planning condition relating effect-size margin, sample sizes, and acceptance probability. A Monte Carlo stress test illustrates calibration under candidate-dependent evaluator optimism; it is a stylised statistical experiment, not an evaluation of a deployed agent. The guarantees are conditional on bounded paired scores, fresh sampling, a valid reference-evaluation construct, and declared evaluation distributions; they do not establish universal agent safety or robustness to arbitrary distribution shift.
authors: Subodh Lonkar
bullets: Separates adaptive candidate generation from confirmatory evaluation and bounded canary deployment.
Tests frozen candidates on fresh paired audits against a prespecified primary objective.
Protects declared capabilities using reference-relative non-inferiority tests and governance constraints.
Provides simultaneous lower bounds for countably many adaptively generated candidates, with evaluator calibration and reference-replacement bridge tests.
Monte Carlo experiments illustrate calibration under evaluator optimism; guarantees are conditional and do not cover universal safety or arbitrary distribution shift.

papers.abstract: Language models rely on finite token contexts, limiting access to earlier interactions. We introduce Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework in which a persistent latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a pretrained language model. A modular read-transition-write architecture separates observation encoding, latent dynamics, and predictor adaptation. We develop deterministic and stochastic formulations. The experiments evaluate only deterministic SALM with frozen GPT-2 small and exclude earlier evidence from its decoder context. On a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, latent-gated LoRA reaches 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a trained full-context LoRA baseline, with earlier evidence available solely through a 64-dimensional state. Zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. In a two-turn task with codewords unseen in training, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance, but rarely generate the exact codeword under the evaluated training schedule. These experiments show that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context.
authors: Omer Haq
bullets: Addresses the limited memory of finite-token contexts by maintaining a state that evolves with each observation.
Uses a modular read–transition–write architecture to encode observations, update latent dynamics, and adapt the predictor.
In deterministic experiments with frozen GPT-2 small, latent-gated LoRA achieved 89.1% accuracy on a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, close to the 88.0% full-context baseline.
Removing or shuffling the 64-dimensional state substantially reduced accuracy, supporting its role in retaining earlier evidence.
On unseen-codeword tasks, interfaces improved candidate ranking over chance but rarely generated the exact codeword under the tested training schedule.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robotic manipulation have enabled increasingly complex and dexterous behaviors, yet existing benchmarks still focus on simple pick-and-place tasks and lack a systematic framework for measuring progress in robot learning along the axis of task difficulty. We present ManiLadder, a large-scale and organized simulation benchmark for robotic manipulation. ManiLadder contains 112 carefully designed tasks stratified into 4 difficulty levels, with 8 categories in each level, spanning rigid-body and deformable-object manipulation, single-arm and dual-arm settings, and gripper and dexterous-hand end-effectors. To calibrate difficulty, we fix the data amount the same for every task and use a unified flow- matching imitation learning policy under the same training and evaluation protocols, then use its evaluation success rate as an operational empirical difficulty signal. All tasks are iteratively refined until they fall into target difficulty ranges, which are then verified across different random seeds, policies, and agentic learning systems. We further analyze the task properties, compare different policy performances and training settings, analyze task transfer and data scaling behaviors, and conduct real-world experiments showing that the designed tasks preserve their difficulty ordering beyond simulation. ManiLad- der provides a calibrated ladder for measuring, comparing, and advancing robotic manipulation capabilities. More results are available at https://maniladder-benchmark.github.io/.
authors: Chongkai Gao, Jieao Shi, Zhaoyu Mu, Yudi Lin, Xuanwei Liu, Wei Ken Ng, Baiye Cheng, Anqi Chen, Kerun Liu, Zhuoran Li, Xuchuan Huang, Haoyang Li, Shengjia Zhu, Nga Teng Chan, Yuxuan Zhang, Xingyu Chen, Lin Shao
bullets: Addresses the lack of systematic benchmarks for measuring progress beyond simple pick-and-place tasks.
Covers rigid and deformable objects, single- and dual-arm setups, and gripper and dexterous-hand end-effectors.
Calibrates difficulty using standardized data, policies, training, and evaluation protocols, with success rate as the difficulty signal.
Validates task difficulty ordering across random seeds, policies, agentic learning systems, and real-world experiments.
Supports analysis of policy performance, training settings, task transfer, and data scaling.

papers.abstract: Accurate plant disease recognition is essential for intelligent agriculture, but few-shot settings provide limited labeled samples that may not capture diagnostic symptoms and intra-class variations. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, offer transferable visual-semantic knowledge. However, existing CLIP-based methods often rely on coarse class semantics and global visual representations, overlooking disease-specific diagnostic information and fine-grained local cues. Excessive few-shot adaptation may also cause over-specialization and weaken the generalization ability of large-scale pre-training. We propose a description-guided, two-stage CLIP adaptation method to address these issues. Symptom and comparative descriptions enrich class semantics with typical visual symptoms and discriminative cues between similar diseases. The enhanced semantics guide the aggregation of class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate global image-text matching with fine-grained cues. For adaptation, we first update the vision-language encoders with lightweight parameters, then freeze them and train a linear classifier. At inference, the classifier is used for in-domain prediction, while class prototypes from the adapted text encoder support cross-domain prediction and retain vision-language transferability. Experiments with two backbones show that our method achieves the highest mean accuracy in most few-shot settings on PlantVillage, Cassava, and Pear, reaching 93.16%, 79.30%, and 96.56%, respectively, with ViT-L/14 under 16-shot. On class-aligned cross-domain evaluation across 21 shared PlantDoc classes, it achieves 56.96% accuracy, outperforming all compared methods. These results demonstrate its effectiveness in fine-grained few-shot plant disease recognition and cross-domain generalization.
authors: Zhenkun Ye, Qian Zhou, Hua Zou
bullets: Addresses limited labeled data, coarse class semantics, and overlooked fine-grained disease cues in few-shot recognition.
Enriches class descriptions with symptoms and comparisons between similar diseases, then aggregates class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate image-text matching.
Adapts CLIP with lightweight encoder updates followed by linear-classifier training; adapted text prototypes support cross-domain prediction.
Under 16-shot evaluation with ViT-L/14, reaches 93.16% on PlantVillage, 79.30% on Cassava, and 96.56% on Pear.
Achieves 56.96% accuracy on 21 shared PlantDoc classes in cross-domain evaluation, outperforming compared methods.

papers.abstract: Accurate forecasting of Earth's dynamic systems is vital in geophysics, where neural operators offer a powerful data-driven paradigm. Standard operators often treat the Earth as a flat Euclidean plane, introducing geometric artifacts. In contrast, Spherical Neural Operators (SNOs) resolve this mismatch by operating within the spherical spectral space, naturally adapting to spherical geometries. However, for computational efficiency, existing SNOs typically rely on the rotation equivariance assumption. This assumption simplifies the transitions of physical states into isolated spectral modal evolutions, thereby over-idealizing the Earth as a homogeneous system. To solve this problem, we no longer rely on the rotation equivariance assumption that isolates spectral modal evolution, but directly derive an explicit modal interaction kernel and propose Diagonal Spherical Neural Operators named DIAGNO. DIAGNO explicitly parameterizes cross-modal interactions through spectral modal decomposition, thereby preserving the inherent heterogeneity of Earth dynamics. Furthermore, leveraging the unique diagonal structure of the spherical spectrum, we design inter- and intra-diagonal interaction mechanisms to natively capture essential zonal and meridional dynamics, respecting intrinsic geophysical regularities. Extensive experiments across simulated fluid dynamics and real-world Earth system reanalysis (including atmosphere and ocean) datasets demonstrate DIAGNO's superior capability, consistently achieving state-of-the-art performance in multi-step forecasting. Beyond this, we validate DIAGNO's practical analytical value in professional geophysical domains by assessing its fidelity in capturing climatological anomalies and maintaining physical consistency.
authors: Herui Li, Bin Lu, Haonan Qi, Lei Zhou, Luoyi Fu, Xinbing Wang, Meng Jin
bullets: Addresses geometric artifacts from flat-Earth operator models and oversimplification from rotation-equivariance assumptions.
Explicitly parameterizes interactions among spherical spectral modes instead of treating modal evolutions as isolated.
Introduces inter- and intra-diagonal interactions to capture zonal and meridional geophysical dynamics.
Performs strongly in multi-step forecasting on simulated fluid dynamics and real atmosphere and ocean reanalysis data.
Also evaluates climatological-anomaly fidelity and physical consistency for practical geophysical analysis.

papers.abstract: Reusing a demonstrated gait can reduce the work of specifying the same motion for each biped. A video captures the timing of a step, but each robot must execute it with its own limbs and actuators. MotionSkill recovers a timed reference once from monocular video and adapts it to each target in simulation. It aligns root motion and body landmarks in a common frame and records which landmarks are available at each instant. At each source timestamp, the mapper preserves limb directions, uses the target segment lengths, and solves inverse kinematics under joint limits and closure constraints. In MuJoCo, we train a separate residual policy for each of ten bipeds on its mapped reference from one four-second walking clip. Each policy uses the measured robot state to correct joint commands during contact. From initial states held out during training, MotionSkill completed 98% of trials on the original video and 26% with the upper body occluded for one second.
authors: Philip Niu, Xiaofeng Han, Sylvie Pan, Yang Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of reusing a demonstrated gait across robots with different limbs and actuators.
Aligns root motion and body landmarks, then maps limb directions to target segment lengths via constrained inverse kinematics.
Trains a separate residual policy per biped in MuJoCo to correct commands during contact.
Using one four-second clip, it completed 98% of held-out initial-state trials on the original video and 26% when the upper body was occluded for one second.
Scope: evaluation is in simulation and depends on a single demonstrated walking clip.

papers.abstract: Multimodal diffusion large language models (dLLMs) generate text through iterative masked denoising with bidirectional attention, offering a compelling alternative to autoregressive vision-language modeling. However, each denoising step requires a full forward pass over long multimodal sequences in which visual tokens dominate the sequence length, and a fixed step budget further compounds this quadratic per-step cost. Existing inference acceleration approaches for multimodal dLLMs characterize attention redundancy implicitly, motivating designs from isolated attention visualizations rather than from measurement. We close this gap with DRAMA, a training-free acceleration framework grounded in a systematic dissection of attention redundancy in multimodal dLLMs. By probing attention tensors along spatial and temporal axes, we reveal two persistent redundancy structures: (i) attention mass consistently concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens, and (ii) attention distributions rapidly stabilize across denoising steps after an initial formation phase. These findings motivate two complementary mechanisms: Spatial-Redundancy-Aware Visual Token Pruning (SVTP) and Sufficiency-Guided Adaptive Stopping (SGAS). Together, DRAMA achieves an average 18.67 times inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks without training, architectural modification, or attention caching, while maintaining competitive accuracy. Our results establish a strong, measurement-grounded acceleration baseline for multimodal dLLM inference.
authors: Yi-Hsin Hung, Fangfu Liu, Shao-Yuan Lo, Chu-Song Chen
bullets: Identifies two redundancy patterns: attention concentrates on a sparse subset of visual tokens and stabilizes across denoising steps.
Introduces SVTP for spatially aware visual-token pruning.
Introduces SGAS for sufficiency-guided adaptive stopping of denoising.
Training-free and requires no architectural changes or attention caching.
Reports an average 18.67× inference speedup across six vision-language benchmarks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

papers.abstract: Calibrated multi-view hand reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet the effectiveness of existing methods depends strongly on real captured data, which is costly to acquire, limited in hand-geometry diversity, and often affected by imperfect annotations. Synthetic data offers a scalable alternative with accurate supervision, but a substantial synthetic-to-real appearance gap hinders its use. To address this, we introduce Hand in Silhouette (SilHand), a calibrated multi-view hand reconstruction framework that operates on binary hand masks, obtainable at low cost either automatically or manually, to reduce the synthetic-to-real observation gap. Rather than relying on RGB features for 3D lifting, SilHand projects metric 3D hypotheses into each view to query and fuse mask-ray evidence for hand reconstruction. This mask-centric formulation enables training on a large-scale synthetic dataset comprising 46.8k grasping poses and 60k free-hand samples, providing broad coverage of hand geometry while directly transferring to real captured hand geometry. Across five real-world benchmarks, SilHand improves relative reconstruction accuracy from 49.2% to 63.4% using masks rendered from reference hands. Moreover, reconstruction accuracy improves consistently as the synthetic training set grows, indicating that broader geometric coverage translates into better real-world performance. While achieving such diversity is difficult with real captured data, it becomes practical under our mask-centric formulation. Finally, SilHand remains robust under mask corruption, with reconstruction error increasing by at most 1.63 mm. Together, these results support binary masks as an effective interface for learning hand reconstruction from synthetic geometry.

papers.abstract: At disaster sites and on unstable slopes, robot contact can collapse uninspected terrain, requiring retreat upon support loss. Massively parallel reinforcement learning of collapse-reactive retreat requires independent state--action experiences. However, on shared rigid-body collapsible terrain, one robot's collapse alters others' contacts without direct interaction. We call this indirect interference. Duplicating terrain objects prevents this but is memory-intensive, limiting parallel sampling. Our key insight is that policy learning does not necessarily require rigid-body collapse modeling, which is feasible but computationally expensive; collapse-induced contact responses can suffice. We therefore propose a memory-efficient parallel policy-learning framework for collapse-reactive retreat via hybrid terrain modeling. Hybrid terrain modeling combines rigid-body simulation of non-collapsible terrain with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions. A State-Multiplexed Contact Model shares terrain geometry and a contact-response law while maintaining environment-specific collapse states, enabling independent experiences without terrain objects for collapsible regions. The framework trains a proprioceptive policy for both normal locomotion and collapse-reactive retreat. It supports over 100 times as many parallel environments as fine-resolution rigid-block terrain within the same GPU memory limit. This scalability and improved sample efficiency enable over 50 times faster policy convergence with comparable retreat performance. Sim-to-sim and real-robot experiments demonstrate retreat under multiple collapse conditions. A supplementary video is available at: https://youtu.be/_RrhwjzEPE0
authors: Yuki Kadokawa, Ritsuki Matsunaga, Yuqi Yang, Edgar Anarossi, Takamitsu Matsubara
bullets: Addresses indirect interference in parallel reinforcement learning caused by shared collapsible terrain altering other robots’ contacts.
Replaces rigid-body collapse simulation with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions while retaining rigid-body modeling for stable terrain.
Uses a State-Multiplexed Contact Model to share terrain geometry and contact laws while keeping collapse states environment-specific.
Supports over 100× more parallel environments and over 50× faster policy convergence than fine-resolution rigid-block terrain under the same GPU memory limit.
Sim-to-sim and real-robot experiments demonstrate retreat across multiple collapse conditions.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Concept of our policy-learning framework. (Top) A wheeled quadruped encounters collapse-prone terrain that cannot be identified before contact. The objective is to learn a policy that enables the robot to retreat to non-collapsible terrain without falling. (Bottom) Comparison of terrain modeling approaches for parallel policy learning. With rigid collapse, shared rigid terrain enables efficient simulation but causes indirect interference, as collapse induced by one robot affects others. Individual rigid terrain prevents interference but increases simulation cost and training time. With virtual collapse on shared rigid terrain, our hybrid approach combines rigid-body simulation for non-collapsible terrain with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions, enabling memory-efficient parallel learning without indirect interference.

papers.abstract: Transferring LLMs into System One decision models typically replaces the language modeling head with a decision head while retaining the full backbone, making every decision pay for all layers. Yet it remains unclear how much depth such decisions require. We find that decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers, with early layers building essential features and the final six layers removable without loss, while independently trained smaller models largely mimic the full model rather than developing specialized decision capabilities. These findings suggest that efficiency requires not simply smaller backbones, but shared computation across different depths. Building on this, we propose \method{}, which jointly trains a full model with prefix sub-models that share its final layers and decision head through self-distillation. A lightweight gate reads the hidden state at each exit to determine whether additional computation is needed, allowing one model to operate at multiple layers. Across seven decision benchmarks, our approach matches or outperforms independently trained models at every depth, while achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs through adaptive computation.
authors: Minh-Anh Nguyen
bullets: Decision information is concentrated in intermediate layers; the final six layers can be removed without accuracy loss.
Independently trained smaller models mostly mimic the full model instead of learning specialized decision representations.
The proposed method jointly trains a full model and prefix sub-models that share later layers and a decision head via self-distillation.
A lightweight gate chooses whether each input needs additional layers, enabling multi-depth inference in one model.
Across seven decision benchmarks, the method matches or outperforms independent models at every depth with improved accuracy-efficiency trade-offs.

The model runs layer by layer, with a lightweight gate evaluating the hidden state at each intermediate exit. If ge ≥ τ , it runs the final block and returns a decision; otherwise, it continues from the saved states without recomputation.

papers.tldr: Adaptive depth with shared computation lets one decision model match or exceed separately trained smaller models while using only as much computation as needed.

papers.abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models through forward-only evaluations, but high-dimensional random perturbations can limit optimization efficiency. Sparse perturbations reduce the search dimension, making the selection of informative coordinates critical. We propose Wanda-Importance Sparsity-MeZO (WIS-MeZO), which uses Wanda weight--activation saliency to construct task-conditioned sparse perturbation masks while keeping the pretrained model dense. We analyze support quality through gradient energy capture and relate it to gradient estimation and convergence. Across 16 benchmarks with LLaMA and Qwen models ranging from 3B to 32B parameters, WIS-MeZO achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and reaches comparable validation losses in fewer optimization steps. Comparisons with random and magnitude-based sparse perturbations further highlight the importance of informative support selection.
authors: Ziqing Wen, Xiaohui Song, Jiahuan Wang, Ping Luo, Junlin Zeng, Dongsheng Li, Tao Sun
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of high-dimensional random perturbations in memory-efficient ZO fine-tuning.
Constructs task-conditioned sparse masks from Wanda weight–activation saliency while keeping the pretrained model dense.
Analyzes support quality through gradient-energy capture and its relationship to gradient estimation and convergence.
Across 16 benchmarks on LLaMA and Qwen models from 3B–32B parameters, it achieves higher aggregate scores than MeZO and comparable validation losses in fewer steps.
Results against random and magnitude-based sparsity emphasize the value of informative support selection.

papers.abstract: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU. We also report how throughput grows with the number of worlds, depth-camera throughput, agreement with closed-form references, and a reliability test over a thousand worlds.
authors: Pranay Gupta, Deepanshu Rohilla
bullets: Addresses the limitation of rigid-body-focused robot simulators and the integration burden of using separate material engines.
Assigns each object to a material-specific solver while coupling all solvers within each control step.
Supports rigid bodies, cloth, cables, liquids, granular materials, and soft bodies, with parallel worlds on GPU or CPU.
Provides world health grades to distinguish physics failures from policy failures and exposes agent-oriented documentation and MCP tools.
Reports tests covering policy training, scaling across worlds, depth-camera throughput, reference agreement, and reliability across 1,000 worlds.

papers.abstract: Video deraining is challenging due to rain streaks, occlusions, and atmospheric effects. Existing methods mainly follow a deterministic restoration paradigm, assuming that clean scenes can be uniquely recovered from rainy observations. However, rain degradation is spatially heterogeneous. Reliable regions require faithful reconstruction, whereas severely occluded regions contain ambiguous content that require stronger prior-driven inference. Therefore, conventional deterministic restoration often produces over-smoothed results, while global generative restoration may introduce unnecessary hallucinations. We introduce a Selective Generative Restoration paradigm for video deraining, where generative priors are adaptively activated according to restoration uncertainty. Based on this principle, we propose Selective Generative Video Deraining (SGVD), an uncertainty-aware diffusion framework that enables adaptive fidelity preservation and generative recovery. Specifically, SGVD exploits stochastic diversity between dual one-step diffusion predictions to estimate region-level restoration uncertainty, which determines where observation fidelity should be preserved and where generative inference should be activated. Furthermore, an anchor-guided trajectory consistency mechanism is proposed to regularize stochastic diffusion evolution across frames, reducing temporal generation drift and improving video coherence. To achieve practical efficiency, SGVD adopts one-step diffusion inference while maintaining uncertainty-aware generative capability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVD achieves superior restoration performance, perceptual quality, and temporal consistency compared with state-of-the-art video deraining methods.
authors: Yi'ang Chen, Han Li, Laibin Chang, Hui Liu, Kui Jiang, Junjun Jiang
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity and spatial heterogeneity of rain degradation, which can cause deterministic methods to oversmooth and global generative methods to hallucinate.
Uses stochastic diversity from dual one-step diffusion predictions to estimate region-level restoration uncertainty.
Preserves observation fidelity in reliable areas and activates generative recovery in severely occluded or uncertain regions.
Introduces anchor-guided trajectory consistency to reduce temporal generation drift across video frames.
One-step diffusion inference provides practical efficiency, with experiments reporting improved restoration, perceptual quality, and temporal consistency over existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overall architecture of the proposed SGVD for video deraining. The rainy video is first encoded into the latent space by a frozen VAE encoder. The Uncertainty-Guided Selective Generation (USG) module estimates a spatial uncertainty map from the discrepancy between dual-noise clean latent predictions, and adaptively combines the generative latent with the fidelity-preserving LQ latent. The resulting conditional latent is injected into the frozen DiT backbone through a lightweight trainable adapter. Meanwhile, AnchorGuided Trajectory Consistency (ATC) regularizes each frame's distance to a shared five-frame anchor across trajectory states, promoting temporal coherence without evaluating this training loss at inference.
Fig. 7: Restoration examples in challenging scenes. From left to right: rain streak map, uncertainty overlay, and reconstruction error.

Fig. 5: Visualization of diffusion posterior uncertainty in SGVD. The uncertainty map is estimated from the discrepancy between two stochastic one-step diffusion predictions. Severely degraded regions exhibit stronger uncertainty responses, while reliable observations remain relatively low-uncertainty, indicating that the estimated uncertainty effectively reflects spatial variations in restoration ambiguity.
Fig. 3: Visual comparisons on synthetic video deraining datasets, including NTURain [6] and RainSynLight25 [18].
Fig. 4: Visual comparisons on real-world rainy videos from the NTURain-Real dataset [6].

Fig. 1: Motivation of Selective Generative Restoration. Deterministic restoration tends to produce over-smoothed details in severely degraded regions, while global generative restoration may introduce content hallucination in reliable regions. In contrast, the proposed paradigm performs region-adaptive restoration by preserving fidelity in low-uncertainty regions and selectively activating generative recovery in high-uncertainty regions.

papers.abstract: AI-generated image detectors face significant challenges when deployed in real-world environments, particularly when test samples are produced by unseen generators that deviate from the source training distribution. Existing detectors often rely on a single type of evidence, such as semantic representations or low-level generation traces, making them vulnerable when the corresponding cue becomes unreliable. Moreover, adapting detectors to newly emerging generators usually requires target labels or retraining, which is costly and impractical. To address these challenges, we propose Dual-Evidence Disagreement-Constrained Adaptation (DEDCA), a test-time adaptation framework for generalized AI-generated image detection. DEDCA constructs a dual-evidence detector by combining CLIP-based semantic evidence with trace evidence extracted from shuffled entropy and residual statistics, and introduces a reliability-aware gate to perform sample-specific adaptive fusion. Our key idea is to exploit the disagreement between the two evidence streams as an unlabeled adaptation signal, enabling the detector to adjust to target-domain shifts without relying on target labels or blindly trusting a single prediction stream. Experiments show that DEDCA achieves superior performance on the GenImage benchmark by outperforming state-of-the-art AI-generated image detectors and test-time adaptation methods with 92.0\% average accuracy.
authors: Hao Tan, Qimin Zhang, Lihuang Fang, Kebing Jin, Jinghui Qin
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts caused by unseen image generators in real-world deployment.
Combines CLIP-based semantic features with generation-trace evidence from shuffled entropy and residual statistics.
Uses a reliability-aware gate for sample-specific fusion of the two evidence streams.
Exploits disagreement between evidence streams as an unlabeled adaptation signal, avoiding target labels or retraining.
Reports 92.0% average accuracy on the GenImage benchmark and outperforms prior detectors and test-time adaptation methods.

papers.abstract: This paper presents an overview of the integrated technologies developed for the Open Platform League at RoboCup@Home 2026 in Incheon. A vision system integrated with learning-based, training-free models enables robust object recognition for both known and unknown objects. We introduce a RoomPlan-based method that semi-automatically registers furniture geometry and labels to generate semantic maps. Additionally, a large language model-based planner interprets the instructions recognized by Whisper and generates primitive skill sequences for execution. A reservoir-computing framework serves as a lightweight temporal-processing model for action recognition. Its field-programmable gate array-based implementation enables low-power, real-time operation. This is key to removing operational time constraints for service robots. Open-source releases, including task environments, dataset tools, and navigation frameworks, enhance reproducibility, reuse, and continuous progress within the RoboCup@Home community.

papers.abstract: We study robot navigation in indoor environments from fixed exocentric cameras (infrastructure-mounted, external to the robot). We show that standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which succeeds with onboard cameras, fails to learn this navigation end-to-end in our setup. This failure results from the perspective mismatch between exocentric observations and egocentric action and goal formulations, which is too complex to resolve from the reward signal alone. To address this, we propose Viewpoint-Invariant Navigation from Exocentric Cameras (VINE). VINE uses an obstacle map estimation network, trained with supervised learning, that takes exocentric images, camera pose, robot pose, and room dimensions as input and produces a viewpoint-invariant obstacle map. This map can be used either by a PPO policy or by a planner such as A*. VINE's map estimation performs better than perspective mapping approaches, handles cameras placed across a wide range of positions and orientations without view-specific tuning, requires only approximate camera pose estimates (noise with a standard deviation of 30cm per axis in x, y, and z and about 20{\deg} of rotation error on average), is robust to intrinsic variation, and extends to two-camera setups with partial coverage. Despite operating from cameras randomized in position during evaluation, VINE surpasses the navigation success rate of PPO with an onboard camera in simulated environments.
authors: Raul Steinmetz, Jair Augusto Bottega, Ayanori Yorozu, Akihisa Ohya
bullets: Standard PPO fails end-to-end because exocentric observations mismatch egocentric actions and goals.
VINE estimates obstacle maps from images, camera and robot poses, and room dimensions using supervised learning.
The maps support either PPO policies or classical planners such as A*.
It works across varied camera positions and orientations, tolerates approximate poses and intrinsic variation, and supports partially covering two-camera setups.
In simulation, VINE outperforms PPO using an onboard camera despite randomized camera placement at evaluation.

papers.abstract: Natural Language Inference models can be sensitive to localized lexical changes. We introduce Shared Multiscale Input-Reference Conditioning (SMIC), which constructs a single input-dependent multiscale reference and reuses it across Transformer layers. Each layer applies its own multiscale transformation to the shared reference and injects the resulting conditioning feature before the attention update. We instantiate SMIC in a token--context Transformer (TCT) and conduct from-scratch comparisons against decoder-based and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) baselines across all three ANLI rounds. TCT-SMIC attains the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy on all three ANLI rounds. The ablations further support the contribution of SMIC. We evaluate a real-valued Llama-style plug-in and extend deletion/insertion diagnostics to pretrained ModernBERT encoder and Llama decoder models with and without SMIC. Across the evaluated perturbation protocols, TCT-SMIC exhibits comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes. We further establish a finite-sample bound on average subset-mass redistribution in terms of the mean Jensen--Shannon divergence between the restricted and renormalized attention distributions.
authors: Xin Zhang, Victor S. Sheng
bullets: Addresses sensitivity of Natural Language Inference models to localized lexical perturbations.
Builds one input-dependent multiscale reference, transforms it per layer, and injects the result before attention updates.
Implemented in a token–context Transformer (TCT) and compared with decoder-based and MLP baselines on all three ANLI rounds.
TCT-SMIC achieved the highest observed ten-seed mean accuracy across all ANLI rounds; ablations support SMIC’s contribution.
Perturbation diagnostics found comparatively low pooled-attention redistribution and smaller signed accuracy changes; a finite-sample redistribution bound is also derived.

papers.abstract: Distinguishing different heat sources in low-resolution infrared (IR) images is inherently difficult, as multiple thermal emitters often collapse into ambiguous and overlapping responses. Existing super-resolution methods hallucinate structures from such ambiguous 2D evidence, leading to thermal drift, boundary merging, and unreliable restoration under infrared degradations. We propose FlowIR, a depth-driven rectified flow framework that resolves thermal ambiguity by injecting 3D geometric cues into the generation process. Pseudo-3D depth lifting and depth-guided 3D convolutions disentangle overlapping foreground objects, while cluster-wise inter-attention suppresses cross-source feature contamination. A Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss further enforces geometric alignment during refinement. Built upon a lightweight rectified flow backbone, FlowIR restores IR images in only a few steps, producing sharply separated, degradation-robust, and geometrically faithful high-resolution results.
authors: Xingyue Zhu, Qinyun Mei, Zhexi Min, Yang Zou, Xingyuan Li, Zhiying Jiang, Jinyuan Liu
bullets: Addresses thermal ambiguity in low-resolution IR images, where overlapping emitters cause boundary merging and unreliable restoration.
Injects pseudo-3D depth cues through depth-guided 3D convolutions to disentangle overlapping foreground objects.
Uses cluster-wise inter-attention to reduce feature contamination between distinct thermal sources.
Applies a Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss to preserve geometric alignment during refinement.
Its lightweight rectified-flow backbone enables restoration in only a few steps and improves robustness to IR degradations.

(c) Grayscale fluctuations show that FlowIR better preserves pixel fidelity in overlapping heat sources regions. papers.title: FlowIR: Depth-driven Rectified Flow for Resolving Thermal Ambiguity in Infrared Super-Resolution
papers.tldr: FlowIR uses depth-guided rectified flow to separate overlapping heat sources and produce sharper, geometrically faithful infrared super-resolution images.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by repeatedly applying a shared block, offering a parameter-efficient approach to language modeling. However, most existing works directly reuse each loop's output as the next's input, which can lead to hidden-state scale growth and perturbation amplification as recurrence deepens. We propose Rectified Looped Transformer (RLT), which redesigns feedback between loops using an interpolation schedule inspired by flow-based modeling. At each loop, RLT forms the next input by linearly interpolating between the current state and its prediction. Such interpolation distributes state changes across loops, encouraging a smoother trajectory from the initial input to the final output. Theoretical analysis proves that, under appropriate assumptions, RLT keeps state magnitudes uniformly bounded across loops and reduces the worst-case perturbation amplification. We evaluate RLT on language modeling corpora and downstream benchmarks. At matched training and inference depths, RLT consistently achieves lower perplexity than a standard looped Transformer, while exhibiting greater robustness to input perturbations and variance in inference depth. Consistent with the theoretical results, latent trajectory analysis shows that RLT maintains more stable hidden-state norms across loops, which also facilitates extrapolation-based decoding strategies. Notably, RLT achieves these gains without requiring additional trainable parameters or extra recurrent block evaluations, thus providing a simple yet more stable feedback mechanism for looped Transformers.
authors: Musheng Li, Jiawei Zhang, Ziyuan Liu, Yuantao Gu
bullets: Looped Transformers reuse a shared block to increase effective depth, but repeated direct feedback can amplify hidden-state scales and perturbations.
RLT interpolates between the current state and its prediction at each loop, producing smoother state transitions.
Theory shows bounded state magnitudes and reduced worst-case perturbation amplification under suitable assumptions.
Experiments report lower perplexity than standard looped Transformers at matched depths, plus greater robustness to input perturbations and inference-depth variation.
Stable hidden-state trajectories support extrapolation-based decoding; the approach adds no trainable parameters or recurrent block evaluations.

papers.abstract: Dynamic reconstruction from casual video must preserve valid subject motion while suppressing transient occluders, shadows, and volumetric effects. Existing methods either suppress valid motion through static-scene assumptions or model all observations jointly, producing ghosting and unstable geometry. We introduce ReCan-GS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates coherent scene content from inconsistent observations. It derives a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score from the learned deformation field, using it as an empirical proxy for reconstruction ambiguity. The score guides separation into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or post-hoc pruning of sensitive Core Gaussians. The same criterion supports removal of spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, and evolving smoke or fog without masks, pretrained segmenters, or medium-specific supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and synthetic smoke/fog scenes demonstrate its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes.
authors: Joel Julin, Liuyue Xie, Ananya Bal, Mose Sakashita, Koichiro Niinuma, Laszlo A. Jeni
bullets: Addresses ghosting and unstable geometry caused by jointly modeling valid motion and inconsistent observations.
Uses a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score as a proxy for reconstruction ambiguity.
Separates coherent dynamic content into Core Gaussians and inconsistent observations into per-view Distractor Gaussians, or prunes sensitive Core Gaussians post hoc.
Handles spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, smoke, and fog across synthetic and real evaluated scenes.
Scope is limited to the distractor regimes and experiments described in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2. An overview of our ReCan-GS pipeline. The scene is modeled with two components: dynamic Core Gaussians (G) and per-view Distractor Gaussians (Gdist). An MLP deforms the core Gaussians over time (t). A Jacobian-based uncertainty signal, derived from the deformation field, guides the optimization to penalize unstable motion in the core layer, effectively forcing transient effects into the distractor layer.

Figure 3. Qualitative results on dynamic scenes with distractors. Columns 2–3 are dynamic reconstruction methods that jointly model all motion, often producing ghosting from transient occluders. Columns 4–5 are standard distractor-removal methods that assume a static scene and therefore struggle with valid dynamic content. ReCan-GS explicitly decomposes inconsistent observations into a distractor layer and recovers a clean, stable core reconstruction.

Figure 4. Smoke removal results. ReCan-GS separates slow-moving volumetric distractors from the core scene by detecting deformationspace instability, enabling clean smoke-free reconstructions where appearance-based methods leave residual haze.

Figure 7. Hierarchical Sensitivity. Post-hoc pruning removes the top 0%, 5%, 7%, and 15% most uncertain Core Gaussians, ranked by accumulated deformation sensitivity. Without pruning, transient hands and moving cast shadows remain. Removing the top 5% primarily suppresses the hands, while pruning the top 7% and 15% additionally suppresses moving cast shadows.

Table 2. Quantitative results on dynamic scenes with distractors, grouped into static distractor-removal and dynamic reconstruction methods. On Jeep, no annotator rated any ReCanGS frame ≥ 3. Per-annotator scores are on the project website.
Table 1. Feature comparison. Our method uniquely supports distractor removal in fully dynamic scenes without pretraining.

papers.abstract: Low-level clouds are one of the largest sources of uncertainty in climate predictions, partly because we lack detailed three-dimensional (3D) measurements of their internal structure. Here, we present HybridCT, a cloud tomographic reconstruction scheme accelerated by machine learning (ML) that recovers 3D cloud extinction directly from passive multi-angle observations. An ML emulator maps radiances from multiple viewing angles to cloud optical thickness (COT), producing path-integrated projections, and a Simultaneous Algebraic Reconstruction Technique (SART) explicitly inverts these projections to retrieve 3D extinction. Training observations are generated from synthetic 3D cloud fields using radiative transfer simulations for nine viewing angles between $\pm$70$^{\circ}$. HybridCT reconstructs extinction with RMSE 13.3 km$^{-1}$ in 3.5 s, compared to 22.7 km$^{-1}$ in approx. 30 min for the state-of-the-art physics-based tomography framework AT3D, a speedup exceeding 500$\times$. HybridCT thus provides a scalable route toward large-scale observations of 3D cloud structure relevant to radiative-budget interpretation and evaluation of high-resolution cloud simulations.
authors: Linda Forster, Nicholas J. LaHaye, Marcin J. Kurowski, Anna Jungbluth, Bernhard Mayer, Anthony B. Davis
bullets: Addresses uncertainty in climate predictions caused by limited measurements of low-level cloud internal structure.
An ML emulator converts radiances from nine viewing angles into cloud optical-thickness projections, which SART inverts into 3D extinction.
Trained using radiative-transfer simulations of synthetic 3D cloud fields.
Reaches 13.3 km⁻¹ RMSE in 3.5 seconds, versus 22.7 km⁻¹ in about 30 minutes for AT3D—over 500× faster.
Scope: the approach is demonstrated with synthetic training observations and aims to support scalable cloud-structure observations.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of HybridCT. (1) Multi-angle passive radiances are first mapped to cloud optical thickness projections using a U-Net. (2) The resulting projections are then inverted with an explicit SART tomography solver to reconstruct the three-dimensional cloud extinction field.

Figure 4: Reconstruction of entire cloud scene showing true vs. reconstructed extinction with correlation coefficient R and slope of the median prediction in each bin (solid gray curve) with 25th–75th percentile range (shaded) for HybridCT with (a) predicted, (b) true COT, and (c) AT3D.

papers.abstract: Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model. Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions, along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.
authors: Jinze Tao, Yuxiao Han, Kangkang Dong, Yancong Wei, Xiaojun Zhu, Bokui Chen, Houde Liu
bullets: Motivation: Calling an LLM planner at every episode adds cost and delay.
Method: Convert planner-driven motions, sub-instructions, detours, and resulting poses into VLA training data under the original task instruction.
Training: Mask losses for goal-averse steps, label states within 1 m of the goal as stops, and update the VLA with low-rank adaptation.
Result: The VLA learns to stop at goals and reach goals the base model misses, across all 3,189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen episodes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of H2E. (a) On training scenes, a frontier LLM planner with a place graph and its own tools calls the base VLA. We keep the sessions that reach the goal. (b) H2E turns one kept session into labels. ① Every step is labelled with the next 8 poses under the original instruction, whether the VLA or a planner tool moved. ② Steps that move away from the goal are drawn dashed. They leave the loss but stay in the history. ③ Visited states within 1 m of the goal are labelled as stops. (c) The VLA keeps its vision encoder and LLM frozen. It trains LoRA adapters and the waypoint head with the masked L1 loss and runs alone at test time.

Figure 5. Examples of better stopping. Each map shows the paths of the base VLA and H2E from the same start on a top-down render of the scene. The dashed ring marks the 3 m goal region. The images below each map show what each VLA sees when it stops and its final distance to the goal. The base VLA passes the goal and stops outside the region, while H2E stops inside it.

papers.title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation

papers.abstract: Shared history in human dialogue is not merely a repository of facts, but the foundation of evolving relationships and mutual understanding. However, mainstream conversational memory systems rely on passive semantic similarity over external fact stores, frequently retrieving topically similar records while missing relationally pivotal experiences. Inspired by cognitive psychology's Self-Memory System (SMS), we propose MindMem, a mental-state-driven memory framework that asynchronously consolidates shared experiences into source-linked mental states of the character, the user, and their relationship. At each turn, a specialized mental-state reasoner (Mind) contextualizes these persistent states to anticipate latent user needs, form proactive intentions, and recover supporting episodic evidence that surface-level matching overlooks. To evaluate history-sensitive adaptation beyond factual recall, we introduce MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark grounded in month-long real-user interactions across dyadic and group scenes. By pairing Direct Question Answering (DQA) with Situated Memory Realization (SMR), it tests whether agents bridge the gap between knowing past facts and naturally using shared history, world rules, and relational trajectories. On MemReal-Bench, MindMem reaches 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, exceeding the strongest memory baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively, and outperforming oracle target-memory injection on SMR. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/jiazhicheng7-ctrl/MindMem.
authors: Zhicheng Jia, Shuchen Wu, Zhuoshi Tong, Haisen Liao, Sicheng Zhou
bullets: Targets the limits of similarity-based memory, which often retrieves topical facts but misses relationship-critical experiences.
Asynchronously consolidates interactions into source-linked mental states for the character, user, and their relationship.
Uses a mental-state reasoner to anticipate user needs, form proactive intentions, and retrieve relevant episodic evidence.
Introduces MemReal-Bench, a longitudinal benchmark evaluating factual recall and situated use of shared history in dyadic and group conversations.
Achieves 59.03% SMR and 82.58% DQA, outperforming the strongest baseline by 24.19 and 9.19 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.
authors: BWM Team
bullets: Addresses the limited controllability and reusability of end-to-end robot video generation.
Converts robot assets, task descriptions, images, motion data, or demonstrations into executable scene programs.

Supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, appearance variation, and reusable modeling rules.
Across 15 tasks and five robot types, it outperformed the compared baseline on most quality, consistency, smoothness, and physical-adherence measures, but had lower dynamic degree.

papers.abstract: Expert-parallel Mixture-of-Experts decoding is latency bound: each layer serializes a token exchange, a grouped GEMM over routed experts, and a combine, while only a few tokens per rank are in flight. Prior GC-MoE fused these phases into one persistent, Green-Context-partitioned CUDA Graph on Hopper (SM90) and datacenter Blackwell (SM100). This paper rebuilds the operator for SM120 (compute capability 12.0, e.g. RTX PRO 5000) over PCIe. SM120 exposes block-scaled tensor cores only through warp-level mma.sync.aligned.kind::mxf8f6f4: no tensor memory, no two-CTA MMA, no cluster multicast. We rebuild the kernel around a swap-AB warp-level block-scaled MMA with FP4 weights in the register A operand and FP8 activations in B, plus SM120-specific mechanisms: scale-byte selection through MMA immediates, a compact-weights path, an adaptive token-tile geometry, an expert-granular streaming dispatch with a batched bulk-pull engine and a 64-bit deduplicating pull cache, full-width BF16 returns drained by resident relay copiers over a position-major arena, and shared experts folded into the compute role. On 8xRTX PRO 5000 over PCIe the operator is 1.522x and 1.387x faster than the FlashInfer CuTe DSL W4A8 MegaMoE and the Cake MegaMoE across 18 decode points (18/18 wins each), and 1.388x faster than Cake with shared experts fused; all 94 numerical cases and 752 per-rank checks pass, at cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.
authors: Yong Li, Haoyu Wang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
bullets: Targets latency from serialized token exchange, expert GEMM, and combine phases in low-concurrency decoding.
Uses warp-level FP8×FP4 block-scaled MMA with register-resident FP4 weights and SM120-specific scale selection.
Overlaps expert-granular dispatch, computation, and returns using adaptive tiling, batched pulls, a deduplicating cache, and resident relay copiers.
On 8× RTX PRO 5000 GPUs, it wins all 18 tested decode points against two baselines and also outperforms shared-expert-fused Cake.
All reported numerical cases and per-rank checks pass, with cross-operator cosine similarity of at least 0.9999997.
