papers.abstract: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present \ourmethod{}, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. \ourmethod{} extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate \ourmethod{} on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.
authors: Sahit Chintalapudi, Xiaoyan Wang, Aryan Zoroufi, Aditya Agarwal, Nancy Kanwisher, Tom\'as Lozano-P\'erez, Leslie Pack Kaelbling

Uses persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map.
Evaluated on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks with heavy occlusion and partial visibility.
Outperforms baselines lacking active perception or persistent memory.

papers.abstract: Motion imitation enables humanoid robots to acquire whole-body skills such as walking and dancing. However, fine-tuning an entire policy for a new skill can affect existing behaviors, while training a separate policy for each skill increases training and maintenance costs. We present PERA, a method for learning new skills by reusing existing motion capabilities. PERA freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an additional task expert and its routing score using task rewards or teacher-action supervision. In Unitree G1 simulation, each added task module contains approximately 1.03% of the parameters of the base actor. Built on our pretrained policy, PERA successfully completes all ten new tasks. Disabling the expert restores the original computation path of the base policy, which still fully executes all 126 original motions. Enabling the expert also improves the execution of some dance motions not used to train that expert, indicating that its benefits extend beyond its training motions. Experiments with HoloMotion further demonstrate the applicability of PERA to different base policies.
authors: Shangchao Hu, Yadan Sun, Xibo Yu, Wei Huang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between catastrophic interference from fine-tuning and the cost of maintaining separate policies.
Freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an added task expert with its routing score using rewards or teacher actions.

papers.abstract: Particle-based volumetric flow measurement techniques have proven their efficacy in quantitatively assessing the dynamic characteristics of unsteady flows within the realm of fluid mechanics. Despite recent advances in multi-frame particle tracking, an open challenge in this area is maintaining trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences, where inter-frame displacements are large. In this work, we develop DiffTR-Flow3D, a diffusion-based model that estimates flow motion from spatiotemporal three-dimensional particle recordings via a stochastic diffusion process. DiffTR-Flow3D conditions the diffusion process with both global and local particle dynamics and enhances flow estimation by leveraging historical particle trajectories. Extensive experiments, including numerical simulations and real-world measurements, demonstrate that DiffTR-Flow3D achieves state-of-the-art displacement estimation accuracy compared with learning-based flow estimators, and, when integrated into particle tracking pipelines, substantially improves their long-term tracking performance, while exhibiting robustness and generalization across diverse flow patterns. This work is expected to provide fluid researchers with an effective tool for the consistent and precise analysis of particle trajectories in temporally under-sampled 3D sequences with large inter-frame displacements.
authors: Jianan Wei, Qiang Zhang, Hao Sun, Yi Yang, Wenguan Wang
bullets: Addresses trajectory loss in temporally under-sampled 3D particle recordings.
Conditions a stochastic diffusion process on global and local particle dynamics.
Leverages historical trajectories to improve displacement and flow estimation.
Experiments on simulations and real measurements show strong displacement accuracy and improved long-term tracking.
Demonstrates robustness and generalization across diverse flow patterns.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of DiffTR-Flow3D. a, Overview of the noise perturbation and reverse denoising processes in DiffTR-Flow3D. The forward diffusion process, q(d1:N |d0), progressively perturbs the flow motion structure d0 ∼ q(d) over N steps to approximate a Gaussian noise distribution. Conversely, the reverse process, pθ(dn−1|dn), iteratively eliminates Gaussian noise from the corrupted flow dN , thereby guiding particles toward their target destinations. b, The flow motion estimation pipeline in DiffTR-Flow3D. This module employs a two-stage flow motion estimator designed to handle diverse displacement distributions in particle dynamics. It first performs a coarse flow estimation between two point sets, followed by a refinement stage that eliminates position offsets using soft alignment operations to capture both local and global correlations. c, Illustration of the feature extraction pipeline in DiffTR-Flow3D. d, The workflow of motion estimation/refinement employed by DiffTR-Flow3D. e, Schematic of the multi-frame trajectory prediction scheme in DiffTR-Flow3D. This scheme first establishes particle trajectories via flow estimation over three consecutive timesteps. Subsequently, particle positions for the next timestep are predicted using temporal fitting functions derived from prior trajectory information. Finally, the proposed flow estimator calculates the residual motion, which is used to correct the trajectories.

papers.abstract: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at https://gooseloc.github.io.
authors: Fabian Deuser, Peter Mortimer, Robin-Nico Kampa, Anna B\"o{\ss}end\"orfer, Mirko M\"ahlisch, Martin Werner, Norbert Oswald
bullets: Targets ground-to-aerial localization when GNSS is unreliable, especially in forests, fields, and rural tracks.
Provides 9,356 georeferenced scenes near Munich across four seasons, pairing aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB and 3D LiDAR.
Includes paved/unpaved terrain labels and seasonal variation to study terrain structure and appearance gaps.
Fine-tuned state-of-the-art baselines degrade substantially off-road, while the proposed RGB–LiDAR baseline improves localization performance.
Data and baselines are publicly released for future research.

papers.title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain

papers.abstract: Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address both challenges with \textit{split-and-scale}, a method that effectively expands latent capacity at inference while keeping training cost tractable. Our key observation is that by representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates, a single pretrained tokenizer can be applied at inference to arbitrarily small sub-regions of a scene, allocating the same latent capacity to a smaller spatial extent and thus capturing far higher detail. We validate this insight by conducting extensive ablations to study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality, demonstrating our inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. We further demonstrate that split-and-scale supports high-quality generative modeling, training an autoregressive 3D generator that performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines.
authors: Dorian Chan, Muhammed Kocabas, Xiaoming Zhao, Oncel Tuzel, Jen-Hao Rick Chang
bullets: Addresses limited latent capacity for modeling fine details in complex 3D objects.
Uses continuous coordinate-based scene representations to tokenize arbitrarily small sub-regions at inference.
Explores trade-offs among compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality through ablations.
Achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits.
Also supports high-quality generative modeling with an autoregressive 3D generator.

papers.abstract: Turbulence modeling relies on human choices of closure form, physical inputs, and tunable parameters. Training closures a posteriori is efficient only with gradients through long chaotic rollouts, which few solvers provide. Most a posteriori approaches therefore resort to gradient-free optimization, and nearly all fix the closure form in advance, learning only its parameters. In this work, we introduce a gradient-aware agentic framework that poses closure discovery as a bilevel problem: a multi-agent large language model (LLM) system searches over closure forms, while a GPU-native differentiable computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solver supplies gradients, making differentiable a posteriori learning an action of the autonomous AI agent. For each proposal, the agents construct a differentiable training program by embedding the analytical, neural, or hybrid closure in the solver, implementing a differentiable objective, and validating the gradient path. They then decide whether to evaluate the closure, compute its parameter sensitivities, or train it a posteriori, select the optimization settings, and revise subsequent proposals using the simulation outcomes and returned gradients. Truncated-horizon gradients make this training usable under chaotic dynamics for closures with tens of thousands of parameters. Demonstrations include dissipation-law and subgrid-scale closure discovery in two-dimensional turbulence and wall-model discovery for large-eddy simulation of three-dimensional channel flow. With gradient-based training, the agent recovers reference coefficients that forward evaluation alone does not reach within the same budget, and autonomously discovers and trains analytical and neural closures that improve agreement with the targeted reference statistics. These results demonstrate the feasibility of end-to-end autonomous turbulence model development in time-resolved flows.
authors: Yi Liu, Xiantao Fan, Mingqi Xu, Jian-Xun Wang
bullets: Recasts turbulence-closure discovery as a bilevel search over closure forms and parameters.
Agents generate differentiable CFD training programs, validate gradient paths, choose evaluations or training actions, and revise proposals from simulation feedback.
Truncated-horizon gradients enable a posteriori training under chaotic dynamics, including closures with tens of thousands of parameters.
Demonstrations cover 2D turbulence dissipation and subgrid-scale closures, plus 3D channel-flow wall models.
The approach recovers reference coefficients and discovers analytical and neural closures with improved agreement to target statistics compared with forward evaluation alone under the same budget.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of the gradient-aware agentic framework, illustrated on a subgrid-scale model discovery task.

papers.abstract: Transformers typically cache an independent key-value (KV) representation for each token at every layer. Recent work reveals that a token's KV representations across neighboring layers are correlated and contain shared information. We hypothesize that this correlation implies incremental inter-layer changes, which can be effectively captured by low-dimensional deltas. Motivated by this, we propose KVPath, a new KV representation paradigm that connects KV representations across the network depth into a path. The path establishes a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, while subsequent layers generate low-dimensional delta KVs to update the preceding KV, thereby constructing their own KV states. By caching the base KV once alongside these compact delta KVs, KVPath preserves distinct layer-specific representations without storing full KV states at every layer. We develop two variants of KVPath: KVPath-Residual, which updates vector values via residual addition, and KVPath-Rolling, which progressively updates feature dimensions in a rolling manner. Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68\% for Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) and 55\% for Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), while maintaining or even improving model performance.
authors: Xuan Luo, Zhiyuan Wang, Hanzhong Cao, Xifeng Yan
bullets: Motivation: KV representations for the same token across neighboring layers share information and exhibit correlated changes.
Method: Store a full-dimensional base KV at the first layer, then generate compact delta KVs for subsequent layers.
Variants: KVPath-Residual uses residual additions; KVPath-Rolling updates feature dimensions progressively.
Result: Under matched parameter counts, KVPath reduces KV-cache storage by up to 68% for GQA and 55% for MLA while maintaining or improving performance.

papers.title: KVPath: Connecting Key-Value Representations Across Transformer Layers

papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on next-token targets from a teacher, a frozen copy of the student that additionally receives privileged information, such as a worked solution, hidden from the student. Whether student gains reflect that information remains unclear. Taking the worked solution as privileged information, we audit four stages across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics: Source, whether the teacher can use the solution; Encoding, whether the resulting token targets are useful; Transmission, whether the student learns from the targets; and Expression, whether the student applies the learned behavior without the solution. With the solution, the teacher solves hard problems and recovers from student errors, yet the teacher does not reliably recognize errors, and its token targets do not favor correct trajectories. Repeated training makes successes within the student's reach more frequent rather than unlocking new ones, and corrections the student learns to predict are not reliably expressed in free generation. To isolate the solution's contribution, we vary its availability separately from teacher and student thinking modes. The largest gains occur when a teacher in thinking mode supervises a student trained and evaluated without an explicit thinking trace, and problem-only teachers often match or exceed privileged-solution teachers: the gain tracks the teacher's thinking mode rather than the solution, a pattern we call reasoning arbitrage. Accuracy gains alone therefore do not establish transfer of reasoning from privileged solutions: bottlenecks lie after Source, across Encoding, Transmission, and Expression. Future evaluations must measure what the solution adds to otherwise identical training.
authors: Haoyi Qiu, Akshat Agarwal
bullets: The audit examines four stages: whether teachers use solutions, encode them into useful targets, transmit them to students, and whether students express the behavior independently.

Across three Qwen3 scales on mathematics, teachers can solve hard problems and recover from errors with solutions but do not reliably identify errors or favor correct trajectories in their token targets.
Repeated training mainly increases successes already within the student’s reach rather than unlocking new capabilities.
Learned corrections are not reliably used during free generation, revealing failures in transmission and expression.
The largest gains come from thinking-mode teachers supervising students without explicit thinking traces; problem-only teachers often match or exceed solution-privileged teachers.

papers.selection_reason: Audits self-distillation of reasoning LLMs and proposes a training-diagnostic view transferable to LLM reasoning research.
papers.title: Privileged Information Does Not Guarantee Privileged Guidance: Auditing On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Models

papers.abstract: Potholes impose billions of dollars in annual vehicle damage, yet detectors report only where potholes are, not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from a single RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded vision-language model (VLM) assessments tend to be over-conservative. We present a five-stage modular framework for the offline assessment of already-detected potholes that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning: perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. We evaluate it on 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes against independent references. Severity agreement with a prediction-free three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.139$, 95% CI [0.00, 0.28]; $n = 101$) and far below the annotators' agreement with one another ($\kappa = 0.605$); against physically measured depth on an independent RGB-D dataset, it is also weak ($\kappa = 0.098$), although the predicted classes preserve the order of measured depths. The severity classes are therefore perceived visual categories, not depth measurements. Geometric grounding does change the warnings: relative to an image-only baseline, it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109% (Stuart-Maxwell $p < 10^{-15}$), and in a blind study, three raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. A six-arm prompt ablation attributes the hybrid prompt's rule adherence to the per-pothole measurements rather than to the rubric or worked examples. At USD 0.105 per scene, it suits large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; its maneuver suggestions are advisory research outputs, not validated vehicle guidance.
authors: Abdalmalek Aburaddaha, Zaid A. El Shair, Ali Al-Bustami, Samir A. Rawashdeh
bullets: Pothole detectors locate defects but generally do not assess severity or recommend actions; single-image severity estimation is inherently ambiguous.

The five-stage offline pipeline applies perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro classification with composite risk scoring, and warning generation.

Geometric grounding substantially changes warnings: it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier, increases critical-tier assignments by 109%, and is preferred 3.5:1 over image-only warnings in a blind study.

Severity agreement is weak with both human references and measured depth, although predictions preserve the ordering of measured depths; the categories should be interpreted as visual perceptions, not depth estimates.
The system costs USD 0.105 per scene and is intended for large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; maneuver suggestions are advisory and not validated vehicle guidance.

papers.title: Pothole Risk Assessment with Geometrically Grounded Vision Language Models

papers.abstract: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding. Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.
authors: Sadegh Rahmaniboldaji, Filip Rybansky, Quoc Vuong, Frank Guerin, Andrew Gilbert
bullets: Introduces sub-action detection, requiring explicit recognition of hand roles and manipulated objects during high-level actions.
Adds FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention module that emphasizes action-relevant visual cues without changing the underlying vision or language encoders.
Uses MetaLoss, a masked object-weighted loss that prioritizes visually grounded terms.
Introduces BiScopeCap-100K, a densely captioned egocentric video dataset with hand-role, object, action, and spatial metadata.
Improves action, hand-role, and object recognition across evaluated Video-LLM backbones, with the strongest aggregate performance among tested configurations on BiScopeCap.

papers.title: Sub-actions in Action: Text-Guided Hand-Role Alignment for Sub-Action Recognition
papers.tldr: BiScopeNet improves egocentric video models’ ability to identify left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within ongoing actions using text-guided feature alignment and targeted supervision.

papers.abstract: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is a widely used regularization-based technique for continual learning, protecting performance on old tasks with a quadratic penalty whose empirical Fisher is usually justified through probabilistic curvature. We instead introduce Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC): new training must preserve chosen functionals of learned behavior. EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).
authors: Davide Wiest
bullets: EWC can underweight well-fitted samples because its empirical Fisher scales importance by loss-gradient magnitude.
CLOC shows that EWC is the first-order form of preserving each old sample’s loss.
IEWC removes this unintended weighting by penalizing output changes along each sample’s loss-level set.
The approach also prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix.

Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC matches or improves EWC and outperforms EWC-DR; on ImageNet-R, uniform IEWC gains 2.00 percentage points over matched EWC (95% CI: 0.93–3.07).

papers.abstract: Autonomous optical networks require monitoring systems capable of adapting to evolving disturbances without repeated retraining or service interruption. We propose a continual event recognition framework for state-of-polarization (SOP)-based optical monitoring based on prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot prototype registration. The framework supports recognition of known disturbances, detection and integration of novel events, and investigates whether overlapping disturbances can be inferred through compositional reasoning from existing prototypes. Experimental validation on a 2600-km ROADM-based optical testbed demonstrates 99.82% closed-set recognition accuracy, successful adaptation to novel disturbances without encoder retraining, and reveals that overlapping optical disturbances exhibit varying degrees of latent compositionality. While some overlaps can be recognized in a zero-shot manner through prototype composition, others require explicit few-shot registration. These results establish continual event recognition as a promising paradigm for future autonomous optical network monitoring systems.
authors: Khouloud Abdelli
bullets: Targets autonomous monitoring that adapts to evolving disturbances without service interruption or repeated retraining.
Combines prototype representations, open-set recognition, and few-shot prototype registration.
Achieves 99.82% closed-set recognition accuracy on a 2600-km ROADM-based optical testbed.
Novel disturbances can be integrated without encoder retraining; overlap recognition varies by event.
Some overlapping disturbances are recognized zero-shot via prototype composition, while others require few-shot registration.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning (IL) typically relies on large-scale offline demonstrations collected from multiple human or algorithmic demonstrators. However, most existing approaches assume these demonstrators are homogeneous or near-optimal experts, a convenient but unrealistic assumption in real-world applications. In practice, demonstrations are often collected from heterogeneous demonstrators with unknown and varying levels of expertise, resulting in highly mixed-quality data. In this work, we study a challenging yet practical setting of imitation learning from such heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators. We propose Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning (LEOS-IL), a principled framework that jointly learns (i) a state-action optimality scoring model and (ii) latent expertise levels for each demonstrator from unlabeled suboptimal offline demonstrations. The learned scoring model is then integrated into an online policy optimization procedure, where the agent is trained to maximize estimated optimality scores while its online rollouts are iteratively leveraged to refine the scoring model, thereby mitigating distributional shift during online adaptation. We further provide theoretical guarantees for optimality score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines across highly heterogeneous and low-quality demonstration regimes.
authors: Cheng Pan, Nan Lu, Kai Arulkumaran, Josie Hughes
bullets: Addresses imitation learning when offline demonstrations come from heterogeneous, imperfect, and unknown-quality demonstrators.
Jointly learns state-action optimality scores and latent expertise levels from unlabeled suboptimal demonstrations.
Uses the learned scores for online policy optimization and incorporates new rollouts to reduce distributional shift.
Provides theoretical guarantees for score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery.
Experiments on continuous-control benchmarks show consistent gains over existing baselines in highly heterogeneous, low-quality regimes.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.
authors: Leonardo Vanni, Stefano Gasperini, Federico Tombari, Chiara Plizzari
bullets: Addresses failures of existing 4DGS methods on splitting, merging, opening, and closing interactions.
Introduces TopoEgo, a benchmark covering fission, fusion, opening, and closing in egocentric video.
Assigns independent rigid motion to interacting parts and activates or deactivates Gaussians as surfaces change.
Outperforms existing 4DGS approaches across topological changes, particularly in post-event frames.
Code and data are planned for public release.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware 4D Gaussian Splatting method for egocentric videos, addressing topological changes (splitting, merging) which is crucial for embodied AI perception and 3D scene reconstruction.
papers.title: Topology-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting for Egocentric Videos
papers.tldr: Topo-4DGS reconstructs egocentric videos with topological changes by modeling moving parts and dynamically changing visible surfaces.

papers.abstract: Language moved from many task-specific models to one unified model: a single generative model with a single generative training task that handles all of them within the same backbone, and keeps improving with data, parameters and compute. We believe the bitter lesson applies just as much to computer vision, 3D and spatial understanding, in the end to visual intelligence: the effort should go into general architectures that solve all these tasks in a unified way, and into scaling them, rather than into task-specific designs. We test this on monocular geometry, a task that has belonged to specialised architectures for years. Iris-Z is a general image generator that produces appearance and geometry together. A single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands the image and its depth at the same time, and one set of weights generates images with their depth, estimates depth from photographs and paints images onto a given depth. At enough scale it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists on established depth benchmarks while keeping the generative abilities of the backbone it started from without specialized layers. We release two models for the community.
authors: Alejandro Ca\~nada, Chema Garabito
bullets: Targets task-specific monocular geometry architectures with a unified, scalable alternative.
Uses one backbone to jointly denoise, reason about, and understand images and depth.
Supports image-plus-depth generation, depth estimation from photographs, and image synthesis conditioned on depth.
At sufficient scale, surpasses specialist models on established depth benchmarks while retaining generative capabilities.
Releases two models for community use.

papers.abstract: GPT-6 Astra can drive a robot arm directly through a fixed harness, and scores of such robot-use agents on RoboDojo have risen quickly since. Reported systems differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is hard to tell which choices produce the gains. We take these designs apart and test them in one framework, along the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model. A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way. Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free lunch, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone. JustRUA starts from the official L3 harness and keeps only what matters most. Even with no learned policy, self-improvement loop or task-specific tuning, this simple harness raises the score on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark substantially, from 29.7 to 50.3.
authors: Zefan Wang, Yufan Dang, Xuanwei Shi, Mingqi Gao, Cheng Yin, SikYuen Tam, Hanyu Liu, Yasheng Wang, Yaxi Lu, Songyang Zhang, Xin Cong, Yuan Yao
bullets: Provides a controlled comparison of harness design, action interface, experience reuse, and scene geometry.
Finds that retaining full episode history and terminating motions early are especially effective design choices.
Experience reuse changes behavior but does not provide universally free improvements.
Scene geometry is highly beneficial, including when depth is predicted from RGB alone.
Raises RoboDojo performance from 29.7 to 50.3 without a learned policy, self-improvement loop, or task-specific tuning.

papers.title: JustRUA: A Controlled Study of GPT-6 Robot-Use Agents

papers.abstract: Satellite constellations now image the Earth daily, capturing the lifecycle of events from deforestation to urban construction. Anticipating these events before completion enables timely intervention, yet existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become, and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Building such a model requires diverse event data, but events are like needles in a haystack, making manual annotation at global scale infeasible. We address this problem by representing change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at distinct time points. This arithmetic approach allows us to search for semantic transformations directly in the latent space, enabling (1) an automated data engine for global event discovery without manual annotation and (2) the largest global satellite event dataset to our knowledge, comprising 21,000+ locations across 64+ event types with ~2M images from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 spanning six continents, to train (3) a novel global-scale event anticipation model. Our model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion. Code: https://github.com/ShreelekhaR/predicting-the-needle
authors: Shreelekha Revankar, Mikhail Klassen, Creon Levit, Ash Hoover, Kavita Bala, Bharath Hariharan
bullets: Targets the challenge of identifying where change occurs, what it becomes, and when it finishes across diverse event types.
Represents temporal change as vector differences between vision-language model embeddings to search for semantic transformations.
Uses this approach to automate global event discovery without manual annotation.
Introduces a dataset with 21,000+ locations, 64+ event types, and approximately 2 million satellite images across six continents.
The resulting model achieves 93.5% maximum F1, 3.6× stronger predicted-event retrieval than baselines, and 3-day median completion-date error up to nine months ahead.

Figure 1: We present our latent-space world model. Trained on a large diverse set of global events, our model allows us to detect change events and predict their future states and completion dates.

papers.abstract: Applications built on large language models assign the model a role through its system prompt, intending to shape how it responds for their use case. We introduce a validation framework for extracting and injecting occupational role vectors, activation-level directions that capture how someone in a given occupational role would distinctively respond to a task or question. We validate these vectors through two complementary lenses, on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. The interpretability lens asks whether each vector is a stable, separable, domain-consistent representation of its role: extracted vectors are highly reproducible across repeated runs and sampling temperatures, remain separable even for very similar roles, and agree more with themselves across in-domain and out-of-domain questions than with other roles' signal. The control lens asks whether injecting a role vector during generation makes the model express the role, and sustain it over a conversation, as well as a role prompt does. On Qwen, injecting the vector alone makes the model express the intended role substantially more often than unsteered, but at best matches a role prompt; on both models, adding the vector to the prompt strengthens the role in single answers but did not slow the role's decline over 30 turns. Together, the two lenses show why both are needed: out of domain the role is expressed only subtly, yet the activations still encode it; and a vector that is stable and separable can still barely steer the model's behavior.
authors: Jose L. Sampedro Mazon, Ilmi Yoon, Nadim Saad
bullets: Introduces a framework to extract, validate, and inject activation-level vectors representing occupational roles.
Evaluates vectors in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using interpretability and behavioral-control tests.
Vectors are reproducible, separable—even for similar roles—and more consistent with themselves across domains than with other roles.
Vector injection increases role expression, but generally does not outperform role prompts and does not prevent role weakening over 30 conversational turns.
Shows that representational stability does not necessarily imply strong behavioral steerability, motivating both validation lenses.

Original rule (committed before any run): the vector steers if, at some strength, the share of answers detected as French is at least 50 pp above the unsteered share and the mean answer length is within 50% of the unsteered mean answer length. The original rule did not name a length unit; the script measured tokens, and French text takes more tokens than English text for the same content, which inflates the token ratio (verdict i); verdict (ii) measures length in characters. Amended rule (verdict iii; amendment dated 2026-10-04 20:28, committed after the original-definition Llama result had been seen at 14:21 and the garbled Llama output had been inspected): an answer is clean French if at least 98% of its letters are Latin script, its share of French function words is above 0.12 and above its share of English function words, and the median of three coherence judge trials is at least 75; the vector steers if the clean-French-and-coherent share is at least 50 pp above the unsteered share at some strength. The amended rule is the primary reading; all three readings are shown. Verdicts are per model and site over all strengths. Printed as two panels.

papers.selection_reason: Studies and steers occupational role vectors in large language models, fitting LLM behavior and foundation-model research.
papers.title: What Roles Do System Prompts Really Assign? Validating and Steering Occupational Role Vectors in LLMs
papers.tldr: The study validates occupational role vectors in LLM activations, finding they reliably encode roles but provide limited and unsustained control over behavior compared with prompts.

papers.abstract: More text-to-video models are available, but many remain limited to low resolutions. Training them for higher resolutions is costly, while existing training-free methods still struggle with fine detail, scene structure, and efficiency. We propose TRACE, a training-free method that synchronizes low- and high-resolution generation trajectories. During early denoising, TRACE aligns predicted scene content at corresponding noise levels. It computes high-resolution updates from low-resolution predictions and the current high-resolution state, without high-resolution model inference. The high-resolution trajectory retains fine-grained variation for generating new details. Local window attention then refines fine details in a shared high-resolution latent state. TRACE checks suspected duplicate subjects against the corresponding low-resolution layout and corrects selected regions and their solver history while preserving detail elsewhere. Experiments across all kinds of video generation backbones and resolutions show improved perceptual quality and text-video alignment over FreeSwim, a state-of-the-art training-free method, with 2.0-2.9x end-to-end speedups. Our code and models will be released at https://github.com/libozhu03/TRACE.
authors: Libo Zhu, Fan Li, Zhixin Wang, Binglu Wang, Weisheng Dong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Addresses costly high-resolution training and limitations of existing training-free resolution extension methods.
Uses low-resolution predictions and the current high-resolution latent state to guide high-resolution updates without high-resolution model inference.
Refines details with local window attention while preserving high-resolution variation for new detail generation.
Detects and corrects duplicated subjects by referencing the low-resolution scene layout and selectively updating regions and solver history.
Reports improved perceptual quality and text-video alignment over FreeSwim, with 2.0–2.9× end-to-end speedups across video-generation backbones and resolutions.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of TRACE. The low-resolution trajectory (Low) provides scene references for the high-resolution trajectory (High). (A) CSTS couples their initial noise and computes early High updates from Low’s predictions, avoiding high-resolution model inferences. (B) Window attention computes high-resolution model predictions. (C) TGSC uses semantic relevance, cross-scale mismatch and betweenstep change to select suspected duplicated subjects. It corrects those latent regions and the corresponding solver history.

Figure 6. Visual comparison of direct inference and training-free resolution-extension methods at 1920×1088 on Wan2.1. Each result pairs two adjacent frames with a detail crop, highlighting wood texture, building facades, and local structure.

Figure 4. Effect of trajectory synchronization during early denoising. Directly upsampling the low-resolution velocity (top) misaligns the clean prediction. The bottom row constructs the velocity from Low’s clean prediction and High’s current noisy state. This aligns their clean predictions while retaining High’s own noisy state. Panels (a–c, e–g) visualize latents; (d, h) show the corresponding decoded results.

Figure 5. Trajectory-guided structural correction during high-resolution refinement. The prediction (a) contains two extra people absent from the low-resolution reference. Matched crops show these duplicated subjects (b), the evidence used to locate them (c), and their removal through regional correction (d). Later denoising adds grass detail in the corrected regions (e).

papers.title: TRACE: Trajectory Synchronization for Training-Free Resolution Extension in Video Generation

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require separating adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained targets. We study this setting as removal manipulation, where progress depends on evolving contact states that are only partially observable from vision and kinematics. We introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. To make multi-finger force observations easier to fuse, we express fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, giving force components consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time. Using an Action Chunking Transformer backbone, policies fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force observations to predict closed-loop action chunks from demonstrations. Evaluation uses six core benchmark tasks for controlled fingertip-input and force-frame ablations, plus three extension scenarios for additional held-out coverage. Across these evaluations, the learned policies achieve consistent removal performance, and ablations show that wrist-frame forces, especially with fingertip pose, improve stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs and no-force baselines. Project website: https://dexremo.github.io
authors: Liman Wang, Hanyang Zhong, Sun Zhaole, Wenting Cao, Babar Jamil, Andy Tyrrell, Shan Luo, Jihong Zhu
bullets: Targets removal tasks involving adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained objects with partially observable contact states.
Provides a high-force robotic hand with modular fingertips, three-axis fingertip force sensing, and nine real-robot scenarios.
Represents fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame to align force meaning across fingers and time.
Uses an Action Chunking Transformer to fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force data for closed-loop control.
Experiments report consistent removal performance, with wrist-frame forces—especially combined with fingertip pose—improving stability and generalization over local-frame and no-force inputs.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of removal manipulation and the proposed framework. (a) DexRemo Hand removes strongly adhered 3D-printed barnacles from a curved turtle mockup, demonstrating variable and partially observable attachments. (b) Representative human removal behaviors reveal task-intrinsic interaction principles. (c) Fingertip forces are transformed from local sensor frames RSi to a shared wrist frame, then fused with vision, fingertip poses, and proprioception. An ACT-based policy generates observation-conditioned action chunks for progressive, edge-initiated debonding.

Fig. 7. Physical objects used in each manipulation task (A1–C2). Each object is photographed alongside a standard ruler to indicate real-world scale. Objects are labeled as seen or unseen according to whether they appear in policy training. Detailed dimensions and preparation parameters are summarized in Table VI and Appendix E.

Fig. 11. Blu-Tack removal (A3): force feedback enables observation-driven switching in an ACT-based policy. (a) P+W (fingertip pose + wrist-frame forces) and (b) P (fingertip pose only). Left: fingertip trajectories for right/middle/left fingers. Right: wrist-frame force components over time (color indicates finger; line style indicates Fx, Fy , and Fz). Vertical dashed lines mark the timestamps of snapshots t1–t4. With P+W, changes in force patterns during side-finger boundary interaction provide an observable cue for switching to a distinct action chunk dominated by the middle finger, which ramps up force and achieves detachment. With P only, the policy exhibits prolonged oscillatory contact and fails to satisfy the success criterion within the time limit.

papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation requires precise alignment and controlled handling of rigid, deformable, and flexible components. Yet, the benefits of pretrained visuomotor policies remain underexplored in settings where limited access to specialized hardware, components, and fixtures constrains demonstration collection and evaluation. Understanding task-specific data requirements is important for assessing their scalability across diverse processes on the factory floor. We investigate whether video pretraining can support reliable industrial manipulation with limited action data. We propose FLUX-mimic, a video-action model, motivated by the potential of video pretraining to capture motion and interaction patterns that enable sample-efficient training. FLUX-mimic is built on a backbone pretrained on large-scale web and industrial task data, and an action expert to generate robot trajectories. We train our policy by joint video-action training. Across four automotive manufacturing benchmark tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, FLUX-mimic outperforms all considered baselines on the dexterous robot platform and matches pi_{0.5}'s average success rate on the gripper-based robot platform. On a deformable part kitting task, FLUX-mimic reaches 77.5% success with as little as two hours of task-specific action-labeled demonstrations.

bullets: Targets precise manipulation of rigid, deformable, and flexible components when hardware and demonstration access are limited.
Combines a backbone pretrained on web and industrial task video with an action expert that generates robot trajectories.
Uses joint video-action training to learn motion and interaction patterns for sample-efficient policy training.
Evaluated on four automotive manufacturing tasks across two bimanual robot platforms.

Outperforms considered baselines on a dexterous platform, matches pi_{0.5}'s average success on a gripper-based platform, and achieves 77.5% success on deformable-part kitting with two hours of demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Learning from paired modalities is commonly equated with aligning them: two encoders are trained until the embeddings of a pair coincide in a shared space. We study whether cross-modal retrieval and classification can instead be obtained while the two encoders' own embedding spaces remain directly unaligned. DuoJEPA trains one encoder per modality with the self-supervised LeJEPA objective and appends to each encoder a single transformer layer that translates its embedding into the other encoder's space, supervised by a contrastive objective computed entirely within that target space. No loss term compares the two own spaces directly, although the encoders are optimised jointly through the translation objective. In our experiments, the translator's residual connections determine where the cross-modal pressure is absorbed: with a residual translator the two encoders become directly aligned, whereas with a skipless (residual-free) translator a paired-cosine test detects no alignment in the final models, and at most a weak one in the ablations, at comparable cross-modal performance. The learned class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation of the source space. We evaluate DuoJEPA on two modality pairs that differ in nearly every respect. On chest radiographs and reports from CheXpert Plus, it attains a zero-shot AUC of 86.6 and a cross-modal retrieval score of 78.5, compared with 60.0 and 64.2 for our reimplementation of LeVLJEPA with the same encoders and data. On Sentinel-2 optical and Sentinel-1 radar imagery, the frozen encoders fall within the range of published Sentinel foundation models under our reproduction of the Copernicus-Bench linear-probe protocol, the translator retrieves the paired image of the other sensor among 4,000 candidates in 77-79% of cases, and a patch-level extension transfers the within-image similarity structure of the scene.
authors: Mahmut S. Gokmen, Mitchell A. Klusty, Evan W. Damron, Caroline N. Leach, Samuel E. Armstrong, V. K. Cody Bumgardner
bullets: Uses LeJEPA self-supervised encoders with a single transformer translator per modality, trained by contrastive loss in the target space.
Residual translators induce direct encoder alignment, while skipless translators preserve largely unaligned native spaces with comparable cross-modal performance.
The class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation.
On CheXpert Plus, it achieves 86.6 zero-shot AUC and 78.5 retrieval, versus 60.0 and 64.2 for the compared LeVLJEPA reimplementation.
On Sentinel-1/2 imagery, it achieves 77–79% retrieval among 4,000 candidates and transfers within-image similarity structure at patch level.

papers.abstract: Deep networks that estimate ground reaction forces and centers of pressure from motion-capture markers are validated within one laboratory, in a seldom-stated coordinate frame, and sometimes with trial-level splits that put the same person in the training and the test set. We measured what each practice costs, and whether such models transfer between laboratories. Three sequence models (convolutional, convolutional-recurrent, and convolutional-transformer) were evaluated on two independent datasets, locomotion (6 subjects) and occupational patient handling (10 subjects), under one pipeline, one tuning procedure, three seeds, and four protocols: trial-level split, leave-one-subject-out, pooled two-laboratory training with matched held-out subjects, and cross-laboratory transfer. At a fixed configuration, trial-level splits overstated the subject-held-out coefficient of determination by +0.040 to +0.194; on occupational data the overstatement exceeded every difference between architectures. With subjects held out, the three models reached values between 0.583 and 0.804; the leader differed between datasets, and gaps lay within subject-to-subject variability. Pooling the laboratories changed neither dataset on matched subjects. Transfer between laboratories was below chance in both directions, including the vertical force, which no in-plane rotation can affect. Leaving force targets in the plate frame while inputs were heading-aligned cost 0.57 of locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance, enough to make that force look hardest; a Newton's-law correlation detected the mismatch before training. Split protocol and target frame changed reported accuracy more than architecture did. Learned force estimators should be validated with subjects held out, checked for frame consistency before training, and tested across laboratories before deployment claims are made.
authors: Hernan David Santos, Yinong Chen, Yu Ding, Xudong Zhang, Jian Tao
bullets: Trial-level splits overstated subject-held-out performance by 0.040–0.194.
With subjects held out, model performance ranged from 0.583 to 0.804, and no architecture consistently led across datasets.
Pooling laboratories did not improve matched-subject performance, while cross-laboratory transfer was below chance in both directions.
A mismatched target frame reduced locomotion anteroposterior-force explained variance by 0.57; a Newton’s-law check detected the mismatch before training.
The findings support subject-held-out validation, frame-consistency checks, and cross-laboratory testing before deployment claims.

papers.abstract: Engineering design studies produce a few tens to a few hundred simulations of one problem, each on its own mesh, and their surrogates are retrained for every study. Tabular foundation models instead infer a new task from its examples in one forward pass, after pretraining on synthetic tasks. We demonstrate the feasibility of in-context learning for physical field prediction on unstructured meshes. A single model, PhysICL, pretrained solely on procedural tasks, predicts fields, with quantiles, directly on each query mesh from labeled simulations, without updating its weights. The same checkpoint accepts variable numbers of context examples, scalar inputs and input fields, and any number of output fields, while mesh size and connectivity can vary within a task. Its procedural prior draws generic laws and boundary-element physical models on morphed 2D and 3D template meshes, evaluated only at the points the model samples, fast enough that tasks generated on the fly by CPU workers keep the GPUs busy throughout pretraining. On five PLAID datasets never seen in pretraining, its field error decreases as the context grows and, from $K = 32$, is below that of the nearest context simulation on every dataset and context draw. It is on par with per-dataset reduced-order models on two of them, behind them where the fields are low-rank. On AhmedML surfaces with a median of 1.1 million nodes, twenty times the largest pretraining mesh, its fixed spatial budgets keep the peak GPU memory at $K = 64$ at 4.27 GiB, against 4.07 GiB on the 6,000-node meshes of 2D\_MSHE. Finally, on 2D\_MSHE, far from the prior, fine-tuning on procedural tasks that reproduce its geometry and loads, without any of its outputs, at a tenth of the pretraining cost, divides the stress error by 2.7.
authors: Fabien Casenave
bullets: Targets engineering studies with limited simulations, where conventional surrogates must be retrained for each problem.
Uses procedural priors over generic laws and boundary-element models on morphed 2D/3D meshes, with quantile field predictions from context examples.
Handles variable context sizes, scalar inputs, input/output fields, mesh sizes, and mesh connectivity in a single checkpoint.

On five unseen PLAID datasets, error improves with more context and beats the nearest context simulation from K=32; performance matches reduced-order models on two datasets but trails them for low-rank fields.
Maintains low peak memory on million-node AhmedML meshes; geometry/load-specific procedural fine-tuning reduces 2D_M​​SHE stress error by 2.7× without using target outputs.

papers.abstract: This work addresses the problem of finding a concealed object in an environment by unifying formalisms for partially observable environments with multi-modal priors drawn from a mix of ontologies, semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs. We propose a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP (CA-MOMDP), a Bayes-adaptive setting where uncertainty is over both object locations and which nodes can conceal them, held as a hypothesis with a bounded ontology prior and resolved only by interaction. We define a hierarchical transition system (HTS) to abstract the environment into room and object nodes that can be planned over via our CA-MOMDP. We further propose a COMBS-score: a multi-modal fusion of a human informed semantic network, LLM, and VLM, to initialize the belief over object locations, which grounds our abstractions and reduces reliance on a single model. Belief is maintained via Bayes' rule, which never lets a look rule out a closed container. We prove a present target is found in a bounded number of searches under exact perception and that its location is never ruled out given missed detection under noisy perception. We ablate each component to demonstrate their significance. Across five simulator configurations, from a gridworld to Matterport3D with a real detector, COMBS finds 92-100% of in-distribution and 92-100% of out-of-distribution targets, matches or beats the baselines in processing speed, significantly outperforms a per-step LLM policy at lower cost on the larger scenes, recovers more out-of-distribution placements than a TidyBot ranking, and matches an LLM-only prior at a fraction of its per-decision latency. COMBS is the only standalone method that can declare a target absent at a stated error level, and the per-step LLM policy offered a termination action abandons 12-22% of targets that were present, against 1.6-3.2% for COMBS on the same episodes.
authors: Taylor Bergeron, Kevin Leahy
bullets: Models uncertainty over both object locations and which environmental nodes may conceal them using a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP.
Plans over room and object nodes through a hierarchical transition system.
Fuses human-informed semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs to initialize location beliefs, then updates them with Bayes’ rule.
Across five simulated settings, finds 92–100% of in- and out-of-distribution targets and generally matches or outperforms comparison methods.
Can declare a target absent at a stated error level; it abandons fewer present targets than a per-step LLM policy.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes COMBS, a multi-modal Bayesian search method that unifies ontologies, LLMs, and VLMs to locate concealed objects in partially observable environments.
papers.title: COMBS: Concealed Object Multi-modal Bayesian Search
papers.tldr: COMBS combines Bayesian search, hierarchical environment abstractions, and multimodal priors to efficiently find concealed objects while avoiding false conclusions that objects are absent.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in robotic manipulation, yet most rely primarily on 2D visual observations and language instructions, leaving scene geometry and obstacle relationships to be inferred implicitly. This limitation is particularly problematic in cluttered environments, where small spatial errors can lead to unintended contacts or collisions. We propose MOSAIC, a modular spatial- and obstacle-aware framework that can be integrated with pretrained VLA policies to improve object-level scene understanding and action generation. Our method augments the VLA backbone with an auxiliary semantic grounding task that predicts role-specific masks for the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles. We further combine the target and destination masks with depth estimated from 3D scene reconstruction to construct role-specific geometric tokens that are injected directly into the action expert. In addition, we propose obstacle-aware attention supervision that emphasizes obstacles near the robot body during task execution. The resulting attention features are subsequently injected into later action-expert layers to further guide action generation. Together, these components provide explicit semantic, geometric, and obstacle-aware cues while preserving the underlying pretrained VLA architecture. We evaluate our framework on pretrained VLA model using the RoboPRO benchmark, including visual perturbation tests, and further validate it on real-world manipulation tasks. MOSAIC improves the success rate by 5.1% in cluttered scenes, and by 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains of up to 25.0% in the most challenging environment. We will release our code and dataset upon acceptance at the following Github page: https://mmahdavian.github.io/MOSAIC/
authors: Richard Shi, Mohammad Mahdavian, Mehrdad Momeni Zadeh, Mohammed Elmahgiubi, Amir Rasouli
bullets: Addresses the weakness of primarily 2D VLA models in reasoning about geometry and obstacle relationships.
Uses auxiliary semantic grounding to predict masks for the target, destination, and surrounding obstacles.
Builds role-specific geometric tokens from masks and reconstructed depth, injecting them into the action expert.
Adds obstacle-aware attention supervision focused on obstacles near the robot during execution.
Improves success by 5.1% in cluttered scenes and 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains up to 25.0% in the hardest environment; also validates real-world manipulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: MOSAIC Model Structure. (a) A vision–language backbone encodes observations, instructions, and robot state, with role tokens supporting semantic mask prediction. (b) The action expert attends to the shared prefix and produces learned attention maps. (c) Object-level depth is extracted using the VGGT-Ω combined with the predicted masks. The depth tokens are generated and injected into the action expert final layers. (d) Contact-relevant expert targets supervise attention through forward KL divergence during training. (e) Predicted attention maps are averaged, detached, and injected through residual cross-attention into late action layers. (f) Flow matching generates actions for robot execution.
Fig. 1: MOSAIC overview. A pretrained VLA is augmented with role-specific masks, object-level depth tokens, and obstacle-focused attention guidance.

The closest point of each object’s bounding box is projected onto pixel space. Disks are centered at these points to highlight potential contact zones. (c) Proximity weight map β. Higher weight for objects closer to the robot body, less weight for farther objects, zero weight for very distant objects. (d) Obstacle contact mask. Using the proximity weight map β to filter out irrelevant objects. (e) Groundtruth attention heatmap H. Obstacle contact mask convolved with a Gaussian kernel with standard deviation σ to represent the spatial distribution of visual attention. (f) Patch-wise distributed groundtruth attention map. papers.selection_reason: Proposes MOSAIC, a framework that augments VLA policies with geometric tokens and obstacle-aware attention to improve manipulation success in cluttered scenes.
papers.title: MOSAIC: Modular Obstacle and Spatial-Aware Framework for Manipulation In Cluttered Scenes
papers.tldr: MOSAIC enhances pretrained vision-language-action policies with explicit object, destination, depth, and obstacle cues to improve manipulation in cluttered and visually perturbed scenes.

papers.abstract: Full-size humanoid robots are being considered for hazardous industrial work such as disassembling electric-vehicle batteries. We describe the safety mechanisms of an open-source autonomy stack for the Unitree H1-2 humanoid and what deploying them taught us. All joint commands pass through a safety layer that runs separately from the control software. It enforces joint position, velocity, and torque limits, and it stops the robot when a state estimate becomes stale or when the hard-wired emergency stop (e-stop) is pressed or disconnected. We pushed the standing robot until it lost balance. With a model-predictive lower-body controller it never recovered, and the operator had to press the e-stop in every trial. Pressing it removes balance control, and the robot falls. The safety layer's own limits trigger the same stop, and limits chosen for manipulation were exceeded during normal walking. Near an operator or a battery pack, the fall can be more dangerous than the cause of the stop. Joint limits bound how much force a robot can apply, but not when applying it is appropriate. Drawing on research on responsibility and on child and adolescent development, we therefore make a case for granting robots force authority in stages, with a person or organization explicitly responsible for its use.
authors: Max Conway, Yutong Zhang, Allen Devaraj, William Xie, Alessandro Roncone, Nikolaus Correll
bullets: An open-source safety layer independently enforces joint position, velocity, and torque limits.
It stops the robot when state estimates become stale or the hard-wired e-stop is pressed or disconnected.
In balance-loss trials, neither the controller nor safety limits recovered the robot; stopping led to a fall.
Limits selected for manipulation could be exceeded during ordinary walking, especially near people or battery packs.
The authors propose gradually increasing robot force authority under explicit human or organizational responsibility.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: (A) Pushes are applied with a rod instrumented with an ATI Mini45 six-axis load cell. (B) Push force (black) and margin of the center of mass (CoM) to the support polygon (green; below the horizontal red line the CoM has left the polygon), mean and spread over 15 trials per controller. Left: under sampling-based MPC (MJPC), the margin decreases steadily after the push and the operator presses the e-stop (vertical red line) at 4.68±2.86 s. Right: the adversarially trained ALMI policy recovers and restores a positive margin in 14 of 15 trials without intervention. The safety layer and interfaces are identical in both conditions; only the lower-body controller differs.

Every joint command they produce passes through the safety layer, a separate process that is independent of the learned and model-based control modules. It enforces joint position, velocity, and torque limits at 90% of the vendor specification, treats a stale state estimate or a lost heartbeat as a fault, and polls a microcontroller connected to a physical e-stop. Losing contact with the microcontroller also stops the robot.

papers.selection_reason: Discusses safety mechanisms and force authority for full-size humanoids, providing deployment lessons relevant to safe robotic control.
papers.title: Runtime Safety and Emergency Stops on a Full-Size Humanoid: Deployment Lessons and a Case for Graduated Force Authority
papers.tldr: Full-size humanoid safety systems can prevent unsafe commands but may cause hazardous falls, motivating staged force authority with explicit human responsibility.

papers.abstract: Recent work suggests that pretrained image generators encode real-world understanding beyond image synthesis. Vision Banana exploits this by framing vision tasks as conditional image editing. However, its data, weights, code, and implementation details are not public. We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others. Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M-3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model's image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class-color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color-class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code, as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints. Project website: https://openvisionbanana.github.io
authors: Arpit Jadon, Valentinos Pariza, Jona Ruthardt, Ryousuke Yamada, A. Sophia Koepke, Andrei Bursuc, Yuki M. Asano
bullets: Identifies interacting design factors for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing.
Trains 4B- and 9B-parameter open-weight models on 2.1M–3.8M public-dataset training pairs.
Surpasses reported Vision Banana Cityscapes zero-shot segmentation performance and approaches state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimation.
Legend ensembling improves segmentation by up to 8.7 mIoU points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining.
Releases data-processing, training, evaluation, and checkpoint resources for reproducibility; instance segmentation remains a weaker area.

papers.selection_reason: Unified recipe for converting generative models into multi-task perception, including depth estimation, relevant to spatial understanding.
papers.title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception
papers.tldr: Open Vision Banana provides a fully open recipe for adapting image generators into unified multi-task vision systems, achieving strong segmentation and depth results with reproducible resources and test-time legend ensembling.

papers.abstract: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) language model uses only a few experts per token, so a server can keep most expert weights in CPU memory and copy an expert to the GPU when the router requests it. Recent methods train the router to keep the same experts for several tokens, and treat fewer routing switches as a proxy for fewer copies. We measure the trade-off directly, in a harness that performs and times real CPU-to-GPU copies for OLMoE-1B-7B. On an L40S GPU, every tested policy that holds an expert set fixed and decodes faster than the least-recently-used (LRU) cache increases next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats. A change that leaves every routing decision intact does better: when the cache must evict an expert, evict the one whose next use lies farthest in the future. This rule copies 2.1x fewer experts than LRU at no loss in quality and is within 3.5% of the fewest copies possible. It needs future requests; the next sixteen tokens of demand recover 96% of its reduction, whereas a rule based on counts of past requests recovers 27%.
authors: Pierre-Luc Bacon, Diego Calanzone, Jean-Maxime Larouche
bullets: MoE offloading keeps most expert weights in CPU memory and transfers requested experts to the GPU.
Reducing routing switches is not a reliable proxy for reducing real transfer cost: faster fixed-set policies increased next-token loss by at least 0.067 nats.
When eviction is necessary, evicting the expert needed farthest in the future outperforms LRU.
The approach achieves 2.1× fewer copies than LRU, with no quality loss, and comes within 3.5% of the minimum possible copies.
Future demand from the next 16 tokens recovers 96% of the reduction; past-request counts recover only 27%.

Points at ∆NLL = 0 preserve every routing decision. papers.selection_reason: Expert eviction policy for MoE offloading that reduces GPU memory transfers during inference, fitting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: Fewer Expert Transfers Without Changing Routing: Expert Eviction for MoE Offloading
papers.tldr: Expert eviction based on predicted future use can cut MoE CPU-to-GPU expert transfers by 2.1× versus LRU without changing routing or model quality.

papers.abstract: Generated touch could extend robot learning beyond recorded contacts. A tactile generator needs a latent space, and we choose one by testing whether a material classifier trained on real GelSight presses still works on encode-decode reconstructions from pretrained image models. On ObjectFolder Real, the classifier loses 6.5 to 9.7 points on reconstructions from three 16x discrete tokenizers and 0.3 points on those from the Stable Diffusion VAE (SD-VAE). The 16x tokenizers again lose far more on Touch and Go and on DIGIT object recognition (YCB-Slide). Retraining the classifier on reconstructions, with no new labels, narrows the discrete gap. SD-VAE reconstructions also keep object identity, with 76.7% object-matching accuracy against 78.9% for real touch and 67.0% for MAGVIT-v2. We therefore select SD-VAE latents and show a photo-to-touch generator trained in them. Code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Wanghao Ye, Aarosh Das, Sihan Chen, Yiting Wang, Bowei Tian, Guoheng Sun, Shwai He, Zheyu Shen, Ziyao Wang, Yexiao He, Zhaoyi Liu, Meng Liu, Yuning Zhang, Meng Feng, Ziyi Wang, Yilong Dai, Yifei Dong, Siyuan Peng, Zhenle Duan, Joshua Liu, Lang Xiong, Daeun Jung, Aditya Sarkar, Parastoo Pilevar, Xiaochuan Gong, Yancheng Zhu, Yingying Fan, Qiong Wang, Ang Li

Reconstructions from three 16× discrete tokenizers reduce material-classification performance by 6.5–9.7 points, while SD-VAE causes only a 0.3-point drop on ObjectFolder Real.
The discrete tokenizers also perform substantially worse on Touch and Go and DIGIT object-recognition tests.
Retraining classifiers on reconstructions narrows the discrete-tokenizer gap without requiring new labels.
SD-VAE preserves object identity well and is used for a demonstrated photo-to-touch generator.
