papers.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly used to automate biomedical research, creating a growing need to benchmark their capabilities on real scientific data and workflows. Their reliability in neuroimaging remains insufficiently characterized, where plausible analytical outputs can conceal errors that affect scientific conclusions. Existing studies have advanced scientific question answering and tool-based automation, but provide limited evidence on workflow reconstruction, acquisition of procedural expertise and evidence-based scientific judgment. Here we present NIBench, a neuroimaging benchmark comprising three complementary evaluations of autonomous agents. First, we benchmark execution and workflow reconstruction using 56 tasks across seven tool ecosystems, covering structural, diffusion and functional magnetic resonance imaging, positron emission tomography and multimodal analyses. Second, we examine whether agents can evolve their procedural skills through distillation of execution trajectories, evaluating the resulting skills on previously encountered tasks, unseen tasks and other models. Third, we assess scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer's disease studies, requiring agents to analyse raw cohort data and provide reproducible evidence. We evaluate 19 language models within a shared agent framework, with selected models undergoing skill distillation and claim evaluation. Leading agents execute supplied analysis protocols nearly perfectly, whereas withholding procedural guidance widens performance differences. Distilled skills improve performance on acquisition tasks and transfer between models, but benefits on unseen tasks are inconsistent. Agents reproduce their reported results yet sometimes reach conclusions inconsistent with expert-derived answers, and access to data does not always improve judgment.
authors: Lujia Zhong, Yihao Xia, Jianwei Zhang, Shuo Huang, Xinyu Nie, Mingyang Xia, Zhiwei Deng, Jiaxin Yue, Xinkai Wang, Junhan Zhao, Yonggang Shi
bullets: Covers 56 execution and workflow-reconstruction tasks across seven tool ecosystems and multiple neuroimaging modalities.
Tests skill evolution through distillation of execution trajectories on familiar, unseen, and cross-model tasks.
Assesses scientific judgment using 36 claims from published Alzheimer’s disease studies and raw cohort data.
Agents perform nearly perfectly with supplied protocols, but performance gaps widen without procedural guidance.
Distilled skills improve acquisition tasks and transfer across models, while unseen-task gains are inconsistent; reproducible outputs can still conflict with expert conclusions.

papers.abstract: Aerial imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) plays a vital role in applications such as surveillance, disaster response, and large-scale environmental monitoring. Automatic generation of textual descriptions for such imagery is essential for reducing manual inspection overhead and enabling better downstream decision-making. However, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite their impressive captioning capabilities, are prone to hallucination, producing descriptions that are inconsistent with the visual input. This problem is significantly amplified in aerial imagery due to its unique challenges such as extreme viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and ambiguous visual entities. Existing hallucination detection approaches either rely on computationally expensive large external models such as GPT-4, which perform poorly on aerial domains, or treat the problem as a rigid binary classification task, ignoring the inherent uncertainty in ambiguous cases. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight, reference-free framework for hallucination detection and correction in free-form aerial image captioning. Our method leverages state-of-the-art MLLMs, specifically InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL, to detect hallucinated content in generated captions with minimal computational overhead. Detected hallucinations are corrected through a dedicated refinement module that improves the factual consistency of the original captions. Extensive experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset (LID) demonstrate that our framework significantly reduces hallucination rates while remaining practical for real-time deployment in resource-constrained environments. Code is available at: https://github.com/Debolena7/Hal_Detect.
authors: Debolena Basak, Somsubhra De, Maunendra Sankar Desarkar
bullets: Targets aerial-captioning hallucinations worsened by viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and visual ambiguity.
Uses InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL to detect hallucinated content without external references or expensive models.
Applies a dedicated refinement module to correct detected hallucinations in free-form captions.
Experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset show reduced hallucination rates and support real-time use in resource-constrained settings.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require carefully controlled contact forces for successful execution, yet large-scale, force-aware datasets remain scarce. Handheld interfaces can help by transmitting interaction forces directly through the operator's arm, but most existing designs are tailored to simple linear grippers and do not match the nonlinear mechanics of widely used robotic grippers. We present RUMI, a handheld universal manipulation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 with exchangeable fingertip sensors that preserves the target gripper geometry while enabling natural input before contact and force measurement after contact. By integrating the tracking system into a virtual reality headset, our method provides real-time augmented reality feedback about the kinematic feasibility of motion on the target robot platform. We further introduce a haptic feedback mechanism that supports force-aware teleoperation for simulated and real robots. A user study shows fewer episodes containing joint-limit violations with live robot visualization and pose initialization (3/50) than without augmented reality (16/50). We additionally train imitation policies from demonstrations, collected using two different fingertip modalities enabled by the gripper-matched hardware, and assess the haptic interface's capability for collecting force-aware teleoperation datasets in simulation.
authors: Kevin Avdiu, Seongjin Bien, Yannik Blei, Philine Meister, Johannes Hechtl, Philipp Schmitt, Kai Wurm, Georg von Wichert, Wolfram Burgard
bullets: Addresses scarce force-aware manipulation data and the mismatch between existing interfaces and nonlinear robotic grippers.
Preserves target-gripper geometry while supporting natural pre-contact input and post-contact force measurement through exchangeable fingertip sensors.
Provides real-time AR feedback on motion feasibility and haptic feedback for force-aware teleoperation in simulation and on real robots.
A user study reports fewer episodes with joint-limit violations using live robot visualization and pose initialization than without AR (3/50 vs. 16/50).
Demonstrates imitation-policy training with two fingertip modalities and evaluates force-aware dataset collection in simulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of RUMI, a gripper-matched handheld interface for collecting force-aware manipulation demonstrations for robot learning. (a) The hardware combines Robotiq 2F-85-matched kinematics with a D405 wrist camera, a rotary encoder, a Quest controller, and fingertip force/torque (F/T) sensing. (b) The device rests on the back of the hand, while the thumb and index finger operate the rear scissor pads. A human-side CoinFT sensor measures force at the index-side input. (c) The nonlinear transmission couples finger motion, while a selectively engaged blocker constrains further closure. (d) The same interface supports three contact domains: virtual contact in VR, remote robot contact during teleoperation, and direct contact with a local object in MR. In VR and teleoperation, contact engages the blocker, providing resistance at the input pads; subsequent squeeze is measured by the human-side CoinFT sensor. In MR, the local object supplies the physical reaction force, and fingertip F/T sensors measure the interaction while the blocker and human-side force-sensing path remain inactive. papers.abstract: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.
authors: Yuzhe Chen, Muxi Diao, Lele Yang, Wenbin Xu, Xuyang Liu, Qile Su, Changyi Liu, Jiankang Chen, Kaiyu Jiang, Haoyu Zhang, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Bingyi Li, Xu Wang, Xuanyu Zheng, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Jiale Cao
bullets: Benchmarks 242 tasks across scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos.
Scores both hidden scene facts via rule-based checks and their visibility in rendered proxy videos via VLM judgment.
Analysis covers 11 frontier coding agents and finds multimodal understanding—especially space and camera motion—strongly differentiates performance.
Agents handle basic staging and camera work but struggle with challenging requests and rarely correct errors after inspecting renders.
Results motivate stronger spatial/camera reasoning, explicit checks, and item-by-item render verification.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation of mobile robots in crowded environments, while preserving pedestrians' psychological comfort, requires distinguishing pedestrians from other obstacles, predicting their future motion, and accounting for uncertainty in the predicted trajectories of both pedestrians and the robot. This work extends a previous MPC framework by integrating obstacle and pedestrian detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online prediction-error estimation directly within the collision-avoidance mechanism. To reduce collision-avoidance complexity in crowded scenarios, nearby obstacles are aggregated, thereby reducing the number of collision-avoidance constraints. Simulation studies evaluate the prediction-error margins and the computational benefits of semantics-aware aggregation. In a paired 300-seed closed-loop comparison with a moving generic obstacle, Markov residual tightening reduces the fraction of runs with physical contact from $10.0\%$ to $1.33\%$, at a mean travel-time cost of $0.68$ s. In a separate crowd-navigation semantic ablation, the offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap occupies $2.11\%$ of observed time with pedestrian-aware handling versus $22.84\%$ with generic-obstacle handling.
authors: Alessandro Febbraro, Federico Rollo, Marcello Farina, Luca Bascetta, Navvab Kashiri
bullets: Targets safe, psychologically comfortable robot navigation among pedestrians and obstacles under prediction uncertainty.
Integrates pedestrian/obstacle detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online residual-based error margins into collision avoidance.
Aggregates nearby obstacles to reduce the number of collision-avoidance constraints and computational complexity.
In a 300-seed comparison, Markov residual tightening reduced physical-contact runs from 10.0% to 1.33%, with a mean travel-time cost of 0.68 s.
Pedestrian-aware handling reduced offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap from 22.84% to 2.11% versus generic-obstacle handling.

papers.abstract: System One models promise fast, general-purpose decision-making without lengthy token generation. However, understanding their capability spectrum and decision reliability requires more than aggregate performance on current benchmarks. Existing evaluations often provide limited insight into the breadth of model capabilities and the reliability of their decisions. We introduce SO-Arena, a benchmark characterizing the capability spectrum and decision reliability of System One models across 11 domains and five capability families. For the capability spectrum, SO-Arena offers evidence-grounded evaluation through reliable sources and manual verification of reference labels against model-visible inputs; fine-grained capability assessment through domain-specific difficulty criteria; and realistic interactive evaluation, where models iteratively execute actions in sandboxes. Reasoning-intensive tasks further enable system one-two comparison. Beyond accuracy, SO-Arena assesses decision reliability through two complementary measures: decision stability under controlled option-set changes and missing-answer recognition when no valid option is available. Evaluations across 21 models reveal that the benefits of scaling and additional reasoning vary substantially across domains. More importantly, strong overall performance does not necessarily imply reliable decision-making: the best-performing System One model ranks only seventh in reliability. Together, these findings highlight the need to characterize capability spectrum and decision reliability as complementary dimensions, providing a systematic view of the strengths and limitations of System One models.
authors: Lichen Li, Ziping Dong, Sicheng Feng, Qi Li, Xinchao Wang
bullets: Benchmarks 21 models across 11 domains and five capability families.
Uses evidence-grounded labels, domain-specific difficulty criteria, and interactive sandbox tasks.
Measures reliability through decision stability under option changes and recognition of unavailable valid answers.
Finds that scaling and added reasoning help unevenly across domains.
The top-performing model ranks only seventh in reliability, separating capability from decision dependability.

papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction holds great promise for accelerating acquisitions, yet its clinical translation remains bottlenecked by poor generalizability across unseen scanners, populations, anatomies, and protocols. Gathering sufficiently diverse clinical datasets to overcome this bottleneck is hindered by high acquisition costs, privacy restrictions, and institutional biases. Here, we introduce Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), a framework that systematically co-designs physics-simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms around scalability--leveraging compute scaling to overcome historical data bottlenecks and achieve robust zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Across 14 public and in-house datasets--spanning seven international centers, five vendors, field strengths of 0.3-7 T, over ten anatomical regions, more than ten acquisition protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular tasks, and a 150-scan blinded radiologist study--SIM demonstrates robust zero-shot generalizability, recovering fine anatomical details while suppressing aliasing artifacts where conventional deep-learning methods fail. Attention-map analyses confirm that SIM learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors. SIM establishes a scalable, privacy-preserving, and democratized infrastructure for universal MRI reconstruction, providing a blueprint for generalizable AI across inverse problems in medical imaging.
authors: Hong Shang, Zijian Zhan, Sen Jia, Xiang Fan, Jintao Meng, Yang Zhou, Xiang Zhou, Tianyu He, Xinran Chen, Qiaoling Zeng, Keyan Yu, Jianhua Yao, Dong Liang
bullets: Addresses poor generalization of deep-learning MRI reconstruction caused by limited, biased, and costly clinical data.
Co-designs simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms to replace historical data scaling with compute scaling.
Evaluated across 14 public and in-house datasets spanning multiple centers, vendors, field strengths, anatomies, protocols, and downstream tasks.
Reports recovery of fine anatomical detail and suppression of aliasing artifacts where conventional methods fail, including a blinded radiologist study.
Attention analyses suggest the model learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of SIM, a compute-scalable framework for zero-shot MRI reconstruction. a, The physics-simulated data engine transforms arbitrary images into paired training data comprising undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements (X) and ground-truth targets (Y ). This pipeline strictly obeys multi-coil MRI forward physics to align simulated and real measurement characteristics, effectively closing the simulation-to-real gap. Simultaneously, it expands image and acquisition diversity to overcome historical data bottlenecks, enabling models to learn fundamental inverse mappings. b, SIM adopts the multi-channel Vision Transformer (mcViT)—a high-capacity architecture with minimal MRI-specific inductive bias—to absorb diverse simulated data and learn robust reconstruction priors at scale, replacing hand-crafted architectures designed for data-scarce regimes. c, Pairing large-scale simulated data with high-capacity architecture reveals power-law scaling relationships with dataset size, model size, and patch count, mirroring scaling behaviors in natural language and vision. Crucially, these scaling gains transfer directly to real clinical data, confirming that the simulation engine effectively bridges the simulation-to-real gap. d, Comprehensive zero-shot evaluation across public and in-house datasets—spanning diverse scanner hardware, populations, anatomies, protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular imaging tasks, and a clinical reader study—demonstrates that SIM achieves vastly superior generalizability over traditional real-data learning paradigms.

Fig. 3 Scaling laws in reconstruction. a, In-distribution scaling for simulated data. Reconstruction performance improves smoothly as dataset and model size increase in tandem. Scaling model size yields sustained performance gains when not bottlenecked by data diversity, analogous to scaling laws observed in LLMs[48]. b, In-distribution scaling for real fastMRI. Scaling model size fails due to pronounced overfitting (Extended Data Fig. A1b) from inadequate data diversity; despite comparable dataset size to simulated data, real fastMRI exhibits high inter-dataset similarity. c, Transfer scaling comparing training data. Scaling behavior learned on simulated data transfers effectively to diverse real-world datasets, successfully bridging the sim-to-real gap. Real fastMRI alone shows no scaling benefit and transfers poorly to OOD test sets; combining fastMRI with simulated data restores OOD scaling, demonstrating that high-diversity simulated data are essential to unlock scaling laws in MRI reconstruction. d, Transfer scaling comparing model architectures. When trained on 1.1 million simulated samples, conventional architectures designed for small-data regimes with hard-coded domain priors (such as E2EVarNet) are outperformed on OOD test sets by mcViT—a generic Vision Transformer with minimal inductive bias—underscoring the need to co-design data and models for scaling regimes. Experiments in a–c utilize mcViT. Across a–d, retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor. ID, in-distribution.

Fig. 4 Zero-shot reconstruction. a, Quantitative comparison. Both SIM and SIM-Zero (trained exclusively on simulated data) outperform all competing baselines across 8 out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks, with SIM exceeding the top baseline by 1.06–3.95 dB in PSNR and 0.008–0.045 in SSIM, and SIM-Zero performing only marginally below SIM. Error bars indicate mean ± s.d. Full comparisons against 9 state-of-the-art methods are in Extended Data Fig. A3. ID, in-distribution. b, Qualitative comparison. Representative reconstructions, error maps, and reference images. SIM recovers fine anatomical detail matching ground truth without perceptible aliasing artifacts (see Extended Data Fig. A4 for additional visual comparisons). XGY, Xingaoyi. c, Cross-protocol transfer. Models were trained on fastMRI Brain data partitioned by protocol (T1, contrast-enhanced T1 [CE], T2, FLAIR). E2EVarNet trained on real data exhibits a diagonal performance, degrading on unobserved protocols due to overfitting. Conversely, SIM displays uniform performance across protocols due to domain-agnostic simulated data. Across a–c, retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor.

Fig. 2 Data simulation pipeline, feature representation, and ablation study. a, Data simulation pipeline. The workflow transforms arbitrary natural images into paired training data comprising undersampled multi-coil k-space measurements and ground-truth targets. The physical mapping between measurement and target strictly obeys multi-coil MRI forward physics. FT, Fourier transform; iFT, inverse Fourier transform; rss, root-sum-of-squares. b, Data visualization in a shared representation space. While real datasets show a clustered distribution with limited diversity, simulated data display diverse local contrast patterns relevant to clinical imaging at the patch level. Each dot represents a 14 × 14 image patch in the DINOv2 feature space[55] after dimension reduction using principal component analysis and linear discriminant analysis to two primary discriminant axes, color-coded by dataset source. LDA, linear discriminant analysis. c, Ablation study demonstrating the effectiveness of key simulated data design features in closing the simulation-to-real gap, as well as the impact of model architectural choices and learning objectives engineered to leverage simulated training data. Error bars represent mean ± s.d. Retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor.

Fig. 8 Visualization of SIM attention maps. a, Attention maps of individual heads across layers, demonstrating that SIM intrinsically captures generic image structures and spatial relationships tied to undersampling physics via large-scale domain-agnostic training, thereby achieving physically explainable and broadly generalizable reconstruction. b, Attention maps aggregated across all layers and heads, showing that SIM dynamically adapts its attention to aliasing source regions as changes in acceleration alter the spatial aliasing distance. Two example query patches are shown under effective acceleration factors of 3.2× and 4.2×. For a and b, arrows and boxes on input images indicate query patches. AF, acceleration factor.

Fig. 5 Zero-shot quantitative MRI. a,b, Representative single-echo reconstructions, derived T ∗ 2 maps, and corresponding error maps evaluated on the public AHEAD dataset (MP2RAGEME sequence, Philips 7 T) (a) and an in-house cohort (MULTIPLEX sequence, UIH 3 T) (b). SIM’s zero-shot capability enables reliable downstream parametric mapping. Skull stripping is applied, and display windowing and leveling are adjusted per echo image and matched between reconstructions and reference images. Retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 3.2× effective acceleration factor. c, Quantitative comparison of T ∗ 2 mapping across all slices evaluated by mean absolute error (MAE) at effective acceleration factors of 3.2×, 4.2×, and 5.1×. SIM consistently outperforms baselines across sequences and acceleration factors. Error bars represent mean ± s.d. AF, acceleration factor.

Fig. 7 Zero-shot clinical applications. a, Representative reconstructions of SIM and E2EVarNet at effective acceleration factors of 3.2×, 4.2×, and 5.1× for an in-house Alzheimer’s disease cohort with three contrasts: T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and T2-FLAIR. Red arrows indicate residual aliasing artifacts. b,c, Quantitative evaluation in terms of PSNR (b) and SSIM (c). Error bars represent mean ± s.d. d–f, Blinded reader study in which 1,050 MRI volumes were evaluated independently by two board-certified radiologists. d, Radiologist ratings of overall image quality evaluated on a 5-point Likert scale (5 = excellent, 1 = unacceptable); each dot represents an individual rating. e, Radiologist ratings of clinical usability evaluated on a 3-point categorical scale (diagnostic, screening-only, non-diagnostic). f, Inter-reader agreement for image quality and clinical usability ratings. Statistical significance was assessed using two-sided paired Student’s t-tests for quantitative metrics (b,c) and two-sided clustered Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for radiologist ratings (d,e); significance levels are denoted as ****P < 0.0001. Inter-reader agreement was quantified using quadratically weighted Cohen’s κ for image quality ratings and linearly weighted Cohen’s κ for clinical usability. For d and e, ratings from two radiologists are pooled for visualization. AF, acceleration factor; VN, E2EVarNet; x3, x4, and x5, effective acceleration factors of 3.2×, 4.2×, and 5.1×, respectively.

Fig. 6 Zero-shot molecular MRI. a, Representative SIM reconstructions of dynamic CEST images (shown at offset frequencies of 1.1 ppm and 3.6 ppm) and derived dynamic maps of PCr and tCr∗ (a weighted sum of PCr and Cr[71]), evaluated on an in-house dataset monitoring calf-muscle recovery using an in-scanner exercise protocol[71] (UIH 5 T). b, Dynamic recovery curves within the calfmuscle region of interest (ROI). SIM achieves image quality virtually identical to the reference across all dynamic timepoints, enabling faithful preservation of dynamic physiological responses. For b, data points represent mean values, and error bars indicate s.d. across all pixels within the calf-muscle ROI. For a and b, retrospective equispaced undersampling is applied at a 5.1× effective acceleration factor. PCr, phosphocreatine; Cr, creatine; τ , metabolic recovery time constant.

papers.abstract: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.
authors: Md Kamrujjaman Mobin, Md Salman Shamil, Md Adnan Arefeen
bullets: Evaluates five EventBench event-camera understanding tasks without using challenge training data.
Renders event bins as red/blue ON/OFF frames, selects and grids bins, then prompts a frozen Qwen3.5 9B model for four tasks; action recognition uses EventGPT-Plus-2B directly.
Achieves 62.28% overall accuracy on 2,084 test questions, ranking 9th of 27.
Performance is strongest on action recognition (80.27%) and causal reasoning (77.22%), and weakest on gesture recognition (54.70%) and event OCR (34.57%).
Post-hoc analysis identifies poorly tightened crops that reduce OCR resolution and a bias toward the first two answer choices in detailed understanding.

papers.abstract: Parameterized-action MDPs (PAMDPs) ask an agent to choose a discrete action together with continuous parameters whose meaning depends on that choice. Model-free PAMDP methods act fast but need many interactions; model-based methods are sample-efficient but plan at every decision, which makes them slow to act. We introduce HyLI (Hybrid Latent Imagination), a model-based agent that learns a hybrid policy entirely in the latent imagination of a world model and acts with a single forward pass. To address learning problems that the PAMDP structure creates, HyLI adds counterfactual mode evaluation, which gives every discrete action a learning signal at every imagined state, and success-window replay, which keeps rare successes in training. On seven standard PAMDP benchmarks, HyLI is within one published standard deviation of, or above, the published score of the strongest model-free baseline in our comparison on all 7 tasks, reaches 90% of that score with 2.4x fewer environment steps than that baseline (5.0x when its reward-free pre-training is counted), and decides 67x faster than the model-based planner DLPA at its published planner settings. It is the only method in our comparison that is both more sample-efficient than that baseline and fast enough for real-time control.
authors: Atahan Cilan, \.Ihsan Mert Muhac{\i}ro\u{g}lu, \"Umit Can Bekar
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between fast but data-hungry model-free methods and slow model-based planners.
Learns a hybrid policy entirely through latent imagination in a learned world model.
Uses counterfactual mode evaluation to train every discrete action and success-window replay to preserve rare successes.
Across seven benchmarks, matches or exceeds the strongest compared model-free baseline’s published score on all tasks.
Reaches 90% of that baseline’s score with 2.4× fewer environment steps and decides 67× faster than the DLPA planner under its published settings.

papers.abstract: Robot mechanics can bias kinematic measures of recovery and limit comparisons across rehabilitation devices. We developed a closed-loop human-robot simulation calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics. Paired runs held motor-control parameters and movement plans fixed to quantify bias in seven metrics relative to a low-impedance reference, normalized using external repeatability benchmarks. Within a subset informed by published device specifications, median log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) bias was 0.93 and 1.79 benchmark units for stroke and healthy profiles, respectively. Sobol analysis identified Coulomb friction and apparent mass as leading contributors; LDLJ bias persisted across 11 robustness variants. LDLJ bias increased as simulated movements became less fragmented. If recovery similarly reduces fragmentation, this effect could partly mask improvement in measured smoothness. Correction combining identified robot dynamics and observed metrics with gradient-boosted trees reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.77 to 0.10 for LDLJ and from 0.24 to 0.08 for spectral arc length (SPARC) in the device-informed subset of a random 20% hold-out. Median smoothness residuals remained at or below 0.15 benchmark units across four separately held-out parameter regions. Under an alternative controller, LDLJ error decreased from 1.60 to 0.17 without retraining, although transfer varied across metrics. These simulation results support mechanical characterization and movement-dependent correction toward more comparable robotic assessments, motivating validation in patients.
authors: David Regev, Alex Scherbakov, Eran Beeri Bamani
bullets: A calibrated closed-loop human–robot simulation quantified bias in seven kinematic metrics against a low-impedance reference.
Coulomb friction and apparent mass were the leading contributors to bias; LDLJ bias persisted across robustness tests and increased as movements became less fragmented.
In a device-informed subset, gradient-boosted correction reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.77 to 0.10 for LDLJ and from 0.24 to 0.08 for SPARC.
Correction generalized to an alternative controller for LDLJ, though transfer varied across metrics.
Findings are simulation-based and require validation in patients.

papers.abstract: Knowing when a large language model's (LLM's) response can be trusted is critical for its safe use. Uncertainty quantification (UQ) can help LLMs recognize if their responses may be unreliable. Existing taxonomies organize UQ methods by uncertainty source or estimation mechanism. They leave unresolved the question of where uncertainty is observed in the model's computation. The answer matters because the observation point determines whether an estimator has access to enough information to recover a given target, and how well it can recover it. Drawing on mechanistic interpretability, we define four mechanistic observation lenses: the structural lens observes component updates, the representational lens observes hidden states, the distributional lens observes token probabilities, and the semantical lens observes distributions over meanings. We relate these lenses through the residual stream and order them by the information they carry, which gives a principle for selecting UQ methods for different targets. We survey existing methods through the four lenses. Furthermore, we distinguish evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics to clarify different UQ evaluation protocols. Finally, we identify open problems and research directions to connect uncertainty estimation to the internal computation and downstream use of LLMs.
authors: Xiaoyu Liang, Virginia Ceccatelli, Aliai Eusebi, Tobias Braun, Nils Loose, Carlo Malagnino, Lorenzo Cavallaro
bullets: Motivates locating the observation point because it determines what uncertainty targets an estimator can recover.
Defines four lenses: structural (component updates), representational (hidden states), distributional (token probabilities), and semantical (meaning distributions).
Relates the lenses through the residual stream and orders them by the information they carry.
Surveys existing UQ methods and distinguishes evaluation targets, criteria, and metrics.
Highlights open problems linking uncertainty estimates to internal computation and downstream use.

papers.abstract: Enterprise agents accumulate memory across dozens of sessions in which facts contradict, get superseded, and blur as similarly named entities collide in embedding space. The field treats this as a retrieval problem; we show it is not. On ENT-310, a synthetic enterprise sales-agent memory benchmark of 310 queries (210 answerable, 100 unanswerable), a vanilla Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) reader over a memory store already matches strong memory systems on the recall pillars. Retention and currency are near-saturated, roughly 0.93 to 0.98 for every competent system, so recall is essentially solved. What remains unsolved is resolution: which entity a query refers to, which time-state is current, and whether to commit an answer at all or decline when evidence is insufficient. We propose DISCERN (DISambiguation and Cross-session Episodic memoRy Navigation), an agent-memory framework built on a single rule: preserve at write, resolve at read. At write time DISCERN builds a strictly additive bi-temporal provenance graph that never merges confusable entities and never drops superseded values. At read time a zero-LLM tool surface drives an agentic loop that navigates this graph and commits exactly one of four gated terminal actions. A four-judge LLM-as-a-Judge council scores two axes: answer correctness on answerable questions, and the answer-versus-abstain decision as a classification problem. On ENT-310, DISCERN is the best-calibrated system on abstention (F1 0.924 versus at most 0.802 across eight baselines) and leads macro answer correctness under equal pillar weighting (0.861 versus 0.806 for the strongest baseline), a lead driven by entity resolution (0.800, where no baseline exceeds 0.40). Applied with zero tuning to the full LoCoMo corpus, the same pipeline again leads macro answer correctness (0.663 versus 0.638) and stays among the best-calibrated on false-premise abstention.
authors: Chirag Ahuja, Vladislav Tanov, Ramcharan Kakarla, Jonathan Taws
bullets: Frames persistent memory as a resolution problem—not primarily retrieval—because retention and currency are already near-saturated.
Builds an additive bi-temporal provenance graph that keeps confusable entities separate and preserves superseded values.
Uses a zero-LLM tool surface and agentic read loop with four gated terminal actions, including abstention when evidence is insufficient.
On ENT-310, achieves abstention F1 of 0.924 and macro answer correctness of 0.861, driven by substantially better entity resolution than baselines.
Also leads macro answer correctness on LoCoMo without tuning, while remaining well calibrated for false-premise abstention.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The DISCERN memory graph. (a) Changed values are kept as bi-temporal edges so both history and current state remain recoverable. (b) Confusable entities are kept co-equal and merely linked, never merged. (c) Episodic turns are preserved and linked to entity nodes.

Figure 3: DISCERN read-time routing. The agent orients (Phase 1, read_profile_summary), runs a mandatory ambiguity check for underspecified queries (Phase 2, find_similar_entities), gathers targeted or raw evidence (Phases 3–4), and commits one of four terminal actions. The EarnedAbstainGate abstains only on demonstrated absence, a DeclineRouter sends a surviving decline to CLARIFY when confusable candidates remain and to ABSTAIN when none do, and a citation-or-abstain renderer requires every committed answer to cite its evidence. This procedure realizes the predicates of Eq. 1.

Right (read time resolves): an adaptive policy navigates the views with a small read-only tool surface and commits one of four governed actions (answer, update, clarify, abstain) under the EarnedAnswerGate and EarnedAbstainGate, the DeclineRouter, and the near-miss guard.

papers.abstract: Post-training can improve rewarded behavior while weakening capabilities users still need. We study two GRPO branches from a shared supervised checkpoint in a multilingual mixture-of-experts model. The released branch gains 36.07 points on MATH but loses 19.32 F1 points on XQuAD-Indic, while XQuAD-English improves under the same scoring rule. An independently trained sibling adds Indic instruction following and language-aware shaping. It recovers the regressing Indic task scores and preserves MATH, but does not restore script compliance and trades off competition mathematics and code. In a later round, judge training is followed by a sharp extraction decline from the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from its earlier checkpoint restores most of the lost F1. A MATH score decomposition associates most of the measured gain with increased boxed-answer emission; accuracy among boxed answers changes little. These results show why benchmark scores should be read alongside the response forms they reward.
authors: Sutanshu Saksena Raj, Purusharth Malik, Pasunuti Prasanjith, Daksh Maan, Parijat Chatterjee, Avinash Benki

Judge training later caused a sharp extraction decline in the Indic branch; reward-free distillation from an earlier checkpoint restored most lost F1.
MATH gains were largely associated with more boxed-answer emission, while accuracy among boxed answers changed little.
Benchmark scores should be evaluated alongside the response forms they incentivize.

papers.abstract: In Gaussian-based semantic occupancy prediction, overlapping primitives can provide ambiguous class predictions, making their joint interpretation important for voxel classification. However, current methods using spatially weighted mixtures neglect explicit modeling of cross-primitive dependencies, limiting the readout's ability to utilize category-specific relational evidence. Hence, we introduce CGOcc, a supervised multi-camera framework that explicitly models Cross-Gaussian dependencies for 3D semantic Occupancy prediction. CGOcc integrates appearance and geometric observations to refine Gaussian states and encodes cross-Gaussian dependencies in a diagonal-plus-low-rank representation. To incorporate these dependencies into voxel classification, CGOcc uses a class-conditional projection to extract diagonal and signed cross-Gaussian statistics without constructing a dense dependency matrix. The readout then refines occupied-class probabilities using these statistics while preserving a learned reference's occupied mass and free probability. Extensive experiments on nuScenes demonstrate CGOcc achieves state-of-the-art performance, with larger gains at high Gaussian overlap and improved predictions near boundaries. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of covariance-aware prediction and support its synergy with geometric interaction.
authors: Zirui Huang, Jiongle He, Yunfan Zeng, Yuanzhi Lu, Guangye Li, Boyan Tang, Weite SU, Pedro V. Sander, Amy Hui Zhang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity from overlapping Gaussian primitives whose class predictions are difficult to interpret jointly.
Refines Gaussian states using both appearance and geometric observations in a supervised multi-camera framework.
Represents cross-Gaussian dependencies with a diagonal-plus-low-rank structure and extracts class-conditional statistics without a dense dependency matrix.
Refines occupied-class probabilities while preserving the learned reference’s occupied mass and free probability.
Experiments on nuScenes report state-of-the-art performance, with stronger gains under high overlap and near boundaries; ablations support covariance-aware prediction and geometric interaction.

papers.abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in https://github.com/gokyeongryeol/BAMOS.

The work informs world-model design for embodied agents operating under uncertain observations.

papers.abstract: Despite impressive advances in large language models (LLM), vision-language models (VLM) still exhibit limited spatial reasoning capabilities. Recent progress in feed-forward 3D reconstruction has enabled precise, real-time geometric understanding from visual inputs. In this work, we propose SpaceMCP, a framework that leverages these advances to introduce an MCP-style paradigm for spatial reasoning. Our approach augments a VLM with structured function calls, allowing it to query a scene graph for spatial information such as distances, object positioning, and camera properties. The scene graph is constructed in real time using feed-forward 3D reconstruction to recover metric geometry, combined with open-vocabulary segmentation to identify and localize relevant objects within the scene. Paired with the VLM's strong reasoning capabilities, the VLM is able to combine this primitive information to solve more complex spatial tasks. Without any training, SpaceMCP achieves state-of-the-art results on VSI-Bench, MMSI-Bench and VSTI-Bench, outperforming recent spatially post-trained VLMs and improving its base VLM by 15-22 points per benchmark. We argue that, given the contrast between the relatively slow progress in native VLM spatial reasoning and the rapid advances in feed-forward 3D computer vision, this paradigm offers a promising path forward for enabling robust spatial reasoning.
authors: Ameen Izhac, Nobuko Yoshida, Ronald Clark
bullets: Addresses the limited native spatial reasoning abilities of current vision-language models.

papers.abstract: This paper focuses on improving the behavioral diversity and effectiveness of language-conditioned manipulation policies trained through imitation learning. Recently, continuous-action policies have become mainstream in robotic manipulation, but the lack of diverse demonstrations tends to restrict their behavioral diversity. For grasping, a fundamental subtask of manipulation, 6-DoF grasp detection provides diverse grasp hypotheses, but open-loop execution constrains responsiveness in dynamic environments. This motivates us to combine the diversity of grasp hypotheses with the adaptability of continuous-action policies. To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight and effective spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as geometric priors. In particular, we employ spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics, and integrate them with grasp hypotheses through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction. On LIBERO, GraSLA achieves an average success rate of 99.30%.

papers.abstract: Embedded perception-to-control systems must combine visual targeting with reliable contact handling under tight computational constraints. We present a shared architecture on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin controlling a Franka Research 3 through Cartesian impedance control. RealSense D435i observations, YOLO11-seg segmentation, depth back-projection, and hand--eye calibration provide metric robot-frame targets. We compare two strategies: compact proximal policy optimization (PPO) policies transferred from simulation for object- and hole-region reaching, and force-guided Cartesian placement using approximately 2 N normal contact and spiral search. The PPO policies achieved 87.2% and 83.1% success over 1000 simulation episodes each. Across 50 real-robot trials per strategy, the learned hybrid and force-guided analytical pipelines achieved 70.0% and 74.0% completion, respectively. Mean perception latency with TensorRT was 34.55 ms. These results support an embedded architecture combining learned free-space reaching with explicit contact correction.

papers.abstract: As memory-augmented agents increasingly support long-term and personalized interactions, reliable recall of emotional experiences while preserving their associated affect becomes necessary. However, existing evaluations usually assess emotion accuracy and factual memory grounding separately, overlooking event-affect correspondence. In this work, we formulate Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as a task that explicitly evaluates the recovery of past events, associated affects, and their correspondence, and define Event-Affect Decoupling as a failure mode where the correct emotion is recalled but associated with the wrong episode. To diagnose Event-Affect Decoupling, we propose EM-TRACE, a stage-wise framework that decomposes AER into retrieval, affect recovery, and realization. On a controlled GoEmotions-based benchmark, Emotion-only retrieval achieves 28.65% affect recovery but retrieves the target episode for only 4.44% of queries, yielding a UAR of 24.21%. Further analysis reveals that event retrieval and affect assignment introduce distinct binding failures. These findings show that reliable AER requires grounded recall of emotional experiences, where episode retrieval, affect recovery, event-affect binding, and generation quality should be evaluated jointly. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/A412/.
authors: Tingna Xie, Ming Wang, Shi Feng, Yongkang Liu
bullets: Defines Affective-Episodic Retrospection (AER) as jointly recovering past events, their affects, and event–affect correspondence.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used across the sciences, but whether their internal computations correspond to known scientific operations or proceed through different mechanisms remains unclear. Understanding these mechanisms is essential for assessing reliability, identifying failure modes, and learning new science from the models. We present, to our knowledge, the first causal mechanistic interpretability study of an astronomy foundation model, AION-1, focusing on its multimodal advantage in redshift prediction, where combining imaging with photometry outperforms photometry alone. We find that this advantage is largest for spatially extended and dust-attenuated galaxies, and that most of it is localized to the first of the encoder's twelve blocks. Within that block, how well a property is linearly decodable does not predict whether it can be localized. Spatial extent is causally used, and one attention head dominates linear probing for it, yet ablating that head has negligible effect on redshift prediction: the information is distributed across heads and is decodable again one layer after we erase it. Dust attenuation shows the opposite pattern: it is only weakly decodable anywhere in the encoder, yet a single head is necessary for most of the multimodal advantage, particularly for the most dust-attenuated galaxies, and keeping that head as the only active head in its block preserves nearly all of the advantage. None of the astrophysically motivated operations we tested explains what this head computes. Whether this reflects a limitation of current interpretability methods or a computation that does not correspond to any known astrophysical operation remains open, and resolving it is a prerequisite for using interpretability as a tool for scientific discovery.
authors: Rachel C. Zhang, Alberto Bietti, Wes Gurnee, Alessandro Favero, Miles Cranmer
bullets: The study examines why multimodal inputs outperform photometry alone, especially for extended and dust-attenuated galaxies.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Interpretability Study of an Astronomy Foundation Model
papers.tldr: A causal analysis of AION-1 shows that its imaging–photometry advantage in redshift prediction relies on distinct, partly opaque mechanisms for galaxy extent and dust attenuation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models are regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, but planning from instructions alone cannot make them reliable. During execution, actions deviate from intended effects, constrained by the embodiment and environment. An embodied brain must understand why execution deviates, identify what can be reliably realized, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision. Current embodied foundation models largely lack these capabilities. To address this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct failure-recovery data by injecting perturbations at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and keeping failures that are observable from public evidence and recoverable from the current state. We align actions, consequences, failure causes, and recoveries into Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model learns Judge and Cause first, then Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate prefixes. Since deployment uses self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate prefixes into that under self-generated ones: the model generates plans from self-generated prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate prefixes compares token probabilities to reinforce or suppress planning tokens. At deployment, this branch is removed. Experiments show stronger failure analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points; with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.
authors: Miao Pan, Kaixiang Yao, Xiaohe Zhou, Xu Wang, Qinfeng Li, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Targets three missing abilities: causal failure localization, capability-aware adaptation, and experience-driven decision revision.
Builds recovery data by perturbing successful trajectories, replaying affected subtasks, and retaining observable, recoverable failures.
Uses Judge-Cause-Sub-Fine supervision with evaluation-first SFT to structure failure diagnosis before recovery planning.
Applies OPD to reduce errors from self-generated planning prefixes without adding a deployment-time branch.
Improves composite task success by 6.1 points with a frozen VLA and manipulation/navigation success by 13.9 points with fixed GPT-5.5 execution.

papers.abstract: Persistent deformation complicates elasto-plastic manipulation by coupling physical interaction with spatially distributed shape changes. We investigate the force--deformation relationship using a standard robot, a single eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, and intrinsic force estimates. A 7-DoF Franka Emika FR3 performs normal indentations while an Intel RealSense L515 captures pre- and post-contact surfaces. Point-cloud processing localizes deformation and estimates displaced volume. Force--volume characterization includes 27 measurements over nine force levels. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP), trained on 52 force--volume pairs at four levels, achieves a held-out RMSE of 1.857 N and $R^2=0.440$. A separate comparison shows lower error for a quadratic model at 16 N and for the MLP at 19 and 23.5 N. An eight-step experiment at 4 N per interaction demonstrates cumulative deformation localization from the second indentation onward. These results establish a practical measurement basis for deformation-aware manipulation using intrinsic force estimates and single-view geometry.
authors: Dezhi Sun, Marijn van Hilten, Kenan Niu
bullets: Addresses persistent, spatially distributed deformation during elasto-plastic robotic manipulation.
Uses intrinsic robot force estimates, pre/post-contact RGB-D surfaces, and point-cloud processing to estimate displaced volume.
Characterizes force–volume behavior from normal indentations across multiple force levels.
An MLP achieves a held-out RMSE of 1.857 N and R² of 0.440; quadratic modeling performs better at 16 N, while the MLP performs better at 19 and 23.5 N.
An eight-step 4 N experiment localizes cumulative deformation from the second indentation onward.

papers.abstract: Language-model agents can share conversational history across sessions, but persistence does not guarantee retrieval of current decisions and their provenance. This engineering study presents Memory-TCG, a Conversation ESAA extension inspired by ringing, resonance and renormalization (RRR), and an exploratory synthetic evaluation comparing chronological retrieval, two simplified baselines (B, recency-aware, and B', authority-aware), full RRR, and variants under three output budgets. With 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, versus 0.06 for chronological retrieval and 0.58 for the oracle ceiling; with 4,096 tokens it recalled all of them. B' and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall across all nine scale-budget combinations, as expected when the active decision set and the adapter ordering are the same. The isolated contribution of ringing to decisions was not measured: comparator D1 cuts facts before the graph is built, and the product retains active decisions by rule. Before the output limit, full-RRR conflict F1 was 0.615 at all three scales; after it, at 480 facts and 1,024 tokens, it was 0.000. Reserving 20% of the budget for conflicts raised that F1 to 0.431 in that scenario, at the cost of lowering decision recall from 0.44 to 0.34, and to 0.930 at 4,096 tokens without decision loss. Fixtures are repetitive, comparators are simplified, and the evaluation was not independently replicated; the results support an engineering analysis, not a claim of selectionist superiority.
authors: Elzo Brito dos Santos Filho
bullets: Persistent conversation history does not ensure retrieval of current decisions and their provenance.
The study compares chronological retrieval, recency- and authority-aware baselines, full RRR, and variants across three output budgets using synthetic conversations.
At 1,024 tokens and 480 facts, full RRR recalled 0.44 of current decisions, compared with 0.06 for chronological retrieval; at 4,096 tokens, it recalled all decisions.
Simplified baselines and the no-resonance variant matched full RRR in decision recall, so the isolated contribution of ringing was not established.
Conflict F1 fell to 0.000 after the output limit in the 480-fact, 1,024-token setting; reserving 20% of the budget improved it to 0.431 but reduced decision recall to 0.34.

papers.abstract: Backpack language models predict with a strictly linear combination of non-contextual per-word sense vectors, weighted by non-negative contextualization scores. We show that non-negativity conflates two properties: the linear readout, which carries the interpretability, and the conic combination, which merely restricts it. We relax the latter by computing the sense weights with differential attention, a difference of two softmax maps with a learned per-sense gain, so context can actively inhibit a sense; we call the result a differential Backpack. At equal parameters on WikiText-103 this cuts the Backpack's perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31%, improves over the softmax Backpack at every sense count, persists with a shrinking margin up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText, and is localized at the sense layer by ablations and controls. The learned inhibition is directly interpretable (a financial context drives the river sense of bank to -0.50), and the preserved per-sense attribution predicts counterfactual removals exactly. We tested a number of combination rules, showing the linear interface is nearly free. Making the readout nonlinear gains only 0.43 perplexity points while invalidating two thirds of the decomposition. The differential Backpack's senses are also better representations, improving zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.
authors: Konstantinos Skianis, Giannis Nikolentzos, Polykarpos Meladianos, Michalis Vazirgiannis
bullets: Backpack models use interpretable linear combinations of non-contextual sense vectors, but standard non-negative weights cannot suppress irrelevant senses.
Differential attention computes signed sense weights as the difference between two softmax maps with learned per-sense gains.
On WikiText-103, the method reduces the perplexity gap to a Transformer by 31% and outperforms the softmax Backpack across sense counts.
Improvements persist up to 350M parameters on OpenWebText and are localized to the sense layer through ablations and controls.
Signed weights remain interpretable: for example, financial context inhibits the river sense of “bank,” while the model improves zero-shot sentence similarity by up to 33%.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding aims to continuously process incoming visual observations, making the retention and retrieval of relevant information increasingly important as the video history grows. Although existing benchmarks include memory-related questions, question-answering accuracy alone does not reliably measure memory capabilities. Incorrect predictions may arise from failures in visual understanding rather than forgetting, whereas correct predictions may rely on linguistic priors or recent observations without requiring historical memory. To address these ambiguities, we introduce MemInStream, a benchmark dedicated to evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding. We develop an evidence-controlled validation protocol that associates each question with temporally localized evidence intervals. The protocol validates evidence solvability and memory necessity by retaining questions that models can answer from the annotated evidence but cannot resolve using recent observations, post-evidence observations, or textual input alone. This helps disentangle memory limitations from understanding failures while reducing memory-independent shortcuts. MemInStream provides a systematic evaluation of memory capabilities through four major categories, covering Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking \& Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory across diverse video scenarios. Overall, \textsc{MemInStream} provides a comprehensive and reliable benchmark for systematically evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding.
authors: Zhenqi He, Dunyuan Xu, Yang Bo, Kien T. Pham, Yanghao Wang, Shuhan Li, Xintong Guo, Yuyang He, Fang Liu, Huankang Guan, Jingyan Chen, Rui Liu, Long Chen
bullets: Existing question-answering accuracy can conflate memory failures with visual understanding errors or linguistic and recency-based shortcuts.
Each question is paired with temporally localized evidence intervals in an evidence-controlled validation protocol.
The benchmark keeps questions that are solvable from the evidence but not from recent observations, post-evidence content, or text alone.
It evaluates four capabilities: Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking & Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory.
The benchmark targets diverse streaming-video scenarios and aims to disentangle memory limitations from other sources of failure.

papers.abstract: Deep neural networks for electromagnetic signal processing are typically developed as single-task experts with fixed inputs and objectives, limiting cross-task transferability. Electromagnetic foundation models offer broader task coverage but incur substantial pretraining and inference costs. To balance accuracy and efficiency, we adopt model routing to dynamically dispatch unknown signals to matched experts within a heterogeneous pool. We construct HeteroSignal-7, a multi-task routing benchmark with 140,000 samples from seven datasets covering six task types, paired with seven classification and waveform-recovery experts and a unified evaluation protocol. We then propose GLCR, a two-stage routing method combining global dispatch with local discrimination of similar tasks. First, a lightweight one-dimensional convolutional neural network (CNN) with an additive-margin head predicts one of seven routing classes. Second, a gradient-boosted-tree specialist uses four physical statistics to re-evaluate samples whose top two candidates match a confusion pair automatically identified from validation errors. The pipeline is trained across the full signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) range and requires neither SNR labels nor noise estimation at inference time. GLCR outperforms all 19 baselines, achieving 96.16% routing accuracy and a 76.30% system score, exceeding the respective second-best baselines by 1.16% and 1.14%. It achieves the lowest routing latency among the compared methods at 1.43 ms per sample and reduces expected overall system FLOPs by 5.9 times compared with executing all experts. This work provides a public evaluation platform and an efficient, reproducible baseline for heterogeneous expert routing in electromagnetic signal processing.
authors: Fang Lu, Yao Lu, Zhuangzhi Chen, Sicheng Zhang, Shanqing Yu, Yun Lin, Qi Xuan, Guan Gui
bullets: Addresses limited cross-task transfer in single-task signal-processing models and the cost of electromagnetic foundation models.
Introduces HeteroSignal-7, a benchmark with 140,000 samples spanning seven datasets and six task types, plus seven heterogeneous experts.
Uses a two-stage router: a lightweight 1D CNN for global classification, followed by a gradient-boosted-tree specialist for automatically identified confusing task pairs.
Trains across all SNRs without requiring SNR labels or noise estimation during inference.
Reports 96.16% routing accuracy, a 76.30% system score, 1.43 ms routing latency per sample, and 5.9× lower expected system FLOPs than running all experts.

papers.abstract: Multiplayer generative world models must produce observations that agree on shared entities despite different camera motions and occlusions. Explicit world representations provide spatial control, but precise modeling of individual game maps limits scene diversity, while shared geometry alone cannot ensure consistent appearance across views. We present CoCode-World, a shared 3D proxy framework that separates structural control from visual synthesis for two-player video generation. Programmable proxies specify scene layout, motion, and occlusion, while RGB references guide character and scene appearance. To coordinate visual details across players, we concatenate paired proxy videos, appearance references, and target views in a consistent spatial layout and generate both views jointly with a pretrained video model. This formulation uses the model's native attention for cross-view communication within a single generation branch, with LoRA adaptation learning proxy adherence and appearance correspondence from paired observations. We construct a two-player GTA~V dataset that pairs synchronized RGB observations with proxy videos derived from shared map geometry and game-engine state. Experiments demonstrate appearance transfer to characters and scene styles unseen during training, with improvements in video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline. Ablations further examine how proxy construction and cross-view communication affect generation. Project page: https://iapple233.github.io/CCW/.

Uses programmable 3D proxies for scene layout, motion, and occlusion, while RGB references control character and scene appearance.

Applies LoRA adaptation to improve proxy adherence and appearance correspondence from paired observations.

On a two-player GTA V dataset, transfers unseen character and scene styles and improves video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline; ablations study proxy design and communication.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. We introduce MemCredit, a decision-centric memory framework that shifts memory selection from semantic relevance to decision utility. MemCredit estimates the state-, reference-context-, and policy-conditional marginal contribution of individual memories through controlled counterfactual interventions, and distills these intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator. At inference time, semantic relevance is used only for high-recall candidate generation, while predicted utility arbitrates which memories are retained under a fixed token budget, without modifying the underlying agent policy or requiring additional environment interaction. We evaluate MemCredit on ALFWorld and WebShop against representative memory baselines. On ALFWorld, MemCredit achieves 86.57 SR@50 under a 500-token historical-memory budget, compared with 65.67% for BM25 retrieval. Counterfactual analysis further shows that memory utility is sparse, strongly state dependent, and poorly captured by semantic relevance. These results suggest that decision utility provides a more effective principle than relevance alone for long-horizon agent memory management.
authors: Quanjiang Guo, Sijie Wang, Qianyang Zhu, Ben Zhang, Jinchuan Zhang, Ke Yan, Zhao Kang
bullets: Targets the mismatch between semantically relevant memories and memories that actually improve actions.
Uses controlled counterfactual interventions to estimate each memory’s state-, context-, and policy-conditional utility.
Distills intervention-derived credits into a lightweight utility estimator; relevance only generates high-recall candidates.
Retains memories by predicted utility without changing the agent policy or requiring extra environment interaction.
On ALFWorld, reaches 86.57 SR@50 with a 500-token memory budget versus 65.67% for BM25; utility is sparse and state dependent.

papers.abstract: In September 2026, TypeSafe announced Jev as the first model in its System One category: unstructured state goes in, and typed, calibrated decisions that software can use directly come out. Jev's architecture and training data are unpublished, but many open typed-decision models have followed, including Nimble, the Decision 1.0--3.0 family and Clef. They answer structured questions about a piece of text, such as a yes/no check, a choice among labelled options or a graded score, by reading the text with a language model and scoring the options with a small readout. Each pairs a different readout with a different backbone, training mix and recipe, so it is unclear which design choices matter. We re-implement five readouts and train all of them under one protocol: the same backbone, the same 15 public English training sources, the same recipe with a per-head learning-rate sweep, and the same seed. Our experiments demonstrate that: The complexity of the head does not affect accuracy: on Qwen3-0.6B every readout reaches 81.3--82.0\% in-domain accuracy, and a 0.5M-parameter cosine head, which scores each option by its cosine similarity to the question, matches the 27M-parameter joint schema head adapted from Clef in-domain at half its inference time. Reading all of a text's questions from one prompt also matches one prompt per question in accuracy, with 1.6 times faster inference and 2.1--2.5 times faster training on one H100. The backbone's size matters more than either choice: moving from Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-4B adds 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources, while the base, instruct and thinking checkpoints of the same model tie. We recommend spending effort on the backbone and keeping the head minimal.
authors: Ritvik Rastogi
bullets: Five readouts were reimplemented and trained under a shared protocol using the same backbone, data sources, recipe, and seed.
On Qwen3-0.6B, all heads achieved 81.3–82.0% in-domain accuracy; a 0.5M-parameter cosine head matched a 27M-parameter joint schema head.
Processing all questions from one prompt preserved accuracy while making inference 1.6× faster and training 2.1–2.5× faster on one H100.
Scaling the backbone from Qwen3-0.6B to 4B improved accuracy by 4 points in-domain and 11 points on held-out sources.
Base, instruct, and thinking checkpoints of the same model performed similarly; the study recommends minimal heads and stronger backbones.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The LM letter readout of Nimble and the learned letter readout of Decision 3.0. Each question gets its own chat prompt, with its options labelled by single-token answer codes, ending right after the assistant’s empty thinking block. Option k scores the dot product between the hidden state at the last token and code k’s row. With Nimble’s frozen LM-head rows, this is exactly the language model’s next-token logit for the code, restricted to the question’s codes; Decision 3.0 learns the rows instead, starting from the same values. Nimble’s prompt also lists the other fields in its schema and names the requested one. In our implementation, a row’s questions share the joint prompt, and each field ends with ANSWER:, read at its colon.

Figure 3: Clef’s joint schema head. From the normalised hidden states it builds a token memory M and pooled question, option, lexical and last-token vectors. Each option gathers evidence from the memory; each question becomes a field vector, and four decoder layers refine the fields jointly. An option’s logit adds a lexical prior to a gated joint score that compares its question’s field with the option (ôp = LN(op)). The width is W=512, with 8 attention heads and sℓ, sf , γ learned scalars, giving 27.3M parameters at H=1024.

Figure 2: The bilinear-MLP head of Decision 1.0/2.0. Each question gets its own plain-text prompt: the state, the question type, the question, one block per option, and an instruction ending in Decision:. The head reads one hidden state per option (the endpoint ei, the closing > of its block) and one per question (the query rj , the final colon), layer-normalises each, and adds a scaled dot product to a small MLP correction; d=256, giving 1.05M parameters at H=1024. No term compares two options, so options interact only through the causal backbone. In our implementation, a row’s questions share the joint prompt: the endpoint is the last token of each option’s JSON and the query is the field’s END FIELD line.

Figure 5: The cosine head. One forward pass encodes the state and every question. For each question, the head pools the question span and each of its option spans, projects both into a shared W -dimensional space, and scores each option by its scaled cosine with its own question. Options are never compared with another question, and the head has no per-type parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Controlled study showing minimal decision readouts match much larger heads at lower inference cost, informing efficient LLM-based decision model design.
papers.title: Small Heads, Strong Decisions: A Controlled Study of Typed-Decision Models
papers.tldr: For typed-decision models, backbone scale matters far more than readout complexity, while a tiny cosine head performs as well as a much larger head at lower cost.

papers.abstract: Compositional diffusion planners extend short-horizon trajectory models to long-horizon goal-conditioned planning by generating and stitching multiple local trajectory chunks. However, in multimodal environments, local plausibility is not sufficient for global consistency: independently initialized chunks may denoise toward incompatible overlap modes, producing plans that are individually feasible but incoherent after stitching. Existing remedies typically add search, guidance, pruning, or graph-based structure at inference time, increasing computational cost or relying on task-specific machinery. We instead investigate graph-structured dependence among chunk-wise initial diffusion noises as a lightweight coordination mechanism for compositional trajectory planning. We propose \textbf{M}arginal-Preserving \textbf{C}oupled \textbf{D}iffusion \textbf{C}omposition (MCDC), a training-free inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners. Instead of sampling chunk noises independently, MCDC constructs coupled Gaussian initializations whose per-chunk marginals remain exactly standard Gaussian, as required by the pretrained denoiser, while neighboring chunks receive positively correlated noise components. This preserves the standard-Gaussian initialization marginal of each chunk while biasing adjacent chunks toward compatible overlap-mode choices. We prove exact marginal preservation and show, under a simple multimodal overlap model, that positive coupling increases the probability of compatible mode selection. On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently improves over independent compositional diffusion sampling while retaining nearly the same inference time, and achieves a favorable success--cost trade-off compared with search-based composition methods.
authors: Hengrui Zhang, Qiyu Wang, Yuhu Cheng, Brooks Paige, Xuesong Wang
bullets: Problem: Independently sampled chunks can select incompatible overlap modes, making globally stitched plans incoherent in multimodal environments.
Method: Couple neighboring chunks’ initial Gaussian noises with positive correlations while preserving each chunk’s exact standard-Gaussian marginal.

Contribution: A training-free, lightweight inference method for pretrained compositional diffusion planners, with proofs of marginal preservation and improved compatibility under a multimodal overlap model.

Results: On OGBench long-horizon stitch tasks, MCDC consistently outperforms independent sampling, with nearly unchanged inference time and a favorable success–cost trade-off versus search-based methods.
