papers.abstract: Vision-based high-speed navigation requires a trajectory planner that can reactively generate smooth, collision-free trajectories from onboard visual observations. Deep reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to vision-based trajectory planning, as it enables the optimization of sequential decision-making policies in complex environments. However, model-free policy gradient methods rely on sample-based policy gradient estimation, which yields noisy gradient estimates and inefficient training. To this end, we propose a framework for learning trajectory planning policies using the analytic policy gradient (APG) method and use it to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed framework leverages differential flatness to analytically reconstruct vehicle states from planned trajectories, thereby enabling differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without requiring an explicit low-level dynamics model. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct a differentiable episode rollout and analytically compute policy gradients from episode-level losses, improving both training efficiency and policy performance. After approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU, APG-Planner demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing baseline methods in simulation and achieves speeds of up to 11\,m/s in real-world flight experiments. We further validate the proposed framework on a skid-steer ground robot, demonstrating its applicability to differentially flat robotic systems beyond quadrotors.

papers.abstract: Navigating off-road trails on a mountain bike requires diverse locomotion skills, including aerial maneuvers, cornering, and slip recovery, paired with sophisticated perception for scene understanding. Translating these capabilities to autonomous, two-wheeled robots remains a formidable challenge. We show that autonomous, high-speed trail navigation can be achieved through a single idea: encoding the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain. In simulation, this layer embeds the navigation task into the training environment; during deployment, it is reconstructed onboard from camera and LiDAR data. First, we introduce a unified learning framework that treats local navigation and locomotion as a joint optimization problem, bypassing the twist or pose command interface of classical control hierarchies. With fixed reward weights, the same framework produces both trail racing and agile parkour, shaped only through terrain semantics and episode length. Second, our perception pipeline combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight dual-head decoder that predicts per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores, which are fused with LiDAR range measurements into an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz onboard an NVIDIA AGX Orin. We validate our framework on the Ultra Mobility Vehicle (UMV), a bicycle robot that autonomously raced across all sections of a kilometer-long, unstructured mountain bike trail at speeds exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s. In simulation, our policy fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.
authors: Fabian Jenelten, Deepana Ishtaweera, Pablo Garcia, Liana Margolese, Igor Bogoslavskyi, Luca Buonocore, Jan Migliazza, Aleksandrs Ecins, Annika Wollschlaeger, Dario Bellicoso, Gabriel Nelson, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter
bullets: Encodes trails as semantic terrain layers used for both training and onboard deployment.
Jointly optimizes local navigation and locomotion without traditional twist or pose command interfaces.
Combines a frozen vision foundation model, lightweight semantic/confidence decoding, and LiDAR into a semantic elevation map running at 30 Hz.
Autonomously traversed all sections of a kilometer-long unstructured mountain-bike trail, exceeding 5 m/s and averaging 3.26 m/s.
In simulation, failed up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Approach overview. (A) Deployment: The policy, parametrized as Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with three hidden layers, observes proprioceptive states, an operator-triggered stand command, and a semantic height scan. Joint action targets are computed at 50Hz to control the rear wheel velocity, the fork angle, and the two DOFs of the torso. (B) Training: Our learning framework utilizes synthetic trails or high-fidelity digital twins and applies to both trail racing and parkour. (C) Semantic pipeline: An incoming RGB image passes through a frozen DINOv3 model and a frozen upsampler to produce high-resolution per-patch features. A lightweight trainable decoder maps these features to a per-pixel segmentation mask. A parallel reconstruction head, scored by cosine similarity to the original features, yields a per-pixel confidence score. A coefficient assignment operation converts the segmentation mask into a traversability image. Finally, an elevation mapping pipeline fuses traversability and confidence scores with odometry and point clouds at 30Hz.

The robot has four actuated DOFs: the rear wheel, the fork, and the lower and upper torso joints, whereas the front wheel is unactuated. The policy jointly combines control and local navigation, while the two-layered grid map encodes a traversable path (third row). (B) With only the episode length and mesh as tuning degrees, the identical learning pipeline generalizes to agile parkour: A single policy navigates a slalom segment, accelerates up a ramp at 5m/s, clears a 1.2m long gap, lands on a five-step staircase, and executes a track-stand, all within an 8 s window.

Figure 4. Mesh generation. (A) The procedural generation of mountain bike meshes is divided into four stages. First, a cross-section polygon is swept along a 4D sweeping path (x, y, z, and yaw). Second, two geometric platforms are welded to the start and end of the trail. Third, the lateral vertices are extended to align with the terrain patch size. Forest objects can optionally be placed. Finally, semantic information is embedded into the vertex colors. (B) Each trail segment may contain one or more skill element(s) of a unique type, such as stairs, pump-track waves, jumps, drops, rocks, curves, skinnies, roots, and ramps. (C) Multiple terrain patches are instantiated across a uniform grid to construct the learning environment. (D) Example of the terrain curriculum for a curved segment. (E) Example of the height-based curriculum for parkour. (F) A high-resolution (17MB) visual mesh is constructed by composing pre-meshed objects. The corresponding semantic mesh is generated by down-sampling the geometry to 5MB and manually encoding high-level navigation signals into the vertex colors.

papers.abstract: We present DroneDiffusion, a perception-aware diffusion planner for local 3-D UAV trajectory generation that explicitly models and avoids failure zones caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces. A vision-language perceptual safety estimator produces a pixel-aligned reliability map that highlights regions of degraded sensing. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) is conditioned on this map together with the onboard RGB image, goal point, and initial velocity to generate egocentric 3-D trajectories. To enforce obstacle avoidance at inference time without retraining, we apply training-free CHOMP guidance over a 3-D Euclidean signed distance field. The model is trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot on a real drone. Reliability conditioning raises the mean perceptual reliability along generated trajectories to 0.71, compared with 0.63 for a geometric baseline, while guidance halves the collision rate of the learned prior from 14.7% to 7.8%. Perceptual safety conditioning and geometric guidance are therefore complementary: treating sensor reliability as a first-class signal reduces incursions into unreliable regions while maintaining competitive navigation performance.
authors: Ivan Valuev, Iana Zhura, Valerii Serpiva, Miguel Altamirano Cabrera, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Targets navigation failures caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces.
Conditions a DDPM on an RGB image, goal point, initial velocity, and pixel-aligned perceptual reliability map.
Uses training-free CHOMP guidance over a 3-D signed distance field to enforce obstacle avoidance at inference time.
Trained only in simulation but deployed zero-shot on a real drone.
Reliability conditioning increased mean trajectory reliability from 0.63 to 0.71, while guidance reduced collision rate from 14.7% to 7.8%.

Right: scene and reliability tokens enter the U-Net bottleneck through two sequential cross-attention blocks, which keeps appearance and perceptual-reliability reasoning separate.

papers.abstract: Small open models suit private customer-service deployments but trail frontier models in two ways: they miss what the written policy requires in a given situation, and they act inconsistently on what they know. We study whether such a model can close both gaps from its own deployment logs and their reference outcomes, without a stronger teacher model. Our starting point is a Gemma 4 12B agent that reads its domain policy from on-demand skills rather than from its system prompt. In each round, the deployed system serves a fresh batch of tasks; the base model diagnoses failed conversations and writes rules into the skills, and a rule survives only if it passes code checks, counterexample self-review, a paired retest, and a noise-calibrated validation gate. Reinforcement learning (GRPO) then trains a LoRA adapter on complete multi-turn, tool-using conversations. On the retail and airline domains of $\tau^2$-bench, without training or selecting on official tasks, the agent after two rounds improves on this starting point by 12.5 pass$^1$ points in retail and 19.5 in airline, and by 18.4 and 22.0 pass$^4$ points. It also exceeds the benchmark's reference agent, which runs the same model with the whole policy in its system prompt, by 11.8 and 8.0 pass$^1$ points and by 22.8 and 16.0 pass$^4$ points, closing most of the gap to three frontier models under the same protocol. A $2\times2$ ablation shows that the rules rescue tasks the agent never solved and carry policy knowledge that RL with the rules in context does not internalize, whereas the trained weights make solved tasks reliable.
authors: Yujia Zhang, Xinqi Ren, Shixiong Zhou, Jia Meng
bullets: Targets two gaps in small open models: missing situation-specific policy knowledge and inconsistent actions.
The agent extracts rules from deployment failures, filters them through checks and retests, then trains on complete tool-using conversations with GRPO.
After two rounds on retail and airline τ²-bench domains, it substantially improves over its starting point and surpasses the policy-in-prompt reference agent.
A 2×2 ablation suggests external rules provide new knowledge, while trained weights make already-solved tasks more reliable.
The study closes most of the gap to three frontier models under the same evaluation protocol.

papers.title: Knowledge in the Harness, Reliability in the Weights: Teacher-Free Co-Evolution of an LLM Agent

papers.abstract: We introduce the multi-head quantum neural network (QNN), a quantum module compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices that can replace transformer blocks inside pre-trained large language models (LLMs) with little loss in accuracy and with far fewer parameters than the blocks it replaces. Encoding a model's $D$ hidden neurons into a qubit register is the obstacle: amplitude encoding scales poorly in circuit depth and angle encoding in qubit count, so neither is practical at production-scale width. We instead partition the hidden space into $k$ disjoint heads, angle-encode each into an $n_q$-qubit register, process the heads in parallel, and couple them through constrained classical linear layers, the mixers. Performing surgery on Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, we show that a single multi-head QNN with $145\,281$ trainable parameters ($D=2048$, $k=32$, $n_q=8$, $L=4$) can replace a contiguous span of eight transformer blocks, displacing $16.33\%$ of the model's parameters. Ablations show that, for a single replaced block, the quantum heads (circuits followed by a learned readout), and not the classical mixers alone, recover the displaced function, whereas for fused spans the mixers alone come within $1$-$3\%$ of the full module in perplexity. Whether this benefit is specific to trained, entangling quantum circuits is not established: controls that switch the entangler off (two seeds), or freeze the circuit at its initial or at uniformly random angles (one seed), beat the full module on held-out perplexity, and a parameter-matched classical multilayer perceptron remains a few percent ahead of the full module. We train classically with exact statevector simulation, then execute the quantum heads of our fusion checkpoints on a $156$-qubit IBM Heron processor, showing that NISQ-scale quantum modules can be installed in a production-scale LLM and run on hardware.
authors: Maforikan Amoussou, Borja Aizpurua, Sukhbinder Singh, Rom\'an Or\'us, Hans-Arno Jacobsen
bullets: Partitions the hidden dimension into parallel angle-encoded quantum heads coupled by constrained classical mixer layers.
A 145,281-parameter module replaced eight transformer blocks in Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, covering 16.33% of model parameters.
For one replaced block, quantum heads were important for recovering the displaced function; for fused spans, mixers alone came within 1–3% of the full module in perplexity.
Controls with disabled, frozen, or random circuits, plus a parameter-matched MLP, sometimes performed better than the full quantum module.
The quantum heads were simulated classically during training and executed on a 156-qubit IBM Heron processor.

papers.selection_reason: Investigates replacing transformer blocks in a 30B LLM with quantum modules, directly relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Multi-head Quantum Neural Networks: Replacing Transformer Blocks with NISQ Modules inside a 30-Billion-Parameter LLM
papers.tldr: A multi-head NISQ-compatible quantum module can replace transformer blocks in a 30B-parameter LLM with far fewer parameters, but its added benefit over classical alternatives remains unproven.

papers.abstract: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.
authors: Shunming Liu, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu
bullets: Addresses domain gaps when transferring discrete diffusion generation to autonomous driving.
Optimizes planning representations during supervised fine-tuning to reduce hallucinations.
Uses metric-guided diversity filtering during reinforcement learning to improve exploration.
Introduces Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding, which adapts decoding to scene complexity.
Reports a 29.7% improvement over the unoptimized model and stronger performance than same-architecture autoregressive baselines across closed- and open-loop benchmarks.

During the processing of training samples, the planning components are discretized and replaced with corresponding special tokens to facilitate supervised learning. Reinforcement Learning: Checkpoints of varying maturity levels are screened based on diversity and accuracy metrics, after which they are fed into the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) training process. Inference: dVLM exhibits distinct confidence trends across different driving scenarios. DAD mechanism transforms these trends into specialized inference sequences to optimize output quality.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a vision-language driving planning system using discrete diffusion, connecting visual-language reasoning to autonomous driving actions and fitting VLA and multimodal LLM topics.
papers.title: Towards Robust Vision-Language Reasoning: A Multi-Stage Optimization Pipeline with Masked Diffusion Model
papers.tldr: MD-Drive uses multi-stage training and adaptive masked-diffusion decoding to improve robust vision-language planning for autonomous driving.

papers.abstract: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.
authors: Shunming Liu, Jianyi Peng, Cheng Li, Lu Hou, Pei Huang, Yajing Sun, Huaxiao Liu
bullets: Targets the gap between front-view-focused MLLMs and the multi-view reasoning required for autonomous driving.
Introduces 12 QA categories spanning low-level perception through high-level driving decisions, with reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation.
Benchmarks 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on high-information-density surround-view videos.
Finds insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning across current MLLMs.
Closed-loop specialist-model evaluations in AlpaSim indicate that stronger multi-view reasoning is associated with better driving performance.

papers.title: Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark

papers.abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.
authors: Haoyi Zhang, Qi Zhang, Yunfan Ren, Yi Bin, Lei Zhu, Heng Tao Shen
bullets: Targets world-model failures when robot dynamics change unexpectedly, such as after grasping an unknown payload.
Uses a fast correction for prompt adaptation and a slow correction for retained dynamics, with prediction errors driving both.
Dynamically reweights pretrained experts without modifying their parameters.
Evaluated on five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, achieving lower multi-step mean error than ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task.
Reported gains cover early adaptation, transient disturbances, and long-horizon retention; code and datasets are planned for release.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an adaptive world model for robot dynamics that responds to sudden changes and retains corrections, directly combining world-model prediction with test-time/continual adaptation for embodied agents.
papers.title: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention
papers.tldr: AFTER-WM adapts world models to sudden, persistent, or transient dynamics changes using error-driven fast–slow corrections that improve prediction and control.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful, and opaque; training-free libraries swap gradients for a textual store but still use trajectory-level, correlation-based admission and flat structure. To address both, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with auditable edits to a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library, where skills are advantage-bearing nodes and compositions are hyperedges. It has three components: training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures; gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them; and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer. On 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/HyperSkill.

papers.abstract: Multivariate time series forecasting often improves the prediction of a target by modeling the interactions among variables, and cross-variable modules such as cross-sectional pooling, inter-variable attention, and graph structures are used to construct such interactions. However, by intervening on the cross-variable reading of existing models at inference time, we find that although these models substantially reduce forecasting error through cross-variable interaction, their reading is nearly identical for all targets: the gain appears to come from dependencies among variables but mainly comes from the common component. We term this phenomenon spurious dependency and attribute it to common-component confounding: present in every variable, the common component affects how reading distinguishes sources, so that reading tends to be shared across targets and concentrates on a few similar averages; dependencies thus make up a small share of the read-in content, and a common component composed of several drivers is only partly captured. Theoretical analysis further shows that the common component and dependencies place different requirements on reading and should therefore be handled in different ways. Accordingly, we propose PRELUDE, a separated-reading framework that estimates the common component holistically through cross-sectional pooling and multiple common factors, and reads dependencies for each target via lead-lag relations in the innovation space obtained by prewhitening. Extensive experiments on 16 real-world datasets from four domains show that PRELUDE effectively mitigates spurious dependency and achieves the best overall performance: it attains the best MSE on 23 of the 24 short-horizon and air-quality settings and reduces the average MSE by 6.1% relative to the strongest baseline.
authors: Dongqing Song, Jianyu Xu, Haobin Ding, Xinyi Guo, Jiahao Du, Ruiqi He, Ruiqi Liu, Yuntong Xie, Chao He
bullets: Existing cross-variable models often improve forecasts through common components rather than truly target-specific dependencies, causing spurious dependency.
The framework models the common component holistically with cross-sectional pooling and multiple common factors.
It captures target-specific lead–lag dependencies in a prewhitened innovation space.
Across 16 real-world datasets from four domains, PRELUDE achieves the best MSE in 23 of 24 short-horizon and air-quality settings.
It reduces average MSE by 6.1% versus the strongest baseline.

papers.abstract: Conditional generative modeling with limited target data can benefit from representations learned in a related source population. We develop a transfer learning framework for conditional flow matching that accommodates distinct source and target response distributions and dimensions. Two procedures exploit a representation learned from source data: TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head with the representation fixed, whereas TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a representation adaptation under a functional anchoring penalty. For explicit neural network classes, we establish bounds on conditional squared Wasserstein risk that account for source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration. When the source representation admits a smooth correction, adaptation replaces the frozen mismatch contribution by the cost of learning the correction and a controllable regularization bias. An information lower bound identifies regimes in which adaptation attains a strictly faster conditional squared Wasserstein risk rate than any generator restricted to the frozen context information. We also develop independent validation procedure for selecting among fitted conditional generators. We show that the selection procedure satisfies an oracle inequality, and the switching rule guarantees, with high probability, no increase in conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator. Simulations and real data applications illustrate the gains from our proposed methods and the effectiveness of target validation in guarding against negative transfer.
authors: Yian Huang, Jian Huang
bullets: Addresses conditional generative modeling when target data are scarce and source and target response spaces may differ.
TFM-Freeze estimates a target velocity head while keeping the source representation fixed; TFM-Adapt jointly learns the head and a regularized representation correction.
Derives conditional squared Wasserstein risk bounds covering source estimation, target fitting, representation mismatch, and numerical integration.
Shows adaptation can achieve faster risk rates than generators limited to frozen context information when the source representation has a smooth correction.

A target-validation and switching procedure has an oracle guarantee and can avoid increasing conditional energy risk relative to a target-only generator; simulations and real-data applications demonstrate practical gains.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in flow-matching Transformers have greatly improved Text-to-Image (T2I) and Text-to-Video (T2V) generation, but unconstrained generation risks producing illegal or unethical content. Safety alignment must therefore suppress unsafe content while preserving legitimate generation. A concept's safety depends on context: a knife used for cooking is safe, whereas its use in violence is harmful. Yet most concept erasure methods indiscriminately suppress static, isolated representations, overlooking evolving semantic interactions. Consequently, safe scenes containing potentially sensitive terms may be unintentionally suppressed, compromising generation quality. To address this, we propose Dynamic Graph Semantic Recomposition (DGSR), which dynamically constructs and updates a semantic interaction graph from evolving text visual states during sampling. Context aware graph reasoning captures semantic dependencies, while paired safe/unsafe supervision distinguishes harmful from legitimate interactions, enabling precise identification of and selective intervention on high risk semantic relationships while preserving benign semantics. DGSR freezes the pretrained backbone and supports both image and video generation. Experiments show that DGSR achieves the lowest Attack Success Rate (ASR) in 10 of 12 T2I evaluations and reduces the average T2V unsafe frame rate by 41.2\% relative to the strongest baseline, while maintaining high generation fidelity and temporal consistency.
authors: Qinghui Gong, Jinshan Lai, Xunlei Chen, Hua Meng, Zhengchun Zhou
bullets: Static concept erasure can over-suppress safe scenes because a concept’s safety depends on its context and interactions.
DGSR dynamically builds and updates a semantic interaction graph during sampling from evolving text-visual states.
Context-aware graph reasoning and paired safe/unsafe supervision enable selective intervention on high-risk relationships.
The method achieves the lowest attack success rate in 10 of 12 T2I evaluations and reduces average unsafe T2V frame rate by 41.2% versus the strongest baseline.
It maintains high generation fidelity and temporal consistency while freezing the pretrained backbone.

papers.abstract: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.
authors: Hengyuan Cao, Biao Gong, Guoshan Lu, Qiyuan Zhang, Lin Liu, Yiding Tian, Yilei Jiang, Yuxin Ma, Chengzhang Wu, Kun Chen, Yiqian Xie, Ting Liu, Xin Zheng, Xijun Gu, Tianren Ma, Jiancheng Pan, Chi Zhang, Xuzhe Zheng, Siyi Li, Zhenzhong Lan
bullets: The Reciprocal World Model treats cognition and physical reality as equally fundamental components of an interactive world.
Its Intent module handles interaction reasoning and participation decisions, while Realization produces coherent audio-visual responses.
Chunk-specific conditions, synchronization tokens, and causal attention masks coordinate both modules without access to future inputs.
Dual rollout distillation reduces distribution shift by training on generated intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories.
Duo supports spontaneous conversation, interruptions, object sharing, virtual-scene manipulation, and audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls.

papers.abstract: Expert review of surgical videos is essential for surgical training but labor-intensive, motivating AI-assisted skill assessment to provide feedback at scale. Although surgical assessment rubrics may use different language to describe similar skills, existing automated methods commonly predict predefined skill levels or numerical scores tied to fixed rubrics, limiting their ability to transfer across semantically equivalent assessment criteria. We propose Predictive Rubric Alignment (PRA), a joint embedding prediction approach that scores surgical videos using natural-language descriptions of skill levels. Rather than matching level probabilities, PRA predicts a rater-weighted combination of skill-level description embeddings. Adjacent description features define a score-parameterized path, and the predicted embedding is projected onto this path to read the score. We introduce two variants: \textit{PRA-item}, which uses learned queries for predefined assessment items, and \textit{PRA-cond}, which generates queries from textual item names to enable assessment of unseen items without retraining. On AIxSuture, a dataset of expert-rated suturing videos, PRA outperforms published baselines in skill classification. We further evaluate zero-shot transfer to the smaller surgical skill assessment benchmark JIGSAWS. Trained on only two AIxSuture rubric items, PRA-cond assesses unseen JIGSAWS items without further training, yielding positive score correlations and greater Grad-CAM overlap with instruments and suture than a description-matching baseline. These results support predictive rubric alignment as a promising direction for flexible and explainable automated surgical skill assessment.
authors: Jiajun Cheng, Haidar M. Abdul-Muhsin, Juha Choi, Shan Lin
bullets: Addresses the limited cross-rubric transfer of methods tied to fixed skill levels or numerical scores.
Predicts a rater-weighted embedding of skill-level descriptions and projects it onto a score-parameterized path.
PRA-item uses learned queries for known items, while PRA-cond generates queries from item names for unseen items.
Outperforms published baselines on skill classification using AIxSuture.
Zero-shot transfer to JIGSAWS yields positive score correlations and better visual alignment with instruments and sutures than description matching.

The rater-weighted target τi combines level-description features, and SIGReg regularizes video and description features. At inference, path projection converts hv(zi) into a score.

papers.abstract: Quadrupedal mobile manipulators can extend their manipulation workspace by coordinating the mounted arm with the mobile base. At the task level, short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories provide an interface for specifying the desired manipulation motion without prescribing how it should be realized by the arm and base. However, executing such trajectories remains challenging because the controller must determine when and how the base should move, and this decision depends on the mounted-arm morphology. We therefore present PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical controller that takes an EE trajectory as the sole task-level motion command and generates coordinated arm--base motions across four families of 6-DoF mounted arms, with extended-reach trajectories beyond the initial fixed-base reach. Within PolyMorphWBC, a trajectory-conditioned coordinator determines the base motion from previewed EE targets, while arm-specific Inverse Kinematics (IK) tracks the current target, and a frozen locomotion backend executes the resulting motion. Cross-arm reuse is enabled by a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF)-derived morphology conditioning, together with online residual-wrench feedback. We train PolyMorphWBC on procedurally generated arms and structured trajectories within and beyond fixed-base reach. In IsaacLab, it achieves 93.95% completion with 2.30cm position error and 4.81{\deg} orientation error on held-out trajectories and arm morphologies. In MuJoCo evaluation against UMI-on-Legs, PolyMorphWBC reduces EE position error by 69--72% and orientation error by 91--97% across four within- and extended-reach trajectories. On a physical Go2--ARX5 system, we demonstrate language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place using EE trajectories from pi_0 without vision-language-action (VLA)-generated base commands.
authors: Heng Li, Yang Li, Yifan Duan, Ren Fang, Matao Duan, Wenhao Yu, Lu Zhang, Jianmin Ji, Yanyong Zhang
bullets: Uses an end-effector trajectory as the sole task-level command, avoiding explicit base-motion planning.
A trajectory-conditioned coordinator selects base motion from previewed targets, while arm-specific IK tracks the current target.
URDF-derived morphology conditioning and residual-wrench feedback support reuse across four families of 6-DoF arms.
Achieves 93.95% completion in IsaacLab with 2.30 cm position and 4.81° orientation error on held-out arms and trajectories.
Demonstrated language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place on a physical Go2–ARX5 system without VLA-generated base commands.

papers.abstract: When robots interact with elastic surfaces such as mattresses and trampolines, changes in loading cause the surfaces to deform and rebound, altering subsequent contact locations and forces. We present Elastra, a simulation framework for modeling this interaction and supporting the training and evaluation of robot control policies. Elastra represents each surface using elements that move only vertically, with elastic connections and damping to model deformation and recovery. Contact forces drive surface motion, and the updated surface geometry is used to compute subsequent contact forces. We systematically validate our simulations against an independent implementation and a real mattress load curve. We further use Elastra to train the Unitree G1 humanoid to stand up on mattresses and trampolines. Using the pretrained HoST policy and ProtoMotions motion tracker as original controllers, we train residual policies through reinforcement learning to add corrections to their joint targets. Adding these residual policies increases the success rate with HoST from 44.1\% to 72.5\%, and from 55\% to 89\% on the trampoline. With ProtoMotions, the success rate increases from 19.0\% to 45.0\% for initial poses not encountered during training. The code and video are available on https://github.com/yichg/elastra.
authors: Youran Sun, Chugang Yi, Xingyu Ren, Haizhao Yang
bullets: Models surfaces as vertically moving elastic-damped elements whose deformation updates future contact forces.
Validates the simulation against an independent implementation and a real mattress load curve.
Uses reinforcement-learned residual policies to correct pretrained HoST and ProtoMotions controllers.
Improves reported standing success for HoST from 44.1% to 72.5% on mattresses and from 55% to 89% on trampolines.
Also improves ProtoMotions success from 19.0% to 45.0% on initial poses not seen during training.

papers.abstract: Generating videos that faithfully convey intended semantics while remaining memorable to viewers is valuable for applications such as advertising, education, and storytelling. However, memorability-oriented text-to-video generation remains underexplored, as human memory involves complex neural processes that are difficult to model and translate into generation guidance. In this paper, we propose MemCrafter, brain-informed approach that enhances video memorability through iteratively agentic prompt refinement. The agentic framework contains two key components. First, we construct a cortical region-based neuro-memorability signal that predicts video memorability from estimated neural responses, providing both an optimization objective and interpretable region-level information. Second, we develop a sensitivity-aware feedback module, motivated by a conceptual sensitivity analysis of the optimization objective, to derive actionable guidance for prompt refinement while preserving semantic fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MemCrafter consistently improves predicted video memorability while maintaining semantic alignment and perceptual quality.
authors: Shengqi Dang, Yi He, Jiaying Lei, Feilin Han, Nan Cao
bullets: Addresses the underexplored challenge of generating videos that are both semantically faithful and memorable.
Builds a cortical-region-based neuro-memorability signal from estimated neural responses.
Uses the signal as an optimization objective with interpretable region-level information.
Introduces sensitivity-aware feedback to provide actionable prompt refinements while preserving semantics.
Experiments show consistent gains in predicted memorability alongside maintained semantic alignment and perceptual quality.

papers.abstract: Generating whole-body gestures that are simultaneously rhythmically synchronized with speech audio and semantically aligned with text descriptions is a fundamental challenge in embodied AI and social robotics. We tackle this Audio-Text-to-Motion (AT2M) problem by composing two independently-trained diffusion models at inference time and refine bias in joint inference by modeling the copula score $s_I$. A rigorous theoretical analysis reveals that naive epsilon blending corresponds to a Product-of-Experts formulation that omits the copula score $s_I$: the cross-modal interaction between audio and text that neither marginal model can capture. We propose CFGComposer: a jointly-trained AT2M diffusion model that estimates $s_I$ via a CFG analogy and injects it as an $\epsilon$-space correction. Experiments on BEAT demonstrate best-in-class semantic fidelity (SRGR $0.9916$, FID $27.18$) with GT-level beat alignment (BA $0.1826$ vs. GT $0.1743$), and 76-83% win rate in blind pairwise human evaluation against all prior methods. Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid confirms direct sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Pengyang Shi, Jinlu Zhang, Chunze Lin, Yizhou Wang, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses Audio-Text-to-Motion generation for whole-body gestures in embodied AI and social robotics.
Shows that naive epsilon blending acts as a Product-of-Experts and misses cross-modal audio–text interactions.
Estimates the missing copula score using a jointly trained diffusion model and injects it as an epsilon-space correction.
On BEAT, reports SRGR 0.9916, FID 27.18, and near-ground-truth beat alignment (BA 0.1826 vs. 0.1743).
Human evaluations favored CFGComposer in 76–83% of pairwise comparisons; deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrated sim-to-real transfer.

papers.abstract: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.
authors: Juntao Xu, Qichai Zhao, Rui Sun, Zhouyang Jiang, Shiwei Wu, Zhi Li, Kaisheng Ma, Yu Liu
bullets: Image–question positional relationships can impair visual access even when the image remains in context.
VPR shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing.
The training-free method works directly on the KV cache without attention-map extraction or extra forward passes.
Static VPR improved 97 of 100 model–task scores across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks.
It increased attention to answer-relevant image regions with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies.

papers.abstract: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.
authors: Chenhui Zhao, Akshay Rao, Akhil Kondepudi, Yiwei Lyu, Xinhai Hou, Rikhil Seshadri, Cheng Jiang, Soumyanil Banerjee, Rushikesh Joshi, Samir Harake, Ashok Srinivasan, Shruti Mishra, Francisco Rivas-Rodriguez, Seunghong Rhee, Nathaniel Roddenberry, Neeraj Chaudhary, Zach Wilseck, Paul Park, Honglak Lee, Vikas Gulani, Aditya Pandey, Todd Hollon
bullets: Addresses the gap between narrow medical AI tools and general-purpose models lacking private clinical imaging expertise.
Interprets complex neuroimaging examinations and communicates findings through natural-language conversation.
Diagnoses, localizes, and describes abnormalities; generates comprehensive radiology reports and assesses disease progression across serial exams.
Outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models across internal and international datasets, including resistance to misleading clinical assumptions.
Scope: focused on neuroimaging and trained on routine clinical-care data; the abstract does not specify detailed evaluation metrics or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 1 | Overview of Neuro-VL training data, workflow, and evaluation. a, We curated the largest neuroimaging dataset to date, containing nearly 1 million studies collected from 450,000 patients, comprising 10 million volumetric scans. The dataset captures the full spectrum of neurological pathology, including neoplastic, vascular, infectious, degenerative, traumatic, and other conditions. b, Neuro-VL was trained to generate robust radiological interpretations of neuroimaging accompanied by an auditable reasoning trace. To reason over image and language input, Neuro-VL integrates a visual encoder with an LLM through a vision-language connector (not shown). The visual encoder incorporates a hierarchical attention mechanism inspired by the inherent structure of neuroimaging data and is pretrained using radiology reports, enabling it to extract semantically rich visual features from complex neuroimaging studies. c, We evaluated Neuro-VL across internal health-system cohorts and 24 international public datasets spanning 21 countries. This evaluation covered diverse tasks, including localization, feature description, diagnosis, report generation, and longitudinal disease monitoring, as well as a comprehensive red-teaming evaluation.

Figure 3 | Neuro-VL for longitudinal disease monitoring. a, Schematic of longitudinal neuroimaging interpretation for disease monitoring. Neuro-VL can integrate imaging findings across multiple time points to assess tumor recurrence following treatment. b, Performance of Neuro-VL-Longitudinal, GPT-5.4, and Gemma 4 on change characterization (n=718), disease trajectory assessment (n=710), and intervention characterization (n=132). Results are mean accuracy with 95% CIs. 𝑃 values compare Neuro-VL with the highest-scoring comparator. c, Performance of Neuro-VL-Longitudinal compared with GPT-5.4 and Gemma 4 on longitudinal report generation (n=734). Results are proportions of pairwise preferences relative to the reference radiologist report as determined by NeuroJudge, an expert-validated LLM-based evaluator. d, Neuro-VL interpreting a pair of brain MRI studies acquired 6 months apart. Neuro-VL identifies disease progression characterized by increased tumor burden, new nodular enhancement, extensive surrounding edema, and new mass effect with midline shift.

papers.abstract: Open-world navigation requires a robot to locate a user-specified target in an indoor scene under open-vocabulary queries. Realistic indoor environments are semi-static: walls and furniture largely persist while smaller objects move, relocate, or vanish between visits. Prior-map systems answer queries from object poses recorded at reconstruction time, which expire as soon as objects move, whereas online methods re-derive where to look from current observations every few steps, often through expensive calls to a vision--language model. Assuming that walls and large furniture do not move, we keep their map to plan paths, but use a target--furniture co-occurrence prior to decide where to search. We present PreNav, an ObjectNav framework on semi-static environments. Rather than invoking a vision-language model at each step, PreNav generates a single global search reference before the robot moves: an LLM converts target--furniture co-occurrence into a spatial prior, a conditional diffusion model turns that prior and the persistent structure into an ordered centerline with a band around it, and the robot approaches the target once it is detected online. Experiments on a Gibson ObjectNav benchmark show that PreNav outperforms a strong online baseline under matched structural priors, using a generator trained only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes and applied to floor-level Gibson without fine-tuning. Real-world experiments under object relocation and open-vocabulary queries further validate the approach.
authors: Yuxuan Feng, Fujing Xie, S\"oren Schwertfeger, Hermann Blum
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between stale object maps and costly step-by-step vision–language-model planning when objects move.
Keeps persistent walls and large furniture for navigation while using target–furniture co-occurrence to predict where to search.
An LLM creates a spatial prior, and a conditional diffusion model converts it into an ordered centerline with a search band before movement begins.
Experiments on Gibson show improved performance over a matched online baseline, despite training only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes without fine-tuning.
Real-world tests with relocated objects and open-vocabulary queries support the method’s practical validity.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video world models are compared and chosen as components for robot learning largely by future-prediction scores. On its own, such a score cannot be read as evidence of prediction, because it mixes encoder quality, the near future's resemblance to the recent past, and the predictor's own contribution. We separate the three with a matched control. On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.
authors: Animesh Maheshwari
bullets: A matched control separates encoder quality, persistence of recent visual context, and the predictor’s contribution.
Across 27,000 household-video future-retrieval trials, models select the true continuation among 11 candidates.
Within V-JEPA, predictor gains vary substantially: +0.291 for V-JEPA 2.1 versus +0.03–+0.04 for V-JEPA 2.
Across five models, predictor contributions range from positive to negative; negative results occur for action-conditioned models tested outside their training regime.
The study recommends reporting the score gap from persistence; downstream planning or control usefulness requires separate evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a persistence-control evaluation for future-prediction scores of pretrained video world models, directly relevant to world-model assessment.
papers.title: Prediction or Persistence? What Future-Prediction Scores Miss About World Models
papers.tldr: Future-prediction scores can reflect persistence and encoder quality rather than genuine prediction, so they should be reported against a matched persistence baseline.

papers.abstract: Agentic video-reasoning frameworks iteratively explore a video, choosing what to observe based on the query and evidence gathered so far. Existing methods are typically evaluated with different backbones, preprocessing pipelines, and computational budgets, making it difficult to determine which components actually drive performance, how much they cost, and whether agentic inference is preferable to native video reasoning in the first place. We conduct a controlled evaluation of a diverse set of recent agentic video-reasoning systems across two strong contemporary backbones, with explicit token and monetary-cost accounting. Across Gemini 3 Flash and Gemma 4, most existing agentic frameworks fail to consistently improve over native video inference and often increase computational cost. We investigate two primary questions: (1) How much agentic framework complexity is necessary for effective video reasoning? (2) When, if at all, is agentic video reasoning preferable to just using the backbone directly? To answer the first question, we introduce a deliberately minimal Active Exploration Baseline and show that it remains competitive with substantially more elaborate agents. We then propose targeted extensions to this baseline, yielding SAVE (Simple Agentic Video Explorer). SAVE outperforms all evaluated prior agentic methods in five of six backbone-benchmark settings. Turning to the second question, our results indicate that the advantage of agentic exploration grows when dense processing would otherwise represent answer-relevant events too sparsely, particularly for long videos and temporally concentrated evidence. Overall, our results suggest that agentic video reasoning should favor simple frameworks over increasingly elaborate pipelines and focus primarily on long-form video, where selective evidence acquisition offers the clearest advantage over native inference.
authors: Tymoteusz Wilk, Sergey Prokudin, Xi Wang
bullets: Existing agentic video-reasoning systems often add computational cost without consistently improving over direct native video inference.
The study provides a controlled comparison across two contemporary backbones with explicit token and monetary-cost accounting.
A minimal Active Exploration Baseline remains competitive with substantially more elaborate agents.
SAVE extends this baseline and outperforms evaluated prior agentic methods in five of six backbone–benchmark settings.
Agentic exploration is most beneficial when dense processing sparsely represents answer-relevant events, particularly in long videos.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Example of both Gemini 3 Flash Native and SAVE answering a question from Minerva (question #34). No timestamp is given in the question, so both methods first have to find the relevant moment in the video. SAVE employs a multi-step search strategy: First, it queries the whole video at low granularity, subsequently isolates the crucial segment from the rest of the video and answers the question correctly. Gemini’s native video processing instead passes the whole video into the model at a higher granularity than SAVE, but nonetheless fails to answer the question correctly, as fine, crucial details get lost in the large amount of irrelevant context passed into the model.

Figure 1: SAVE exploring Minerva video. A video-wide query locates Game 4 (five of 15 sampled frames shown). A focused query distinguishes Ian’s opening EKE from Mack’s response AXE, which the transcript also confirms. SAVE stops with the correct answer.

Figure 7: Example of both Gemini 3 Flash Native and SAVE answering a question from Minerva (question #1357). In this case, two moments from the video are crucial to answering the question. Neither timestamp is given in the question. SAVE employs a multi-step search strategy: First, it queries the whole video at low granularity and subsequently isolates the first crucial segment from the rest of the video. After having correctly interpreted the first relevant segment, it proceeds to search for the second relevant segment later in the video. After 6 iterations, the second relevant moment is found and SAVE answers the question correctly. Gemini’s native video processing instead passes the whole video into the model, manages to correctly identify the first moment, but the second moment is lost among the large amount of irrelevant visual context presented to the model.

Figure 5: Example of both Gemini 3 Flash Native and SAVE answering a question from Minerva (question #24). In this example a specific timestamp is directly given in the question. Gemini simply downsamples the whole video to 1 FPS and therefore has no possibility of efficiently querying only the relevant segment. SAVE uses its range query to specifically observe the relevant part at high granularity and correctly answers the question.

Figure 4: Example of both Gemini 3 Flash Native and SAVE answering a question from Minerva (question #7). In this example a specific timestamp is directly given in the question. Gemini simply downsamples the whole video to 1 FPS and therefore has no possibility of efficiently querying only the relevant segment. SAVE uses its range query to specifically observe the relevant part at high granularity and correctly answers the question.

Bars show accuracy; n denotes the number of samples in each bin.

papers.selection_reason: Studies agentic video-reasoning frameworks and proposes a simple active-exploration baseline for long-form video understanding.
papers.title: SAVE: Less is More in Agentic Video Reasoning
papers.tldr: SAVE shows that simple, selective video exploration can outperform complex agentic frameworks, especially for long videos with temporally concentrated evidence.

papers.abstract: Real-world robot imitation learning is often limited by the cost of collecting physical demonstrations, which typically yield only one action label per visited state. We present CrowdMAPS, a web-based crowdsourcing paradigm for augmenting real-robot datasets with Multiple Actions per State (MAPS). After or during standard robot data collection, CrowdMAPS distributes visited robot states to remote annotators through a web-based 3D interface, where they specify alternative valid actions without requiring access to physical robot hardware. This expands robot datasets along a complementary "width" dimension--by increasing the number of actions per visited state--rather than only by collecting more trajectories. We evaluate CrowdMAPS using keyframe-centric goal-pose annotations supplied by non-expert annotators and train imitation policies on the resulting MAPS data. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, increasing MAPS width from one to ten actions per state improves sample efficiency and increases average success rates by 35.6 percentage points for keypose policies and 33.0 percentage points for trajectory policies. These results show that software-mediated human annotations can augment physical robot data to afford denser supervision, establishing CrowdMAPS as a scalable digital layer for real-robot data collection.
authors: Yilong Song, Harshvardhan Chandirasekar, Karthik Desingh, Chen Zhu-Tian
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited action diversity of physical robot demonstrations.
Remote annotators provide alternative actions for visited robot states without using robot hardware.
Expands datasets in “width” by adding actions per state rather than collecting more trajectories.
Across five real-world manipulation tasks, increasing actions per state from 1 to 10 improved average success by 35.6 percentage points for keypose policies and 33.0 points for trajectory policies.
Uses non-expert, keyframe-centric goal-pose annotations to provide denser supervision.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of multimodal large language models, but answer accuracy only partly reflects its effect. Pruning can change the probabilities of alternative response tokens even when greedy answers remain correct and unchanged. We compare full and pruned response distributions under shared reference prefixes. Average predictive drift grows with compression on fixed correctly answered samples. Separate analyses associate larger drift with more confidence-decision disagreements and sampling failures. We propose DiFiT (Distribution-Fidelity-guided Token pruning) to learn discrete selection from reference answers and full-token response distributions. Dual-View Distillation matches probabilities across the vocabulary, while answer supervision supports task quality. A learned scorer and differentiable Top-$K$ learn which visual evidence to retain. A multi-budget mask objective supports different retention ratios through one shared ranking over a frozen model. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, DiFiT reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% relative to FastV at 10% retention on four-task greedy-correct controls. It preserves 98.74% of baseline performance on MME at 30% retention.
authors: Jingyuan Zhang, Nihao Niu, Xinyang Lv, Beibei Han, Xiaoyun Wang, Yanning Hou, Ke Xu
bullets: Visual token pruning can alter alternative-token probabilities even when greedy answers stay unchanged.
DiFiT learns which visual tokens to retain using full-model response distributions and reference-answer supervision.
Dual-View Distillation aligns vocabulary-level probabilities, while differentiable Top-K selection supports discrete pruning.
A shared ranking supports multiple retention budgets with one frozen model.
On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it reduces sampling-induced negative flips by 30.3% versus FastV at 10% retention and preserves 98.74% of baseline MME performance at 30% retention.

papers.selection_reason: Presents visual token pruning for multimodal LLMs guided by distribution fidelity, directly fitting token pruning and multimodal LLM interests.
papers.title: DiFiT: Distribution-Fidelity-guided Visual Token Pruning for Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: DiFiT prunes visual tokens for multimodal LLMs while preserving response distributions, reducing sampling errors under aggressive compression.

papers.abstract: 6-DOF pose estimation of large and heavy industrial objects, such as large piping systems in shipyards and structural components in petrochemical plants, remains relatively underexplored in robotic perception. Repeatedly repositioning large objects is physically and spatially demanding, making it difficult to acquire real training data with sufficient pose diversity. Synthetic data offer a scalable alternative, but faithfully reproducing real RGB-D observations, particularly the structured measurement errors of real depth sensors, remains difficult. We propose MiniPose, a practical pipeline for miniature-based real RGB-D data collection that addresses both the data-acquisition burden and the sim-to-real gap. We fabricate a scaled-down replica and capture RGB-D data of it in diverse poses using a real RGB-D camera. RGB images are used directly, while depth maps are converted to a geometrically consistent representation of the full-scale object via a simple inverse scaling transformation. This allows training to incorporate real appearance and sensor measurement characteristics that are difficult to reproduce using synthetic data alone. To examine whether the benefit depends on a particular network, we evaluate two RGB-D pose estimators with different formulations, PVN3D and RDPN6D. Mixing at most 1,000 miniature images per pipe type, less than 10\% of the training data, with 10,000 synthetic images improves the mean ADD-S AUC across pipe types over synthetic-only training for both estimators. A comparison with training on full-scale real data further suggests that miniature data can serve as a proxy where full-scale collection is difficult, reducing the data-collection burden for large industrial objects.
authors: Hyunjun Kim, Youngjin Seo, Sungwon Seo, Jiyou Shin, Kunwoo Kim, Chanyong Park, Hyungpil Moon
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of physically repositioning large objects to obtain diverse real training poses.
Captures miniature RGB-D observations with a real sensor, using RGB directly and inversely scaling depth to represent the full-scale object.
Combining up to 1,000 miniature images per pipe type with 10,000 synthetic images improves mean ADD-S AUC over synthetic-only training for both PVN3D and RDPN6D.
Results suggest miniature data can proxy full-scale real data while reducing collection effort.
Scope: evaluated on large industrial pipe types and two RGB-D pose estimators.

The scale equivalence between the miniature and the full-scale object is illustrated (right).

Green boxes denote the ground truth, while red and blue boxes show the inference results of the model trained on simulation data only (Simulation Only) and on simulation and miniature data (Ours), respectively. papers.abstract: Deep neural networks typically realize dense computation by propagating information through all intermediate channels, while many approximation methods rank and retain individual computational components. We ask whether dense neural computation can instead be represented exactly as an expectation over a combinatorial state space, and approximated by evaluating only its most probable configurations. We introduce a novel probabilistic state-space framework for Transformer MLPs. The framework partitions the intermediate dimension into channel groups, defines an input-dependent distribution over binary inclusion states, and uses importance-corrected masked outputs such that the full expectation exactly recovers the dense MLP output. The key algorithmic novelty is NORDER-II, which enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without constructing or sorting the exponentially large state space. Truncating this ordering yields an anytime approximation governed by cumulative probability mass and a state budget. On Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, NORDER-II at a state budget of B=2048 achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output approximation accuracy, compared with 76.9% and 79.8% for Channel Top-k. When the first, middle, and last MLP layers are approximated jointly, WikiText-2 perplexity remains within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference. Relative to expected-count Grouped Top-k, NORDER-II yields 82.6% to 126.4% relative accuracy gains with only 0.18% to 0.19% additional local analytic FLOPs. These results establish the significance of joint-state structure beyond atomic salience and point to a new paradigm for neural computation: dense layers can be viewed as structured probabilistic inference over combinatorial computational states. This framework opens a path toward adaptive, probability-mass-controlled computation in pretrained neural networks.
authors: Victor O. K. Li, Yang Han, Jacqueline C. K. Lam
bullets: Partitions MLP channels into groups and defines input-dependent binary inclusion states with importance-corrected outputs.
NORDER-II enumerates complete joint states in decreasing probability without materializing the exponential state space.
At budget B=2048, it achieves 92.4% and 93.8% MLP-output accuracy on Llama-3.2-1B and Gemma-2-2B, outperforming Channel Top-k.
Joint approximation of selected MLP layers keeps WikiText-2 perplexity within 0.06% and 0.54% of dense inference.
Results support probability-mass-controlled, adaptive computation based on joint-state structure rather than individual channel salience.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) object tracking faces modality-induced appearance discrepancies and abrupt target-position shifts that can arise from modality switching, UAV motion, and inter-sensor offsets. Although existing methods model modality and spatial variations, they primarily rely on offline representation learning and offer limited localization-oriented adaptation during testing. To address these challenges, we propose Test-Time Selective Adaptation with Token Shift (TSAT), which derives spatial and temporal adaptation signals from unlabeled test sequences for online optimization. Specifically, we design a controllable token shift auxiliary task, which imposes explicit spatial correspondence between predefined token translations and resultant localization offsets, generating stable annotation-free spatial adaptation signals. Furthermore, we introduce a temporal backward prediction auxiliary task to exploit frame-wise temporal dependencies, effectively mitigating cumulative localization errors in continuous tracking. To suppress interference from unreliable tracking samples, we develop a reliability-aware update gating strategy to screen valid adaptation signals and stabilize online parameter updates. Experiments on CM-UOT demonstrate that TSAT achieves state-of-the-art performance against existing test-time adaptation methods, exhibiting superior robustness under frequent modality switching and severe spatial displacement. Experiments across tracking frameworks and datasets further validate the effectiveness and generalization capability of TSAT.
authors: Yun Xiao, Hailong Ye, Zhicheng Zhao, Lei Liu, Amir Hussain
bullets: Addresses appearance discrepancies and abrupt target shifts caused by modality switching, UAV motion, and sensor offsets.
Uses a controllable token-shift auxiliary task to generate annotation-free spatial localization signals.
Adds temporal backward prediction to exploit frame dependencies and reduce cumulative localization errors.
Applies reliability-aware update gating to exclude unreliable samples during online adaptation.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on CM-UOT and effectiveness across tracking frameworks and datasets, especially under frequent switching and severe displacement.

papers.abstract: Modern machine learning models for global weather forecasting achieve remarkable predictive accuracy, yet they frequently produce states that violate fundamental physical laws, including conservation of mass, hydrostatic balance, or spectral energy scaling. We term these outputs physical hallucinations and propose PhysXAI, a rigorous diagnostic framework that detects, localises, and attributes such inconsistencies. Unlike existing post-hoc metric suites, PhysXAI is a learnable system that explicitly decouples forecast error from physical plausibility. We formalise the problem through a novel joint condition on numerical and physical residuals, and introduce a multi-branch encoder that extracts representations from conservation, dynamical, spectral, cross-variable, and spatiotemporal residuals. A key innovation is a physics-consistency contrastive learning objective, which we theoretically show the latent representation to be approximately isometric to the physical residual space, ensuring that diagnostic decisions remain grounded in physically meaningful deviations. We further derive an adaptive multi-objective loss with gradient-based weighting to balance competing diagnostic objectives. The framework produces spatially resolved hallucination maps, violation-type classifications, and calibrated Bayesian uncertainty, enabling both detection and interpretable attribution of physical inconsistencies. We conduct a comprehensive comparative evaluation of PhysXAI across ERA5, WeatherBench 2, and MERRA-2, using forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and NeuralGCM, with Python-written code and a fully reproducible experimental protocol. Our theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation establish PhysXAI as a principled framework for diagnosing physical hallucinations and advancing trustworthy AI for weather forecasting.
authors: Anjan Mahapatra, Nikhil Raj
bullets: Targets violations of mass conservation, hydrostatic balance, spectral energy scaling, and other physical constraints.
Decouples forecast-error assessment from physical plausibility using joint numerical–physical residual conditions.
Combines residual representations across conservation, dynamics, spectra, variables, and space–time with contrastive learning and adaptive multi-objective weighting.
Produces spatial hallucination maps, violation-type classifications, and calibrated Bayesian uncertainty for attribution.
Evaluated across ERA5, WeatherBench 2, and MERRA-2 forecasts from GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and NeuralGCM; the abstract reports theoretical and empirical validation but no specific numerical results.

papers.abstract: Intelligent fault diagnosis models are typically developed for a single machine under a specific set of operating conditions, such that each new machine or condition requires retraining from scratch. This one-machine-one-model paradigm scales poorly. Although transfer learning and domain generalization can reduce the labeling burden, they primarily seek domain-invariant commonality, potentially discarding machine-specific characteristics that are critical for diagnosis. This paper proposes TFC-MMFD, a time-frequency-condition multimodal fusion foundation model for rotating-machinery fault diagnosis under multi-element heterogeneous scenarios. Statistical indicators, time-frequency images, vibration sequences, and textual machine and condition descriptions are tokenized into a unified language-like space, allowing inputs of different physical origin to be represented as a single sequence. A LLaMA backbone, together with cross-modal bidirectional attention and a Q-Former, then distills this sequence into fault-mode queries. Diagnosis is performed by matching these queries against natural-language fault-mode anchors rather than fixed class indices, while regression-adversarial condition disentanglement and condition-conditioned masked pre-training improve robustness to changing conditions. Across four progressive tasks on ten public bearing datasets spanning diverse bearing types, speeds, and loads, TFC-MMFD attains 99.40% accuracy and 99.16% macro-F1, maintains over 80% accuracy on most interpolated unseen conditions without adaptation, and improves from 20.26% to 95.63% accuracy on an unseen machine with only five labeled samples per class. It outperforms the strongest of eight domain-generalization baselines by 10.57 percentage points and compares favorably with a recent bearing foundation model while using less than half of its fine-tuning data.
authors: Xinyu Zou, Jian Ma, Liang Ma, Chen Lu, Tao Peng, Yingjie Li

Condition disentanglement and condition-conditioned masked pre-training improve robustness to changing and unseen operating conditions.
Across ten public bearing datasets, reports 99.40% accuracy and 99.16% macro-F1; it also reaches 95.63% accuracy on an unseen machine using five labeled samples per class.
