papers.abstract: Humanity has long sought to explain natural phenomena. Reliable prediction of experimental outcomes is a central test of our understanding of the processes that produce them. If artificial general intelligence (AGI) is to surpass human scientific capabilities, it must also predict experimental outcomes more reliably than humans. Such capabilities could accelerate scientific discovery across disciplines, help address humanity's most pressing challenges, and improve human well-being. We introduce Science Prediction Universe (SPU), a benchmark of hidden experimental outcomes with 100 public verified tasks from chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine, and 16 private tasks from unpublished wet-lab experiments. Given an experimental setup and candidate conditions, an agent works with any resources it needs to rank the candidates by a measured outcome. We evaluate thirteen agent configurations spanning twelve frontier models across two harnesses (Codex and Claude Code). Current agents remain far from saturating wet-lab outcome prediction, with substantial performance disparities across models: on the public benchmark, configurations separate into two distinct tiers, with task-adjusted Spearman correlations ranging from 0.227 for the lowest-performing configuration to 0.478 for the best. Analysis of 1,155 scored public trajectories (227,103 tool calls) suggests that the bottleneck lies in scientific judgment rather than tool execution: agents rely on shared monotone priors, agreeing far more with one another than with experimental reality (0.52 vs. 0.33), and frequently compute trivial physical or chemical proxies that do not influence the final outcome.

Yu, Tong-Yi Zhang, Hao Cheng, Qin Han, Yanye Feng, Chenru Duan, Chuncheng Liu, Yan Liu, Yuchen Gao, Zhao Li, Ronghua Zhang, Tory Xu, Renjian Song, Yaokai Fu

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for LLM agents predicting experimental outcomes, relevant to evaluating frontier language models.
papers.title: Science Prediction Universe
papers.tldr: Science Prediction Universe benchmarks AI agents on predicting hidden wet-lab outcomes and finds that current systems remain substantially unreliable, primarily due to weak scientific judgment rather than tool-use limitations.

papers.abstract: Embodied world models (WMs) are implicit learning systems that predict the next future latent state directly from observations and actions. Unique from other end-to-end learning systems, the dynamics predictor of WMs can simulate the environment's response to alternative actions without physical deployment nor pre-specifying states of the dynamical system. Current metrics focus on the quality of model outputs, e.g., clarity of reconstructions or task success, but fail to assess the fidelity of modeling consequences of counterfactual actions. Inspecting the forced response to action perturbations through sensitivity analysis is one way to audit how well WMs can predict the consequences of counterfactual actions. Deploying WMs on hardware will require new evaluation frameworks to analyze the tradeoffs between state error and accurate sensitivity prediction.
authors: Ayush Gaggar, Jared Berry, Todd D. Murphey
bullets: Existing metrics overlook fidelity to counterfactual action consequences.
Sensitivity analysis can audit model responses to perturbed actions.
Evaluation should assess the tradeoff between state-prediction error and sensitivity accuracy.
The framework is motivated by reliable deployment of world models on physical hardware.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Designing world models will often involve a tradeoff between low state error and low error in predicted action sensitivity. For four example scenarios: a) Structured environments, like open-loop pick and place, only require low state error. b) High accuracy in both action sensitivity and state prediction is only possible when robot motion can be modeled and is repeatable. c) Poor performance in both dimensions is acceptable with effectively unlimited time and compute for non-critical tasks. d) Action sensitivity is more relevant than state error in unstructured, unknown environments, where environmental uncertainty dominates error.

Figure 1: The dynamics predictor of world models uniquely enables roboticists to audit end to end learning systems through observables alone. However, current metrics measure planning utility through one isolated component of the WM stack. Thus, new metrics that evaluate a system’s dynamics fidelity of counterfactual actions are needed.

Figure 2: Current metrics give false signals of planning utility. Left: Visualizing ground truth interactions from an underfit decoder shows planning fidelity and reconstruction accuracy are distinct evaluations. Right: An overfit, brittle action policy shows task performance and planning utility are distinct evaluations.

papers.title: Does Your World Model Know Actions Have Consequences?
papers.tldr: The paper argues that embodied world models should be evaluated on whether they accurately predict the consequences of alternative actions, not just on output quality or task success.

papers.abstract: Frozen vision-language models often match concepts mentioned in a caption without respecting their negation: a query "a kitchen with no toaster" favors an image containing a toaster. Yet these models are substantially stronger at matching affirmative descriptions. We exploit this asymmetry with Negation-Aware Evidence Scoring (NAES), which reformulates negated descriptions into affirmative queries and combines their evidence by caption structure. A lightweight text decomposer, NegSplit, identifies this structure by extracting negated spans and the remaining affirmative context. For captions with an affirmative remainder, NAES matches that content and applies a presence-based correction for the denial. When no affirmative content remains, it queries the denied object's presence and reflects the evidence around a reference to score the negated description. With LAION-2B CLIP, NAES achieves 82.4% accuracy on COCO-MCQ and 93.0% on VOC2007-MCQ, surpassing KTN by 2.9 and 0.9 percentage points; with OpenAI CLIP, it exceeds PeakPatch accuracy by 4.4 and 26.0 points, respectively. NAES also improves negated-description retrieval on COCO and MSR-VTT, with gains extending to SigLIP, SigLIP 2, and larger CLIP encoders. The strongest multiple-choice results use competing descriptions to center and align evidence; retrieval improvements persist without this conditioning. These findings show that explicitly separating affirmative matching from denied-object evidence can substantially improve negation-aware ranking.
authors: Aashish Pokhrel, Tejas Anvekar, Shivanand Venkanna Sheshappanavar
bullets: Addresses CLIP’s tendency to favor images containing objects described as absent.
NegSplit extracts negated spans and remaining affirmative context from captions.
NAES scores affirmative content directly and corrects for the denied object’s presence; fully negated queries use reflected evidence.
Improves multiple-choice accuracy and negated-description retrieval across CLIP-family models and benchmarks, with gains over prior methods reported in the abstract.
Multiple-choice scoring benefits from competing descriptions for evidence alignment, while retrieval gains persist without this conditioning.

Stage 2: frozen CLIP scores positive and hybrid remainders against crop-grounded, candidate-specific image vectors, with a fixed λ = 0.3 presence correction for hybrid options. papers.selection_reason: Focuses on improving negation-aware ranking in frozen CLIP, a multimodal foundation-model behavior.
papers.title: Saying No by Asking Yes: Affirmative Decomposition and Evidence Reflection for Frozen CLIP
papers.tldr: NAES improves frozen CLIP’s understanding of negation by decomposing descriptions into affirmative context and denied-object evidence, then reflecting presence evidence when needed.

papers.abstract: Mechanistic localization does not by itself yield usable control: causal sensitivity may occupy little activation energy, an accurate local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable numeral target may be wrong. We introduce AROMA (Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation), a frozen-VLM control framework separating where to intervene, which geometry and gain to use, how to reach a target, which target to pursue, and when to act. In Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, four dimensions of a causally validated cross-attention head explain 89.82% of cardinality sensitivity but only 9.52% of median activation energy; magnitude-normalized causal subspace actuation converts this mismatch into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy on untouched procedural data by +8.00 pp. Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation (MEA) reaches 81.25% of oracle targets versus 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched step budgets. With target and gate frozen before evaluation, targeted MEA improves the previous frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% on a new natural Stage-2 cohort (N=630; paired p=4.63e-7) and yields 65.741% versus 65.153% over all 7,992 examples while editing only 63 inputs. Prospective routing, replication across heads and models, and comparisons with attribution-steering baselines further characterize each stage, separating localization, actuation, reachability, target quality, and selective deployment as distinct control problems.
authors: Zhaoning Zhang
bullets: Addresses why identifying causally sensitive components alone may not enable reliable finite-scale control.
Uses a frozen VLM framework that separates localization, actuation geometry and gain, target reachability, target selection, and gating.
Magnitude-normalized actuation converts a low-energy causal subspace into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy by 8.00 percentage points on untouched procedural data.
Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation reaches 81.25% of oracle targets, compared with 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched budgets.
On a new natural cohort, targeted actuation improves the frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% while editing only 63 inputs; gains are modest overall.

figures.caption: Figure 7. From low-rank sensitivity to independently confirmed control. (a) Same-α rank-4 CSA severely underactuates; magnitude normalization restores and slightly exceeds whole-head accuracy on the v3 development intervention subset. (b) The learned Top-4 subspace exceeds every one of 20 frozen random rank-4 controls; random mean is 27.18% and random maximum is 30.78%, versus 52.53% for Top-4. (c) After the CSA method is closed, a newly generated v4 confirmation set yields 50.25% baseline, 57.25% whole-head, and 58.25% MN-CSA. (d) MN-CSA obtains 174 repairs and 14 breaks versus 150 repairs and 10 breaks for whole-head, producing 20 additional net repairs.

Figure 8. Utility-aware routing confirms adaptive control within the frozen low-rank candidate family. (a) The router improves over the fold-selected global comparator in grouped OOF development and the frozen global comparator in external validation and the untouched final population; only the last stage is the primary confirmatory test. (b) On the final N = 294, the advantage combines six additional repairs with eleven fewer breaks, yielding 17 router-only versus 0 global-only paired wins. (c–d) The learned policy does not collapse to a single method or gain: it selects identity, MN, and SA and uses every nonzero gain in the frozen grid. Final primary effect: +5.782 pp, 95% CI [+3.401, +8.503] pp, exact McNemar p = 1.53 × 10−5.

Figure 1. AROMA at a glance. Mechanism (top): a frozen VLM exposes a causally validated cross-attention head; its Top-4 sensitivity subspace supports magnitude-normalized MN/SA edits, while WHOLE is an alternative full-head intervention geometry on the same actuator. Policy (bottom): a ground-truth-free gate decides when to act; on gated examples, either a target rule selects which target to pursue and MEA determines how to reach it, or a candidate router selects geometry and gain without an explicit target.

Figure 3. Local projected geometry is quantitatively valid at small scale, but global target control requires iterative re-linearization. (a) Pearson agreement between first-order predicted and realized numeral movement is near-perfect at β = .05 and declines as intervention scale grows. (b) Oracle MEA accumulates reachability as it recomputes the current target–competitor margin and projected gradient. (c) Matched-budget controls under the same realized per-step norms: iterative MEA, a frozen initial target-gradient direction, and activation-aligned control.

Figure 4. Target quality converts controllability into prospectively confirmed deployment utility. (a) Accuracy on the prespecified N = 630 Stage-2 population (+4.286 pp over old Unified; 29:2 paired discordance; exact McNemar p = 4.63×10−7). (b) Repairs and breaks relative to identity. (c) Correct predictions on the 63 frozen APPLY cases under the same gate; the GrAInS minimal port, the counting-adapted GrAInS-inspired comparator, and the constant-zero rule are post-confirmation controls.

Figure 11. Cross-model replication and held-out gain calibration in IDEFICS-9B-Instruct. (a) Independently screened B2H28 shows held-out bidirectional actuator behavior. (b) Sensitivity trace rises monotonically with rank (point labels), but finite causal steering peaks at rank 4 and deteriorates at ranks 8 and 16. (c) On the development-only screen set, larger gain substantially increases balanced low-rank steering; only the top two configurations are carried forward. (d) Independent dev validation selects r = 4, β = 2 before the final cohort is touched. On the untouched final set, the fixed low-rank intervention reaches 79.67% directional consistency in both directions and recovers about 81% of same-run whole-head mean shift. Because β = 2, this is a gain-calibrated, not equal-norm, comparison.

Figure 2. Sensitivity is not activation energy. (a) The top four dimensions explain 89.82% of the uncentered cardinalitysensitivity second moment and 86.78% after centering; both are far above the rank-matched null distribution. (b) The same Top-4 subspace contains little of the pooled activation norm: median ρ = 0.309, corresponding to only 9.52% median projected activation energy. This mismatch predicts why same-α low-rank scaling under-actuates and motivates magnitude normalization.

Figure 15. Natural hierarchical UGR converts complementary action-space capacity into an untouched gain. On the prespecified N = 631 Stage-2 population from a new 8,000-example TallyQA cohort, frozen Unified routing improves over frozen Whole-only routing by +1.902 pp (95% CI [+0.792, +3.170] pp; exact McNemar p = 0.00418; 14:2 paired discordance). The unified candidate oracle adds +6.181 pp over the Whole oracle. The realized policy is sparse (52/631 interventions), increases repairs while reducing breaks, and does not collapse to WHOLE: 48.1% of its non-identity selections use MN or SA.

Figure 12. Transfer separates geometry from deployment policy. (a) Frozen Llama rank-4 geometry retains positive natural-domain utility, though below whole-head control. (b) The synthetic router fails zero-shot on a separate TallyQA set even while the same actuator/action family retains large oracle headroom. (c) Relearning only the lightweight utility map is sample-efficient; K = 500 is frozen as an efficiency elbow before a new confirmation set. (d) HoloCount preserves large oracle headroom while the transferred policy is essentially neutral, exposing a stronger routing/readout boundary.

Figure 6. Frozen procedural confirmation. The synthetic router is frozen before evaluation on the untouched 2,000-example Proc-Count-Causal v3 set. (a) Accuracy increases from 999/2000 = 49.95% to 1161/2000 = 58.05% (+8.10 pp; paired 95% CI [+6.85, +9.40] pp). There are 173 repairs, 11 breaks, and +162 net repairs, with interventions on 32.65% of examples. (b) All prespecified visual conditions improve: dense, +10.25 pp; distractors, +7.25 pp; grid, +12.00 pp; random_sparse, +7.00 pp; and row, +4.00 pp. These gains support generalization beyond v2 within the procedural benchmark family.

Figure 9. Prospective unified geometry routing improves the strongest development-selected restricted policy. (a) Development OOF and untouched-final exact accuracy for the prospectively selected full-head restricted comparator and UGR; triangles show candidate-oracle upper bounds. The paired final gain is +2.212 pp (95% CI [+0.316, +4.265] pp; exact McNemar p = 0.0385), with 27 unified-only versus 13 restricted-only correct examples. (b) Selection shares show that the unified router uses the prespecified intervention families non-degenerately. These shares are descriptive rather than an attribution of the paired improvement; the primary claim is the frozen comparison in (a).

Figure 14. Lightweight natural-domain calibration restores routing utility. (a) With the actuator and routing model family fixed, mean development gain rises from +0.33 pp at K = 50 to +2.12 pp at K = 500 and then largely saturates. The selected K = 500 is a sample-efficiency elbow, not the maximum-gain point; error bars denote across-run standard deviations. (b) Frozen evaluation on a new 4,000-example image-disjoint TallyQA set improves accuracy from 64.925% to 67.050% (+2.125 pp; paired 95% CI [+1.50, +2.775] pp), with 130 repairs, 45 breaks, and +85 net repairs (exact McNemar p = 9.176 × 10−11). (c) Both prespecified subsets improve: Simple by +1.10 pp and Complex by +3.15 pp. (d) The policy retains identity (α = 1) for 80.0% of examples and applies non-identity actions to 20.0%.

Figure 5. Bidirectional cardinality steering. (a) In the 300-sample characterization, α = 0.5 shifts the normalized expected numeral downward on 91.33% of samples, and α = 1.5 shifts it upward on 90.67%. Strict ordering µ0.5 < µ1 < µ1.5 holds on 88.67%; downward and upward response magnitudes are strongly coupled (Spearman ρ = 0.9514, p = 1.59 × 10−154). (b) On Proc-Count-Causal v2, gains α ∈ {0, 1, 1.5, 2, 4} produce monotonic mean expected-numeral shifts, from −0.151 at α = 0 to +0.439 at α = 4; α = 1 exactly reproduces baseline. These results support a bidirectional, dose-responsive cardinality actuator.

Figure 10. Bidirectional actuator behavior generalizes across the frozen historical candidate pool. (a) Attenuation (α = 0.5) and amplification (α = 1.5) directional consistency for all seven candidates on the same fresh N = 300 cohort; the dashed line marks 0.5. Six heads pass both one-sided exact directional tests after Holm correction across the 14 head-by-direction tests. (b) The stricter per-example ordering µ0.5 < µ1 < µ1.5 varies substantially across heads and is not itself the replication criterion. L8H30 provides a useful negative case: historical causal candidacy does not automatically imply stable finite controllability.

Figure 16. Finite-step response geometry explains selective repair and failure. (a) AROMA intervenes selectively rather than globally. (b) Larger expected-numeral movement creates both repair opportunity and break risk. (c) Repairs are strongly concentrated in target-aligned movement directions. Target alignment is a post-hoc diagnostic using ground truth and is not available at inference time.

Figure 13. Diagnosing limited zero-shot policy transfer. (a) The frozen synthetic router improves procedural v3 accuracy by +8.10 pp but changes zero-shot TallyQA accuracy by −2.975 pp. The post hoc natural action oracle reaches 71.575% (+6.725 pp over the 64.85% baseline), indicating retained actuator headroom. (b) Baseline errors shift from 93.76% undercounts and 6.24% overcounts on synthetic v2 to 21.12% undercounts and 78.88% overcounts on natural TallyQA. (c) Selected-score/realized-utility Spearman correlation is positive on v2 and v3 (ρ ≈ 0.409 and 0.411) but near zero and slightly negative on natural data (ρ ≈ −0.0667). (d) Without fitting or tuning parameters, SPUC-v1 clips standardized features to empirical v2 training support. Clipping affects 39.825% of samples; accuracy remains 61.875%, while intervention rate changes from 65.275% to 63.275%. Support violation contributes to extreme extrapolation but does not explain the accuracy decrease, indicating a conditional-utility shift.

papers.abstract: The visual world is cluttered: robust vision-language reasoning requires ignoring irrelevant information. Yet vision-language models (VLMs) can suffer substantial accuracy losses when answering questions about a target image with distractors present. Existing mitigations focus on selecting relevant images or limiting information exchange between images. Through a systematic analysis of three open 7-8B VLMs on five perception benchmarks adapted to include distractor images, we show that distractors reduce accuracy even when models correctly identify the relevant image, suggesting that selection alone is not enough. To understand the mechanism behind this interference, we combine attention analysis with targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL and identify middle-layer distractor-to-text connections as a pathway through which irrelevant visual information affects reasoning. We introduce answer consistency regularization, which encourages consistent answer distributions with and without distractors. Without directly constraining attention, this objective reduces middle-layer attention from question tokens to distractor images, consistent with the pathway our analysis implicates. With five distractors, our approach improves circular accuracy by an average of 16 percentage points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline across the five benchmarks while preserving single-image performance.
authors: Marie Amale Huynh, Regev Cohen, Serena Yeung-Levy, Sivan Doveh
bullets: Distractors lower accuracy even when the model correctly selects the relevant image, so image selection alone is insufficient.
Analysis of three open 7–8B VLMs across five distractor-adapted perception benchmarks traces interference to middle-layer distractor-to-text connections.
Targeted knockouts in Qwen2.5-VL support these connections as a pathway for irrelevant visual information to affect reasoning.
Answer consistency regularization reduces middle-layer attention from question tokens to distractors without explicitly constraining attention.
With five distractors, the method improves circular accuracy by an average of 16 percentage points over the Qwen2.5-VL baseline while preserving single-image performance.

papers.selection_reason: Analysis and regularization of visual distraction in vision-language model reasoning.
papers.title: Back to the Question: Tracing Visual Distraction Through Text Tokens
papers.tldr: Distractor images can disrupt VLM reasoning through middle-layer connections to text tokens, and answer consistency regularization substantially improves robustness without hurting single-image performance.

papers.abstract: Federated learning often assumes that data is fixed in advance, which is unrealistic in many real-world scenarios where new data continuously arrives, causing catastrophic forgetting. To address this challenge, we propose FCLPF (Federated Class Incremental Learning with Pseudo Features), a method that uses pseudo features generated from prototypes to mitigate catastrophic forgetting. Our approach reduces communication costs and improves efficiency by eliminating the need for past data and avoiding computationally heavy models like GANs. Experimental results on CIFAR-100 show that FCLPF achieves an average accuracy of 51.87% and an average forgetting of 9.62%, significantly outperforming existing baselines with an average accuracy of 47.72% and forgetting of 20.46%. On TinyImageNet, FCLPF achieves 37.56% accuracy and 3.14% forgetting, compared to the baselines' 27.69% accuracy and 24.46% forgetting, demonstrating the superior performance of FCLPF.
authors: Min Kyoon Yoo, Yu Rang Park
bullets: Addresses continual arrival of new classes in federated learning, where fixed-data assumptions cause catastrophic forgetting.
Generates pseudo features from class prototypes to retain knowledge without past data.
Avoids exemplar storage and computationally heavy GAN-based approaches, reducing communication and computational demands.
On CIFAR-100, achieves 51.87% average accuracy and 9.62% forgetting, versus baselines’ 47.72% and 20.46%.
On TinyImageNet, achieves 37.56% accuracy and 3.14% forgetting, compared with 27.69% and 24.46% for baselines.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and the potential for cross-provider adaptability. Achieved without memory, evolution, or extensions, these results establish EvoX as a competitive multi-model agent runtime and underscore the importance of harness-level operational control in realizing foundation-model capabilities.
authors: Haoyang Zhang, Qumeng Sun, Xiao Zhang, Xiang Liu, Zhidong Fan, Junjie Wang
bullets: Addresses failures caused by tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims.
Combines model-facing guidance with Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding.
Introduces Contrast, an auditable harness-evaluation framework with fairness constraints, request verification, and evidence-based adjudication.
Across five benchmarks, six models, and six harnesses, EvoX reached a 56.2% success rate over 691 task–model pairs—about 3 percentage points above the other harnesses’ average.
Results varied by model, with larger gains for GLM-5.3 and Kimi K3, indicating model-dependent harness effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Architecture and runtime design of EvoX. The system integrates a model-driven Semantic Policy with a harness-level Operational Policy to coordinate decisions and environment interactions. The operational policy comprises three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization mediates executable tool calls, Execution Continuity coordinates recovery and runtime control, and Outcome Grounding aligns reported outcomes with observed execution. The runtime supports diverse tools and optional persistent adaptation through long-term memory and GEP-based experience evolution. The right panel illustrates the conceptual distinction between a minimal execution loop and explicit harness-level operational control.

Figure 2: Overview of Contrast for controlled and auditable harness evaluation. A fairness contract distinguishes locked, shared, and harness-native conditions, preserving native execution behaviors while controlling external evaluation factors. Versioned tasks undergo qualification and integrity checks before execution through native harnesses in controlled environments. A model bridge mediates model requests, enforces applicable configurations, and audits provider-bound request parameters. Execution traces, model-call records, verifier results, and runtime diagnostics provide evidence for failure attribution, validity decisions, and auditable result selection. Only valid, scored task–model combinations enter paired statistical comparisons, while excluded or quarantined records remain available for audit and disclosure.

papers.tldr: EvoX treats the agent harness as an operational policy, using deterministic runtime controls to make LLM tool use more reliable and achieve the highest reported success rate across evaluated harnesses.

papers.abstract: Reference capacitively coupled plasma (CCP) simulations provide spatially resolved plasma fields but are costly to generate across operating conditions. We compare the data efficiency of five surrogate architectures--Coordinate MLP, PCA-Net, U-Net, Fourier neural operator (FNO), and Transolver--for predicting RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature in 1D planar and 2D axisymmetric GEC CCP benchmarks. We assess the number of reference simulations needed to achieve 1% and 2% mean relative L2 error for parameter-interior and parameter-boundary test cases, and examine architecture-specific mechanisms. FNO achieves the lowest or joint-lowest reference-case requirement in seven of eight comparisons. In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 training cases, compared with 100 for Transolver and 200 for U-Net. In 2D, FNO and U-Net each reach 1% interior error with 100 cases; FNO and Transolver each reach 2% parameter-boundary error with 200 cases, compared with 400 for U-Net. At the stricter 1% 2D parameter-boundary target, Transolver requires 400 cases versus 800 for FNO. Additional analyses investigate FNO spectral modes and padding, U-Net skip connections, Transolver adaptive slicing, and PCA-Net projection versus prediction error. The results support FNO as a data-efficient baseline for the tested CCP settings, while showing that the preferred architecture depends on the accuracy target and operating-parameter region.
authors: Zhenyu Zou, Junjue Liao, Hao Yang, Luowei Yin, Chenyu Wang, Yufeng Wei, Zhichao Peng, Chun Chen, Daniel Zhengyu Huang, Kangxin Liu, Haoran Guan, Rubing Han, Yipei Chen, Peiting You, Yuwei Fan
bullets: Five architectures are compared for predicting RF-cycle-averaged electron density, ion density, electric potential, and electron temperature in 1D and 2D CCP benchmarks.
Data efficiency is evaluated by the number of reference simulations needed to reach 1% or 2% mean relative L2 error for interior and boundary parameter cases.
FNO requires the fewest or tied-fewest reference cases in seven of eight comparisons.
In 1D, FNO reaches 1% interior error with 50 cases; in 2D, FNO and U-Net reach it with 100 cases.
For the strictest 1% 2D boundary target, Transolver needs 400 cases versus 800 for FNO, highlighting target- and region-dependent trade-offs.

papers.abstract: When people face a hard problem, they often restate it in a clearer way before solving it. We study whether the same habit helps large language models by rewriting the statement of a problem. A legal rewrite must keep the meaning, the constraints, and the correct answer unchanged. We test three kinds of rewrites. Decomposition makes hidden subgoals explicit. Typed Reformulation casts the task into a more suitable solving frame. Concept Reduction removes surface detail and exposes the task structure. We evaluate them on eight math, logic, and code benchmarks with eight models, all under the same chain-of-thought solving prompt. The effect is large but depends on the problem type. An oracle that picks the best rewrite after the fact raises accuracy by +27.6% on average. Yet no single rewrite helps every problem, and a mismatched rewrite can hurt. Still, the effect follows clear patterns. Each kind of rewrite fits certain problem types. A simple fixed rule learned from one set of problems transfers part of the gain to new problems. It gains +11.0% on the problems it chooses to rewrite, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share of problems. Rewriting is therefore not a universal way to solve problems. The question is when and how to rewrite.
authors: Wentao Zhang, Xiaoyu Zhang, Chengwei Liu, Yutao Hu, Tao Zhang, Junsheng Wu, Hongping Gan, Yang Liu
bullets: Studies three meaning-preserving rewrites: Decomposition, Typed Reformulation, and Concept Reduction.
Evaluates eight models across math, logic, and code benchmarks under a common chain-of-thought prompt.
An oracle selecting the best rewrite achieves an average accuracy gain of 27.6%.
No rewrite works universally: mismatched reformulations can reduce performance.
A simple rule transfers part of the benefit, gaining 11.0% on selected problems, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share.

papers.abstract: Deep-learning-based 3D MRI reconstruction is limited in practice by the GPU memory and compute cost of full-volume training; 3D acquisitions are thus most often reconstructed by 2D models applied slice-by-slice and then stacked, which ignores through-plane (stacking-axis) structure. We reconstruct in full 3D and ask whether a model can be trained at low resolution (fast and memory-feasible) yet deployed at higher resolution. This coarse-to-fine strategy needs reliable cross-resolution performance, but standard networks are resolution-specific and degrade substantially when evaluated outside the training setting. We therefore use resolution-agnostic neural operators (NOs) and propose KIR-NO (k-space-to-Image Reconstruction Neural Operator), a discretization-agnostic framework for accelerated 3D MRI reconstruction. KIR-NO is trained with full backpropagation on low-resolution volumes and applied zero-shot to higher-resolution volumes at inference. Its core building block is a 3D neural operator based on discrete-continuous convolutions: convolutional filters are parameterized in a continuous basis and sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions while preserving the local inductive bias of convolution. KIR-NO integrates these learned operators with physics-based consistency: a k-space neural-operator head first refines the undersampled Fourier measurements, and image-space neural-operator cascades then refine the reconstruction through interleaved data-consistency updates. Across 3D knee and brain MRI benchmarks, KIR-NO improves over classical and CNN baselines: it improves over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN by 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains persisting at 8x and 16x. These results show that resolution-agnostic operators make coarse-to-fine 3D MRI reconstruction - cheap low-resolution training with high-resolution deployment - practical across anatomies.
authors: Jiayun Wang, Ram Daftari, Weijie Gan, Valentin Duruisseaux, Ruibo Wang, Armeet Singh Jatyani, Boris Bonev, Anima Anandkumar
bullets: Addresses the high GPU cost of full-volume 3D MRI reconstruction, which often leads to slice-wise 2D processing that misses through-plane structure.
Uses resolution-agnostic neural operators with continuous-basis 3D convolutions that can be sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions.
Combines a k-space neural-operator head with image-space operator cascades and interleaved physics-based data consistency.
Trained on low-resolution volumes and deployed directly at higher resolution without retraining.
Outperforms classical and CNN baselines across knee and brain MRI benchmarks; gains over a 3D CNN reach 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4× acceleration on SKM-TEA, and persist at 8× and 16×.

papers.abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are compared mainly by accuracy averaged across findings, a summary that can hide complete failure on a single diagnosis. We audit five open medical VLMs (MedGemma-4B, Lingshu-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and MedVLM-R1) on 6,048 ChestX-ray14 questions balanced by sex, age, finding, and label. On the 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detect zero cases while MedGemma and Lingshu detect 38% and 67% of the same images. The two failing models answer "no" to all 864 pneumothorax cases (balanced accuracy 0.500, chance), yet produce fluent, anatomically specific explanations that name the signs of a collapsed lung and then deny them, with no hedge or abstention. This failure is not an artifact of prompting, image resolution, label ambiguity, or model scale. It persists across four prompt formats, at native resolution, and on single-label cases. A within-model control shows the same forced prompt gives HuatuoGPT 79% recall on nodule but only 6% on pneumothorax. It survives a tenfold scale increase (Qwen2.5-VL-72B detects 4%) and replicates on SIIM-ACR, an independent dataset with radiologist-drawn masks, where the failing models detect 0 of 432 confirmed pneumothoraces, including 0 of the 144 largest lesions. Reading the models' logits and internal states shows this is not blindness. The two failing models are highly confident yet no better than chance and a linear probe recovers pneumothorax from their hidden representations even where recall is zero, so the finding is represented internally but suppressed at the output. Aggregate accuracy therefore cannot establish that a medical VLM can see a given finding, because a model that misses one can still describe it convincingly. Reporting per-finding recall and specificity on balanced cases is needed to tell the difference.
authors: Shreya Ajay Kale, Angad Ripudaman Singh Bajwa
bullets: Five open medical VLMs were audited on balanced ChestX-ray14 questions across findings and patient attributes.
HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detected zero of 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, while MedGemma and Lingshu detected 38% and 67%.
The failing models consistently denied pneumothorax with fluent, specific explanations and no abstention, despite chance-level balanced accuracy.
The failure persisted across prompts, resolutions, single-label cases, model scale, and an independent SIIM-ACR dataset.
Hidden-state probes recovered pneumothorax information, suggesting output suppression rather than visual blindness; per-finding recall and specificity are therefore necessary.

papers.abstract: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.
authors: Jie Ren, Jonathan Rosenfeld, Neil Thompson
bullets: Parallel test-time scaling wastes compute by fully expanding low-quality reasoning paths before evaluation.

PreG generates short prefixes, ranks them by internal confidence, and completes only the strongest candidates.
Theoretical analysis shows PreG can widen the effective decision-boundary margin under a fixed compute budget.
Experiments report consistent gains over standard parallel TTS with improved token efficiency and lower computation.

papers.abstract: The geometric understanding of a scene is a crucial component for safe and efficient robotic operations in novel and unstructured environments. The recent emergence of foundation models for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) has provided an opportunity to enrich robotic perception capabilities with dense long-range depth predictions, replacing expensive onboard hardware (e.g., LiDARs and stereo cameras). However, these offline models are primarily trained on affine-invariant depth representations, and their generalization to novel scenes remains unclear. In this work we present EM-ViT, a monocular depth estimation model that learns to adapt online relative depth inputs from a foundation model prior to the metric scale with observations collected during robotic operations. Motivated by the stereo camera parameterization, our method decomposes depth prediction via dense disparity refinement to recover the scene's relative structure and an effective baseline scalar prediction to determine the missing metric scale. The learning process leverages sparse LiDAR points and, optionally, the robot's Ego-Motion (EM) to rapidly train a lightweight Vision Transformer (ViT), while an internal gradient matching loss preserves the fine-grained semantic structure of the input disparity in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on publicly available sequences, such as KITTI, and show that our online learning pipeline can adapt to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models. The code and supplementary materials will be publicly available at https://emvit-mde.github.io.
authors: Dimitrios Chatziparaschis, Georgios Georgakis, Adnan I. Ansar, Shehryar Khattak, Konstantinos Karydis
bullets: Addresses uncertain generalization of affine-invariant monocular depth models in novel, unstructured environments.
Refines dense disparity to recover relative scene structure and predicts a baseline scalar for metric scale.
Trains a lightweight Vision Transformer online using sparse LiDAR, with optional ego-motion and gradient matching to preserve fine details.
Evaluated on public sequences including KITTI, showing faster and more accurate adaptation than existing foundation MDE models.
Code and supplementary materials are planned for public release.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Self-supervised virtual stereo system for online metric adaptation in MDE. Based on an affine-invariant inverse depth input da and camera’s focal length f , our Ego Motion (EM)-ViT framework decodes depth reconstruction into dense disparity refinement d̂ and an effective baseline prediction B̂, achieving scale-to-structure disentanglement. The integrated disparity refinement module (e.g., dRefNet) uses a single image It, with optionally previously captured frames Iref and their corresponding poses p, to metrically fine-tune generated depth D̂t, while pose corrections can be provided in real-time via the odometry refinement module (e.g., odomNet). Our lightweight EM-ViT framework is self-supervised by sparse LiDAR annotations, photometric reconstruction, and gradient matching loss, to provide real-time, accurate, and fine-grained monocular depth estimation.

Fig. 6: Moments during online training. We demonstrate our model’s online MDE adaptation in the unexplored garage environment, by presenting the total training loss (top left), the δ1 score (top right), and depth prediction instances on unseen images (bottom).

Specifically, in cases of low solar phase angle and poor area texture, the applied Flight Stereo [11] method shows depth discontinuities, in contrast to the EM-ViT. papers.abstract: Aerial spatial intelligence (ASI) requires models to understand objects and spatial relationships across changing viewpoints and scales. Evaluating these abilities as models evolve calls for fresh physical observations, yet producing new aerial spatial questions requires repeatedly establishing entity identities, geometric references, and cross-view correspondences. We introduce \textbf{RSLiveBench-UAV}, a continually evolving vision-language benchmark driven by recurring acquisition of real UAV imagery. Its update protocol admits images captured after the preceding release and delays answer disclosure. An entity-centered production workflow uses geometry-assisted association to link repeated observations of physical vehicles, reuse human-verified attributes, and combine them with view-specific annotations and spatial references for traceable question generation. All tasks use deterministic scoring without model judges. We evaluate 30 general-purpose, remote-sensing, and embodied models on 35,491 question records from ten scenes, covering 17 tasks across 2D perception, 3D perception, cross-view perception, and reasoning. All 18 tested embodied models outperform the three selected remote-sensing comparators in Overall, although the strongest embodied model scores 43.29 versus 59.88 for GPT-6-Astra. Fine-grained vehicle recognition remains challenging, and performance varies across heights and camera pitches. Retrospective scene-group comparisons and rolling-window replay characterize score-pattern consistency under scene renewal. RSLiveBench-UAV connects fresh physical observations, entity-centered answer production, and systematic model evaluation to support continual assessment of ASI. Benchmark will release at https://rslivebench.space
authors: Yue Zhou, Jiawei Liu, Jue Chen, Ziyang Gong, Haojia Wei, Jingxiang Li, Xue Jiang, Zhihang Zhong, Pai Peng, Xue Yang, Yansheng Li, Jonathan Li

Covers 17 deterministic-scoring tasks spanning 2D, 3D, cross-view perception, and reasoning across ten scenes.
Evaluates 30 models on 35,491 question records; fine-grained vehicle recognition remains difficult, with performance varying by height and camera pitch.
Rolling-window replay and retrospective scene comparisons assess score consistency as scenes are renewed.

papers.abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.
authors: Binghang Lu, Lang Cao, Changhong Mou, Yige Sun, Cindy Xiangrui Kong, Zheyuan Deng, Tian Yuan, Bing Hu, Runyu Zhang, Na Lu, Guang Lin
bullets: Benchmarks 1,001 cases across 42 classical and fractional PDE templates.
Tests noise-free data, substantial Gaussian noise, and hard out-of-distribution settings.
RSI-PDE shortlists equations by residual loss, refines coefficients and solvers using relative L² feedback, and gates policy or memory updates with validation.
Across four frontier models, RSI-PDE raises average pass rates over single-run baselines and native harnesses while using fewer recorded model calls.
The benchmark targets workflows requiring equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration.

papers.abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.
authors: Qi Zhang, Bohan Wang, Qianru Sun, Hanwang Zhang
bullets: Across 10 multimodal configurations and 6 model families, the study contrasts spatial-imagery tasks with symbol-manipulation tasks.
Ablating a vision-language direction in hidden states sharply harms spatial navigation while preserving—and slightly improving—boolean reasoning in Chameleon-7B.
The effect is direction-specific, layer-localized, and extends to mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective-taking.
Vision-shaped thinking is concentrated at 7–8B in the tested models and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in a tested 32B model.
In dual-path models, the causal signal lies in the generation pathway; probe-decodable information in the understanding pathway is not necessarily causally used.

papers.abstract: AI-manipulated video detectors are typically evaluated on clean, curated datasets. In deployment, however, videos have usually passed through repost compression on social-media platforms and sometimes were captured by imperfect hardware. To measure detection under these conditions, we introduce Reality Perception Gap (RPG), a benchmark of 10,000 videos from frontier generators and partially synthetic edits, processed with cross-platform repost compression and paired with real footage that carries camera-side optical artifacts. RPG also includes socially fragile content, such as crime and wartime footage, where fabricated videos can cause severe social harm. Across 18 detectors, none catches more than 15% of fakes at a 1% false-positive rate. A positive control and a re-encoding sweep separate two sources of failure: generator and content shift degrades detectors before any compression, and repost compression erases the low-level traces that the artifact-based detectors relies on. Existing detectors therefore struggle when deployment conditions strip away the generation artifacts they rely on. These complementary failures suggest that robust detection requires training under deployment conditions and combining low-level, temporal, and semantic evidence, where passive detection may have reached its limits.
authors: Xiangrui Liu, Xinmiao Luan, Xinyuan Wang, Zhiyuan Fang, Chi-Yao Huang, Douglas C. Montgomery, Yanjie Fu, Felix Juefei-Xu, YeZhou Yang
bullets: Introduces Reality Perception Gap (RPG), a 10,000-video benchmark covering frontier-generated videos, partially synthetic edits, repost compression, camera artifacts, and socially fragile content.
Evaluates 18 detectors under deployment-like conditions; none detects more than 15% of fakes at a 1% false-positive rate.
Generator and content shifts already degrade performance, while social-media re-encoding further removes the low-level artifacts detectors rely on.
The findings point toward training under deployment conditions and combining low-level, temporal, and semantic evidence.
The study suggests passive detection alone may be approaching its practical limits.

papers.abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.
authors: Zahraa Selim, Menna Hamed, Wesam Ahmed, Sohyla Said, Sara Basheer, Rami Zewail
bullets: Addresses VRAM and bandwidth constraints that prevent co-locating models, vector indices, and KV caches on edge GPUs.
Finds GPTQ offers higher throughput but becomes unstable for contexts of 2048+ tokens, while NF4 provides more reliable long-context behavior.
Integrates Florence-2 vision processing with only 430 MB of additional VRAM.
Structured prompting reduces latency by 47% and improves quantization-affected mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.
The complete architecture uses 8.37 GB of memory, targeting 12–16 GB GPUs, with evaluation focused on Turing hardware such as the Tesla T4.

papers.abstract: Large language models trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) with verifiable rewards exhibit strong reasoning ability and broad generalization, whereas models trained with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) are often viewed as more prone to memorization and limited transfer. This paper rethinks this distinction through the lens of SFT training data on widely used Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 series models. First, we study the role of data source and show that it is critical: a carefully mixed SFT dataset substantially outperforms data generated solely by a larger model. Second, we study the role of data scale and show that matching the number of correct rollouts between SFT and RL greatly improves SFT generalization, while matching the total rollout budget enables SFT to generalize as well as RL. Combining these two factors further enables SFT to generalize even better than RL. Third, by using LLM annotations to characterize the solution methods in training rollouts, we show that larger datasets cover more tail methods and that these tail methods provide generalizable reasoning signals. Finally, we support these empirical findings theoretically by analyzing the training dynamics of shallow transformers under both RL and SFT.
authors: Yunlong Hou, Fengzhuo Zhang, Yuan Cheng, Jiachun Pan, Xingyao Li, Zhuoran Yang

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.

Introduces a Conflict Index to quantify geometric interference between editing tasks.
Uses conflict-aware task ordering to reduce cumulative interference.
Applies dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the available null space when needed.
Experiments across five domains and three backbones show improved multi-task editing while preserving general capabilities and handling incremental task arrival.

papers.abstract: We present Hy ASR 3.0, a large language model (LLM)-based automatic speech recognition (ASR) system that delivers strong recognition accuracy, supports flexible contextual conditioning, and maintains robust recognition performance across diverse speech conditions. Hy ASR 3.0 supports Mandarin Chinese, English and 13 Chinese dialect groups, including Cantonese. Among the evaluated systems, it achieves the lowest aggregate error rates on public Mandarin Chinese, English, and Cantonese benchmarks and the lowest error rates on the corresponding internal test sets, alongside first-tier dialect recognition performance. Beyond audio-only transcription, Hy ASR 3.0 supports multiple forms of external context, including hotword lists, question--answer dialogues, and summaries, enabling the use of task-relevant information during recognition. The model also leverages intra-utterance context to disambiguate homophonic and phonetically similar keywords using information from other parts of the same utterance, without requiring a separate contextual input. Evaluations demonstrate strong contextual recognition in both external-context and intra-utterance settings, as well as robust recognition of long-form speech, children's and older adults' speech, low-volume speech, and speech in noisy environments. This report describes the model architecture and training methodology and presents evaluations across recognition accuracy, context utilization, and robustness.

papers.abstract: Safe trajectory tracking (STT) aims to enable autonomous vehicles to follow a reference trajectory accurately while avoiding collisions. This problem is particularly challenging for Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) in highly dynamic environments. Existing non-learning-based STT methods often use simplified vehicle and interaction models to meet real-time requirements, which may result in suboptimal tracking accuracy. Although Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) can help address this limitation, widely used Lagrangian DRL methods often suffer from unstable training because increasing Lagrange multipliers amplify policy-gradient magnitudes. To address these issues, we propose a novel reinforcement learning framework for STT, called STT Control Epigraph Form RL (STTC-EFRL). In this framework, the STT problem is formulated as an epigraph-form min-max optimization problem. Based on this formulation, we develop a learning mechanism that uses a decreasing scalar related to the epigraph to adjust the policy gradient descent direction without increasing the gradient magnitude, thereby improving training stability. We also develop a computationally efficient ray-casting method to compute a polyhedron scaling factor for safety quantification. Experimental results, including Vehicle-in-the-Loop tests, show that STTC-EFRL achieves higher tracking accuracy than the considered non-learning-based baseline and more stable training than widely used Lagrangian DRL methods, while satisfying safety requirements in connected environments.

papers.abstract: AI-generated content (AIGC) has substantially narrowed the visual gap between natural and synthetic images, while existing detectors often rely on generator-specific artifacts and exhibit limited generalization to unseen models. This motivates a fundamental question: which intrinsic physical image characteristics provide stable, discriminative cues for distinguishing natural from AI-generated images? We investigate this by systematically identifying robust physical features and incorporating them into a vision-language representation without external textual prompts at inference. We first analyze 15 handcrafted physical descriptors across images from over 20 generative models. Based on cross-generator stability and real-fake discriminability, we propose a Feature Stability-Discriminability Validation Assessment (FSDVA) to select a compact set of reliable features. Five core features, including Laplacian variance, Sobel statistics, and residual-noise variance, are then used to construct structured textual descriptions encoding physical evidence for CLIP-based learning. We integrate these physics-enriched descriptions with image representations via a native physics-guided multimodal framework, adapting CLIP ViT-L 14 with LoRA. At inference, the model requires only the input image, with no external captions or manual prompts. On GenImage, our method achieves 99.0 percent accuracy on SDv1.4 and 96.7 percent on Wukong, with a mean of 97.23 percent across eight generative models versus 95.8 percent for C2pCLIP under the same setting. On UniversalFakeDetect, it maintains strong, stable generalization across diverse and unseen generation settings. These results show that carefully selected physical image statistics provide complementary forensic evidence to pretrained vision-language representations, enabling interpretable, more generator-agnostic AIGC detection.

On GenImage, the method reaches 99.0% accuracy on SDv1.4, 96.7% on Wukong, and 97.23% mean accuracy across eight generators, exceeding the cited baseline.

papers.abstract: Autonomous cyber defense is widely studied with deep reinforcement learning, but most work trains policies inside simulators because learning requires many trial-and-error interactions. Simulator-based training carries a fidelity gap: trained policies face authentication delays, partial action failures, service dependencies, and user traffic patterns that the simulator did not represent, and degrade on transfer. Training directly in the network being defended removes the gap but makes every interaction slow and costly, so sample efficiency becomes the binding constraint. Model-based reinforcement learning has reduced sample requirements on games and physical robots by orders of magnitude by planning inside a learned world model, but it has not been applied to defenders trained in operational networks. We present FOE-Dreamer (Factored Opponent-Enhanced Dreamer), a model-based reinforcement learning framework that trains a defender online and directly in a network on cloud infrastructure, without a simulator stage. FOE-Dreamer separates three sources of variation in the latent state: a controllable component driven by defender actions, an exogenous component driven by benign user activity, and an opponent embedding inferred from defender-observable signals alone. Separating the components reduces the variance in policy gradients during planning in imagination. Against two scripted attacker profiles with user activity emulated by the GHOSTS framework on an 8-host OpenStack testbed, FOE-Dreamer trains within a 3-day budget on a single GPU and achieves about 2$\times$ better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN baselines under matched compute. Both the factoring and the opponent model contribute to the gain, and the learned latents are consistent with the intended separation.

On an 8-host OpenStack testbed with two scripted attackers, it trained within a 3-day single-GPU budget.
Achieved about 2× better episode loss than Rainbow and IQN under matched compute; both factoring and opponent modeling contributed.

papers.abstract: Generative large language models are widely used for multilingual text evaluation, yet whether decision models that directly output judgment probabilities can serve as multilingual judges has received limited attention. We evaluate Jev against generative LLM judges on four multilingual benchmarks with human annotations, covering up to 47 language varieties and three evaluation formats: binary decisions, pairwise comparisons, and graded ratings. At approximately $1/31$ to $1/61$ of GPT-6.1's evaluation cost, Jev is competitive on most multilingual judging tasks, but falls behind GPT-6.1 on knowledge-intensive answer verification. Further analysis shows that Jev is more likely to accept incorrect answers in low-resource languages than in English and that its probability outputs help identify errors across tasks. Based on these findings, we offer recommendations on evaluation instructions, confidence-based selection, and model routing, providing empirical guidance for using Jev as a multilingual judge.

papers.abstract: Cross-domain video deepfake detection increasingly uses frozen foundation-model experts, combined by calibrated score averaging, a per-video router picking one expert, or a learned head over concatenated features. Expressive routing and feature fusion are often reported to beat plain averaging. Across a 22-dataset frozen-expert testbed, we find those gains are largely evaluation artifacts. A corner theorem locates the gap routing aims to close: because AUC depends only on score ordering, the best any score-space router can do is an oracle reading the test label to pick each video's expert, a ceiling no realisable, label-blind router reaches. The theorem does not order real routers against a calibrated global average; the case against routing is empirical, and no router we test beats that average. Feature fusion reads raw features, falls outside the theorem, and is audited empirically. Reported gains trace to leakage: holding out one dataset leaks siblings sharing identities and reals (over-crediting routing), while holding out one manipulation keeps that dataset's reals in training (over-crediting feature fusion). A $2\times 2$ over fold and evaluation granularity pins the $+2.6$pp feature-fusion "win" to the fold alone: 12/12 significant under leaky folds vs. 0/12 under honest family-held-out folds, where both gains vanish. Fusion still pays off in the tail of hard videos and families: as experts are added, videos every expert misclassifies drop from 15.2% to 2.3%, and global calibrated fusion (InvB) beats the best single expert on worst-family AUC, selective risk (AURC), and low-false-positive recall, stably across protocols. Practitioners should calibrate and combine globally, hold out whole dataset families, and measure tail performance. For score-space routing under ranking metrics, honest evaluation and expert diversity matter more than combiner complexity.
authors: Luke Collins, Chang-Tsun Li, Duc Thanh Nguyen
bullets: Leakage from dataset-family splits can falsely credit routing and feature fusion.
A theorem shows score-space routers have an unattainable label-aware oracle ceiling under AUC; it does not prove they beat averaging.
Across 22 datasets, no tested router beats calibrated global averaging.
The reported +2.6 percentage-point fusion advantage disappears with honest family-held-out folds.
Adding experts reduces videos missed by all experts from 15.2% to 2.3%; calibrated fusion improves worst-family AUC, selective risk, and low-false-positive recall.

papers.abstract: Forward-KL language-model distillation normally computes dense teacher and student scores over the full vocabulary at every supervised position, making training and stored teacher targets expensive. We instead distill from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing the retained mass as we sweep support from 100% to 0.01%. Our main study distills Qwen3 4B -> 1.7B. We confirm the broader support-reduction finding on larger Qwen3 8B -> 4B and Nemotron Nano 12B -> 9B pairs and under answer-only supervision. We evaluate generation primarily on MMLU-Pro and secondarily on GPQA-Diamond. Across the Qwen3 settings, retaining 0.01% of the vocabulary causes no observed MMLU-Pro degradation relative to full-vocabulary distillation, although disagreement with the complete teacher distribution increases. Nemotron Nano matches full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro at 0.1%, but smaller fractions fail to emit the closing reasoning tag, showing that the reliable cutoff depends on the model family. At 0.01% support, caching the retained next-token scores from the teacher forward pass cuts training step time by 38%, while restricting student output computation to those tokens cuts peak memory by 24%; neither causes observed MMLU-Pro degradation.
authors: Lavinia Ghita, Dhruv Desai
bullets: Full-vocabulary forward-KL distillation is expensive because it uses dense teacher and student scores at every supervised position.
The method retains and renormalizes only the teacher’s highest-probability tokens, sweeping support from 100% down to 0.01%.
Across Qwen3 model pairs, 0.01% support caused no observed MMLU-Pro degradation; results were also confirmed on larger pairs and answer-only supervision.
For Nemotron Nano, 0.1% matched full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro, while smaller supports disrupted closing reasoning-tag generation.
At 0.01% support, cached teacher scores reduced training step time by 38% and restricted student computation reduced peak memory by 24%, without observed MMLU-Pro degradation.

papers.abstract: Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: speculative decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share.
authors: Igor Sadalski, Minghao Guo, Benjamin Jones, Wojciech Matusik
bullets: Recasts algorithms as proof graphs whose assumptions are explicit and auditable.
Uses an LLM to relax one assumption, re-derive and re-prove the algorithm in Lean, then generate code.
Formalizes 89 algorithms spanning KV-cache eviction, weight pruning, and speculative decoding.
Improved on every evaluated published algorithm in KV-cache eviction and weight pruning.
Matched OpenEvolve within a point at equal budget, with lower repeat-to-repeat variability.

papers.abstract: Embodied continual learning requires controllers to infer changing situations, retain prior behavior and reuse motor skills without task labels or known boundaries. The challenge is deciding when to recover earlier behavior and which skills can support new learning. We introduce Situation-guided Primitive Integration for Recurrent Embodiment (SPIRE), a recurrent-spiking system that infers latent contexts from action-outcome evidence and learns context-specific motor actors online. Mature actors become protected sources that combine with a target-context residual to drive recurrent-spiking motor populations. Across coordinate, three-joint and hidden-force control, SPIRE maintained control, autonomously inferred situations, retained prior behavior and accelerated acquisition of an unseen source composition, reducing mean interactions to criterion by approximately 40% relative to matched fresh controllers. Rewinding compatible source actors impaired early acquisition in every matched intervention, demonstrating causal reuse. Against seven recurrent continual-learning and modular-control comparators, SPIRE achieved 2.4 times the mean prior-learning advantage of the strongest eligible task-free alternative selected for each paired stream. These results demonstrate autonomous recovery and causal reuse of motor skills for new learning in continuous embodied control.
authors: Yiyang Jia, Mingyang Lyu, Gongce Cao, Feifei Zhao, Yinqian Sun, Yi Zeng
bullets: Addresses continual control without task labels or known task boundaries.
Infers latent contexts from action–outcome evidence using a recurrent-spiking system.
Learns online context-specific motor actors and combines protected source actors with target-context residuals.
Across three control settings, it retained prior behavior and reduced interactions to criterion by approximately 40% versus matched fresh controllers.
Rewinding compatible source actors impaired early learning, supporting causal motor-skill reuse; SPIRE also outperformed task-free comparators on prior-learning advantage.

papers.abstract: Open-weight Vision-Language Models (VLMs) score 85-94% on spatial benchmarks (BLINK Spatial, What's Up CLEVR) yet collapse to chance on simple geometric questions when object, scene, and texture priors are stripped away. We introduce and open-source Sophon, a procedurally generated diagnostic of paired colored point-cloud stimuli across three coordinate systems (1D linear, 2D Cartesian, 2D polar) and four question types (binary, categorical, comparative, quantitative). Across four open architectures (LLaVA-NeXT, LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2.5-VL, Idefics3), accuracy clusters at 47-52% while frontier models (Opus 4.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5.4) clear 77-83% and humans reach 84-94%. We use linear probes and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to trace the open-weight failures. Probes of the vision encoder (ViT) and language decoder (LLM) recover Sophon spatial information at 83-85% and 80-86% accuracy, respectively, and the language tower's reasoning circuit answers text-only controls (point clouds as sets of coordinates) at +40 pp over visual stimuli. Language tower per-layer attention attribution localizes visual integration to mid-stack layers. At readout, models elevate the correct answer-set tokens but select among them randomly. We localize the mechanism by tuning individual and grouped components across every architecture's stack, including the vision tower (ViT workspace and reader), the projector, and the language tower (LLM workspace and reader). These experiments demonstrate that this mid-stack workspace holds circuitry capable of organizing the spatial signal so that the frozen reader can decode it. LoRA fine-tuning adjusts that circuitry such that 7B-class VLMs answer Sophon spatial reasoning questions at frontier aggregate accuracy. This work suggests that these models do not have a capability gap for spatial reasoning but suffer from a routing bottleneck that targeted fine-tuning repairs.
authors: J. Zach Gazak, Ryan Swindle, Justin Fletcher
bullets: Introduces an open, procedural diagnostic using colored point clouds across 1D and 2D coordinate systems and four question types.
Open-weight VLMs perform near chance (47–52%), despite much higher scores on conventional spatial benchmarks.
Probes show spatial information is recoverable in both vision and language components, while text-only controls substantially outperform visual inputs.
Attention and component-tuning analyses localize the failure to mid-stack visual-integration and reasoning workspaces, where models identify answer sets but choose randomly.
LoRA fine-tuning brings 7B-class VLMs to frontier-level aggregate accuracy on Sophon, supporting a routing-bottleneck explanation.

Figure 5: Per-layer GT vs competitor logit gap, five LoRA conditions, four architectures. Each panel projects the answer position hidden state through the unembedding WU at every decoder layer and reports the mean gap between the ground truth direction token and its same axis competitor (e.g. “left” vs “right”). The shaded region marks the reader band. In every architecture BASE and READER sit at or below zero throughout, so reader-band training installs no contrast. The three trained conditions rise late in the stack and largely coincide, and WORKSPACE’s contrast appears despite the reader band and WU being frozen. The reader band’s contrast emerges when the workspace is reorganized to feed it (§5.3).

Filled = stimulus engaged: Perceiver (r≥0.5, top-1<50%), Direction perceiver (r≥0.5, top-1≥50%). Hatched/outline = engagement failure: Noisy (r<0.5), Few anchor (top-3≥50%), Constant (top-1≥85%). Labels above bars are answer uniqueness (nunique/n). Human scale r reflects rater unit ambiguity. See all models version in Appendix U.
