papers.selection_reason: Procedural diagnostic for spatial reasoning in VLMs, identifies routing bottleneck and shows fine-tuning improves spatial intelligence, directly relevant to spatial intelligence in multimodal models.
papers.title: Sophon: A Procedural Diagnostic for Spatial Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Sophon reveals that open-weight VLMs often contain spatial information but fail to route it through their reasoning circuitry, a bottleneck that targeted LoRA fine-tuning can repair.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3\% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6\%.
authors: Wen-Han Hsieh, Ken Jiankun Zheng, Chia-Chien Chen, David M. Chan, Trevor Darrell
bullets: Addresses ineffective sampled action sequences and the latency of computationally expensive action verification.
Collects autonomous rollouts from the frozen VLA and trains a compact verifier to predict task-success scores for action chunks.
At inference, the verifier scores candidate actions and selects the highest-scoring one for execution.
Achieves 82.3% average success across four LIBERO-10 tasks and improves average success by 22.6% over the baseline on three real-world tasks.

(d) The robot executes the first H actions of the candidate with the highest predicted task-success score.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to lack diversity in open-ended text generation, a limitation that is especially consequential in education, where homogeneity can narrow the kinds of thinking and disciplinary work students are invited to do. We study diversity in two educational generation tasks: math items and essay feedback. We compare frontier and open-weight models with human-authored reference distributions using lexical, semantic, and domain-grounded measures. For math, we examine the mathematical activities students are asked to perform; for feedback, we examine the revision work requested and the rhetorical strategies used to communicate it. We evaluate direct prompting, two diversity prompting methods, and post-training. Across both tasks, directly prompted model outputs are markedly less diverse than human-authored content--78% higher on lexical (Self-BLEU) and 51% higher on semantic (embedding) similarity--and represent a narrower range of instructional forms. Diversity prompting and post-training increase variation largely through surface features without broadening the instructional repertoire. Models inherit and amplify the most normative routines of human instruction. Overcoming mode collapse in education will require richer instructional data and investment in teachers' creative capacity and professional judgment.
authors: Mei Tan, Hyunji Nam, Hari Subramonyam, Dorottya Demszky
bullets: Studies two tasks: math-item generation and essay feedback.
Compares frontier and open-weight models with human references using lexical, semantic, and domain-grounded measures.
Direct prompting produces markedly more homogeneous outputs and a narrower range of instructional forms.
Diversity prompting and post-training increase surface-level variation but do not substantially broaden instructional repertoires.
The authors call for richer instructional data and greater investment in teachers’ creative capacity and judgment.

papers.abstract: Morphology-aware tokenizers are expected to help morphologically rich languages, and their reported gains over byte-pair encoding (BPE) are usually credited to their linguistic units. A comparison with BPE cannot support this attribution, since such a tokenizer also segments text more finely (granularity) and, on token-level tasks, changes how much the sub-token readout matters. We separate both factors from the effect of grouping words by their roots (root assignment) in Amharic, a Semitic language whose Ge'ez abugida hides consonantal roots inside syllabic glyphs, with Latin-script Hausa as an orthographic contrast. Our design combines a lossless root-and-pattern tokenizer with controls that change one factor at a time, in two independent implementations. In both, real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots (+4.9 and +4.7 F1), and root-frequency structure explains little of this gain. In small from-scratch models, the readout choice moves F1 by up to 13.4 points and reverses the sign of every comparison of the root-and-pattern arms with BPE, whereas in two pretrained encoders it moves F1 by less than one point. The granularity effect changes sign across languages and implementations. We recommend decomposing tokenizer effects, and reporting the readout, before a gain is attributed to linguistic structure.
authors: Abdul Rehman Antall, Baidya Nath Saha
bullets: The study compares morphology-aware tokenization with controlled alternatives in Amharic and Hausa.
Real root assignment improves Amharic named-entity recognition over scrambled roots, while root-frequency structure explains little of the gain.
Word-level readout has a major impact in small from-scratch models, changing F1 by up to 13.4 points and reversing comparisons with BPE.
Readout effects are much smaller in pretrained encoders, and granularity effects vary by language and implementation.
The authors recommend reporting readout choices and isolating tokenizer factors in future evaluations.

papers.title: What Do Tokenizer Comparisons Measure? Disentangling Granularity, Root Assignment, and Word-Level Readout across Amharic and Hausa

papers.abstract: Driving world models aim to simulate how a scene unfolds under different ego actions. This requires plausible motion of surrounding vehicles as well as precise ego-trajectory control. Learning vehicle motion from perspective video alone is challenging because motion is entangled with appearance and vehicles can be occluded. Prior work therefore conditions video generation on layouts that specify vehicle motion, providing control over surrounding vehicles but requiring their future trajectories as inputs. We introduce BirdDreams, an autoregressive driving world model that jointly generates perspective video and a schematic bird's-eye-view (BEV) video, making scene layout part of the predicted future. The BEV, rendered from scene annotations for training, depicts roads and vehicles as simple shapes at a fixed metric scale, providing a top-down view of their positions and motion with reduced occlusion between vehicles. Perspective video, by contrast, retains scene details that the BEV omits, such as traffic signals and object appearance. Joint attention between two video diffusion transformers, one per stream, lets each stream inform the other during generation. The predicted BEV also provides a geometric interface for ego control: we translate and rotate its latest frame along an input ego trajectory and use the resulting frames as a soft condition that shows how the scene would appear to move if only the ego vehicle moved. At inference, BirdDreams generates both videos from a single camera image without requiring an HD map or vehicle-state inputs. On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, BirdDreams follows input ego trajectories more faithfully than prior driving world models and generates more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning. Human evaluation shows that BirdDreams outperforms a perspective-only baseline in generating realistic surrounding-vehicle behavior.
authors: Junyoung Seo, Jaewoo Seo, Seungryong Kim, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Xiuming Zhang, Seung Wook Kim
bullets: Addresses the challenge of modeling surrounding-vehicle motion and precise ego control from perspective video, where appearance and occlusion confound motion learning.
Uses two autoregressive video diffusion transformers with joint attention: one generates detailed perspective video, while the other generates a metric-scale schematic BEV video.
Uses the predicted BEV as a geometric interface for ego control by transforming its latest frame along a requested ego trajectory as a soft condition.
At inference, requires neither an HD map nor vehicle-state inputs.

On PhysicalAI-AV and nuScenes, it follows ego trajectories more faithfully, produces more plausible ego motion without ego-action conditioning, and improves surrounding-vehicle realism in human evaluation versus a perspective-only baseline.

papers.abstract: BEST-RQ, based on random projection and quantization, has been a well-established self-supervised learning approach to learn speech representations from large-scale unlabeled audio due to its high performance and efficiency. However, in BEST-RQ representations learned by random quantization can be sensitive to the choice of quantization targets. To address this issue, we propose a distributionally robust extension of BEST-RQ that seeks representations robust across multiple quantization configurations. Specifically, we define groups by codebooks and formulate the training as a group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) problem. Rather than optimizing solely for the average loss across groups, our approach adaptively reweights groups to emphasize those performing poorly. Additionally, we regularize DRO with a Kullback-Leibler divergence to prevent excessive distribution deviation. We evaluate our approach on the Multilingual LibriSpeech dataset and show that the distributionally robust BEST-RQ achieves superior performance over the conventional uniform average across multiple codebooks.
authors: Muhammad Khan, Xiaodong Cui, Brian Kingsbury, George Saon
bullets: BEST-RQ can be sensitive to the choice of random quantization targets.
The method groups training examples by codebook and formulates learning as group Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO).
It adaptively upweights groups with higher loss and uses KL-divergence regularization to limit excessive reweighting.
Experiments on Multilingual LibriSpeech show improved performance over uniform averaging across codebooks.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed DRO-BEST-RQ with KL regularization. For an utterance i, the acoustic features xi are first projected into a lower-dimensional space using a shared projection matrix P . The resulting representations are then quantized using multiple fixed random codebooks Cg to generate group-specific pseudo-labels yi g . The input acoustic features are processed by a shared encoder and group-specific prediction heads. The cross-entropy loss is computed for each codebook on those masked frames which are then combined through the KL-regularized DRO objective.
Table 2: Illustration of the Group DRO weighting mechanism across four BEST-RQ codebooks at an arbitrarily selected iteration.
Table 3: WER (%) on the MLS test sets

papers.tldr: A distributionally robust version of BEST-RQ improves speech representations by emphasizing poorly performing quantization configurations instead of treating all codebooks equally.

papers.abstract: Agents that perform state estimation using pretrained perception models, e.g., Vision-Language Models (VLMs), face the fundamental challenge that predictions are uncertain. Still, most approaches determinize these predictions into a single best-guess state and make decisions as if it were ground truth. This is brittle because when the guess is wrong, the agent's decisions may be unsafe or infeasible. At the other extreme, maintaining a full probability distribution over symbolic states is often intractable. We propose a middle path, drawing on the underlying probabilities the perception model already produces (e.g., a VLM's output-layer token distributions) to construct a $\theta$-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS$_\theta$), a minimal subset of states whose cumulative probability meets a user-specified belief-mass threshold. The minimality of an MBS$_\theta$ ensures that the agent considers only the most likely states, enhancing robustness in downstream decision-making while maintaining computational tractability. Using a novel three-layered belief system, we efficiently approximate individual state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints. On this belief construction, we base our MBS$_\theta$ construction, while maintaining only a lean factored representation of the belief. Our algorithm, Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), takes advantage of the unique structure of this belief system to construct an MBS$_\theta$ with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case. Using a VLM as the backbone of our state estimator, we validate our method's theoretical properties, scalability with problem size, and improvement of downstream decision-making when used in a task-planning pipeline.
authors: Guy Azran, Sarah Keren
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of committing to a single estimated state and the intractability of representing full symbolic-state distributions.
Builds a θ-confidence Minimal Belief Set containing the smallest set of likely states whose probabilities reach a user-specified belief mass.
Approximates state probabilities from per-feature predictions and task-level constraints using a three-layered, factored belief representation.
Introduces Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS), with correctness guarantees and polynomial complexity in the unconstrained case.
Experiments with a VLM-based estimator evaluate theoretical properties, scalability, and downstream task-planning improvements.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$\mu$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering. We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).
authors: Anish Saxena, Hritvik Taneja, Christos Kozyrakis, Aamer Jaleel
bullets: HBF offers much higher capacity than HBM but its roughly 20× higher read latency can severely slow on-demand LLM inference.
SlipStream profiles repeatable weight-page demand order and uses a staging warp to prefetch pages through a producer-consumer pipeline.
Hardware retires tracking entries when demand first accesses a page, keeping prefetching closely paced with consumption and limiting lead distance.
Across seven dense models, SlipStream reaches 92.4% of ideal HBM-latency HBF performance with a 40 MB buffer, versus 43.1% for H3 with 320 MB.
A 16 MB buffer remains within 4% of the 40 MB configuration; SlipStream also reaches 91.2% of ideal performance on Mixture-of-Experts models.

papers.abstract: Full-duplex spoken dialogue, in which a system listens while it speaks and can backchannel, yield the floor, and be interrupted, is usually obtained by training on hundreds of thousands to millions of hours of speech. This is costly, rewrites the language model that supplies the system's knowledge, and still leaves turn-taking either implicit or decided coarsely rather than word by word. We show that a frozen, general-purpose multimodal LLM can instead be adapted into a word-level full-duplex system with little data. Our system is a thinker-talker cascade on an 80 ms frame clock. The thinker keeps the LLM frozen and trains only lightweight adapters and a few new token embeddings (97M parameters); at every frame it emits one token of agent text, with pauses, yields, and onsets represented as tokens of the same vocabulary and kept legal by a finite-state machine. A four-stage curriculum, each stage anchored to the model's own behavior under the previous format, performs the conversion in about 30 GPU-hours. The talker reads only the thinker's discrete tokens, so the two halves are trained independently. On Full-Duplex-Bench and InteractionBench, the system is competitive with open-source full-duplex systems built through large-scale speech training: among them, it is the least likely to take the floor when the user merely pauses, backchannels most often, and leads in spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and coherence over long conversations.
authors: Tairan Chen, Richard Yucheng He, Yihang Liu, Baodong Cao, Chen Xu
bullets: Full-duplex dialogue requires listening while speaking, backchanneling, yielding, and handling interruptions at word-level timing.
The system uses a frozen LLM with lightweight adapters and new token embeddings, operating on an 80 ms frame clock.
A thinker emits text, pauses, yields, and onsets as constrained tokens; an independently trained talker converts them to speech.
A four-stage curriculum completes adaptation in about 30 GPU-hours.

On two benchmarks, it is competitive with large-scale speech-trained systems and performs strongly in floor-taking restraint, backchanneling, spoken-task accuracy, groundedness, and long-conversation coherence.

Each stage card shows what the model reads and emits at that stage as one cell per frame (user codec tokens, agent words, pause, SE/SS, and PAD cells), which modules it trains, and which model anchors its KL term; the frozen core is never changed. The resulting thinker emits agent text and timing tokens frame by frame, and the talker turns them into speech, so that the agent listens and speaks at the same time.

Figure 1: Illustration of the two behaviors on a shared timeline (user above, agent below; schematic: timings and text are illustrative). (a) A free-running conversation: the agent backchannels (“mmhm”, “yeah”, in the backchannel color) while the user is still talking and takes the turn when the user finishes, with no external turn detector. (b) A user interruption: the agent yields the floor when the user cuts in (silence-start token, SS) and takes it back to answer the new request (silence-end token, SE). SE/SS markers are drawn at the start and end of each agent turn.

Figure 3: Data flow and frame-level token structure. A frozen codec encoder turns the user’s waveform into per-frame audio tokens. The thinker reads the user-audio stream together with its own agent-text stream (pad, text, and control tokens on one lane per frame) and extends the text stream by one token per frame. The talker reads the agent-text stream and its own previous audio tokens and extends the agent-audio stream by one frame; a frozen codec decoder renders it as a waveform. The control tokens SS and SE open and close the agent’s silences, and pause tokens mark short gaps; the example includes a short backchannel (“Mhm”) produced while the user is still speaking.

Figure 4: The thinker’s turn-taking state machine. In SILENCE the legal tokens are PAD (stay silent) and SE (take the floor, entering CONTENT after one automatically fed EPAD frame). In CONTENT they are word pieces and pause0 (stay), pausem withm > 0 (enter PAUSE), and SS (yield, entering SILENCE). PAUSE samples nothing: it feeds its queued PAD and EPAD frames and returns to CONTENT when the queue is empty.

papers.tldr: A frozen multimodal LLM can be efficiently adapted into a word-level full-duplex spoken dialogue system using lightweight components and limited training.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) perform strongly on multimodal tasks, Document Understanding (DU) among them, but the benchmarks that measure them mostly cover English documents and narrow problems. How well current VLMs generalize across languages, tasks, styles and layouts therefore remains unclear. We introduce MDU, a multilingual DU benchmark of 23146 examples spanning 13 tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish. The tasks isolate complementary capabilities, from surface-level text and Markdown extraction through summarization, classification and named-entity recognition to layout-sensitive passage and layout extraction. We evaluate 45 state-of-the-art open-weight VLMs from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system under the same protocol. The benchmark is far from saturated: the best average is 69.0, only eight of the 45 evaluated systems reach 65, and the two best results come from 27B models rather than from the largest systems we evaluate. Performance is uneven in ways that scale does not fix. The gap between the strongest and weakest language does not close as models grow, and it survives controlling for the domain composition of each language. Capabilities also do not improve together: once we partial out overall model quality, per-task scores are largely uncorrelated, and transcription ability in particular trades off against semantic extraction.
authors: Matteo Gabburo, Daniela Baiamonte, Stefano Simonazzi, Silvia Gardini, Sean Cesare Lazzeri, Andrea Zugarini
bullets: Introduces MDU, a benchmark with 23,146 examples across 13 document-understanding tasks and five languages: English, French, German, Italian, and Spanish.
Covers capabilities from text and Markdown extraction to summarization, classification, named-entity recognition, and layout-sensitive extraction.
Evaluates 45 open-weight VLMs ranging from 1.7B to 235B parameters, plus one commercial system, under a shared protocol.
The benchmark is not saturated: the best average score is 69.0, only eight open-weight systems reach 65, and the top two results come from 27B models.
Language and task performance remain uneven as models scale; transcription ability can trade off against semantic extraction.

papers.tldr: MDU shows that current vision-language models remain far from robust multilingual document understanding, with performance varying substantially by language and task rather than simply improving with scale.

papers.abstract: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.
authors: Jaiaid Mobin, Avinash Maurya, M. Mustafa Rafique, Bogdan Nicolae
bullets: Targets evolving sensor distributions in deadline-constrained surrogate workflows, where concurrent serving and fine-tuning cause GPU contention and latency variability.
Fuses inference and training samples into one forward pass, applying backpropagation only to training samples.
Uses a polynomial-time offline scheduler that exploits nonlinear batch-size latency and repetitive workloads.
Evaluated on real-world Ptychographic reconstruction with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.
Improves reconstruction MSE by up to 30%, inference MSE by up to 50%, and reduces deadline misses by 13%–22% versus a multi-context baseline.

papers.selection_reason: Unified inference and fine-tuning on a single GPU reduces latency variance and deadline misses; relevant to efficient AI and streaming adaptation.
papers.title: UniPipe: Unified Inference Serving and Fine-Tuning for Deadline-Constrained DNN Surrogate Workflows
papers.tldr: UniPipe unifies DNN inference and fine-tuning in one GPU context to improve surrogate accuracy while reducing deadline misses in real-time scientific workflows.

papers.abstract: User research and system testing reveal whether products and services meet user needs, yet recruiting specialized participants, designing controlled what-if comparisons, and repeating studies as designs evolve often bottleneck design iteration and data-driven decision-making. We present a framework and execution infrastructure that translates real-world industry inquiries into controlled experiments with simulated users. Our methodology formally defines the target cohort, experimental stimuli, and decision-relevant metrics, while the pipeline supports large-scale concurrent runs over cohort-stimulus-environment combinations (survey, web, chatbot, and OS app), auditable trial-level logging, cohort-level outcome aggregation, and cross-cohort and cross-variant statistical reports. Across twelve industry partner cases spanning five domains, we show how constructing hard-to-reach or what-if persona cohorts supports exploratory studies and distills simulated responses into testable design hypotheses. Cross-model comparisons on selected cases largely preserve primary conclusions, whereas perturbing or ablating persona attributes alters service outcomes, effect sizes, and inter-group differences, indicating that grounding target cohorts in detailed personas materially shapes simulation results. Together, these studies show that persona-enabled agents can test specified cohorts at design speed, diagnose systems under test, and deliver directional evidence that focuses problem definition, steers design and strategic decisions, and guides further study.
authors: Julie Zhu, Jianheng Hou, Zhixu Silvia Tao, Shi Bo, Yilan Fan, Yixuan He, Zhiyuan Hu, Shirley Huang, Fangyu Liu, Yijun Wang, Zibu Wei, Haimingyue Xu, Zhen Xu, Zichen Yuan, Jierui Zuo, Jintao Huang, Yifan Wang, Qianfeng Wen, Jiahan Li, Zhejian Peng, Bowen Yang, Shushu Liang, Yuexing Hao, Xiaomin Li
bullets: Addresses the cost and iteration bottlenecks of recruiting specialized participants and repeatedly running controlled user studies.
Formalizes target cohorts, experimental stimuli, and decision-relevant metrics across surveys, websites, chatbots, and OS apps.
Supports concurrent cohort–stimulus–environment experiments, trial-level logging, aggregation, and statistical reporting.
Twelve industry cases across five domains show that simulated persona cohorts can support exploratory research and produce testable design hypotheses.
Results are sensitive to persona attributes, while selected cross-model comparisons generally preserve primary conclusions; findings are directional and intended to guide further study.

papers.title: Probe What-If Worlds Before You Ship: Persona Simulation for Real-World Decision Making
papers.tldr: A persona-based simulation framework enables fast, auditable what-if studies with simulated users to generate directional evidence for real-world design decisions.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models such as CLIP can classify images into categories they were never explicitly trained to recognize, but accuracy degrades when test images differ in style or source from their training data. A common remedy generates randomly cropped and flipped copies of each test image, called views, and combines their predictions. Since some views miss the object, methods must identify which views to trust. The dominant approach uses prediction entropy to measure confidence and retains the most certain views. Other methods use signals such as embedding typicality. Despite repeated refinements of these scoring functions, the information they rely on, the model's own response to each view, remains largely unexamined. We investigate this choice while holding other pipeline stages fixed. First, we show that view selection, rather than the gradient update, accounts for almost all accuracy gains. We then examine whether entropy identifies useful views when predictions are wrong, despite at least one view predicting the correct class. In these cases, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones no better than chance, recovering only about one-twentieth of the accuracy recovered by an oracle over the same views. This finding holds across two image encoders and under a control ruling out an obvious statistical artifact. An exact analysis explains this limitation: entropy measures confidence but not which class a view favors. We identify an unused signal already available in the augmentation pipeline: the fraction of the original image retained by each crop. Ranking views by this quantity improves accuracy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets over entropy and on 11 of 15 over the strongest scoring function tested. A pre-method measurement also predicts which datasets benefit.
authors: Sivasuthan Sukumar, Uthayasanker Thayasivam
bullets: View selection, not the gradient update, accounts for nearly all reported accuracy gains in the evaluated pipeline.
When at least one augmented view is correct, entropy ranks correct views above incorrect ones about as well as chance.
Entropy recovers only about one-twentieth of the accuracy achievable by an oracle selecting among the same views.
Ranking views by the fraction of the original image they retain improves accuracy over entropy on 14 of 15 benchmark datasets.
A pre-method measurement predicts which datasets benefit from this alternative signal.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The pipeline, and which of its stages produces the accuracy. (a) The augment, score, select, aggregate recipe TPT, ZERO and ADTE each declare. (b) Each stage measured with the other two held fixed, on ImageNet-A, in percentage points: the absolute gap between two accuracies, so 40% to 59% is 19 of them. Selection produces almost all of the gain; the gradient step is indistinguishable from no update under a paired McNemar test [McNemar, 1947]. Concurrent work agrees by different means [Huang et al., 2026]; we claim the decomposition and its mechanism, not the direction.

Figure 3: The gain is predictable before the method is run. One point per dataset; the horizontal axis is how well a view’s crop area separates correct from incorrect views on reducible errors, an AUC computed with no method in the loop. Datasets left of the chance line gain nothing, as a real signal rather than a tuning artefact should. Per-dataset gains are in Tab. 1.

Figure 4: What the model’s response cannot see. Both arms use the same regressor, the same training rows, and feature sets of identical dimension holding the identical value multiset; only the ordering differs. (a) Every configuration improves when class identity is preserved. (b) The gap, sorted: positive in 40/40, mean 8.60 percentage points. The capacity ladder had saturated in all 40, so under-fitting does not explain it. Per-configuration numbers in Tab. 5.

Figure 2: The entropy score separates useful views from useless ones only where a better choice cannot help. (a) The control: reducible errors are defined on one random half of an image’s views and the score evaluated on the disjoint half, so restricting the population cannot contaminate the measurement. (b) Area under the ROC curve (AUC, Sec. 3), where 1.0 orders correct views perfectly above incorrect ones and 0.5 carries no information; on reducible errors it falls to chance on both encoders. (c) The consequence in accuracy on those images.
Table 3: How much a better choice of views could buy. The oracle keeps the same number of views as the deployed method but selects them knowing the label.

Table 2: The entropy score is at chance exactly where a better choice would help. Mean AUC over six datasets per encoder, where 0.5 means the score orders correct and incorrect views no better than chance. Orientation matters: a value below 0.5 is anti-predictive, and reversing the imagefeature row gives 0.546 and 0.532. That row tests statistics computed from the cached embeddings rather than the output distribution, and the crop-area row a quantity that is not a function of the model at all.

Table 5: Keeping class identity is worth 8.60 percentage points, positive in 40/40. “Sorted” and “Unsorted” are the two matched feature sets; “Oracle” ranks by the true-class mass directly. Share of the oracle gap: 8.4% for the best class-symmetric fit, 21.7% for the class-asymmetric one.

Table 4: Closed forms agree with automatic differentiation at machine precision. Maximum absolute disagreement, float64 (machine epsilon ≈ 2.2× 10−16). An algebra slip would produce an order-one disagreement, not one at this scale.

The baseline is never tuned; our parameters are cross-fitted. ∗ marks p < 0.05 under paired McNemar [McNemar, 1947]. Crop geometry is positive on 14 of 15 datasets and its largest gains are those the label-free measurement flags in advance (Fig. 3).

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies test-time adaptation for vision-language models, fitting the test-time learning subtopic.
papers.title: What Entropy-Based View Selection Cannot See: An Audit of Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: Entropy-based view selection for test-time adaptation cannot reliably distinguish confidently wrong views from correct ones, while simple crop-area information is often more effective.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is now a standard stage of language model post-training, and the compute devoted to it is growing rapidly. While it has been shown to improve capabilities, particularly for tasks with verifiable rewards, it can also change behaviours and internal properties that the reward does not explicitly target. We present a formalism to describe the evolution of "traits" during RL post-training and, in doing so, recover the Price equation from evolutionary biology. We use this to develop a mathematical model for what we call "trait hitchhiking": the amplification or suppression of non-targeted traits as training redistributes probability across completions. We evaluate this Price update expression on language models trained with GRPO and show that the Price estimates closely track the sampled trait dynamics. These results identify trait hitchhiking as a mechanism by which RL post-training can silently amplify undesirable traits.
authors: Adil Soubki, Elizabeth S. Z. Tan, Miles Cranmer
bullets: Motivation: RL improves rewarded capabilities but may silently alter non-targeted behaviors and internal properties.
Method: A trait-evolution formalism based on the Price equation models how probability redistribution across completions changes traits.
Evaluation: The authors test the resulting Price update on language models trained with GRPO.
Result: Price-equation estimates closely track the observed dynamics of sampled traits.
Implication: Trait hitchhiking may amplify undesirable traits even when they are not directly rewarded.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Trait hitchhiking follows the same law in evolution and in RL. Left: long tails are correlated with other traits that make a widowbird ‘fit’, although long tails themselves do not lead to increased fitness of a widowbird. Right: RL leads to an increased probability for outputs that achieve a high reward. Behaviours or traits that appear consistently in highly rewarded outputs will thus also gain a greater prevalence, even though the reward function does not necessarily reward these traits. The change in the average trait exhibited by the model is the covariance of reinforcement (specifically ω from Definition 3, which defines how the probability of an input-output pair changes after a training step), and •, the trait.

Figure 4: Cumulative change in wrong hint influence throughout training across conditions with different hint accuracies. We measure the effect of changing an incorrect hint on the model’s answers using a fixed validation set. Blue curves show directly measured changes from initialization, while orange curves show cumulative Price estimates. Faded curves show the three individual seeds and bold curves show their means.

Figure 3: Expected trait level Tt (blue), expected reward Rt (green), and the exact Price equation reconstruction (orange) across initial trait prevalences p (rows) and trait–quality correlations γ (columns). Although only reward is optimised, the trait rises for γ > 0 and falls for γ < 0, while the reconstruction overlaps the observed trajectory. Curves show means over five seeds with standard-error bands; gray dashed lines mark T0.

Figure 6: Cumulative activation-trait change for three layer-12 SAE features during GRPO on GSM8K: initially positivecorrelated feature 30882, negative-correlated feature 22348, and neutral control 10288. papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and models 'trait hitchhiking' during LLM post-training using the Price equation. This provides a formal framework for understanding how RL post-training amplifies non-targeted traits in language models.
papers.title: Trait Hitchhiking in LLM Post-Training
papers.tldr: RL post-training can unintentionally amplify or suppress behaviors unrelated to its reward, a phenomenon formalized as “trait hitchhiking.”

papers.abstract: Today's AI workloads are rapidly changing: new models are released more often, model architectures are increasingly diverse, and traffic distributions change frequently. The challenge we face at Together AI is continual optimization for these changing workloads. Compiling a deployment into an optimized forward pass is a challenge that is well-suited for agent hill-climbing. Existing systems struggle with continual compilation due to a tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. Many systems use agents to optimize individual kernels from the inference forward pass using offline benchmarks, but timings are low-fidelity because of data-dependent behavior in primitives like mixture-of-experts (MoE). On the other hand, systems use agents to directly optimize end-to-end engines but suffer from slow engine launch times. To address these challenges, we build Together Compiler (TKCC), the first truly continual agent loop designed for AI inference optimization. To address the throughput-fidelity tradeoff, we propose: (1) a Tiered Persistent Engine that decouples engine launch overheads from forward pass computation; (2) a cost model to select the parallelism configurations that seed the optimization process. We also conduct extensive ablations on agent context management and present our insights on deploying TKCC in production. TKCC outperforms highly-optimized hand-written Megakernels on the Llama 1B workhorse workload by up to 1.7x and the best open source engines on the latest frontier models (Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash) across hardware platforms by up to 2.6x higher TPS on the InferenceX benchmark. TKCC also sets the state-of-the-art performance at batch size 1, with 1111 TPS on M3.1 Flash and 1205 TPS on DeepSeek v4.1 Flash. Finally, TKCC generalizes beyond frontier language model inference. TKCC serves trillions of tokens across our production fleet.
authors: Reyna Abhyankar, Dylan Lim, Drew Wadsworth, Venkata Hasith Vattikuti, YuTong Julia Zhang, Jung Hwan Heo, Taeksang Kim, Kesavan Ramakrishnan, Evangelene Stanley, Xinyu Fang, Daniel Y. Fu, Simran Arora
bullets: Targets frequent changes in models, architectures, and traffic distributions that make one-time compilation insufficient.
Uses a Tiered Persistent Engine to separate engine-launch overhead from forward-pass computation.
Uses a cost model to seed optimization with suitable parallelism configurations.
Reports up to 1.7× improvement over hand-written Megakernels and up to 2.6× higher throughput than open-source engines across evaluated workloads and hardware.
Has been deployed in production, serving trillions of tokens, and generalizes beyond frontier language-model inference.

The kernel scores every earlier token in the context and must return the indices of the k highest-scoring tokens. It groups the scores into histogram bins and keeps every bin above the one that contains the k-th largest score. Within that bin, it ranks each score by comparing it against every other score in the bin, breaking ties by lower token index, so the run time grows quadratically with the bin’s size. papers.abstract: Regular time-series generation from irregular time series is typically reduced to one-shot imputation: complete each partial sequence once, freeze the completions, and train a generator on the resulting surrogate dataset. We show that this open-loop strategy is structurally flawed. Point imputers collapse ambiguous missing regions to conditional averages, while stochastic imputers become stale as the generator evolves; the binding constraint is therefore iteration, not imputer design. We introduce a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework that closes the imputer-generator loop. Each E-step samples missing values from the posterior of the current generator, and each M-step retrains the generator on these completions, preserving unconditional generator training. Since our diffusion prior operates in a lifted 2D representation while observations live in time-series space, we further introduce Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR), which enforces operator-consistent conditioning, uncertainty preservation, and manifold consistency during the E-step. Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes, our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving over the strongest baselines by 59% in discriminative score, 15% in predictive score, 73% in Context-FID, and 71% in feature-correlation error. Ablations show that our approach reduces average discriminative score by 73% over single-step baselines, closing most of the remaining gap to the clean-data oracle. Code is available at https://github.com/azencot-group/PSLR.
authors: Idan Arbiv, Gal Fadlon, Omri Azencot
bullets: Open-loop one-shot imputation is flawed because deterministic imputations collapse ambiguity and stochastic imputations become stale as the generator changes.
The method alternates posterior sampling of missing values with generator retraining, preserving unconditional generator training.
Posterior Sampling for Lifted Representations (PSLR) enforces consistent conditioning, uncertainty preservation, and manifold consistency between lifted and time-series spaces.
Across ten datasets and four corruption regimes, it reports substantial improvements over the strongest baselines across discriminative, predictive, Context-FID, and feature-correlation metrics.
Ablations indicate that co-evolution closes most of the gap to a clean-data oracle.

papers.selection_reason: Develops a co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework for irregular time series generation using a diffusion prior in lifted representations. This learns and generates future temporal dynamics, fitting the video world models category.
papers.title: Closing the Loop: Co-Evolving EM for Irregular Time Series Generation in Lifted Representations
papers.tldr: A co-evolving Monte Carlo EM framework jointly imputes missing values and trains a generator, enabling high-quality regular time-series generation from irregular observations.

papers.abstract: Tool-using language-model agents accumulate histories of their own mistakes, and a system that compacts, repairs or hands off such a history decides what it says about those mistakes while their effects stay in the world. Prior work cleans the history at a fixed world, where showing a corrected step and saying it is done move together. We ask whether the same correct content helps or hurts depending on how the history states it and what the world holds. We freeze an agent mid-task with its exact world state, edit the history or the world, and let a receiver model continue. On AgentCE-Bench, after the agent commits a wrong value, we hold the world fixed and add the correct value by two natural edits: a truthful note beside the preserved error or the agent's own completed action. The note raises recovery, the share of remaining targets the receiver gets right, from 51% under a matched neutral note to 66%. The completed action lowers it below the unedited history, from 50% to 44%, so the value's presence alone does not predict the effect. On AppWorld, after a database write, we vary whether its receipt reports success or failure and whether its effect is present. A success receipt lowers whole-task success from 45% to 28% while the effect is absent and raises it from 38% to 49% once present. The two effects differ by 27 points pooled over two receivers, a difference positive in six of eight receivers at 97.5% and seven at 95%. A history edit's effect thus depends on the world it describes, and a history made to look clean while the world still holds the error can leave an agent worse off than no edit at all.
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Anurag Koul, Hongjun Liu, Bo Pang, Shafiq Joty, Erik Nijkamp
bullets: The study tests whether identical information helps differently depending on how it is represented in history and whether the world reflects it.
With the world fixed after a wrong value, a truthful note improved recovery from 51% to 66%, while presenting the correction as a completed action reduced it from 50% to 44%.
In AppWorld, success receipts helped when their effects were present (38% to 49%) but hurt when effects were absent (45% to 28%).
History edits and world state interacted across receivers, showing that the value alone does not determine recovery.
Scope: results concern mid-task, tool-using agents and history/world edits evaluated on AgentCE-Bench and AppWorld.

papers.abstract: StructRL turns the experience collected during reinforcement learning into an explicit replay graph. Once the graph contains a path to the task goal, dynamic programming selects actions on the observed part of the state space; these actions form a graph policy that is defined only where the required transitions have been observed. StructRL transfers these actions to model-free learners: as action preferences for a DQN Q-model and as target directions along shortest observed paths for a SAC actor. For DQN on three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, final success rises from 0.10 to 0.90 (DoorKey), 0.10 to 0.80 (KeyCorridor) and 0 to 0.50 (ObstructedMaze); plain DQN does not catch up with three times the budget. For SAC on continuous PointMaze, graph-derived direction labels raise final success from 0.17 to 1.0 on seven matched runs that reached the goal. Distilling the graph policy into a fresh Q-model gives a DoorKey 6x6 controller that reaches the goal from 91% of reachable states, against 38% for plain DQN. Scaling experiments identify three bottlenecks: incomplete graph support, structural aliasing, and loss of graph information in high-dimensional inputs.
authors: Ivo Nowak
bullets: Builds an explicit graph from collected experience and uses dynamic programming to derive policies over observed states.
Transfers graph guidance to DQN through action preferences and to SAC through shortest-path direction targets.
On three sparse-reward MiniGrid tasks, DQN success improves to 0.90, 0.80, and 0.50, versus 0.10, 0.10, and 0 for baseline DQN.
On PointMaze, graph-derived SAC guidance raises final success from 0.17 to 1.0 across seven matched runs that reached the goal.
Key limitations are incomplete graph coverage, structural aliasing, and loss of graph information in high-dimensional observations.

papers.abstract: Classification of lung adenocarcinoma into poorly differentiated (PD) and well-to-moderately differentiated (WMD) subtypes plays an important role in patient survival; however, consistent classification is difficult due to inter-observer variability among pathologists. Collecting data from multiple hospitals is also challenging due to patient privacy concerns. This study proposes a web-based federated learning system that shares only locally trained model weights without sharing patient data between institutions. The UNI2 foundation model and CLAM-SB were used to classify pathological whole slide images. A four-client federated learning system was constructed, and the NLST cohort was reserved exclusively for external validation. In centralized evaluation, joint training with CPTAC and TCGA outperformed single-institution training on external validation, confirming the necessity of multi-institutional data integration. FedAvg, FedProx, FedBN, and FedNova were compared as federated learning algorithms under identical experimental conditions. Test AUC ranked as FedBN, FedProx, FedNova, and FedAvg. FedNova showed the most balanced classification performance between PD and WMD. L1-norm structural pruning at 20%, 30%, and 40% sparsity was applied to reduce model transmission size. FedAvg, FedProx, and FedBN showed a tendency of decreasing Test AUC under pruning, while FedNova achieved improved Test AUC across all sparsity levels. A web-based application was developed supporting slide upload, local training, AI classification, and attention heatmap-based visualization. The combination of FedNova and 40% pruning was confirmed as a practical approach that improves communication efficiency and classification performance while protecting patient privacy.
authors: Moon-Il Joo, Md Ariful Islam Mozumder, Hee-Cheol Kim
bullets: Addresses inter-observer variability and the difficulty of sharing pathology data across hospitals.
Uses UNI2 and CLAM-SB within a four-client federated learning system, with patient data remaining local.
FedBN achieved the highest reported test AUC, while FedNova provided the most balanced PD/WMD classification.
L1-norm pruning improved FedNova’s test AUC across 20%, 30%, and 40% sparsity levels.
The platform supports slide upload, local training, classification, and attention-heatmap visualization; NLST was used for external validation.

papers.abstract: Second-order optimizers improve deep neural network training using curvature information, but their practical efficiency is limited by GPU execution overhead. AdaFisher reduces Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) approximation costs through diagonal Kronecker structures and exponential moving averages, yet its PyTorch implementation requires sequential CUDA kernel launches, intermediate tensor allocations, and repeated memory accesses. We introduce CAFIN, a GPU-native CUDA kernel fusion framework that improves AdaFisher execution efficiency without changing its optimization formulation. The proposed approach progressively integrates FIM preconditioner construction, exponential moving average updates, gradient preconditioning, momentum accumulation, weight decay, and parameter updates into fused CUDA kernels. Shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation, and in-place operations further reduce memory traffic and intermediate allocations. Experiments using ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet across NVIDIA GTX 1660 Ti and RTX 3060 Laptop GPUs demonstrate up to 78.4% lower isolated FIM construction latency and 2.1-26.9% lower optimizer-step latency. The implementation also eliminates approximately 18.91 MB of intermediate GPU memory allocations per optimizer step. Numerical validation confirms consistency within the predefined FP32 tolerance, while convergence accuracy remains comparable across evaluated datasets and random seeds. These findings demonstrate that CUDA kernel fusion can substantially accelerate second-order optimization while preserving AdaFisher's underlying mathematical formulation and learning behavior.
authors: Maryam Arshad, Muhammad Khuram Shahzad
bullets: Targets overhead from sequential CUDA launches, intermediate tensors, and repeated memory accesses in AdaFisher.
Fuses FIM preconditioning, moving averages, gradient preconditioning, momentum, weight decay, and parameter updates.
Uses shared-memory reuse, register-resident computation, and in-place operations to reduce memory traffic and allocations.
Experiments with ResNet-18 across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny ImageNet show up to 78.4% lower isolated FIM construction latency and 2.1–26.9% lower optimizer-step latency.
Numerical consistency and comparable convergence accuracy are maintained under the evaluated FP32 settings.

papers.abstract: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = \rho / (\mu_i + \rho)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $\Delta_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $\Psi(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $\omega^* = (4\nu^2 \Sigma / c')^{1/3}$, $c' = \sigma^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho)$, and the plug-in strength $\rho^* = \sigma^2 / (n\delta^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $\rho_{\mathrm{eff}} = \rho (e^{\zeta q} - 1) / (\zeta q)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.
authors: Mrigank Shekhar Singh
bullets: The method analyzes how periodic anchor refreshes affect forgetting, lag, and estimation variance in each spectral direction.
It derives an optimal refresh rate, plug-in prior strength, and a finite-dimensional random-matrix correction for the anchor.
The online SPAR procedure calibrates window length and prior strength from residuals.
Across a 27-configuration grid, the calibrated window responds to drift without divergence; defaults also transfer to hourly electricity and BCI IV 2b streams.
The algebra, refresh dynamics, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4; reported approximation error is within 5% at fixed operating points and 13% at the method’s own operating points.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text one token at a time, and each token reads every weight from memory, so on edge devices, decoding is limited by memory bandwidth. 2:4 semi-structured sparsity keeps two of every four weights, but Apple-silicon GPUs have no sparse matrix hardware, so pruning helps only if a kernel actually reads fewer bytes. We present metalSPARSE, to our knowledge the first 2:4 sparse kernels for Apple GPUs, together with a fused decoder written in Metal. The kernels stream weights in compressed form and expand them in registers. On Qwen2.5-1.5B with 2:4 sparsity on every decoder linear layer, decoding runs 3.6x faster than HuggingFace Transformers on PyTorch-MPS on an 8 GB M2 MacBook Air and 1.52x faster than MLX on a 16 GB M4. The same engine on dense weights matches MLX, so the gain comes from the compressed weights, and sparsity delivers 97% of the speedup its byte reduction allows. Prompt processing, which is compute-bound, does not speed up. To preserve quality, we combine a Wanda mask with block-wise reconstruction and low-rank adapters trained jointly with the surviving weights and quantized to 4 bits. On WikiText-2 this brings perplexity from 3.01x dense after one-shot pruning (Wanda with a closed-form refit) to 1.34x, and the whole pipeline runs on the same laptop/hardware.
authors: Tek Raj Awasthi (Friedrich-Alexander-Universit\"at Erlangen-N\"urnberg), Babita Awasthi
bullets: Targets memory-bandwidth-limited, one-token-at-a-time LLM decoding on Apple-silicon edge devices.
Uses Metal kernels that stream 2:4 compressed weights and expand them in registers, plus a fused decoder.
Achieves 3.6× over PyTorch-MPS and 1.52× over MLX on tested Qwen2.5-1.5B configurations; dense performance matches MLX.
Sparsity realizes 97% of the speedup theoretically enabled by reducing weight bytes, while prompt processing does not accelerate.
Combines Wanda pruning, block-wise reconstruction, and jointly trained 4-bit low-rank adapters to reduce WikiText-2 perplexity from 3.01× to 1.34× dense.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly capable of automating end-to-end OpenFOAM workflows for computational fluid dynamics (CFD). However, current progress is bottlenecked by two critical limitations. First, existing evaluations are dominated by tutorial-level cases and execution-oriented metrics, masking a substantial executability--acceptability gap: successfully executed simulations often fail to satisfy prescribed numerical or quantity-of-interest (QoI) criteria. Second, domain expertise in existing systems is tightly coupled with bespoke agent architectures, limiting its reuse and continual refinement across agent implementations. To address these challenges, we introduce ExtFoamBench, a challenging benchmark for OpenFOAM agents that spans five axes of workflow variation, and separately assesses execution completion, numerical soundness, and QoI satisfaction. Complementing this, we propose EasyFoam, an agent framework that decouples CFD expertise into modular, externalized skills driven by a dual-loop mechanism. An execution loop constructs workflows from explicit task requirements and uses structured simulation evidence to diagnose failures and guide targeted repairs. Meanwhile, an evolution loop distills task experience into reusable skill updates selected through paired evaluation. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that EasyFoam achieves substantially higher task acceptance rates than baseline agents, establishing this work as a starting point for future research toward self-improving CFD agents.

papers.abstract: Task success is not a sufficient measure of safety for embodied artificial intelligence (AI), because robots may complete objectives while violating safety requirements. Existing evaluations often emphasize performance and robustness, but lack a systematic route from documented safety hazards to executable, verifiable tests. We present EAST (Embodied AI Safety Testing), a digital-twin framework that converts literature-grounded safety evidence into fault-injection tests across perception, instructions, environments, actions, and timing. EAST combines an expert-reviewed safety-fault taxonomy and eight executable operators with applicability and validity constraints. Its three-stage workflow generates test specifications, verifies fault realization during simulated execution, and independently assesses safety challenges, violations, task outcomes, and behavioral signatures using simulator-state evidence. The framework preserves execution traces and replayable records, supporting attribution and reproducibility across experiments. We evaluate EAST on six RoboTwin manipulation tasks and two policy architectures, ACT and RDT, against alternative testing strategies under matched budgets. Across five comparative campaigns, EAST targets all 74 admissible task-policy-operator combinations and obtains valid evidence for 63, while achieving safety-challenge exposure rates close to Random-Legal and Rule-Based. Moreover, 82 valid EAST executions complete their tasks despite safety violations, revealing risks concealed by success-oriented evaluation. These findings support systematic, validity-aware, reproducible safety testing beyond task-completion metrics.

papers.tldr: EAST systematically turns documented safety hazards into reproducible fault-injection tests for embodied AI, revealing safety violations that task-success metrics can miss.

papers.abstract: Learning safe policies that generalize to unseen environments is difficult under bounded actuation, where an unsafe decision may become unrecoverable. Conventional control barrier function (CBF) filters enforce only instantaneous safety and ignore future recoverability. We propose SAFTER (Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability), which embeds a differentiable, closed-form backup-CBF filter into Soft Actor-Critic training. SAFTER unifies current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input admissibility into a single differentiable certificate. Its CBF condition yields an exact minimum-intervention projection without iterative online optimization. In quadruped navigation, SAFTER reaches 90% training success with 30.6% fewer transitions than Vanilla SAC and 34.1-35.1% fewer than current-state CBF-filtered SAC baselines. Across unseen simulated environments, SAFTER improves success by up to 42.4 and 61.4 percentage points over the state-of-the-art methods CBF-RL and SEA-Nav, respectively, and achieves 73.3% and 76.7% success on two real-world navigation maps. Ablations identify accurate differentiation through the safety filter as a key contributor to robustness, in which replacing the projection Jacobian with the identity approximation reduces success rate in a High-Shift environment from 61.4% to 6.2%. These results show that recoverability-aware filtering serves as both a runtime safety mechanism and a learning mechanism for sample-efficient, robust policies.
authors: Benedictus C. G. Cinun
Bin Hu
bullets: Addresses unsafe, potentially unrecoverable actions under bounded actuation and unseen environments.
Integrates current safety, finite-horizon backup safety, terminal recoverability, and input limits into one differentiable certificate.
Uses a closed-form backup-CBF filter with exact minimum-intervention projection, avoiding iterative online optimization.
In quadruped navigation, reaches 90% training success with fewer transitions and substantially improves success in unseen simulated environments and two real-world maps.
Accurate differentiation through the safety projection is critical; an identity Jacobian approximation sharply reduces performance in a high-shift setting.

papers.title: SAFTER: Safety-Aware Filtering Through Explicit Recoverability for Robust Reinforcement Learning under Distribution Shift

papers.abstract: Query-based segmentation models achieve strong performance even under real-time inference on workstation GPUs. On edge devices, however, we show their transformer decoders are deeply memory-bandwidth-bound, a bottleneck invisible to standard FLOP analysis that worsens with input resolution and limited DRAM bandwidth. An FP16 roofline analysis with tensor-core GEMMs active and hardware DRAM counters shows that the non-tensor-core aggregates of FastInst and Mask2Former reach only $2.5\%$ to $6\%$ of the CUDA-core ridge yet account for $53\%$ to $70\%$ of decoder time and $61\%$ to $71\%$ of decoder bytes. The largest individual kernels sustain up to $90\%$ of nominal peak DRAM bandwidth, effectively saturating the memory bus. The bottleneck is therefore not primarily low GEMM intensity, but cross-kernel activation traffic. CompactInst addresses this bottleneck using parameter-free spatial pooling at $4{\times}$, which reduces the bytes moved within the transformer decoder, while a two-convolution refinement head recovers spatial detail. Under TensorRT FP16 on Jetson Orin Nano, CompactInst delivers decoder speedups from $2.35{\times}$ to $4.74{\times}$ and model speedups from $1.57{\times}$ to $2.62{\times}$ as input resolution grows, while closely matching accuracy ($-0.4$ AP on COCO val2017, $+0.2$ AP on Cityscapes test). A heavier variant with $2.57{\times}$ more decoder FLOPs still runs its decoder $1.74{\times}$ faster on the most bandwidth-constrained device, confirming at the deployment level that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, govern latency.
authors: Oliver Busemann
Torben Töniges
Martin Atzmueller
bullets: Roofline analysis identifies DRAM bandwidth as the dominant decoder bottleneck, especially at higher resolutions and on bandwidth-limited devices.
Non-tensor-core decoder operations consume most decoder time and bytes despite low CUDA-core utilization, with large kernels nearing peak DRAM bandwidth.
CompactInst uses 4× parameter-free spatial pooling plus a two-convolution refinement head to reduce activation traffic and recover detail.
On Jetson Orin Nano with TensorRT FP16, it achieves 2.35–4.74× decoder speedups and 1.57–2.62× end-to-end model speedups as resolution increases.
Accuracy remains close to baseline on COCO and Cityscapes; a higher-FLOP variant further supports that decoder bytes, not FLOPs, determine latency.

papers.selection_reason: Profiling and reducing memory bandwidth of transformer decoders on edge GPUs directly fits efficient AI and token-level cost reduction.
papers.title: Memory Bandwidth, Not FLOPs: Profiling and Accelerating Query-Based Segmentation Decoders on Edge GPUs

papers.abstract: The rapid evolution of video generation has narrowed the perceptual gap between authentic and synthetic videos, making generalizable AI-generated video detection increasingly challenging. Existing detectors predominantly rely on visual representations, leaving caption-derived textual semantics underexplored. Meanwhile, temporal regularity in fine-grained visual representations has received limited attention. We find that caption-derived textual representations provide complementary discriminative cues to global visual representations. Our analysis further reveals that AI-generated videos exhibit stronger temporal persistence and lower temporal variability, a pattern we term temporal over-regularity (TOR). Based on these findings, we propose MTOR with a multimodal branch and a TOR component. The multimodal branch integrates global visual and caption-derived textual representations, while the TOR component models temporal over-regularity at three levels: coarse inter-frame continuity, fine-grained token correspondence, and frame-to-video stability. Extensive evaluations on five benchmarks covering 46 generator variants demonstrate state-of-the-art overall performance against 16 representative baselines, while robustness experiments confirm strong resilience to twelve real-world video perturbations. Code and models will be released at https://github.com/hwang-cs-ime/MTOR.
authors: Hang Wang
Chao Shen
Lei Zhang
Zhi-Qi Cheng
bullets: AI-generated videos show stronger temporal persistence and lower temporal variability than authentic videos, termed temporal over-regularity (TOR).
The multimodal branch combines global visual features with caption-derived textual representations for complementary detection cues.
The TOR component models coarse frame continuity, fine-grained token correspondence, and frame-to-video stability.
Evaluations across five benchmarks and 46 generator variants report state-of-the-art overall performance against 16 baselines.
Robustness experiments show resilience to 12 real-world video perturbations.

papers.abstract: GAMBIT is an opening chess move in which a player sacrifices a piece, typically a pawn, to gain a positional advantage later in the game. Analogously, in multi-robot coordination, individual robots may need to forgo locally reward-maximising behaviours to improve overall team performance. Such self-sacrificial behaviours are difficult to capture with manually designed heuristics, particularly in dense, interaction-rich environments. Focusing on double-integrator continuous dynamics, this work studies how to learn such coordinated heuristics over motion primitives for multi-robot trajectory execution. Our framework, GAMBIT, first learns coordinated motion-primitive selection through imitation learning and subsequently fine-tunes the policy through reinforcement learning. We further introduce a safeguarded rollout mechanism with backup trajectories that guarantees collision-free execution at all times. Experiments demonstrate that GAMBIT substantially outperforms a range of baselines, including centralised motion planners and decentralised reactive planners, while exhibiting strong scalability. In particular, it coordinates over a thousand robots with planning latency below a few hundred milliseconds in continuous domains.
authors: Rishabh Jain
Akmaral Moldagalieva
Lorenzo Magnino
Michael Amir
Keisuke Okumura
Ajay Shankar
Wolfgang Hönig
Amanda Prorok
bullets: Addresses coordination in dense, interaction-rich environments where locally optimal robot actions can harm team performance.
Uses imitation learning to initialize coordinated motion-primitive selection, followed by reinforcement-learning fine-tuning.
Introduces safeguarded rollouts with backup trajectories to guarantee collision-free execution.
Outperforms centralized and decentralized planning baselines and scales to over a thousand robots with sub-second planning latency.
Scope: multi-robot systems with continuous double-integrator dynamics; the abstract does not specify experimental datasets or detailed limitations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. GAMBIT framework overview. We aim to learn a coordination-aware GNN policy that provides heuristic preferences over motion primitives. The framework consists of (a) imitation pretraining and (b) RL fine-tuning. The former step learns from demonstration trajectories by treating motion-primitive selection as a classification task. The latter uses multi-agent RL to maximise multi-robot navigation performance through our safeguarded rollout mechanism. The resulting policy, combined with the safeguarded rollout, enables collision-free execution while retaining high scalability.

Fig. 2. Main result. For each scenario, an example instance is shown at the top, where filled circles represent robots and unfilled circles connected by lines indicate their corresponding goals. Grey circles, rectangles, and cylinders represent obstacles. The remaining plots show, from top to bottom, CSR (complete success rate), SOC (sum-of-costs; normalised by lower bounds based on start–goal distances), and computation time to derive the entire trajectories. SOC and computation time are averaged over successful instances for each planner, with shaded regions indicating one standard deviation; to ensure meaningful comparisons, we report these metrics only when the corresponding success rate exceeds 50%. db-LaCAM’s SOC often exceeds the displayed range; we use an orange dot and arrow to indicate the clipped value to preserve readability of the remaining curves.

Fig. 3. Scalability assessment with up to 1,024 robots in the Forest scenario. The left panel shows a snapshot of the entire workspace at a certain timestep. Circles represent robots, with solid lines indicating their trajectories as tails. The upper-right panel depicts the trajectory evolution within a specific region, highlighting coordinated behaviours produced by GAMBIT; e.g., the ⋆ robot temporarily moves away from its goal to let others pass. The lower-right panel presents individual success rate (ISR) evolution for n = {256, 512, 1,024}; i.e., the percentage of robots that have reached their goals, as a function of elapsed simulation time. We run the planners on 32 instances, with each curve representing the solution over a different instance. The bottom-right panel shows the distribution around the median inference time/step (and the corresponding loop frequency) for computing actions for the entire team.

Fig. 4. Snapshot from a GAMBIT deployment with eight multirotors planning at 10Hz. (left-inset) Speed profile (m/s) for the robots in this instance. (right-inset) Top-down view of the arena and trajectories.

papers.title: GAMBIT: Learning to Plan Continuous Multi-Robot Trajectories

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation. They act by first predicting how a task should be performed and then decoding the actions from that future. However, the remaining actions are invalid once execution drifts from the prediction. Simply replanning from the already out of distribution state rarely restores what the task still requires; existing execution monitors decide when to stop, but not what to restore. We observe that the answer is already in hand: the future the WAM predicted before acting depicts exactly the states it intended to pass through. We introduce FAVOR (Future Anchored Verification and Online Recovery), a lightweight framework that keeps these predicted frames as anchors and uses them for verification and recovery. An Anchor Verifier compares each observation with its anchor, together with the executed actions, to flag deviations that break the task. Anchor-Guided Recovery uses a vision-language model to turn the flagged anchor into a short corrective instruction. Under strengthened instruction guidance, the WAM executes this instruction to return to the intended future. It then resumes the task. FAVOR raises the task success of the base WAM from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus without modifying the policy.
authors: Zhibin Qin
Zhenxiong Tan
Xinchao Wang
bullets: Addresses the problem that execution drift invalidates remaining actions and replanning from the deviated state may not restore task progress.
Stores the WAM’s predicted future frames as anchors for monitoring and recovery.
An Anchor Verifier compares observations and executed actions against anchors to identify task-breaking deviations.
A vision-language model converts flagged anchors into corrective instructions, after which the WAM resumes execution.
Improves success from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus without changing the policy.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of FAVOR. (a) The frozen WAM predicts future frames and the IDM decodes an action chunk; the predicted frames are retained as anchors. Every ∆ steps, the verifier compares the observation with its anchor: a pass continues execution, and the failure interrupts the remaining actions and triggers recovery. (b) The Anchor Verifier encodes the prediction–observation pair with DINO, fuses it with action and horizon embeddings, and outputs a failure score through a causal GRU; an alarm is raised when the score exceeds τ . (c) Anchor-Guided Recovery: a VLM reads the alarmed anchor, the current observation, and the task, and issues a corrective instruction.
Figure 3: Effect of the guidance scale on recovery predictions. All branches start from the same trigger state and the corrective instruction “pick up the cup”.

Figure 4: Qualitative examples of Anchor-Guided Recovery on LIBERO. In each case, the top row shows the observed execution and the bottom row the WAM’s retained prediction up to the alarm (orange frame); red circles mark where the observation departs from its anchor. Right of the alarm, native continuation under the original instruction fails (top), while the corrective instruction issued by the VLM (green) restores the anchored condition and the task succeeds (bottom). Both branches start from the same simulator state at the alarm.
